News.title: Two left injured after UPS cargo jet crashes with plane on tarmac at Miami airport
News.content:
Next

TWO people have been injured after a cargo plane crashed into a passenger jet on the tarmac at Miami International Airport.

The pilot of a Copa Airlines flight arriving from Panama City declared “somebody hit us” on the radio while crossing a taxiway.



Its wing had clipped the nose of a Bogota, Colombia, bound UPS plane at an intersection on the tarmac around 9.15pm yesterday.

An air traffic controller asked the cargo plane pilot: “UPS 358, did you hit that aircraft?”



He immediately admitted fault, saying: “Yeah we went too far and he clipped us with his wing.”

A shocking image from the aftermath shows a massive hole in the UPS plane’s nose, with debris scattered across the tarmac.



The airport’s communication director, Greg Chin, said two people were treated for minor injuries by Miami-Dade Fire Rescue.

It was not clear if the incident had anything to do with ripple effects of Friday’s national aviation ground stop.

News.title: Tanker owners sued for $1m over terrifying cruise ship collision which left passengers stranded in water after capsizing
News.content:
Next

A $1MILLION lawsuit has been filed after a tanker crashed into a cruise ship docked in New Orleans.

Nearly 200 passengers on board the cruise survived the Mississippi River horror as the packed liner capsized and left people stranded in the water.



The port is now claiming the M/V Atlantic Asphalt is at fault for the disastrous smash, according to court documents.

A total of 32 people were treated at local hospitals following the catastrophe, but none had critical injuries.



All 197 passengers and crew on the American Heritage cruise ship survived as well as the employees aboard the tanker.

Officials called the dramatic rescue a “miracle on the Mississippi”.

The exact reason for the crash remains unknown, but US Coast Guard Captain Melanie Burnham said the tanker appears to have had “some type of a loss of steering”.

The National Transportation Safety Board has launched an investigation into the capsize.



Terrifying clips showed passengers clinging to the sides of the partially submerged ship and being pulled from the water in a frantic rescue.

Court documents allege the port terminal “was significantly damaged” in the ordeal with more than $1million (£756k) in damages.

The M/V Atlantic Asphalt, its owner Nave Shipping SA, and its management company, Thome Ship Management Pte Ltd, are all named in a federal court lawsuit filed on Friday in Louisiana.



Records show the port is demanding money to cover cleanup, inspections, repairs and other expenses.

The lawsuit also suggests the tanker should be seized and sold to pay for the damage.

It claims the collision “occurred as a result of the negligence, gross negligence, fault or carelessness” of the ship and its operating companies.

The lawsuit alleges that the tanker and companies failed “to use all available means to avoid the risk” of ramming the riverboat.

In shocking footage of the incident, the huge tanker is seen steaming towards a smaller river cruiser as bystanders watch on in horror.



The huge Atlantic Asphalt slams straight into the side of the docked cruiser, reportedly punching a hole that pierced through to the ship’s dining room.

Emergency services rushed to the scene of the horror collision near the Port of New Orleans in Louisiana at around 12.30pm on Friday.

The ship tilts at a sharp angle and can be seen sinking rapidly.

It then falls fully on its side just feet from the port as rescuers scramble to save passengers from the river.

Passengers can be seen clinging to life rafts and attempting to swim to safety as their huge vessel begins to slip beneath the waves.



Footage recorded inside the river cruiser from the moments before the disaster shows the huge tanker heading straight for the smaller ship.

The passenger recording the video backs away from the window in fear before running for her life.

The Atlantic Asphalt capsized the American Heritage, a river cruise ship operated by American Cruise Lines.

Cruise ship restaurant manager Zayvion told ABC passengers were “scared” during “chaotic” scenes after the crash.

He said: “There was a hole in the hull of the other boat in the dining room.”



“It was a little chaotic, but our team knew what we were doing.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Zayvion added: “A lot of people were just scared, especially as the boat tipped over.

“It was scary for a lot of people. Even me, like, when it was tipping, I was like, it was getting real.”

News.title: Sprawling 19th century farmhouse to be knocked down TODAY after planners ruled it was illegally built on green belt land
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

FEELING GREEN Sprawling 19th century farmhouse to be knocked down TODAY after planners ruled it was illegally built on green belt land







Next

A SPRAWLING farmhouse is set to be demolished today after planners ruled it was illegally built on green belt land.

The charming 19th century property on Dones View Farm in Dutton, Cheshire, will be knocked down at a cost of £20,000.



Retired builder Barry Devine bought the barn in 2000 and spent 19 years transforming the pad into a substantial house with separate wings.

Mr Devine claims he never needed planning permission, but council planners argued it’s an entirely new house and ordered its demolition in 2019.



Cheshire West and Chester Council also demanded the removal of boundary walls and fencing.

The retired builder spent four years battling the order through the planning inspectorate, High Court and Court of Appeal, but lost every challenge.

Mr Devine’s final appeal was dismissed in March 2023, but the house remained standing.

The council then prosecuted him for failing to comply with the enforcement notice.



Mr Devine was found guilty of one breach and appeared at Chester Crown Court for sentencing on November 6.

The offence is punishable by an unlimited fine.

However, Recorder Eric Lamb delayed sentencing after Mr Devine produced documents showing demolition work was scheduled.



The work is due to start today (November 14) and finish on November 28 to the tune of an estimated £20,000.

The judge also raised concerns that Mr Devine was unrepresented, having “spent all his money” appealing the case.

Sentencing was adjourned until December 21, with inspectors authorised to visit on December 14 to check the property has been knocked down.

Mr Devine said he was “not going to talk about” the case.

News.title: Jimmy Mizen’s killer given fresh  parole hearing despite being branded ‘known bully’ behind bars
News.content:
Next

JIMMY Mizen’s drill rapper killer has been given a fresh parole hearing just months after he was labelled a “known bully” behind bars.

Jake Fahri will go before the Parole Board in early 2027.



The thug, now 37, killed 16-year-old Jimmy at a bakery in Lee, South East London, in 2008.

He was jailed for life and served 14 years.



Fahri was released on licence in June 2023 but recalled in January 2025 for boasting about his crimes on drill rap songs.

He won a move to an open prison before Justice Secretary David Lammy blocked it.



But Jimmy’s mum Margaret Mizen, 74, told The Sun on Sunday last night: “When we hear there will be another parole hearing it brings all the emotions back, and it always comes around Christmas time.

“I just hope the Parole Board get it right this time, because last time they didn’t.

“They need to look at it seriously, and if they genuinely think he is ready to come out, we have to accept it.

“But they did say he was a bully last time, and if that hasn’t changed then it’s hard to see how he can come out.”



Millwall fan Jimmy was attacked by Fahri after the thug walked into the bakery and started an argument in May 2008.

The wannabe gangster, then 19, hurled a glass oven dish at Jimmy, severing an artery in his neck.

Fahri, who lived near the Mizens and already had convictions for burglary and assault, ran out of the shop and was described by a witness as “walking with a swagger”.

Fahri is entitled to one parole hearing at least every two years while on recall.

A Parole Board spokesman said: “Protecting the public is our priority.”

News.title: Senior US airman removed from Britain by Americans ‘sent video of himself committing sex act on bus’

EMBASSY 'PAEDO' Senior US airman removed from Britain by Americans ‘sent video of himself committing sex act on bus’







Next

A SENIOR US airman spirited out of Britain by the Americans sent a video of himself committing a sex act on a bus, a court martial heard.

Lt Col Michael Morris, 39, who was working at the US embassy in London, was allegedly in uniform in the footage.



He is also accused of swapping dozens of abuse images of children as young as two with his brother Benjamin, 33.

US spies flew Lt Col Morris to America without telling British police.



Claims aired in a military court at Joint Base Andrews near Washington DC make it clear he is accused of committing crimes on British soil.

A justice source said: “This makes it even more shocking the Americans acted without telling us.”

Benjamin, who was arrested in the US, is also charged with child abuse image offences.

The dawn raid in August, which The Sun on Sunday exclusively revealed, came after his brother Benjamin Morris was arrested in a sting, in June.

He denies the charges.

The charges relate to a period between March and April of this year.

News.title: Son of anti-Trump ex-CIA director arrested after ‘FBI uncovers sickening trove of child sex abuse images’
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

TWISTED FIND Son of anti-Trump ex-CIA director arrested after ‘FBI uncovers sickening trove of child sex abuse images’







Next

THE son of ex-CIA Director John Brennan has been arrested for allegedly possessing a trove of child sex abuse material.

Kyle Brennan, 40, has been charged with transportation of child pornography, according to a federal complaint.



The case started when an account linked to Brennan was flagged to authorities by Adobe CyberTipline.

It reported the suspect for allegedly uploading illicit files of child abuse online.



The claims were submitted to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) in April and June, 2024.

The FBI’s Washington field office is involved in the probe.



On April 7, three files allegedly containing the illegal material were uploaded to the Adobe account.

A review of the files appeared to show a morphed image combining the face of a girl with the naked body of another child.

The girl was later identified as just 12 years old.

Comcast records also showed the IP address used to upload the files was registered to Brennan at an address in Virginia.



Apple also shared records confirming the private relay account was linked to the suspect.

In October, the FBI was alerted and a judge signed off on a warrant.

Investigators were then allowed to examine the files and seize Brennan’s phone.

On Friday, an analysis of his device, named “Kyle’s iphone (2)”, revealed 88 images of girls under the age of 18 engaging in sexual acts, prosecutors said.

A police complaint stated one image appeared to be a “fully nude, pubescent minor girl on a locker bench”.



It read: “The girl’s wrists and ankles were bound and her mouth was gagged.”

The Justice Department is also probing the suspect’s dad John Brennan, who once served under former President Barack Obama, over unrelated matters.

The investigation on Brennan Snr focuses on whether he lied to Congress in 2023 regarding the 2017 intelligence assessment on Russian election interference.

News.title: Two US tourists, 38 & 40, drown in holiday hotspot after being dragged under water by strong current on Caribbean trip
News.content:
TOURIST TRAGEDY Two US tourists, 38 & 40, drown in holiday hotspot after being dragged under water by strong current on Caribbean trip







Next

TWO American tourists have drowned in a holiday hotspot after being dragged under the water by strong currents during a Caribbean trip.

A 38-year-old man and 40-year-old woman were swimming with several others before they were pulled beneath the waves.

Police said the two victims were swimming near Bimini Island in an area where a sign had been placed warning of strong currents.

Some of the swimmers were rescued by a nearby ferry boat.





But the US swimmers were unresponsive when the vessel arrived to pick them out of the water.

Emergency services performed CPR on the pair when they arrived at hospital.

But they remained unresponsive and later died.

Local cops said: “Both victims were transported to the local clinic, where medical personnel continued life-saving efforts.



“Unfortunately, despite their efforts, both individuals were pronounced deceased by the attending physician shortly before 4pm.”

Police do not suspect foul play.

But an investigation has been launched to determine the full circumstances of the ordeal.

An autopsy will reveal their exact cause of death.



It comes after the heartbroken husband of a missing American tourist revealed she was allegedly seen alive more than four hours after she vanished on a dream vacation.

Elizabeth Waddell disappeared while going for a swim in the sea on the Caribbean island of Grenada on July 22.

News.title: PM hailed Milburn’s benefits recommendations – but it WON’T reduce Britain’s ballooning welfare bill
News.content:
Milburn’s Neet idea but costs still rising







Next

A GAGGLE of leftie Labour rebels are up in arms about Alan Milburn’s big welfare report.

The jobs czar is about to deliver his long-awaited inquiry into the causes of the shameful Neets crisis, which has seen a million young people locked out of jobs and education.



And, shock horror, Mr Milburn is actually proposing a reduction of some benefit cash for young people.

It is the first time a senior Labour figure has made genuine overtures towards reducing welfare since Keir Starmer tried to trim benefits by £5billion two years ago.



That proposal was shot down in flames by a rebellion of leftie backbench MPs faster than you could say “Universal Credit”.

It was the first nail in Starmer’s coffin.



But this time, his replacement Andy Burnham seems likely to accept Milburn’s recommendations and see off any minor rebellion.

The PM is hailing the report as a “watershed moment” for benefit provision.

He says: “It’s starting to point to a very different way of thinking about welfare.”

There is no doubt Mr Milburn will make many worthwhile and sensible proposals.



His aim to double the number of apprenticeships for young people is the type of policy The Sun on Sunday has long campaigned for.

But, despite the rebels, don’t imagine that these vital changes will reduce a welfare bill which is heading towards a staggering £430BILLION a year.

Mr Milburn proposes to cut benefits for some Neets which presently cost £4billion.

Even if he cuts half of them, that would only save £2billion.

The start-up costs of the report’s proposals are themselves estimated to be £6billion — and it may take a decade for them to be effective.



In the meantime, Britain’s benefits bill just keeps growing and growing.

Not so very different after all then, is it Prime Minister?

Got to be kidding

BRITS are used to being constantly chivvied along by the nanny state.

But this time the bureaucratic mollycoddling has gone too far.

A new Government guide warns students to take the bins out, clean the fridge and polish their phones.



Food Standards Agency officials have spent taxpayer cash advising freshers to wash their hands and stock up on cleaning products.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

But they should remember one thing:

If you treat people like toddlers, they will throw their toys out of the pram.

News.title: Energy expert shares exact temperature to set your thermostat for 'comfortable' winter
News.content:
Energy expert shares exact temperature to set your thermostat for 'comfortable' winter

The Energy Saving Trust has shared the best way to heat your home 'comfortably' - and save £120 while you do it

View 3 Images Some people have been turning up the thermostat to try to heat their home more quickly (Image: Getty)

Autumn is well and truly here, with falling temperatures along with the leaves. It can also spark what can be a battle in many households over exactly when to switch on the heating and at what temperature to set it.

‌



‌



Over recent years, one viral social media trend has seen influencers advising people to "crank up the heating" and turn up the thermostat in a bid to heat the house more quickly. But energy experts are warning that this not only doesn't work but it also will actually leave you out of pocket.

‌



The Energy Saving Trust advises: "A room thermostat stops your central heating system using more energy than it needs to. It turns the heating on until the room reaches the temperature you’ve set. Once it reaches the set temperature, it turns the heating off until the temperature drops again."

‌



View 3 Images Many people have turned on the heating over recent weeks (Image: PIKSEL via Getty Images)

And it dismisses the trend as a myth explaining: "You don’t need to turn your room thermostat up when it is colder outside. Your home will heat up to your chosen temperature whatever the weather, but it may take a little longer on colder days.

"Remember: turning up your room thermostat won’t make your home heat any faster! Also, bear in mind that room thermostats need a free flow of air to get a better sense of the temperature. Therefore, it’s important to make sure they’re not blocked by curtains or furniture and to keep them away from heat sources like radiators."

‌



What temperature is best?

The organisation also has advice on setting the correct temperature - and it could save you a decent amount of cash. It says: "You should set your thermostat to the lowest comfortable temperature for your needs.

"For most people, this is between 18°C and 21°C. If you can, turning down your thermostat from 22°C to 21°C can save £120 a year in GB and £80 in NI on energy bills."

‌



Timing can save

The Energy Saving Trust says a timer or programmer can help as it lets you control when your heating and hot water comes on and when it goes off. It says: "This is useful because it means you can programme your central heating based on when you need it. For example, you can programme the heating system for when you want warmth and switch off when you’re not at home or at night.

"While these controls are found in many heating systems, the advice for using them varies if you have heat pump or electric heating. Using a programmer, you can set ‘on’ and ‘off’ time periods for your central heating." It explains that typically, with a boiler you should set the central heating programme to:

‌



Turn on around half an hour before you get up.

Turn off around half an hour before you go to bed.

Check that the clock on the programmer is correct before you set your programmes. Many programmers will change automatically when the clocks change in spring and autumn. But if it doesn’t, you will need to remember to adjust it.

‌



View 3 Images The Energy Saving Trust has a recommendation for the best temperature (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

When you should turn your heating on will depend on your circumstances, but generally you should put it on when you start to feel cold, it recommends.

‌



Check your settings

The Energy Saving Trust says a boiler should have a dial or a digital temperature setting, sometimes marked in numbers or from minimum (min) to maximum (max). It advises: "This sets the temperature of the water that’s pumped from the boiler through the radiators to heat your home. This is known as the boiler flow temperature.

‌



"If your boiler thermostat is set higher than needed, lowering it could save you money. This is because a lower flow temperature helps your boiler work more efficiently.

"But if it’s not set high enough when it’s very cold outside, your home may not reach the temperature you need to be comfortable. Don’t lower it below 65C if you have separate hot water cylinder, as lower temperatures can lead to the growth of harmful bacteria."

Article continues below

Service your boiler or heat pump

The organisation adds: "We recommend getting your boiler or heat pump serviced every year to make sure it’s running properly. The cost of a service will vary depending on where you live and how much work is needed. This will help make sure your system is running at its most economical.

"Renting your home? Your landlord should arrange and pay for the service. They also have to provide gas safety checks for your boiler and all other gas appliances."

News.title: Dentist issues urgent 21-day warning over common sign on your tongue
News.content:
Dentist issues urgent 21-day warning over common sign on your tongue

Many people pay little attention to their tongue but it can hold a wealth of health information

View 3 Images The tongue can indicate several health problems (Image: Getty)

A tongue is often part of the body that gets little thought or attention. However a dentist is warning it is something people should take note of as it might have something to tell you about your health.

‌



‌



And while most of the time changes are harmless, there are occasions it can point to an infection or low iron or vitamin levels which should always be checked. Dr Nilesh Parmar. clinical director of Parmar Dental Group in Essex, who also works with Emergensee a network of private emergency dental practices, said: "Dentists look at the tongue as part of a routine check-up because it can tell us a lot, from an infection to low iron or vitamin B12.

‌



View 3 Images Most symptoms that appear on the tongue are harmless (Image: Getty)

‌



"Most changes are harmless and clear up on their own, but anything new that doesn't settle is worth getting checked. Persistent ulcers, unexplained lumps, or red or white patches should also be assessed by a dentist, particularly if they persist for three weeks."

Why the tongue changes

The tongue is covered in tiny projections called papillae. According to the British and Irish Society for Oral Medicine, every tongue carries a coating of mucus, cells, bacteria and other debris, which the tongue's movement and saliva normally clear away.

A 2016 review in The Open Dentistry Journal links a smooth tongue, where the tiny bumps on its surface have been lost, with conditions including iron and vitamin B12 deficiency. Dr Parmar has shared some common issues, what they might be and what you need to do about them.

‌



A white coating

The NHS says a white tongue is not usually serious, and suggests brushing your tongue or using a scraper to help improve it. A dry mouth makes a coating more likely, according to the British and Irish Society for Oral Medicine, and the NHS lists breathing through your mouth at night. which can happen with a blocked nose, among the main causes of a dry mouth. A white tongue can also be a sign of oral thrush, or of leukoplakia, white patches that cannot be rubbed or scraped away.

‌



A black, brown or 'hairy' tongue

Hairy tongue happens when the papillae grow longer than usual, and it can look yellow, dark brown or black. The British and Irish Society for Oral Medicine lists smoking, drinking a lot of tea or coffee, a dry mouth, poor oral hygiene and some medicines among the factors that make it more likely, and says it is harmless and not linked to mouth cancer.

‌



Ensure our latest health news always appears at the top of your Google Search by making us a Preferred Source. Click here to activate or add us as Preferred Source in your Google search settings

Dr Parmar explained: "A black or brown furry tongue looks worrying, but it's usually harmless. The tiny bumps on the tongue grow longer and pick up staining from tea, coffee, smoking and some medicines. Gently cleaning your tongue each day and drinking more water can help."

‌



Map-like patches

Geographic tongue is a common, harmless condition that causes smooth red patches with pale or white edges, which can look like the outline of a map, according to the Oral Health Foundation. It happens when the surface of the tongue sheds and renews itself unevenly, the patches can change shape or move over time, and it cannot be passed on. Some people notice soreness or burning, particularly with acidic, hot or spicy food.

‌



A sore, red or smooth tongue

The NHS lists a sore or red tongue among the symptoms of vitamin B12 or folate deficiency anaemia, and a sore tongue among the less common symptoms of iron deficiency anaemia. It says B12 or folate deficiency anaemia should be diagnosed and treated as soon as possible, as some of the problems it causes can be irreversible if left untreated.

‌



View 3 Images Dr Nilesh Parmar (Image: Parmar Dental Group)

Dr Parmar said: "A sore, red or unusually smooth tongue can be a sign of low iron, vitamin B12 or folate. If it doesn't settle, see your GP, especially if you're also tired or short of breath. A blood test is better than treating it with supplements yourself, as the reason your levels are low also needs to be found."

‌



A 'strawberry' tongue

Scarlet fever occurs most often in winter and spring, according to the UK Health Security Agency. The NHS says it can start with flu-like symptoms such as a high temperature and a sore throat, followed by a rash that feels rough, like sandpaper.

‌



A white coating appears on the tongue and then peels, leaving it red, swollen and covered in little bumps, known as "strawberry tongue". It is less common in adults than in children. The NHS advises seeing a GP if you have symptoms, and checking with the surgery before you go in, as scarlet fever spreads very easily. It is treated with antibiotics.

When to get your tongue checked

Article continues below

The NHS says mouth ulcers should clear up on their own within a week or two, and advises seeing a dentist or GP about one that lasts longer than 3 weeks. It also advises getting a red or white patch in the mouth, a lump, or pain that is not going away checked by a GP or dentist. It says to call 999 if your lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly become swollen, as this can be a sign of a serious allergic reaction.

News.title: Joanna Page's 'invisible' health condition as she enters I'm A Celeb jungle
News.content:
Joanna Page's 'invisible' health condition as she enters I'm A Celeb jungle

The star requires lifelong medication to keep the symptoms from 'returning'

View 3 Images Gavin and Stacey star Joanna Page is going into the I'm A Celebrity jungle (Image: © ITV)

As well as taking part in Bushtucker Trials, Gavin and Stacey star Joanna Page will face her own challenge when roughing it in the Australian jungle for I'm A Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here! The mum-of-four will have her own "invisible" health issue to manage while away from home.

‌



‌



The TV star will be entering the famous ITV jungle when the show returns to screens this Monday, November 16. She will share the camp with the likes of footballing legend Wayne Rooney, soap star Claire Sweeney and Paralympian Ade Adepitan.

‌



But the Swansea-born actress, who also featured in the festive rom-com Love Actually, previously spoke about "losing her signature energy" one year and began experiencing bouts of chronic fatigue. She also noticed her tendency to shiver.

‌



Joanna will likely continue to manage her underactive thyroid during her stint in the jungle. The condition, known as hypothyroidism, is common, according to the NHS, and requires medication for life to "prevent symptoms returning". An underactive thyroid is widely described as an 'invisible' health condition because many of its most severe symptoms cannot be seen by others.

View 3 Images Joanna Page recently arrived in Australia ahead of the ITV show (Image: Tim Merry/Staff Photographer)

Speaking about the situation previously, Joanna told Wales Online that she constantly felt like she was "in slow motion all the time." She added: "I just had no energy.

‌



"I’d get out of bed, load the washing machine, and then be so drained I’d have to sit around staring into space for the rest of the day. I was continually freezing cold.

"I’d have the central heating on full blast, be wearing three layers of clothing including thermals. My husband James would have to walk around in shorts because it was so hot in the house.”

‌



Ensure our latest shopping news always appears at the top of your Google Search by setting us as a Preferred Source. Click here to activate or add us as a Preferred Source in your Google search settings.

View 3 Images Joanna is best known for her role as Stacey Shipman in the hit show Gavin & Stacey (Image: BBC/Toffee International Ltd./Tom Jackson)

‌



Symptoms of an underactive thyroid are often similar to those of other conditions, and they usually develop slowly, so you may not notice them for years. For example, if you are at an age where you may be expecting the menopause, you may think you have started the menopause rather than having an underactive thyroid.

Treatment for an underactive thyroid involves taking daily hormone replacement tablets, called levothyroxine, to raise your thyroxine levels. You'll have regular blood tests until the correct dose is reached.

Article continues below

Once you're taking the correct dose, you'll usually have a blood test once a year to monitor your hormone levels. People usually need treatment for the rest of their life, but are often able to lead a normal, healthy life.

News.title: Man forced to sell huge private island he won in prize draw after realising issues
News.content:
Man forced to sell huge private island he won in prize draw after realising issues

Matthias Ross won a 16-acre Canadian island in a Haribo prize draw in 2005, but travel bills and upkeep have prompted him to put the retreat on the market for £184,000.

View 3 Images Aerial drone view of a long forgotten cottage on an island (Image: Getty Images)

Winning a private island might sound like a dream, but the bills that followed have prompted one lucky prize draw winner to put his Canadian retreat up for sale. Matthias Ross, 44, is asking £184,000 for the roughly 16-acre island on Black Lake in the Shelburne region of Nova Scotia. He won it in a lottery organised by sweet maker Haribo in 2005.

‌



‌



The prize came with a two-bedroom wooden house, a flight to the island, a canoe and fishing gear. There were even some gummy bears included in the package. But after years of holidays there, Matthias, from Bavaria in southern Germany, has reportedly decided the expense of keeping it is too much.

‌



He told German newspaper Bild that flights to Canada, onward journeys by car and boat, and maintenance costs had made it too expensive to hold on to. On top of that, the annual property tax bill is €2,500, or roughly £2,000.

‌



View 3 Images A calm lake in Northern Nova Scotia where the private island is situated (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

His parents helped look after the island and its property for years, but travelling there has become harder as they have grown older. Matthias is also said to be keen to explore other parts of the world after spending numerous holidays at the retreat over the past two decades.

‌



For a buyer willing to take on those costs, the island offers a secluded escape with opportunities for fishing, swimming, hiking and evenings around a campfire. It can only be reached by boat. Solar panels provide power, while water is drawn from the lake.

The sale includes a two-bedroom, one-bathroom log cabin, two small boats, a shed, a generator and a small dock. Marshland belonging to the island also offers space to explore.

‌



View 3 Images Aerial view of Powder Mill Lake (Image: Getty Images)

The property listing describes the setting as: "Escape to your own private island paradise, only 30 minutes from the amenities of Shelburne."

Article continues below

It adds: "A quick boat ride from shore will land you at your own island retreat where you can enjoy at least three seasons each year of lakeside living. The adjacent marshland belonging to the island invites you to go on extensive nature explorations, simply unique."

For those drawn to outdoor pursuits, the listing says: "Wilderness enthusiasts will be excited by the many recreation opportunities accessible from the island such as swimming, canoeing, fishing, or hiking (to name a few). Included with the island, and cabin, are two small boats, one shed, one generator, and a small dock."

News.title: 'I was abandoned as a baby in a phone box - now I want to find my mum'
News.content:
A woman abandoned in a phone box as a baby and the good samaritan who found her are launching an appeal to find her birth mother. April Paul, 32, from north west London, asks: “Where are you, Mum? Please come forward, I’d love to talk to you. She adds: “Every time I walk past a phone box I think of her and wonder where she is, and if she ever thinks of me too.”

It is estimated that about 16 babies are abandoned in the UK each year and the majority are newborns. April is a foundling - a term for infants who are left by their parents in places where they will likely be discovered, such as hospitals, parks, public toilets, or phone boxes, and subsequently raised through adoption or foster care.

She says: “As a foundling, you’re left with so many questions. Who am I? No-one knew my race, my ethnicity, in the beginning, because Mum didn't come forward. As I’ve grown older, things like medical history remain a mystery. Meeting my mum would help answer questions like, what will life be like when I am old?”

View 3 Images April and Joe are super close, and consider each other family (Image: Philip Coburn)

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

Ariel Bruce, lead search and social work consultant on the ITV documentary series Long Lost Family says April’s experience is common for a foundling. She explains: “When an adopted person reaches the age of 18, they're entitled to access their original birth certificate, which tells them the name of at least one parent. Usually, there's a social work file too, that gives a context to how the adoption came to take place - parents, ethnic background, medical histories. For a foundling, none of that stuff exists.”

As well as medical questions going unanswered, Ariel says: “There's a human need to know where we come from. Who we are.” On April 30 1994, only a few hours old and still with her umbilical cord attached, she April was found in the early hours of the morning by a civil service worker Joe Campbell, then 30, who had intended to make a call from the Newham phone box.

View 3 Images Joe with baby April, who he found in a phone box (Image: Supplied)

‌



Bank worker April, who is married to her childhood sweetheart and has two children, aged 12 and six, with him, says: “My mum had wrapped me in blankets, called the Samaritans on the phone and then fled into the night.” She had left an abusive relationship and then fled from North London’s Newham General Hospital after giving birth to April, her eighth child - disappearing into the night without a trace.

Joe called the police and stayed until help arrived - calling her April after the month when she was found. Now a bus driver, Joe, 62, a father of seven from Bell Green, south London, says: “I attempted to adopt April, but my request was denied by authorities because I was a single man. My biggest regret is that I couldn't raise her, but I never stopped thinking about her.”

April was fostered and later adopted by a Pakistani family, who named her Kiran Sheikh. Then, in 2016, at 22, she made a public appeal for her birth mother - and she and Joe were reunited.

A colleague, who didn’t know Joe’s story, spotted the appeal. He says: Joe says: “He said, ‘Joe, that's you.’ I reached out immediately, of course. It was so emotional to see her again after all those years. I introduced her to my family, and she fitted right in, like she’d always been there.”

‌



View 3 Images April as a tiny baby. She was abandoned in a phone box just hours after she was born (Image: Supplied)

The pair have been close ever since and see each other most weeks. This year, April launched a fundraiser to help Joe in retirement - surprising him with almost £50k on ITV’s Good Morning Britain last month. April, calling him “my dad,” says: “I owe him my life.”

Always curious about her roots, through various appeals on social media and word of mouth, April has managed to track down all but one of her biological siblings. She says: “Five older children who actually lived with Mum and Dad were taken into care. Then, later, two were given up at birth and I was abandoned. Connecting with them has been incredible. I’ve found a sense of who I am. And I was able to know my ethnicity for the first time.”

Last year, April met her biological father for the first time. She says: “He’s in prison serving life for attempted murder, but he said sorry for what he’d done. But my mum is a different story. She is still nowhere to be seen.”

‌



Now April is calling for her birth mum to get in touch, with Joe by her side, as she launches a fresh appeal for information. Joe says: “It was divine intervention on that day in 1994. I consider her my daughter. But I understand that, for April, many questions are left unanswered. I will always be here for her.”

April adds: “My mum abandoned me in a phone box, and while I don’t understand why she did it - I do think people deserve a second chance.”

News.title: Shepherd's pie will be tastier if you add a splash of unusual drink to the meat
News.content:
Shepherd's pie will be tastier if you add a splash of unusual drink to the meat

Shepherd's pie is a classic comfort food, but adding a splash of port wine to the lamb sauce can elevate the dish, according to HelloFresh recipe developer Mimi Morley.

View 3 Images Shepherd's pie will be transformed if you add just one extra ingredient (Image: GMVozd via Getty Images)

A chilly Sunday in November is the ideal time to rustle up a hearty, warming dish that the whole family can enjoy. Shepherd's pie is always a firm favourite, with its rich, meaty filling, fluffy mashed potato topping and golden, crispy cheese crust.

‌



‌



It may require a couple of hours in the kitchen, but much of that time is largely hands-off, and it's brilliant for batch cooking and enjoying over several days. But if you truly want to elevate your shepherd's pie to new heights, there's one secret ingredient that makes all the difference.

‌



It may seem a little unusual, but adding a dash of port to the meaty sauce is an absolute game-changer, according to Mimi Morley, a recipe developer for Hello Fresh.

‌



View 3 Images You don't get much more comforting than a shepherd's pie (Image: Getty)

She said: "Shepherd's pie is a classic comfort food and it's easy to see why so many of us Brits turn towards it during the colder and darker months of the year.

"One simple trick often used by chefs to add more depth to lamb dishes is adding a splash of port. Its rich and slightly sweet taste works particularly well alongside lamb, it instantly helps to balance the savoury flavours and create a more delicious and full bodied gravy."

‌



How to use port in shepherd's pie

The simplest way to introduce port into your shepherd's pie is to pour a small amount into the lamb filling and allow it to reduce before adding your gravy.

"You don't need to completely change your recipe or spend a ton of money on other additional ingredients, using this small addition of port can make all the difference and this is a great example of that", Mimi added.

‌



To achieve this, she recommends beginning by preparing your pie filling in the usual way, browning the minced lamb alongside your chosen vegetables.

Once the meat has visibly browned and the vegetables have softened, add the small splash of port to the pan and let it simmer for a few minutes until it has reduced down.

‌



After reducing, carry on preparing your pie as you normally would, allowing the filling to simmer until the gravy has thickened and all the flavours have melded together.

View 3 Images Shepherd's pie will be much tastier if you add a splash of port (Image: Getty)

‌



Ensure our latest food headlines always appear at the top of your Google Search by making us a Preferred Source. Click here to activate or add us as Preferred Source in your Google search settings

Extra tip for tastier shepherd's pie

For that golden, crisp and flavourful finish we all crave in our shepherd's pies, try mixing a little fresh thyme into melted butter before lightly brushing it over the mashed potato topping.

‌



Then, use a fork to create ridges across the mashed potato before popping the dish in the oven.

"Adding a little thyme to melted butter before brushing it over your mashed potato is such a simple way to bring even more flavour to your shepherd's pie," said Mimi.

Article continues below

"It creates that lovely golden topping but the thyme also compliments the lamb perfectly."

News.title: Russell Brand's former flatmate 'witnessed more crimes' and appeals to victims to call cops
News.content:
Russell Brand's former flatmate 'witnessed more crimes' and appeals to victims to call cops

Mark Pinheiro, who previously lived with Russell Brand in London, has appealed to other women following the disgraced former comedian's convictions last week

View 6 Images Brand lived with former pal Mark Pinheiro in London for around 16 months from the end of 1999 (Image: Netflix)

Russell Brand’s former flatmate says he saw the sexual predator commit more crimes and is appealing to other potential ­victims to come forward.

‌



‌



Mark Pinheiro, a one-time pal who was the first to give evidence at the trial of the disgraced entertainer, says he is willing to back women up.

‌



He claims he once saw Brand, now serving 10 and a half years for rape and sex assaults, try to drag a woman into his bedroom against her will.

‌



Mark, who lived with Brand in London for 16 months from 1999, urged victims: “If you’re out there and you’re listening and you want to come forward, do come forward and I will support you. I’ll say it now as I said it back then, ‘I saw what happened’. It’s not a he-said she-said argument... there was a third party to bear witness.”

View 6 Images Mr Pinheiro was the first witness to give evidence in Brand's trial at Southwark crown court (Image: Netflix)

Judge hails victims' bravery as sex predator Russell Brand is caged for 10 years READ MORE :

Mark speaks about the alleged attack he witnessed in new Netflix documentary, Russell Brand: Open Secret. He says he heard a girl shouting “Let go of me”, and “wrestling herself away from him [Brand]”.

‌



He claims: “I open up my door, and I see Russell basically holding on to the girl with both of his hands, gripping hold of her arm trying to pull her back in like a tug of war. And she’s wrestling herself away from him, and then as I switch the light on, the light comes on and he lets go.”

Mark told us: “There’s so many incidents that I can remember.”

‌



View 6 Images Brand is now serving a ten and a half year sentence for one rape and three sex assaults against four women (Image: Netflix/Press Association)

Mark first met Brand in December 1998 and they performed together in a cabaret group. Brand moved in with him at the end of 1999 until early 2001. They remained pals and Mark even celebrated several Christmases together with Brand and his doting mum Barbara, who raised the comic after his dad, Ron, walked out when he was just six months old.

‌



But they drifted apart around 2010 when Brand met pop star Katy Perry and Mark last saw him during his Messiah Complex tour in 2015.

He says: "I didn’t speak to him, but was backstage and I got to witness a lot of his antics... seeing a lot of girls who are taking the invite to come back to stage to meet him and were queueing up and patiently waiting their turn. Mark says Brand made no attempt to hide what he was doing and accused his entourage of enabling his behaviour.

‌



View 6 Images Brand was questioned by police on four separate occassions before being charged and sent to trial (Image: Metropolitan Police/AFP via Getty Images)

He said: “They were happy to tolerate it and that’s as far back as 10 years ago. I wasn’t the only person who saw things.

‌



“I was kind of disappointed more people didn’t come forward.” On Monday, Judge Mr Justice Joel Bennathan sentenced Brand for attacks on four women; a fan he raped at his London home, another he groped in a Soho bar, and two employees he assaulted at Choice FM and Channel 4.

The attacks took place between 2004 and 2009, at the height of his fame.

‌



Brand, 51, was cleared of raping a woman in a hotel in Bournemouth in 1999 during the Labour Party conference, where he had been performing in a cabaret. His trial heard that his wife Laura Gallacher, 39, with whom he has three children aged between three and 10, is standing by him.

View 6 Images Brand was taken to HMP Wandsworth in a prison van on Monday after being sentenced (Image: James Veysey/Shutterstock)

‌



Mark had told the jury at Southwark crown court Brand had bragged about being a ladies’ man who wanted to bed 5,000 women.

He recalled how the star often slept with up to three women a week in the flat. He believes Brand is a narcissist who suffers from other disorders, including sex addiction and a messiah complex.

‌



He said: “He enjoys manipulating people to do what he wants them to do for him and he just enjoys it. And it’s a skill perfected and mastered.

“I don’t know of any time where Russell’s actually kind of honoured his word. I don’t think there’s any doubt that he’s a narcissist. I’ve seen the nasty side of Russell, somebody who’s in denial and who would say, ‘oh, you know, I despise violence’ or whatever, but he could snap”.

‌



View 6 Images How the Mirror reported Brand's sentence earlier this week (Image: Geoffrey Swaine/Shutterstock)

At least six more alleged victims have come forward since Brand’s sentencing, and prosecutors are now considering more charges. Some of the cases are believed to date back to when he was hosting Channel 4’s Big Brother’s Big Mouth in 2006.

‌



Mark, who now works as a video FX supervisor, fears there could be more victims. He said: “I used to say to him, ‘Russell, you skirt really close to the bars’, meaning the prison bars.

“‘One day, you’re gonna get yourself in trouble’... Russell, stay away from the bars’. Here we are. It’s like some kind of self-fulfilling prophecy, in a way. It’s all kind of unfolded and ended up where he is now.

Article continues below

“He wasn’t above the law after all.”

In a direct message to possible victims coming forward who may be fearful they will not be believed, Mark urged: “I support them. I encourage them to come forward.”

News.title: Ex-Met Police inspector lied about wife's death in Barbados hotel room, BBC learns
News.content:
An inquest in the UK later found that Rebekah's organs had been inexplicably "chopped up" into small pieces by a pathologist in Barbados.

This served no medical purpose and destroyed vital evidence, according to a UK pathologist who examined her body after it had been repatriated.

The inquest also established that key toxicology and histology tests - to look for signs of disease, injury or other changes in the body - were not conducted.

The coroner, Andrew Harris, said this raised the prospect of "deliberate concealment or obstruction of further investigation".

He also said that while bloodstains on bedclothes may be consistent with vomiting, he could not accept the cause of death determined by Barbadian authorities, aspiration pneumonitis - inflammation of the lungs - and delivered an open verdict.

He concluded that Rebekah's death likely involved intoxication and said unlawful killing could not be ruled out.

The inquest did not, however, consider Arter's alleged sexual exploitation of several other women whose cases he had investigated, to be within its scope.

Police in Barbados have previously said no marks of violence were found on Rebekah's body and there was nothing to suggest anything untoward - adding that they did not order toxicology tests because they believed she died from natural causes.

A week after Rebekah died, Arter flew back to the UK where he was arrested at Heathrow in connection with alleged sexual offences against another woman whose case he had investigated as a police officer in 2010. He was found dead in Wandsworth prison three days later.

In response to the BBC, Metropolitan Police Commander Simon Messinger said: "Our thoughts at this time remain with Rebekah Arter's family, who understandably have questions about the circumstances of her death.

"We would urge any victim survivors of rape and sexual offences - no matter how long ago a crime may have occurred - to reach out."

Elliot says his two young children will never know their grandmother.

"My daughter, my son - they're never gonna actually have any memories of her," he says.

"For the rest of my life, I'm never going to know how she's passed away."

News.title: Alleged Russell Brand rape victim wants age of consent law changed
News.content:
Warning - this story contains graphic content

A woman who alleges that she was raped by Russell Brand when she was 16 has waived her right to anonymity and is campaigning for a staggered age of consent in an interview with the Sunday Times.

Mia Latter was one of six women who made allegations against Brand in 2023 as part of a Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches investigation. She was known under the pseudonym 'Alice'. Brand denied the allegations at the time.

None of the women in the 2023 media investigation were complainants in Brand's recent criminal trial.

Reacting to the proposal, Cabinet Office Minister Louise Haigh said it would be a "massive step" to change the age of consent law, but that it "deserves proper consideration and scrutiny".

Speaking to the Sunday Times, she added that it was "disgusting" that a culture existed in the 2000s that "normalised and celebrated" celebrities having relationships with teenagers.

On Monday the entertainer was sentenced to 10 and a half years for one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. He was acquitted of two counts of rape and one allegation of attempted indecent assault.

The Sunday Times reported that Latter had initially described the allegation about Brand to them as a sexual assault and that is how they reported it in their 2023 investigation.

Latter, 37, "now calls this allegation rape", the paper said.

Latter said she was 16 when she met Brand, who was 30 at the time, when she was on her way home from a shopping trip. She said Brand was working at MTV.

She told the paper: "I think people were so struck by my story because of the age difference and the clear imbalance [in power],"

She said Brand told her to keep their relationship secret from her school friends and claimed that he referred to her as "the child" in front of his entourage.

It was towards the end of their relationship that Latter was allegedly orally raped by Brand, according to the Sunday Times.

Latter said that she was now campaigning for the introduction of a "staggered" age of consent that would prohibit relationships between 16- and 17-year-olds and adults.

"I don't want to criminalise teenagers having sex with each other," she told the paper. "If you're between the ages of 16 and 18, it seems reasonable that you can have relationships with each other, and [teenagers] are always going to. But â¦ if you're in your thirties, forties and fifties and you're trying to have a relationship with someone under the age of 18, it [should be] a criminal offence."

She also told the paper that she would not continue with the criminal process so she could focus on her campaign.

In her interview with the Sunday Times she said that the CPS decided not to include her as part of Brand's criminal trial but the police wanted her to be part of a "subsequent trial".

A Met Police spokesperson said: "Officers launched an investigation in January 2026 after receiving an allegation of rape.

"Detectives sought advice from the Crown Prosecution Service to determine how best to proceed, and officers were advised that further information was needed before a charging decision could be made.

"This investigation remains ongoing. We understand the delay has been distressing for this victim-survivor. However, our focus has been on putting forward the best possible evidence."

A spokesperson for the Crown Prosecution Service said it would "continue to work closely with investigators to provide advice and make sure cases progress as quickly as possible".

News.title: Neets review won't be for the faint-hearted - and will test Burnham's appetite for a welfare fight
News.content:
It's an ugly acronym. And it's an even uglier situation.

The reality of so-called "Neets" in the UK - young people who haven't got jobs, aren't studying or being trained up - has seen hundreds upon hundreds of thousands in their late teens or early-20s struggle to find a decent future for well over a decade.

It costs the taxpayer billions. And the human cost is variously described as a disaster, a national shame, even a moral crisis.

When the phrase Neet was first coined by Tony Blair's Downing Street in 1999, the focus was on 170,000 or so teenagers who were not in education, employment or training. After many attempts at solving the problem, add in a pandemic and years of a sluggish economy, it's acute - with nearly a million under-25s in that situation.

A tome full of proposals to try and fix it once and for all will be published on Tuesday, after a year in the making.

How the government reacts will test its appetite and capacity for radical change, and the prime minister's real, not rhetorical, hunger for tricky political arguments.

The canny smooth talker behind the huge review, former Labour MP Alan Milburn, wants you to know that Andy Burnham knows exactly what's coming.

Speaking to me in Liverpool, where in Merseyside 14.5% of 16 to 24-year-olds are unemployed,, external he tells me: "All the way through, the prime minister, the chancellor, all the ministers, they know what's going on. It won't be a surprise to them when this is launched and that gives it a fighting chance of actually being implemented."

But his collection of proposals is not for the faint-hearted.

On top of a plan to stop under-25s claiming the main sickness and disability benefits, Milburn will argue for a dramatic shift in the balance of what the taxpayer spends on benefits for young people compared with what is spent on support to help them get into work.

He says the amount spent on young people's benefits is 25 times as much as that on employment support - and he wants to shift it to a drastically different two to one.

He won't put specific numbers on it yet, but accepts openly that means a significant number of young people losing their benefits or facing cuts.

But that would come with a chunky expansion of the amount of further education, training, health support and likely jobs subsidised by the taxpayer too. A big cut to state support on one side of the ledger, but a big increase on the other.

And to make sure that government gets really serious about improving the mess, Milburn is asking for a new law that would give young people a guarantee of help and support - a job, an apprenticeship, a training place, or perhaps health treatment so they are able to work - an "opportunity guarantee".

He told me he won't fall into the "elephant's trap", where a feisty teenager could sue the prime minister if they didn't get the job they fancied. But the idea is to put a legal duty on the authorities in a similar vein to councils' obligation to look after children in care, or to provide accommodation or advice to homeless people.

News.title: Hannah Fry feels 'unbelievably lucky' after cervical cancer treatment
News.content:
Prof Hannah Fry has described feeling "unbelievably lucky" after being treated for cervical cancer.

The mathematician and BBC presenter, who recently took part in the second season of the Celebrity Traitors, said cancerous cells were discovered after she attended a cervical screening in 2020.

She underwent a hysterectomy, describing the experience to BBC Radio 4's Desert Island Discs as "horrific".

"As awful as that was, it had a full stop at the end of the sentence," the 42-year-old added. "I had my five-year clear the other day. I feel so unbelievably lucky."

In Sunday's episode, Fry told show host Lauren Laverne that she had delayed a cervical screening examination for months in 2020. After she attended one, the results "didn't come back for a few weeks," she said.

"Then I got a call from my GP telling me they needed me to come back and do another test, and they did a biopsy.

"I was trying hard not to panic but when they found it was in the lymphatic systemâ¦ that was when it really started to come down."

The broadcaster said she was told that her chances of survival depended on the cancerous cells not having spread to her lymph nodes, although it was not clear "how bad it was at that point".

"It's all about, basically, how far into your lymphatic system has it got. If it had not got into any lymph nodes, then the odds were in my favour and I had a really good chance of survival," she said.

Fry explained that this meant "if it was in one it would drop to a 60% chance of survival and two â the odds would go against me and it would be a 40% chance".

News.title: Israel kills Hamas commander in strike on Gaza camp, officials say
News.content:
A senior Hamas figure who helped plan and oversee the 7 October 2023 attack on Israel has been killed in an Israeli airstrike, officials in Israel and Gaza have said.

Samir Abu Younis, the newly appointed commander of the Rafah Brigade, was killed on Saturday in Al-Mawasi in the southern Gaza Strip, according to Hamas's Al-Qassam Brigades military wing.

A local Hamas official confirmed Younis's death. The Israeli military said it had targeted him and that prior to the strike "steps were taken to mitigate harm to civilians".

Eyewitnesses in Gaza said four missiles struck a tent in the Al-Waha camp, which shelters hundreds of displaced people in Al-Mawasi, causing a fire to break out.

A medical source at Nasser Hospital in the southern city of Khan Younis said three injured people had arrived there, as well as a dead body.

The Israel Defence Forces (IDF) and Israel's security agency, the ISA, confirmed in a statement on Telegram that it had "eliminated" Younis.

Describing him as a "central figure among Hamas's senior figures", it said he had "acted with the aim of trying to restore the strength of the brigade and the Hamas terrorist organisation".

It added: "Younis directed the brigade's terrorists to advance and carry out terror attacks against Israeli civilians and IDF troops."

Al-Qassam Brigades wrote on Telegram that Younis had "participated in numerous high-profile operations and resisted enemy incursions", and was "one of the most important commanders involved in planning and overseeing the 7 October attack".

It described his killing as a "cowardly assassination".

Younis, 53, had been in his position since 15 September, following the death of the brigade's previous commander, Nael Abu Obeid.

He joined Hamas' armed wing in 1991 and held several senior operational roles before becoming commander. His funeral will be held on Sunday afternoon in Khan Younis, Hamas said.

The Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed an 251 others taken hostage, triggered the most recent war in Gaza.

Since then, more than 74,650 people have been killed in the Palestinian territory, the health ministry there says.

Though a ceasefire was reached last October, Israel has continued occasional strikes it says are targeting remaining Hamas militants, which it argues it has the right to do under the terms of the ceasefire agreement.

News.title: Beauty advent calendars can cost hundreds - but are they value for money?
News.content:
It's easy to see the appeal of a beauty advent calendar. Like many women at this time of year, Julia says she often finds herself tempted to splurge on one - especially a perfume calendar. But she takes quite an unsentimental approach.

"I always look at what's in them. If I like enough of the fragrances, I'll buy it," says the 39-year old, who works as a senior commercial manager in engineering.

Luxury advent calendars are supposed to offer the thrill of a surprise but, for Julia, it is more important she actually wants the items inside - a thought that is also striking more and more customers in the wake of the scandal over the Skims calendar.

News.title: How to shake hands and make eye contact - the lessons preparing pupils for the world of work
News.content:
There is a sudden buzz of conversation in a Year 10 class as teenagers split into pairs, sit down opposite each other and start conducting mock job interviews.

It is not for a forthcoming exam. These 14- and 15-year-olds at Sandbach High School and Sixth Form College are working on skills that should help them when they leave school and try to enter the workforce.

Today, they are learning the art of a successful job interview. Around the room, pupils are practising firm handshakes and making good eye contact.

They are rehearsing how to answer questions that you might expect to be asked in a job interview, such as "When was the last time you worked in a team?" and "Tell me about a time you made a mistake at work".

None of them has even reached working age yet, but in forthcoming lessons they'll also be learning about how to write a CV and what their rights at work are. It is all part of dedicated career lessons that they get every fortnight alongside their usual classes.

There are nearly a million young people across the UK - one in eight of all those aged 16 to 24 - who are not in education, employment or training - or Neet - according to the latest estimates.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has called the high number both a "moral failure" and an "economic catastrophe".

News.title: My mother told me I would die if I sought treatment for Ebola - I am proof you can survive
News.content:
When Dr Raymond Kasereka Kamwanga told his family he suspected he had Ebola and was going to a treatment centre in the city of Butembo in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, his family were horrified.

They regarded the specialised unit as a "death house" as not many patients do recover - especially those admitted in the late stages of the illness. His 50-year-old mother was in tears, pleading with him not to go there.

"Why are you choosing to die at the Ebola treatment centre?" Masika Ndungo had asked him.

But as a doctor at Butembo's Katwa Hospital, he knew that if stayed at home, he was unlikely to survive.

This was in July, two months after the World Health Organization (WHO) had declared the Ebola outbreak in DR Congo a public health emergency of international concern. Since then 5,400 people have died and 11,000 have been infected, making it the second-most deadly outbreak ever recorded.

Butembo is in North Kivu province, the epicentre of the crisis, with the highest number of reported cases, according to the Congolese health ministry.

Dr Kamwanga is one of 3,031 people who have survived - and is evangelical about sharing his story in an effort to help stop the spread of infections devastating his community.

After staring death in the face and overcoming ostracisation, he has even started writing a book about his experience.

"As someone who has recovered, I am living proof that the disease exists, but also that it is possible to recover from it," he tells the BBC outside Katwa Hospital where he still works.

The 30-year-old medic believes he contracted the virus through contact with a patient in a setting where protective measures are not always adequate.

News.title: Young people should have legal guarantee of job or training, Milburn tells BBC
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has described Milburn's forthcoming report as a "watershed moment," but stopped short of committing to implementing its recommendations in full.

Burnham also insisted paying for the reforms would not mean "more money" but "spending differently" in government when pressed on the large upfront investment they are expected to require.

Asked whether he would accept the politically sensitive report in full, Burnham declined to provide that "blanket assurance".

Speaking at the Welsh Labour conference on Saturday, Burnham said that the report addressed the "youth detachment" that has been on the rise since the pandemic.

"It can't be right that we've stripped away support from young people as a society, as life is getting harder for them and growing up is getting more difficult," he said.

The prime minister added that the government was also looking at a new vision for schooling that is "not focused solely on the university route" and which offers technical education alongside traditional academic learning.

Lord Blunkett, a former Labour home secretary, told the BBC that money from cutting benefits spending should be reassigned to supporting employment "at least in the immediate future".

Speaking on Radio 4's Today programme, he said reforms should focus on "transferring resource that currently goes into paying for failure, keeping youngsters at home, isolated, lonely, into actually putting the money in and the resource and the commitment in to making those jobs available".

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch has previously said the government should not be spending "lots of time" on employment schemes, which she said would ultimately fail.

Her party and Reform UK have argued for significant cuts to welfare, including to fund a boost to defence.

Reform economy spokesman Robert Jenrick said: "This review is pointless unless we get action from Burnham straight away.

"It cannot be right that this continues for another 10 years before the youth benefits bill comes down."

Green Party leader Zack Polanski said it was "disappointing" the Milburn review had "come up with the same tired conclusions" on youth unemployment.

Polanski added: "Using benefit sanctions to force young people into low-paid, insecure work doesn't solve the structural inequalities they face, and it deepens poverty."

The Liberal Democrats want the government to introduce a 100-hour work experience guarantee and a careers coach for every young person.

They believe this would equip youngsters with the best possible skills before they leave school.

The TUC - the umbrella group for unions in the UK - welcomed Milburn's proposal of a legal guarantee as a "game changer", describing the country's number of Neets as a "national emergency".

But it stressed that funding for additional support for young people should not come from public service budgets. "In further education, funding needs to be targeted at the workforce, as well as provision, to tackle the recruitment and retention crisis and massive pay disparities in the sector," it said.

"A zero sum approach would be wrong and counter-productive."

News.title: Man dies after being stabbed by gang of masked men
News.content:
A murder investigation has been launched after a 27-year-old man was stabbed in Manchester.

Officers were called to Moss Bank in the Crumpsall area of the city shortly after 01:30 GMT following reports that a man had suffered several stab wounds. He later died from his injuries in an ambulance.

Greater Manchester Police (GMP) said initial inquiries suggested the victim had been attacked by "a number of males" all believed to have been wearing dark clothing and balaclavas.

The suspects are believed to have fled the scene in the direction of Ash Tree Road, said a force spokesperson who added that no arrests had been made and inquiries were continuing.

News.title: UK ethics watchdog chief steps back from role over sexual misconduct claims
News.content:
The head of the government's main ethics watchdog has stepped back after it emerged he was investigated in a previous job over alleged sexual misconduct involving female colleagues, and had, in one case, been sanctioned.

Stuart Sterling was appointed as the first chief executive of the newly formed Ethics and Integrity Commission in October 2025.

The existence of the allegations against Sterling, and the investigations into them, were first reported by the Sunday Times.

Following the report, a government spokesperson said: "These are serious allegations. Stuart Sterling has stepped back from his role while we swiftly establish the facts."

The Labour Party promised in its 2024 manifesto to create the commission to "ensure probity in government" in response to scandals during the Covid pandemic.

As its head, Sterling's role included advising the prime minister on tackling misconduct in public life.

The Sunday Times reported that, in 2003, Sterling had been subject to a "full misconduct hearing" when he was a junior officer with Northamptonshire Police in what was treated as a case "of sexual harassment".

The paper said he had been accused of inappropriately touching the breasts of a female colleague in a police station, and a male colleague who allegedly witnessed the event had reported him to his superiors. It reported that he had been suspended on full pay.

A representative for Mr Sterling said: "Stuart states that a full disciplinary process was held regarding the complaint in 2002. He complied with this fully. It resulted in a sanction."

The Sunday Times reported that he was given a financial penalty of two weeks' pay. It said that, at the time, that was the maximum sanction possible short of forced resignation. He then received two police commendations and was promoted to be a detective sergeant.

The Sunday Times said that by 2008 Mr Sterling had been reported to the force again after another allegation of sexual misconduct against a female colleague, this time at a social gathering outside work.

Mr Sterling's representative said: "He denies that the alleged incident in 2008 ever took place. He was never subject to any criminal investigation, but the allegation was examined by professional standards".

The representative added: "He was not required to resign from the force. He left voluntarily".

Northamptonshire Police has confirmed that it holds a digital record of a misconduct process from 2002.

It did not comment on the later allegation.

In 2009, Sterling joined the Cabinet Office. It is not clear what vetting process he underwent. He has since served in a variety of senior roles and in 2019 was seconded to the National Police Chiefs' Council. In 2023 he received an OBE for helping to plan the funeral of Queen Elizabeth.

It is understood the Cabinet Office will now examine whether appropriate and correct disclosures of information were made.

News.title: King jokes with Elton John as he marks 78th birthday with radio show
News.content:
King Charles and Sir Elton John joked about the problems of ageing as the pair joined for a special radio show to coincide with the monarch's 78th birthday.

Sir Elton, 79, was joined on his regular Rocket Hour radio show for a special episode during which the King shared his musical memories as the pair chose 14 songs together.

The programme also marked the 50th anniversary of the King's Trust and highlighted how musicians have supported the charity's efforts.

"We and the Trust are definitely still standing," the King said, as he highlighted Sir Elton's track I'm Still Standing as one of his favourites because of the song's "message of resilience".

The music legend joked in reply: "I'm still sitting now, though" giving a large laugh, with the King chuckling: "With occasional bits dropping off here and there. I know this is a terrible problem as we get older."

The special was recorded last month at Apple Music Studios in south London and premiered on Saturday morning.

The King recalled Sir Elton's 1986 performance at Wembley Arena, which marked the charity's 10th anniversary.

"I suspect that no-one who was present on that night in 1986 could possibly forget your performance of I'm Still Standing," King Charles said.

"I know people in all kinds of circumstances find this song inspiring, not only for its marvellous spirit, but also its message of resilience. And certainly, 40 years on from that remarkable concert, we and the Trust are definitely still standing."

News.title: Magnificent Wales end 73-year New Zealand hoodoo
News.content:
Nations Championship

Wales (21) 35

Tries: T Williams, Lake, Griffin, James, Rees-Zammit Cons: Costelow 5

New Zealand (21) 28

Tries: Ratima, Sititi, Fineanganofo, Lakai Cons: Mo'unga 4.

Wales celebrated a first victory against New Zealand in 73 years with a brilliant performance to spark astonishing scenes in Cardiff.

Steve Tandy's unfancied side lifted a nation as they broke a 34-match losing sequence against the All Blacks that stretched back to 1953.

In a nine-try Nations Championship thriller at the Principality Stadium, Wales led 14-0, 21-7 and 35-21 before they held off New Zealand with a wonderful defensive display in the final quarter, led by flankers James Botham and Jac Morgan and lock Dafydd Jenkins.

The home side produced a stunning start with tries from inspirational scrum-half Tomos Williams and captain Dewi Lake inside the first six minutes.

Prop Archie Griffin also added a first-half try, but New Zealand responded with scores from scrum-half Cortez Ratima, number eight Wallace Sititi and wing Fehi Fineanganofo to level the score 21-21 at half-time.

Wales centre Eddie James and wing Louis Rees-Zammit scored early second-half tries before New Zealand flanker Peter Lakai pulled one back.

The remarkable Wales defence followed as they held up the All Blacks three times over the line to stop New Zealand scoring, to evoke wild celebrations.

News.title: Burnham suggests Welsh Labour lost sight of devolution as review criticises ex-first minister's strategy
News.content:
The prime minister has told members of his party that Welsh Labour may have lost sight of some of the principles of devolution before it was thrown out of power in a historic election defeat.

On Saturday morning Andy Burnham addressed the first Welsh Labour conference since May's Senedd election.

He suggested the previous Labour government did not do enough to pass powers down to communities, and said it was "hard" to accept the party was no longer in power after 27 years of running the Welsh government.

He spoke before a review into what went wrong concluded that former First Minister Eluned Morgan's political strategy of calling out Westminster played a role in the party losing power.

The report by Prof Anand Menon, of PF Global, said Morgan's calls for constitutional change like the devolution of policing and the Crown Estate did not get through to voters.

A source close to the former first minister said it was "ludicrous" to suggest that Morgan was focused on constitutional issues.

Meanwhile, Welsh Labour leader Ken Skates has criticised his party for focusing too much on powers for the Senedd.

In a subdued speech, Burnham said he wanted to see "one Labour team" where "everyone" was "signed up and on the same page".

He spoke ahead of the publication of a review of what went wrong at the election.

Since he became prime minister he has been lobbying the Welsh government to devolve more powers to local councils.

"Somewhere along the way perhaps we lost sight of some of the principles that drove devolution in the first place.

"We probably stopped listening as much as we should have, and actually stopped driving power down into every Welsh postcode which is what the vision to me really should always have been about - about people and places."

He said the party would accept its defeat and "come back stronger" with a "vision for a stronger Wales in a fairer United Kingdom".

Burnham said he wanted to achieve the sense of a "one Labour team for Wales" where the party is "pulling in the same direction".

"Where I'm pulling with you and not creating problems for you or going against what Ken or colleagues want to achieve.

"We will put forward a vision for communities up and down Wales, as well as giving Wales a stronger national voice."

News.title: Family's two-year fight to bring killer driver back from Latvia
News.content:
Days after her 12-year-old son was killed by a BMW driver travelling at 70mph, Louise Slater sat outside the suspect's home, gathering the courage to plead with his family to hand him in.

She had been given the name and address of Aleksanders Dolars after her son Keaton was killed in a hit-and-run in Coventry.

Distraught, she was preparing to knock on the door when a neighbour approached and asked what she was doing.

When she explained, he told her the family, from Latvia, had packed up and left a day or two earlier.

Keaton's suspected killer had fled just hours after leaving him dying in the road.

What followed was a relentless two-year fight by his parents to track him down and bring him back to England to face justice.

He was finally jailed on Friday, for nine years and four months.

This article contains upsetting details

Dolars' name had been already circulating locally before police identified him as their main suspect on 18 June 2024, four days after Keaton was killed.

A family waiting at nearby traffic lights said their seven-seater "shook violently" as a BMW driver sped past at what appeared to be far more than the 30mph limit. Moments later, they saw something fly into the air behind them.

The car did not stop.

As it disappeared from view, the family noticed a black rucksack and a single shoe lying in Radford Road and realised a child may have been hit.

News.title: Thousands turn out in Edinburgh to protest against AI data centres
News.content:
Thousands of people have joined a protest in Edinburgh against the building of large-scale AI data centres.

Demonstrators with placards - and some dressed in costume - assembled at the top of the Royal Mile before marching towards the Scottish Parliament.

The event comes at a time of widespread debate about the environmental impact of data centres and is part of a wave of protests across Europe.

The Scottish government will soon publish new planning guidance on data centres and said it was developing a strategy to maximise the "public benefit".

News.title: Russell Brand secretly moved to new prison days after being jailed for rape
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in
