Sports.title: Russell partners with BRDC to launch karting academy
Sports.content:
Formula 1 star George Russell has launched a karting academy in partnership with Silverstone to make motorsport more accessible and discover the next young superstar.

The eight-time grand prix winner launched his GR63 Karting Academy on Thursday with it open to boys and girls aged eight to nine, based at the kart track in Silverstone.

It features a “four stage path to the top” and will start in December with an open-access format inviting every eligible driver to Silverstone, where 80 will be selected for stage two.

That will see the 80 drivers compete in the “GR63 Shootout” on 31 January to determine the 25 slots for an eight-round championship at Silverstone from March to November in 2027.

The championship is fully-funded for each driver and the top five will go head-to-head in stage four next December, where the winner will receive a fully-funded karting campaign in 2028.

“Karting is where it all started for me,” said Russell, who won titles on a national and international level before progressing into single-seater competition.

“It taught me everything I’ve relied on throughout my career. I know how hard it is for talented young drivers to get that first opportunity, especially when budgets are tight.

George Russell, Mercedes Photo by: Michael Potts / LAT images via Getty Images

“With the GR63 Karting Academy, I want to give something back by finding those hidden talents and giving them the support and platform they need to reach their potential.

“I'm really grateful to Silverstone and the British Racing Drivers’ Club for helping make this happen."

The academy is designed for those who “may not have the budget required to progress through the sport” with the costs in motorsport, both at grassroots level and at the top, increasing.

So costs to enter the academy’s opening stage are £25 with that rising to £75 for the “GR63 Shootout”, before everything is fully-funded from stage three onwards.

BRDC president David Coulthard said: “As owners of Silverstone and guardians of British motorsport, the BRDC has always been committed to reinvesting in the sport and nurturing home-grown talent.

“That commitment has played a big part in Britain’s long record of success in motorsport, and it is a great source of pride for the Club and its Members.

“The GR63 Academy captures that ethos perfectly, and we are delighted to work with George to support the next generation of drivers here at Silverstone."

All drivers must be a citizen of a commonwealth country and to book oneself for stage one, an arrive and drive session, click the link for the Silverstone website here.

Sports.title: Lawson to stay in F1 as Racing Bulls announces 2027 driver pairing
Sports.content:
Racing Bulls has confirmed Liam Lawson will stay with the team for the 2027 Formula 1 campaign, partnering Arvid Lindblad for a second, straight season.

They have formed a formidable duo this year having propelled Racing Bulls to fifth in the championship, which is set to be the Anglo-Italian team's best-ever result.

Despite sitting on 89 points, however, compared to 38 for rookie Lindblad, Lawson's future was in doubt thanks to junior driver Nikola Tsolov starring in F2 this year.

The 19-year-old Bulgarian is second in the standings and has been handed private testing opportunities and a rookie FP1 session in Mexico as part of his junior driver duties.

So Racing Bulls was weighing up its need for short-term performance against its explicit goal of training young drivers for parent team Red Bull.

But with Lawson rising to the occasion in recent weeks, performing some of his strongest races under constant pressure, the 24-year-old has effectively been too good for the team to ignore.

Nikola Tsolov Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

Sources indicated to Autosport in Brazil last weekend that amid a big push for the company's top leadership to back Tsolov, the pendulum swung back towards Lawson's favour with his performances over the Americas triple-header.

Read Also: Formula 1 How the Racing Bulls pendulum is swinging back towards Lawson

So the Kiwi has now signed a fresh deal for 2027 with team boss Alan Permane saying he had "no doubt" that the squad will field the strongest possible line-up next season.

"We’re delighted to be continuing with Liam and Arvid for 2027," he said. "Both have demonstrated their ability and potential throughout the season, and we’ve seen the progress they’ve made, both individually and as a pairing.

“I have no doubt that this is the best driver line-up for us, bringing a strong combination of experience and ambition.

“Together, we have a solid foundation to build on the progress made this year, continue pushing ourselves forward and take the next step towards achieving our ambitions in 2027."

Next year is set to be Lawson’s third, full season in F1 having made his debut at Zandvoort towards the back end of the 2023 campaign - having another partial season in 2024.

Arvid Lindblad, Racing Bulls, Liam Lawson, Racing Bulls Photo by: Rudy Carezzevoli / Getty Images

"I’m very happy to be continuing with Visa Cash App Racing Bulls next year,” he said. “We’ve had a brilliant season together and the team has worked very hard to produce a fast car, which I’ve loved driving.

“It feels great to be part of a historic season for the team as we continue our fight for P5 in the constructors' championship. It's a testament to the hard work of everyone both at track, and back at the factory.

"I’m looking forward to carrying this moment forward with Arvid through to 2027. We’re building something super positive and I’m excited by what we can achieve together.”

Lawson is currently eighth in the drivers’ standings with Lindblad in 11th ahead of the final three rounds: Las Vegas, Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

"Looking back on my first season in Formula 1, it's been a truly special year, full of new experiences and learnings since the very first pre-season test," said 19-year-old Lindblad.

"I can't wait to get started next year, building on everything I've learned during my rookie season. It's set to be an exciting year, and I look forward to continuing to drive alongside Liam."

Sports.title: What the Brazilian GP revealed about F1's ability to cope with rain
Sports.content:
The question of what might happen in a wet race has vexed Formula 1's stakeholders since before the beginning of the season. It's also prompted some unnecessarily hysterical commentary throughout the year, peaking in the run-up to last weekend's Brazilian Grand Prix at Interlagos, where rain for qualifying and the race was a virtual certainty for the first time this season.

Although the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia was interrupted by rain and the discovery of a software glitch, by the time the race got going the track was drying quickly. This was not the case in Brazil.

Qualifying at Interlagos was red-flagged for 80 minutes after a downpour coincided with the start of the session, and many media outlets alighted on a spicy George Russell quote in the aftermath.

"I love driving in the rain here but, at some point, if that was a race, there was no way we should be driving in that because the chances of seeing a really, really horrific incident are very, very high," he said.

Perfect headline material for a noisy story, but context was lacking. The general consensus within the paddock after that session was that the FIA made the right calls at the right time, immediately suspending Q1 during the initial downpour, then applying great rigour to identify a safe ‘window' to restart it.

"In general, I want to race, but yesterday [Saturday] I think it was the perfect call," said Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur after the race. "When we did the first [Q1] lap before the red flag, we came back with two centimetres of water in the car…"

Charles Leclerc, Ferrari, Carlos Sainz, Williams, Arvid Lindblad, Racing Bulls Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

Those conditions were too wet to stage any kind of track activity beyond a boat race in the pitlane. The real questions surrounded how the cars and the latest generation of tyres would perform in the kind of wet and/or rapidly changing circumstances in which qualifying and the race could actually be staged.

Historically, Pirelli's heavily treaded ‘extreme' wet tyres are rarely seen, since too much of their operating window sits outside the margin of what is considered to be acceptable racing conditions. They displace massive quantities of water but the tread blocks overheat too quickly as the track dries. By the time the track is wet enough to justify the ‘extreme' tyre, a red flag is usually imminent.

The intermediate tyres have therefore been the wet-weather boots of choice, but this year's are understood to be too ‘hard' and slow to come up to operating temperature. Pirelli just hasn't been able to accomplish like-for-like running with the narrower wheels mandated for this season, given the testing restrictions.

It's long been feared that lack of grip from the new intermediates, combined with the more brutal torque delivery of the latest generation of engines, would make the 2026 F1 cars dangerously undriveable in the wet. Hence the outbreak of hysteria ahead of the Brazil weekend.

What actually transpired was less dramatic, and more nuanced. The nature of the track surface at Interlagos meant driveability was occasionally an issue, but not always. In the background, the FIA has been doing a lot of work since the beginning of the year to manage power delivery in these conditions.

Alexander Albon, Williams, Carlos Sainz, Williams Photo by: Colin McMaster / LAT Images via Getty Images

While qualifying – once it got started – offered some hope that the ‘extreme' wets are now more useable, the intermediates were a little more problematic. Kimi Antonelli went off at Turn 12 on his lap to the grid, and several other drivers reported their cars became a handful again when rain in the last 10 laps dictated a return to the intermediates.

"I think what is good is that we can use the 'big wet' much more than in the past," said Vasseur. "And this is good because it's not pushing you to use inter when it's a more 'big wet' situation, or mix between the two, and then you are taking risks.

"I think the quali was pretty good… but also the grip was completely different. You saw in the lap to the grid today that everybody was completely like hell. I think it's a difficult track with these conditions."

Pirelli's target for next year is to bring the performance of the wet-weather compounds closer together, so the intermediate warms up faster and the ‘extreme' is more resistant to wear. But this is a challenge to engineer because the tracks differ so much in terms of the energy going through the tyres.

"It was difficult to fire them up but they also wore quite quickly," said Alex Albon, who finished 15th in Brazil.

"So even when they're cold, they're wearing and it just feels like they never overheat, or they never level up to temperature. And then by the time you're circulating, the tread's already come off the tyre and then you're already struggling, you're sliding around. So, you never feel good at any point in the race; it never feels like it comes alive."

This would explain some of the peculiarities of the opening laps, where those at the front of the grid found themselves having to be super-cautious because they couldn't feel the grip – while some of those towards the rear, who spent less time waiting for lights-out, got strong getaways.

Even among those there was a variance: Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton quickly broke through to the top 10 from 20th and 21st on the grid, only for Hamilton to then go backwards as his car developed massive oversteer snaps. Verstappen, like Antonelli, then found his car less performant on the slicks.

Wet conditions added to the drama of qualifying Photo by: Sam Bloxham / LAT Images via Getty Images

This mixed spread of performance over the wet and dry tyre compounds will be tricky to unpick, but the consensus remained that the wet-weather rubber needs more development. There were minor gripes but not the disasters that were feared and noisily predicted.

"I think the level of the wet and the inter is not good enough and we need to work with Pirelli on finding a better tyre," said Carlos Sainz, "because in the mixed conditions the inter is still a very weak tyre at the rear. By the time it warms up, the front is gone.

"And the extreme, honestly, yesterday we had so much sliding and a big lack of rear grip, so still missing a bit of development on these two tyres."

While the data gathered through running in many different conditions this weekend will be useful, it's still an isolated example. What worked or didn't work at Interlagos may not translate elsewhere, given variances in surfaces and ambient temperatures.

"Quite tricky I would say," was Liam Lawson's take on racing in the wet in a 2026 F1 car.

"The biggest problem today is the [ambient] temperature was much cooler than yesterday. And so even though there was less water, on the laps of the grid the cars were nearly undriveable, and the temps were just going down.

"So, we survived the start of the race but at points when it rains a lot, the inter becomes... it's not that the standing water's too much, it's that you can't actually keep the temperature in it. So, if we're on a track like Vegas and it rains, honestly, I think we're in trouble.

"But overall, obviously we got through a weekend for the first time with these tyres."

Additional reporting by Roberto Chinchero and Guilherme Longo

Sports.title: F1 2026 calendar update: Imola off the table, no plan B if Iran war escalates
Sports.content:
The Qatar and Abu Dhabi grands prix which will conclude Formula 1’s 2026 season are set to proceed as planned, provided there is no dramatic escalation of the Iran war.

The Middle Eastern conflict, which started in late February as the United States and Israel launched strikes on Iran, has destabilised the region. The calendars of many motorsport championships have been impacted – not least F1’s, whose Saudi Arabian race was cancelled while Bahrain’s round was postponed and hosted in Malaysia.

F1 has been monitoring the situation closely, with a chilly Imola as an alternative season finale on the first weekend of December if Qatar and Abu Dhabi were unable to host their respective events.

Lusail did run its MotoGP round without major issues last weekend, though both Yamaha teams withdrew from the competition due to the geopolitical situation.

10 November was F1’s deadline to provide Imola with a final answer as to whether the Italian track would have to prepare for a grand prix in the next three weeks; it will not.

Charles Leclerc, Ferrari, Isack Hadjar, Racing Bulls Photo by: Zak Mauger / Motorsport Images

So the 2026 season will end with the planned Las Vegas-Qatar-Abu Dhabi triple-header, with travel insurance and governments’ travel advice currently allowing it.

However, there’s a caveat: F1 is aware it cannot guarantee the situation won’t change by early December and insists it will prioritise safety if the conflict escalates.

Team bosses have been maintaining a straightforward stance on the matter – they trust F1 and the FIA to make the right calls.

“I trust them to take the best decision for all of us,” Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur commented in Mexico. “Me, personally, I want to race. It doesn't matter where, but I want to race. Now, I will go where they will tell us to go.”

“Stefano and Mohammed have been pretty clear about the situation that Formula 1 follows what the international guidelines are, whether there are travel restrictions, airlines not flying, any warnings in the region, the kind of feedback that local governments are making,” his Mercedes counterpart Toto Wolff added in Friday’s press conference at Interlagos. “So not only the promoters, but what the local governments are making. And this is what you need to rely on, in my opinion, and I'm fully with that.

Toto Wolff, Mercedes Photo by: Mark Sutton / Formula 1 via Getty Images

“I think that if riders stand up, who know nothing geopolitically about what's going on, but have an audience that listens, I think that is something that creates media value. But I would have done the same as MotoGP management has done. You want to ride or drive, go. If you don't want to, don't go. It's as simple as that, and everybody can take their personal decisions on that, and I respect that.

“Of course, you've got to be wary of what's happening in the next few days, a few weeks, and Stefano has his finger on the pulse to monitor that. If things were to get more dangerous and we would get that feedback, then he's going to be the first one, together with Mohammed, to protect the people that were meant to travel. So that's why I'm following their guidance.

“From what I'm hearing internally, it hasn't been raised. It hasn't been a topic. But also there, if someone feels they don't feel comfortable, he or she doesn't feel comfortable travelling, then it's something that I would always respect. And maybe that's an opportunity to give somebody else a chance. It wouldn't change anything for the relationship. I've always respected that some people didn't want to go to certain grands prix, and that's how I see it at the moment.”

Additional reporting by Ronald Vording

Sports.title: Ignore social media echo chamber and trust F1 over Middle East races – Wolff | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff says Formula 1 is right to go ahead with its plans to race in the Middle East.

Many sports including other motor racing series cancelled events in the region due to the US-Iran war. However F1 commercial rights holder Liberty Media held its Moto GP event in Qatar last weekend, despite one manufacturer staying away due to concerns over the safety of travelling to the region.

F1 confirmed this week it has abandoned its back-up plan to relocate the final round of 2026 to Imola in Italy if its planned events in Qatar and Abu Dhabi cannot go ahead.

Wolff said those questioning the wisdom of racing in the Middle East should pay less attention to media coverage and listen to those in charge of the series.

“For me, with our social media feed, we are always at risk of seeing what we want to see,” he told the BBC. “I believe you need to trust what the authorities say. You need to rely on the commercial rights holder, that’s F1, and the FIA as our governing body.”

However Wolff said no staff will be forced to attend the final two rounds and anyone choosing not to could hand an opportunity to a replacement.

“I strongly support that if someone doesn’t want to go to Qatar or Abu Dhabi, personally doesn’t want to, then I’m very fine with that,” he said. “We don’t want to oblige anyone. There’s not going to be any sanctions, or so on, on teams.

“If you don’t feel right about going there, then I have respect for that, and don’t go. It gives an opportunity maybe to someone else to be tested and to see how another person would perform in the future. That’s how I would approach it.”

Sports.title: Spotlight: FIA pulls F1 reporter’s pass over column calling Leclerc a ‘sneaky b*****d’ | Brief
Sports.content:
The Daily Mail says the FIA has barred its Formula 1 reporter from attending the final three rounds of the world championship as a media representative.

It quotes a letter sent yestreday by FIA general manager Alberto Villareal regarding an article the newspaper published about Ferrari driver Charles Leclerc , whom its F1 correspondent Jonathan McEvoy called a “sneaky little b*****d”.

“The FIA considers that your article falls short of the standards of professionalism expected of media representatives accredited to cover the FIA Formula One World Championship,” said Villareal, quoted by the newspaper.

“Accordingly, the FIA has decided to exercise its discretion under the 2026 FIA Formula One World Championship Accreditation Guidelines to withdraw your media accreditation for the remainder of the 2026 season, with immediate effect.”

Three rounds of the season remain in the USA, Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

Earlier this year Max Verstappen ordered the removal of another journalist, Giles Richards of The Guardian, from a Red Bull press conference. Verstappen was unhappy Richards asked him three months earlier whether he regretted colliding with George Russell during last year’s Abu Dhabi Grand Prix.

Update: The Daily Mail has now announced it will not cover the final three rounds of the championship

Sports.title: Grosjean admits his single-seater career is likely over after ending IndyCar season 19th | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Former Formula 1 driver Romain Grosjean, who survived a fireball crash six years ago in Bahrain, is preparing to call time on his single-seater racing career.

Grosjean raced in F1 between 2009 and 2020, then switched to IndyCar. He completed his fifth season in the series this year but the 40-year-old admits he is unlikely to return.

“The reality is, this is probably the end for me with single-seaters,” Grosjean told Racer.

Grosjean finished on the podium three times in his first season in IndyCar with Coyne, earning the attention of top team Andretti, who hired him for the 2022 season. The team replaced him after he finished 13th in the championship for two years running,

After spending one year at Juncos Hollinger, Grosjean lost his drive for 2025, but returned with Coyne this year. The season began promisingly when he reached the final round of qualifying in St Petersburg, but a string of finishes outside the top 10 followed.

The Coyne driver finished on the podium just once all year. He ended the season 19th in the standings ahead of just six other full-time drivers, including RLL’s Mick Schumacher, who replaced him at Haas in 2021.

Grosjean said it had been a “tough” season overall. “I had [a] few amazing moments. I got the chance to lead the Indy 500. I finished in the top 10. I ran [in] the top five most of the last 60 laps. Amazing! I got a podium in Markham, which was incredible with my ‘tractor.’

“But then we go to Milwaukee and Laguna Seca, and [at] Laguna Seca, I qualified dead last, almost. I know it’s one of my fastest tracks, so I’m like, ‘I don’t want that anymore.’ I’ve had enough of those moments where you just don’t have the tools to play.”

Grosjean was supposed to contest his final grand prix at Abu Dhabi in 2020. However the burns he suffered in his Bahrain crash forced him out early. His former team Haas gave him the opportunity to test one of its cars at Mugello last year.

Sports.title: Court of Appeal to hear Audi’s case over Tsunoda decision on November 25th | Formula 1
Sports.content:
The International Court of Appeal has set a date to hear Audi’s appeal over the Italian Grand Prix stewards’ decision regarding Yuki Tsunoda.

Audi is challenging the decision not to penalise Tsunoda, who finished the race in 10th position, for triggering an extra formation lap before the start of the race.

The ICA will hear the case on November 25th at the FIA’s headquarters in Paris.

Tsunoda, who substituted for Racing Bulls’ Liam Lawson at Monza, finished seven seconds ahead of Gabriel Bortoleto. Therefore the Audi driver could gain a point if Tsunoda is penalised.

Bortoleto previously said Audi’s case was “straightforward”.

F1’s sporting regulations state any driver who causes an extra formation lap must start the race from the pit lane and will receive a Stop-and-Go penalty if they fail to. As Tsunoda did not start from the pit lane, Audi believes he should receive a penalty.

The stewards ruled Tsunoda “was not the ’cause’ of the extra formation lap” and therefore did not have to start from the pit lane.

This is the second time this year the ICA has been asked to rule on a decision taken by the stewards at a grand prix. In September they reinstated two penalties which were originally issued to Pierre Gasly during the Monaco Grand Prix and later rescinded.

ICA hearing announcement

On 6th September 2026, at the end of the formation lap during the race restart following a red flag, the race director ordered an additional formation lap Following the race, the stewards investigated a potential breach of Article B5.9.4 of the 2026 FIA Formula 1 Sporting Regulations by Mr Yuki Tsunoda (driver of car number 22), which requires any driver who caused an extra formation lap to start from the end of the pit lane. Failure to do so, a Stop-and-Go penalty should be imposed on the driver. In decision number 69, the stewards decided to take no further action against Mr Yuki Tsunoda. On 9th September 2026, Audi Revolut F1 Team lodged an appeal against that decision, arguing that Mr Yuki Tsunoda had caused the extra formation lap and should therefore have received the prescribed Stop-and-Go penalty.

Sports.title: Racing Bulls keep Lawson and Lindblad as Tsolov gets Red Bull reserve role | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Racing Bulls has confirmed an unchanged driver line-up for the 2027 Formula 1 season.

Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad will continue to drive for the team next year.

The news ends speculation Red Bull’s second Formula 1 team would replace either of its drivers with Nikola Tsolov. The Red Bull junior driver lies second in the Formula 2 standings with four races remaining.

Shortly after Racing Bulls confirmed its driver line-up, Red Bull announced Tsolov as its reserve driver for 2027. Red Bull also announced Tsolov will be Racing Bulls’ reserve driver.

Racing Bulls is on course to score its best championship result under any of its identities, including its time competing as Minardi, before it was purchased by Red Bull at the end of 2005.

However Lawson’s future at the team came into doubt as Racing Bulls delayed its decision on its driver line-up for next year. Lawson made his F1 debut in 2023 and gained promotion to Red Bull in 2025 but the team dropped him after just two rounds. Lawson made a temporary return to Red Bull this year as a substitute for the injured Isack Hadjar.

During his time at Racing Bulls, Lawson has scored enough points to single-handedly put Racing Bulls fifth in the constructors’ championship. However he clashed with Red Bull driver Max Verstappen during a practice session in Mexico earlier this month, which his rival said was “not very smart behaviour” for a driver who was “fighting for [his] seat”. Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies denied his team would have any say in its junior squad’s driver line-up.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Racing Bulls team principal Alan Permane said Lawson and his rookie team mate Lindblad form “the best driver line-up for us, bringing a strong combination of experience and ambition”.

“Together, we have a solid foundation to build on the progress made this year, continue pushing ourselves forward and take the next step towards achieving our ambitions in 2027.”

Tsolov said he hopes to make the step up to F1 after next year. “My ambition is clear: I want to become an F1 driver,” he said. “Having the opportunity to spend next year preparing for that next step is incredibly exciting.

“I’m confident that with the team’s support and experience, I’ll have the best possible preparation to make sure I’m fully ready to take the next step onto the F1 grid when the time comes.”

Mekies said Red Bull has been highly impressed by Tsolov. “Nikola is an exceptionally talented young driver, and we have been hugely impressed by his development and performances over the past few years,” he said.

“To fight for the championship in F3 and now challenge for the F2 title in his first full season says a great deal about his ability and determination. What has impressed us just as much is his maturity, his approach to racing and his willingness to keep learning and improving.

“We have enormous belief in Nikola’s potential and see him as a driver with a very exciting future in F1. This appointment reflects our confidence in him and our commitment to his continued development. Our focus in 2027 will be on giving him the experience, tools and support he needs to be ready to race in F1 next.”

Sports.title: Pacheco Exposed: Fulghum Hands Prospect First Loss in Carson
Sports.content:
Darius “DFG” Fulghum handed Diego Pacheco his first professional loss by unanimous decision Saturday at Dignity Health Sports Park in Carson, California. Two judges scored the 12-round main event 115–112, and the third had it 114–113 for Fulghum. On the same Matchroom Boxing card, Anthony Olascuaga retained his WBO flyweight title with a unanimous decision over Yuberjen Martinez.

Darius Fulghum vs. Diego Pacheco

Fulghum (16–1–1, 13 KOs), the WBA’s No. 4 contender from Houston, took the WBC Silver and WBO International super middleweight titles from Pacheco (26–1, 19 KOs) in a bout that also served as a WBA final eliminator.

Fulghum opened a cut under Pacheco’s right eye with a left hand midway through the third. His left hand gave Pacheco trouble throughout the first four rounds. Pacheco did better in the fifth until Fulghum caught him on the chin with a right in the final minute. They traded clean right hands midway through the sixth, by which time Pacheco also had swelling around his left eye.

Referee Ray Corona deducted a point from Fulghum in the ninth for hitting behind the head. Fulghum drew blood from Pacheco’s nose with a right hand late in the round. He outworked Pacheco in the 11th and rocked him with a right to the chin midway through the 12th.

Anthony Olascuaga vs. Yuberjen Martinez

Anthony “La Princesa” Olascuaga (13–1, 9 KOs) retained his WBO flyweight title by unanimous decision over Colombia’s Yuberjen Martinez (7–1, 7 KOs), a two-time Olympian and 2016 silver medalist. The judges scored it 115–112 twice and 114–113.

Martinez landed several punches with Olascuaga against the ropes in the second before the champion hurt him with a counter. Olascuaga caught him with a counter right early in the third, but Martinez rallied over the third and fourth and shook the champion twice with uppercuts in the sixth.

Olascuaga hurt Martinez with a body shot in the seventh and went back downstairs with a combination in the eighth. The two traded in the tenth, when Olascuaga went down after their feet caught. Referee Thomas Taylor ruled it a slip. With the fight still close in the final round, Olascuaga dropped Martinez with a short right to the chin in the closing seconds.

Undercard Results

Charlie Sheehy def. Jose Matias Romero, 10 rounds. Sheehy (14–0, 8 KOs) won the WBA Continental North American lightweight title by decision over Romero (31–5–1, 11 KOs). Sheehy rocked Romero with a right in the second, trapped him on the ropes with a flurry in the eighth, and buckled his knees with a right uppercut late in the ninth. Romero was still returning right hands in the tenth. Gerard White was the referee.

David Adeleye def. Alexander Flores, UD 10. Adeleye (15–2, 13 KOs) won the WBA International heavyweight title by scores of 100–89 on all three cards. He dropped Flores (21–7–1, 13 KOs) with a jab midway through the third. Adeleye controlled the middle rounds and repeatedly used his forearm against Flores at close range. Flores landed a right hand in the final exchange. Ray Corona was the referee.

Zaquin Moses def. Manuel Lerma, TKO 4. The southpaw Moses (9–0, 5 KOs) controlled the first three rounds of the scheduled eight-round super featherweight bout. Lerma’s corner called a halt between rounds, and referee Thomas Taylor stopped it at 0:01 of the fourth. Lerma fell to 5–4–1.

Nishant Dev def. Sona Akale, KO 3. Dev (8–0, 6 KOs) dropped Akale (10–6, 5 KOs) with a right hand in the third round of their scheduled eight-round junior middleweight bout. Referee Robert Hoyle counted Akale out at 2:52.

Federico Pacheco Jr. def. Jack May, KO 5. Pacheco (12–0, 9 KOs) dropped May (11–2, 8 KOs) in the fourth and again in the fifth of their scheduled eight-round heavyweight fight. Referee Thomas Taylor waved it off at 2:59 of the fifth.

Frank Espinoza def. Abisai Torres Diaz, TKO 2. Espinoza (6–0, 6 KOs) dropped Torres Diaz (5–3–2, 1 KO) with a right to the chin in their scheduled six-round middleweight bout. Referee Gerard White stopped it at 0:50 of the second.

David Diamante was the ring announcer.

Sports.title: Darius Fulghum Upsets Diego Pacheco in Carson
Sports.content:
Darius Fulghum handed Diego Pacheco his first professional loss by taking away the space the taller man needed to box. Fulghum walked Pacheco down behind his jab and landed the cleaner punches inside to win a 12-round unanimous decision at Dignity Health Sports Park in Carson, California.

Two judges scored it 115–112, and the third had it 114–113 for Fulghum, who improved to 16–1–1. Pacheco fell to 26–1. Fulghum won the WBC Silver and WBO International super middleweight titles in a bout that also served as a WBA final eliminator.

Fulghum’s Jab Keeps Pacheco Backing Up

Pacheco landed a clean right hand and a body shot in a close second round, but Fulghum was already making him work at a distance he didn’t want. Fulghum pressed inside and landed left hands to the body and head as Pacheco tried to tie him up. In the third, a stiff Fulghum jab opened a cut below Pacheco’s right eye.

Fulghum kept Pacheco from getting set in the fourth, using feints and changing angles to get his jab through. He followed with one of his best rounds in the fifth, catching punches on his gloves and coming back with right hands that landed flush on Pacheco’s chin. Pacheco could still get through with his right hand, but he spent too much time backing up to build on those shots.

Pacheco had a better finish to the sixth, forcing Fulghum back after spending much of the round giving ground. That spell was brief. Fulghum was back on the front foot in the seventh, finding Pacheco’s swelling left eye with the jab. By the eighth, Fulghum was again staying close enough to keep Pacheco from extending his punches.

Fulghum Finishes Strong After Deduction

The closest the fight came to turning late was in the ninth. Referee Ray Corona deducted a point from Fulghum for punches to the back of the head, a call some observers questioned because Pacheco was dipping as the punches came in. Pacheco picked up his pace and won the round on the Boxing News 24 card, making it a 10–8 round and cutting Fulghum’s lead to two points.

Fulghum took the initiative back in the tenth. Pacheco’s face was swollen and his mouth was bleeding as Fulghum backed him up and landed cleanly. The same pattern held through the final two rounds. Pacheco never put together the sustained rally he needed, and the fight went the distance without a knockdown.

Boxing News 24 scored it 116–111 for Fulghum. The point deduction made the official result especially tight on the 114–113 card, but Fulghum gave the judges three strong rounds after it. Whenever Pacheco found a little room to punch, Fulghum went back to his jab and made him give it up again.

Sports.title: Diego Pacheco vs Darius Fulghum Live Results: Round-by-Round Updates
Sports.content:
WBO flyweight champion Anthony Olascuaga (13-1, 9 KOs) retained his title by unanimous decision over Yuberjen Martinez (7-1, 7 KOs). The scores were 115-112, 115-112, and 114-113. Olascuaga landed hard shots to the head and body early.

Martinez picked up the pace in the middle rounds and traded with the champion. Olascuaga hurt him with a body shot in the eighth, forcing him to back away. Martinez stayed on his feet in that round and kept firing back down the stretch. Olascuaga dropped him in the final seconds of the 12th.

Lightweight Charlie Sheehy (14-0, 8 KOs) defeated Jose Matias Romero (31-5-1, 11 KOs) by unanimous decision over 10 rounds to win the WBA Continental North America title. All three judges scored the fight 100-90 for Sheehy. The unbeaten Bay Area prospect controlled the distance with his jab and built a clear lead through six rounds.

Romero found more opportunities at mid-range as the fight became more competitive in the later rounds. Both fighters landed clean right hands to the head in the eighth. Romero took Sheehy’s best shots without going down and kept firing back through the final rounds. Sheehy’s steadier work earned him every round on all three cards on the Diego Pacheco vs. Darius Fulghum undercard.

David Adeleye (15-2, 13 KOs) defeated Alexander “The Great” Flores (21-7-1, 19 KOs) by unanimous decision over 10 rounds to win the WBA International heavyweight title. All three judges scored it 100-89 for Adeleye. The British heavyweight dropped Flores with a jab in the third round, sending him backward onto the canvas.

Flores outweighed Adeleye by more than 26 pounds but rarely came forward after the knockdown. Adeleye appeared to hurt his biceps midway through the fight but continued to press as Flores offered little in return. The win came in Adeleye’s first fight in the United States and his debut with Matchroom Boxing. It was his first victory since losing a unanimous decision to Filip Hrgovic.

Zaquin “Zaybop” Moses (9-0, 5 KOs) stopped Manuel “El Tomate” Valentine Lerma (5-4-1) when Lerma’s corner kept him on his stool after three rounds. The official time of the TKO was 0:01 of the fourth round. The junior lightweight bout was scheduled for eight rounds.

Moses controlled the fight from his southpaw stance and broke Lerma down with steady pressure over the first three rounds. Both fighters are 21, but Lerma spent much of the bout on the defensive. Moses, a Matchroom prospect from Newark, is the younger cousin of Shakur Stevenson. He spoke with the DAZN broadcast team after the win.

Nishant Dev (8-0, 6 KOs) dropped and stopped Sona “Slink Proper” Akale (10-6, 5 KOs) in the third round of a scheduled eight-round junior middleweight bout. The 6-foot-1 southpaw controlled the action against Akale, who gave up six inches in height. Dev scored the knockdown in the third and finished the fight before the end of the round.

Akale, 38, had previously faced Nico Ali Walsh. Dev, 25, was coming off a first-round stoppage of Cesar Diaz in July, when he scored three knockdowns. The unbeaten Matchroom prospect has now stopped six of his eight professional opponents. Dev discussed the win with the DAZN broadcast team after the fight.

Frank “Knuckles” Espinoza (6-0, 6 KOs) stopped Abisai “El Talisman” Torres Diaz (5-3-2, 1 KO) by second-round TKO in a scheduled six-round middleweight bout. Espinoza hurt Torres Diaz with a barrage of punches in the second. Referee Gerard White stepped in at 0:50 to end the fight.

Torres Diaz came in with more professional experience, but he couldn’t withstand the 21-year-old’s power and pressure. The Sacramento prospect has now stopped all six of his professional opponents. It was Espinoza’s second stoppage win on a Diego Pacheco card this year, following his July victory over Luis Caraballo Ramos. Espinoza celebrated the quick finish with fans at ringside.

Heavyweight Federico Pacheco Jr. (12-0, 9 KOs) stopped Jack “The Outlaw” May (11-2) with a left hook to the body in the fifth round of their scheduled eight-round bout. Pacheco took his time early against the taller, heavier May, who outweighed him by nearly 18 pounds. Both landed punches in a busier second round, with Pacheco catching May with a solid right hand.

Pacheco dropped May with an overhand left late in the fourth. May beat the count, but he was still hurt when the bell rang. Pacheco stalked him in the fifth and folded him with a left hook to the body for the second knockdown. May stayed down through the count.

Sports.title: Anthony Olascuaga Drops Yuberjen Martinez Late to Retain Title
Sports.content:
Anthony “Princesa” Olascuaga needed all 12 rounds and a knockdown in the final seconds to keep his WBO flyweight title Saturday night. Olascuaga (13-1, 9 KOs) beat Yuberjen Martinez (7-1, 7 KOs) by unanimous decision, with scores of 115-112, 115-112, and 114-113 in the co-feature of Diego Pacheco vs. Darius Fulghum at Dignity Health Sports Park in Carson, California.

The one-point card showed how much was still at stake when Martinez went down. The Colombian beat the count and made it to the final bell after spending much of the fight trading with the champion. It was Olascuaga’s sixth successful defense and his first professional bout in the Los Angeles area.

Olascuaga’s Body Work Slows Martinez

Olascuaga landed hard punches to the head and body early, but Martinez began letting his hands go more freely in the middle rounds. The challenger was willing to trade when Olascuaga came forward, and he landed enough of his own power shots to make the champion work for the rounds.

Martinez came into the fight with seven stoppages in seven professional outings, and he was still firing back after Olascuaga had carried him deep into his first world title fight.

The eighth was one of Olascuaga’s best rounds. A body shot hurt Martinez and sent him retreating, giving Olascuaga a chance to follow him and keep the pressure on. Martinez stayed upright and kept the fight competitive into the championship rounds, but the champion had found a target he could return to when the challenger stood his ground.

CompuBox counted 67 body shots among Olascuaga’s 203 landed punches, nearly a third of his total. Only eight landed power punches separated the two men over 12 rounds. That narrow margin spoke to how often Martinez answered back, while Olascuaga’s work downstairs gave him one of the clearest moments of the fight before the knockdown.

Olascuaga, 27, won the vacant WBO belt by knocking out Riku Kano in three rounds in July 2024 and had already beaten former champion Hiroto Kyoguchi by decision. The Carson bout was his Matchroom Boxing debut, with Teiken co-promoting him, and brought him home after a title run fought mostly in Japan.

Martinez, 35, brought two Olympic appearances and a silver medal from Rio to his first world title challenge. His seven professional wins had all ended inside the distance, including a WBO Latino title win, so this was his first time hearing the final bell as a pro. He was still in the fight when the 12th round was almost over.

Olascuaga sent him to the canvas with seconds left, and the narrowest card came back with just one point between them. Before the knockdown, Martinez was getting the better of Olascuaga and looked to be on his way to victory. The ending kind of shows you how important it is to stay dialed in. Martinez looked like the better fighter.

Sports.title: David Adeleye Drops Flores and Wins Wide Decision
Sports.content:
David Adeleye (15-2, 13 KOs) dropped Alexander Flores (21-7-1, 19 KOs) with a jab in the third round and won a unanimous decision to claim the WBA International heavyweight title on Saturday night in Carson, California. All three judges scored the 10-round fight 100-89 for Adeleye, and fans booed at the lack of action on the Diego Pacheco vs. Darius Fulghum undercard.

The knockdown was the clearest moment of a fight that rarely opened up. Adeleye caught Flores with a jab that sent him backward to the canvas, where he tried to prop himself up with an arm. Flores got up and made it through the round, but he seldom came forward after that, leaving Adeleye to do most of the pressing.

Adeleye Controls the Fight After the Knockdown

Flores weighed 266.8 pounds to Adeleye’s 240.5, a difference of more than 26 pounds. The heavier man spent long stretches on the defensive. With Flores rarely pressing forward, Adeleye could keep working at his own pace and bank rounds without having to fight his way out of much trouble.

Adeleye appeared to hurt his biceps midway through the bout and continued to press. Flores was still there at the final bell, but he offered little sustained offense to make the later rounds competitive. The crowd let the fighters hear its frustration as the bout went the full distance at Dignity Health Sports Park.

The three identical cards reflected how little the balance of the fight changed after the third. The judges gave Adeleye every round, with the knockdown accounting for the extra point in the margin. For Flores, the rounds lost early left him needing to take more chances in the second half. He rarely did, and Adeleye had little reason to abandon a pace that was winning him every round.

For Adeleye, the result was a return to the win column after his unanimous decision loss to Filip Hrgovic in August 2025. The former British heavyweight champion was making both his United States debut and his first appearance with Matchroom Boxing. Flores, a 36-year-old veteran from Southern California, entered with 19 knockouts, but he spent too much of the fight backing off to give himself many chances to use that power.

Adeleye had stopped 13 of the 14 opponents he had beaten entering Saturday. This time he had to go 10 rounds against a heavier man who was content to give ground after getting dropped. The third-round jab showed how quickly Adeleye could hurt Flores. The rest of the bout showed how rarely Flores was willing to risk getting caught again, even as the rounds slipped away and the boos came from the crowd.

Sports.title: Diego Pacheco Seeks To Outshine Darius Fulghum
Sports.content:
Diego Pacheco (26-0, 19 KOs) returns to the War Grounds in Carson, California to get one step closer to his aspirations of becoming a world champion. He’s delayed a world title fight, wanting to ensure he’s fully prepared for what is coming.

He turned down a title fight against Hamzah Sheeraz during a time he was changing trainers and did not want to commit to the fight under those conditions. He wanted to have more time and become acclimated to his new trainer, Buddy McGirt. In his first fight under Buddy in July of this year, a much-improved Diego stopped the very tough and gritty Immanuwel Aleem in the eleventh round. Pacheco controlled the range and utilized his jab well, connecting on 44.2 percent of his total punches (Compubox).

The Spit Bucket Podcast asked Pacheco about the recent changes Darius Fulghum (15-1-1, 13 KOs) has experienced, changing his training from Houston, Texas, and relocating to the Brickhouse Gym in North Hollywood under co-trainer Julian Chua. Diego said of Darius, “I’ll be honest with you I’ve never seen Darius before. I didn’t see not one fight, not one tape, you know so…I’m not worried about him. I’m worried about me and what I have to do and making sure I’m ready and I’m good money.”

This is surprising considering Fulghum is an opponent who can present many challenges within the ring. He gave Bektemir Melikuziev all he could handle, fighting him on the inside and giving him a bloody nose.

At Thursday’s Press Conference, Darius made it known that he believes team Pacheco made a mistake in choosing him as an opponent, as he is a dangerous opponent and believes he can surprise many and score the upset. Fulghum is a boxer who can box at range or on the inside. He has good size and power and does present stylistic challenges. Darius has his own world title aspirations and knows another loss will set him back a few steps. Although Diego himself may not have watched tape, his trainer Buddy would have done his homework and prepared him for what will be a tough match. If Pacheco can continue on the improvements from his previous fight, he can demonstrate improved skills, which will be boxing at range, utilizing the jab, and using a controlled attack that uses timing and precision to counter his opponents.

Fulghum struggled against David Stevens, demonstrating difficulties on the inside when given the right amount of pressure. Diego must exploit this weakness. He’s always performed well at the War Grounds and must shine bright tonight if he intends to gain that super championship title match he’s been seeking. Promoter Eddie Hearn would like to pin Pacheco against the WBA super middleweight champion Jaime Munguia in a Los Angeles super fight or against the WBC super middleweight titleholder Canelo Alvarez. Huge title fights are on the horizon for Diego, but he must first perform great against the very game Fulghum.

Sports.title: Viddal Riley vs. Seydi Coupe Full Card Results
Sports.content:
Viddal Riley retained his EBU European cruiserweight title with a unanimous decision over Seydi Coupe on Saturday, November 14, 2026, at OVO Arena Wembley in London. The judges scored the 12-round main event 116-112, 117-111 and 119-109 for Riley, who improved to 15-0 (7 KOs). Coupe suffered his first defeat, falling to 14-1.

Coupe rocked Riley with a right to the chin midway through the third. Riley found room for his left hook against Coupe’s jab in the sixth, and both men landed clean punches late in the seventh. By the eighth, Coupe had swelling under his right eye.

Riley used his movement and landed right hands to the chin in the ninth and tenth. He pressed for a stoppage in the final round, but Coupe made it to the bell with swelling under both eyes. Giuseppe Quartarone refereed the main event of the MF Pro card, which streamed on DAZN.

Wembley undercard results

Zelfa Barrett (36-3, 19 KOs) stopped Gavin Gwynne (19-5-2, 5 KOs) in the fifth round to win the vacant WBA Intercontinental lightweight title. Barrett dropped Gwynne with a right uppercut to the chin in the final minute of the round. Gwynne went down again and his corner threw in the towel. Bob Williams refereed.

Ben Marksby (15-0, 3 KOs) beat Yaser Al Ghena (16-1, 3 KOs) by unanimous decision over 12 rounds to win the Commonwealth and WBO European super lightweight titles. The scores were 114-113, 116-111 and 117-110. Marksby caught Al Ghena with a left hook late in the second and hurt him with a right in the sixth, prompting referee Howard Foster to give Al Ghena an eight-count. Al Ghena landed a good right in the ninth, but Marksby countered him as he pressed forward late and opened a cut above his left eye in the final round.

Dan Toward (9-1-1, 6 KOs) won a 10-round split decision over Jak Corrie (9-1-1, 6 KOs) for the vacant WBA Continental Europe super welterweight title in a rematch of their May draw. Two judges scored it 98-92 for Toward, while the third had it 96-94 for Corrie. Toward had the better of the early rounds and stunned Corrie with a combination midway through the eighth.

Tom Welland (12-1, 6 KOs) stopped Jack Dillingham (7-1-1, 2 KOs) at 2:50 of the seventh round to win the vacant English featherweight title. The fight was close through five rounds. Welland bloodied Dillingham’s nose in the sixth and dropped him with body shots late in the seventh, prompting referee Steve Gray to stop the bout.

Preliminary results

Frankie Stringer (12-0, 1 KO) outpointed Kurt Jackson (7-5-1) over eight rounds. Referee Rocky Israel scored it 80-72 for Stringer.

Kieran Molloy (16-0, 9 KOs) dropped Steve Suppan (17-6-1, 8 KOs) three times with right hooks in the first round. Suppan’s corner pulled him out before the fight resumed.

JP O’Meara (9-0, 1 KO) beat Jorge Luis Huerta Balleza (4-28, 1 KO) on points over six rounds. Referee Kieran McCann scored it 60-54 for O’Meara.

Arjon Basi (4-0, 1 KO) outpointed Fernando Joaquin Valdez (1-35-1) over four rounds. Basi rocked Valdez with a right uppercut to the chin in the final round.

Derrick Osadolor (2-1, 2 KOs) stopped Tomas Podlas (5-16-1, 5 KOs) at 1:49 of the second round. Osadolor dropped Podlas in the first and put him down again in the second, when referee Rocky Israel waved it off.

Sports.title: Zelfa Barrett Stops Gavin Gwynne in Fifth Round
Sports.content:
Zelfa Barrett won the vacant WBA Intercontinental lightweight title with a fifth-round stoppage of Gavin Gwynne on Saturday, November 14, at OVO Arena Wembley in London. Barrett dropped Gwynne with a hard uppercut in the fifth to finish a fight scheduled for 12 rounds, improving his record to 36-3 with 19 knockouts.

Gwynne (19-5-2) had five inches in height on Barrett and tried to make that size count by pressing forward and keeping his hands busy. Barrett had the quicker hands and landed the harder punches. The difference told as the fight wore on, with Barrett breaking down the Welshman before the uppercut brought the chief support bout to an early finish.

Barrett makes his power count at Wembley

Gwynne came in with a good win of his own. The former British, Commonwealth and European lightweight champion had beaten the previously unbeaten Khaleel Majid by majority decision in May. He tried to put Barrett under steady pressure at Wembley, but his work rate could only do so much once Barrett began landing the more damaging shots.

Barrett, 33, has now won five straight since losing to Jazza Dickens in 2025. The Manchester fighter had gone the distance with Owen Durnan in July. Against Gwynne, a more accomplished opponent coming off a notable win, he showed how quickly his power could settle a fight. Barrett and Gwynne showed each other respect after the stoppage.

The regional belt gives Barrett, a former world title challenger at super featherweight, a chance to move up the WBA rankings at lightweight. The performance was as important as the belt. A decisive stoppage over a former European champion gives Barrett a stronger case for a bigger fight at 135 pounds.

The bout was the chief support on the MF Pro card streamed on DAZN and headlined by Viddal Riley against Seydi Coupe for the European cruiserweight title.

Ghana News.title: SNARSA targets illegal mining reclamation, forest monitoring, and flood prevention through technology
Ghana News.content:
The School of Natural Resource Students’ Association (SNARSA) at the University of Energy and Natural Resources (UENR) seeks to deploy modern technology to help address illegal mining, forest degradation, flooding, and other environmental challenges confronting Ghana.

The association says it intends to use high-powered Geographic Information System (GIS) equipment and scientific research to identify environmental hotspots, monitor forest depletion, map disaster-prone communities and provide data to support government interventions.

SNARS President, Kingsford Nana Oduro Dickso, outlined the plans during theassociation's official launch at UENR in Fiapre, near Sunyani in the Bono Region, where executives were sworn in.

The launch was held under the theme: “Natural Resources Students at the Forefront of Sustaining the Environment: Partnering Government Against Environmental Backlashes.”

Mr Dickson said the association wanted to move beyond conventional student activities and position its members as technical partners in addressing the country's environmental challenges.

He explained that a major component of the association's vision was the establishment of a state-of-the-art Natural Resources Laboratory equipped with soil and water testing facilities, an Environmental Impact Assessment and reclamation centre, and advanced GIS technology.

The proposed laboratory, estimated to cost GH¢2.5 million, would provide facilities for assessing degraded lands, determining their suitability for restoration and generating scientific information to support environmental management.

According to him, the technology would also enable students to monitor changes in vegetation and identify areas vulnerable to environmental disasters.

He cited the Normalised Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), a remote-sensing technique used to assess vegetation health, as one of the tools the association intends to explore.

“We will be able to use our technology to determine the rate at which our forest is depleting and advise the Forestry Commission,” he said.

He added that GIS technology could help identify fire-prone areas and flood-risk zones, providing useful information to institutions such as the National Disaster Management Organisation (NADMO) and the Ghana National Fire Service.

Mr Dickson said flooding was not limited to major cities, pointing to poor sanitation and choked gutters in Sunyani as examples of local environmental challenges that required both technological and community-based interventions.

“If you pass through the streets of Sunyani, you see how gutters are being choked. So we are not only going to use technology; we will serve as volunteers to help these gutters and reshape our communities,” he stated.

The SNARSA president said the association was interested in supporting land reclamation initiatives by conducting soil assessments to determine the potential uses of restored lands.

He explained that scientific testing could help establish whether reclaimed sites were suitable for agricultural activities.

According to him, such interventions could help return degraded lands to productive use, create economic opportunities and support national development.

He said the association had drawn inspiration from ongoing land reclamation initiatives, including the Ghana Gold Board's Land Reclamation Project.

Mr Dickson stressed that the ultimate objective was to ensure natural resource students applied their academic knowledge to real-world problems rather than graduate and depend entirely on government for employment.

“Government should not invest so much in our education, pay our lecturers and their research allowances, and at the end of the day, we become no use to society,” he said.

He added that SNARSA intended to establish partnerships with government agencies, industry players and other relevant institutions to translate research and technology into practical environmental solutions.

Ghana News.title: Abibinsroma Foundation congratulates government on Solar Energy Tax exemption in 2027 budget
Ghana News.content:
Dr Cassiel Ato Forson, the Minister of Finance

Foundation says the decision is an important step towards climate action, affordable renewable energy and a Just Transition for all Ghanaians.

AbibiNsroma Foundation welcomes and congratulates the Government of Ghana on its decision, announced in the 2027 Budget Statement, to remove import duties and Value Added Tax (VAT) on solar panels and batteries.

We consider this an important step towards making renewable energy more affordable and accessible to Ghanaians, while demonstrating the country’s commitment to promoting clean energy and addressing the growing impacts of climate change.

For us at AbibiNsroma Foundation, this announcement goes beyond tax exemptions. It is an opportunity to accelerate Ghana’s transition to renewable energy, reduce dependence on fossil fuels and make clean energy a realistic option for more households, businesses and communities.

Ghana, like many other African countries, continues to experience the effects of climate change, including flooding, rising temperatures, coastal erosion and other environmental challenges. We believe that investing in renewable energy is part of the practical action needed to address these challenges and build a more sustainable future.

We are particularly encouraged by the potential of this decision to create opportunities for households, small businesses, farmers, women and young people who often face financial barriers to accessing clean energy.

As a Foundation, we believe that the energy transition must be fair, inclusive and beneficial to everyone, not just those who can afford it.

A STEP FORWARD IN GHANA’S CLIMATE ACTION

Expanding access to solar energy and battery storage can contribute significantly to Ghana’s climate ambitions. It can help reduce greenhouse gas emissions, improve energy security, support local businesses and create new opportunities in the growing green economy.

We also see this decision as an opportunity for Ghana to strengthen its contribution to the goals of the Paris Agreement and demonstrate leadership in Africa’s transition towards cleaner and more sustainable energy systems.

However, the success of this policy should not be measured only by the number of solar panels imported into the country. It should also be measured by how many ordinary Ghanaians, particularly those in underserved communities, can actually afford and benefit from solar energy.

A JUST TRANSITION MUST LEAVE NO ONE BEHIND

At AbibiNsroma Foundation, we strongly believe that climate action must put people and communities at the centre of decision-making.

Women, young people, low-income households, rural communities, coastal populations and small-scale businesses must not be left behind in Ghana’s transition to renewable energy.

We therefore encourage the Government to build on this announcement by introducing additional measures that will make the benefits of this policy reach ordinary people.

In particular, we encourage the Government to:

1. Make solar energy affordable: Promote accessible financing and credit facilities to help households and small businesses acquire solar systems.

2. Support women and young people: Create opportunities for women-led businesses and youth entrepreneurs in the renewable energy sector.

3. Invest in green jobs: Strengthen technical training and skills development in solar installation, maintenance and battery management.

4. Promote local industries: Encourage local assembly, manufacturing, innovation and investment in renewable energy technologies.

5. Reach vulnerable communities: Give particular attention to rural, coastal and underserved communities that face energy access challenges.

6. Protect the environment: Strengthen battery recycling, electronic waste management and responsible disposal systems to prevent future environmental pollution.

OUR CALL FOR EFFECTIVE IMPLEMENTATION

While welcoming this announcement, we encourage the Government to ensure that the tax exemptions are implemented effectively in 2027 and that the savings are reflected in the prices paid by consumers.

We also call on government agencies, civil society organisations, development partners, the private sector and community organisations to work together to ensure that this policy delivers real benefits for the people of Ghana.

We believe Ghana has an opportunity to make renewable energy a major driver of sustainable development, climate resilience, job creation and economic transformation.

Our message is simple: climate action must not only be about protecting the environment; it must also improve people’s lives.

AbibiNsroma Foundation remains committed to working with government, civil society, development partners and communities to advance climate justice, renewable energy advocacy and a Just Transition in Ghana and across Africa.

We congratulate the Government on this policy announcement and look forward to seeing it translated into practical benefits for all Ghanaians.

ABOUT ABIBINSROMA FOUNDATION

AbibiNsroma Foundation is a Ghana-based organisation committed to environmental sustainability, climate justice, community development and inclusive sustainable development. The Foundation works to promote locally led climate action, strengthen community participation in environmental decision-making and advocate for policies that respond to the needs and priorities of vulnerable communities in Ghana and across Africa.

Ghana News.title: El Niño: West African governments urged to prepare for food and health threats
Ghana News.content:
West African governments have been urged to strengthen preparations for the potential impacts of the 2026–2027 El Niño event, amid concerns that changing rainfall patterns and rising temperatures could put food production, water supplies and public health under pressure.

Climate and public-health specialists say delayed rainfall and prolonged dry spells could disrupt farming activities, particularly among farmers who depend on rain-fed agriculture and have limited access to irrigation.

The warnings come as countries across the region are being encouraged to strengthen early-warning systems, food reserves and emergency health preparedness before the potential impacts materialise.

Speaking at a virtual expert discussion organised by the West African Journalists for Environment, Science, Health and Agriculture (WAJESHA), climate scientist Dr Caleb Mensah warned that the interval between early rainfall events could be long enough to affect crop establishment.

“The interval between the first and second rainfall events could extend to two or three weeks,” said Dr Mensah, a Senior Lecturer at the University of Energy and Natural Resources (UENR).

Such a gap could create difficulties for farmers who plant in response to the first rains, particularly if subsequent rainfall is insufficient to support crop growth.

Dr Mensah said farmers could struggle to achieve their usual production levels if rainfall is delayed or inadequate while temperatures remain high.

The consequences could extend beyond individual farms, putting additional pressure on food availability and the movement of agricultural produce to markets.

Farmers' access to drought-resistant seeds remains a concern

Although agricultural research institutions have developed crop varieties capable of tolerating drought conditions for longer periods, Dr Mensah said access remained an important consideration.

He pointed to drought-tolerant seed varieties developed by the Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), but questioned how widely farmers could obtain them.

“The CSIR has developed seed varieties that can withstand drought for longer periods. The question is how many farmers will have access to these seeds,” he said.

He also raised concerns about agricultural pests, including termites, army ants and other insects, which may thrive under high-temperature and low-water conditions.

Agricultural experts, he said, would need to identify appropriate control measures and ensure farmers had the resources to respond.

The potential consequences of reduced rainfall could also affect water resources and electricity generation.

Dr Mensah said lower-than-expected rainfall could affect hydrological systems, including water inflows into the Volta and Lower Volta systems.

For Ghana, where hydroelectricity is an important part of the energy mix, reduced inflows could create additional pressure on electricity generation.

However, he stressed that the scale of the impact would depend partly on the preparedness measures taken by governments and other stakeholders.

“The extent of the impact will depend on the measures we put in place. That is why our efforts must begin now,” he said.

WHO warns countries are not fully prepared

Beyond agriculture and water, health specialists are warning that climate-related hazards could place additional demands on already vulnerable health systems.

Dr Patrick Otim, Programme Area Manager for Emergency Response at the World Health Organization's Regional Office for Africa, described El Niño as a risk modifier, explaining that its health consequences would depend on the hazards experienced, existing vulnerabilities and the capacity of health systems to respond.

Potential health concerns include heat-related illnesses, malnutrition linked to food insecurity, and waterborne, foodborne and vector-borne diseases.

Floods and landslides could also cause injuries and deaths, damage health facilities and interrupt access to essential healthcare.

Dr Otim said the WHO had been issuing early-warning alerts to member states and encouraging governments to take appropriate preparedness measures.

He disclosed that the organisation had classified the event at Grade 3 under its internal three-level emergency grading system, the highest level.

The WHO was also supporting 18 countries with readiness assessments to identify gaps in their emergency response capacities.

“I do not think any country in West Africa is fully prepared to deal with this,” Dr Otim said.

He identified inadequate food storage and limited national food reserves as major preparedness concerns.

According to him, governments need to consider how to strengthen food reserves and provide basic social support to vulnerable populations who could face severe food insecurity following crop failure.

He called for a coordinated, whole-of-government response involving the health, agriculture, water and disaster-management sectors.

Such preparations, he said, should include contingency plans, risk maps, identification of high-risk communities and the pre-positioning of essential supplies before emergencies occur.

He also urged countries to strengthen health alerts, nutrition screening and disease surveillance while ensuring that essential health services remain operational.

Meningitis surveillance among health priorities

Dry conditions could also increase concerns about meningitis, particularly in countries within Africa's meningitis belt.

Dr Otim noted that Ghana lies within the meningitis belt and stressed the importance of effective surveillance to identify suspected cases, confirm the bacteria responsible and guide an appropriate response, including vaccination where necessary.

“Effective surveillance is essential for detecting the first cases and enabling a timely response,” he said.

He urged people experiencing symptoms such as headaches, neck pain or neck stiffness to seek medical attention promptly for assessment and confirmation.

The WHO official also highlighted the need to protect communities with limited access to healthcare.

He said risk assessments and vulnerability mapping should help authorities identify populations requiring additional support, including displaced people, residents of peri-urban communities and people living in urban settlements with inadequate housing.

Mobile health services, outreach programmes and temporary clinics could help bring healthcare closer to vulnerable populations, particularly in areas expected to face climate-related hazards.

However, he stressed that such interventions would require advance planning, adequate resources, equipment and trained personnel.

Journalists urged to turn climate warnings into practical information

The experts also highlighted the role of the media in ensuring that early warnings translate into practical action at community level.

Dr Otim said journalists needed to move beyond technical explanations of climate phenomena and communicate what potential risks could mean for people's everyday lives.

He encouraged the use of local languages where appropriate and called for reporting that provides practical guidance on safe water, mosquito nets, protection from heat, access to medical care and emergency preparedness.

“The next step is to take this information to communities and make it local and actionable,” he said.

However, he cautioned against sensational reporting that could create unnecessary public anxiety.

“It is important to inform the public without creating panic. Informing without alarming is key,” Dr Otim said.

The discussion was held during the third edition of WAJESHA's Expert Knowledge Exchange Series, under the theme El Niño 2026–2027: Understanding Its Implications for Ghana and West Africa.

The initiative brings journalists and specialists together to strengthen public understanding and improve reporting on environmental, climate, science, health and agricultural issues.

Ghana News.title: Ahmed Ibrahim calls for stronger government-academia partnership to tackle environmental challenges
Ghana News.content:
The Minister for Works, Housing and Water Resources, Ahmed Ibrahim, has called for stronger collaboration between government, universities, industry and civil society to address Ghana’s growing environmental challenges.

He said tackling issues such as climate change, illegal mining, deforestation, land degradation, pollution, flooding and water resource depletion requires collective action, with academia and the youth playing critical roles.

Speaking at the official launch of the School of Natural Resources Students’ Association (SNARSA) at the University of Energy and Natural Resources (UENR) in Fiapre, near Sunyani in the Bono Region, the Minister urged students to use their knowledge and expertise to develop practical solutions to the country’s environmental problems.

The launch was held under the theme: “Natural Resources Students at the Forefront of Sustaining the Environment: Partnering Government Against Environmental Backlashes.”

Mr Ibrahim described the theme as timely, given the increasing environmental pressures confronting Ghana and other parts of the world.

“As future environmental scientists, resource managers, policymakers, planners and development practitioners, you have a critical role to play in shaping a more sustainable future,” he told the students.

He stressed that sustainable national development could not be achieved without protecting the country's natural resource base, noting that economic growth, public health, food security, energy production and urban development were all closely linked to responsible resource management.

The Minister also raised concerns about Ghana’s water security, revealing that the country’s per capita water availability is estimated at 1,509 cubic metres annually, below the globally accepted benchmark of 1,700 cubic metres per person.

He said the situation underscored the need to prioritise water security through sustainable management, protection and equitable distribution of water resources.

Mr Ibrahim indicated that the government remained committed to investing in water supply infrastructure, rural water systems and urban water expansion initiatives to improve access to safe and affordable water.

However, he cautioned that government interventions alone would not be enough to protect the country's water bodies and ecosystems.

“Safeguarding our rivers, wetlands, and watersheds requires responsible behaviour from all stakeholders,” he said, urging students to become ambassadors for water conservation and environmental stewardship.

The Minister also called for increased investment in climate-resilient systems capable of withstanding floods, droughts and other environmental shocks.

He said roads, housing, drainage systems, water supply networks and sanitation facilities were essential to national development, adding that infrastructure planning must increasingly respond to the effects of climate change.

“Safe and sustainable infrastructure not only protects lives and property but also promotes economic growth, productivity and social inclusion,” he stated.

Mr Ibrahim further highlighted the importance of responsible natural resource management, warning that deforestation, environmental degradation and unsustainable resource extraction posed significant threats to Ghana's development.

He identified universities, particularly UENR, as important partners in addressing these challenges through research, innovation and capacity building.

The Minister therefore encouraged SNARSA members to embrace interdisciplinary thinking, scientific inquiry and community engagement to generate practical solutions.

He assured the university community that the Ministry was ready to deepen strategic partnerships with academic institutions and student organisations to promote knowledge generation, innovation and evidence-based policymaking.

“The Ministry stands ready to engage with and support initiatives that promote sustainable natural resource management, environmental protection and the development of practical solutions to national challenges,” he said.

He congratulated the leadership and members of SNARSA on the launch, expressing optimism that the association would contribute meaningfully to environmental sustainability and responsible resource management in Ghana.

Ghana News.title: Senyo Hosi commends gov’t over NACOC expansion, warns of growing synthetic drug threat
Ghana News.content:
Convener of the OneGhana Movement and Trustee of the Ghana Coalition Against Galamsey, Senyo Hosi, has commended the government for strengthening the operational capacity and nationwide presence of the Narcotics Control Commission (NACOC).

He says the Commission has made significant progress in expanding its operations, although it remains confronted with resource constraints in the fight against drug trafficking.

Speaking on JoyNews’ Newsfile on Saturday, November 14, Mr Hosi said NACOC’s presence had grown from about eight districts before the current government assumed office to 81 districts.

His comments follow the arrest of a 43-year-old freight forwarder in Tema in connection with the seizure of approximately 2.6 tonnes of cocaine in Valencia, Spain, in August 2026.

The suspect, who operates a freight forwarding business at Community 1 in Tema, was arrested by NACOC officers at about 3 pm on Wednesday, November 11, after investigations linked him to the processing of customs documentation for the shipment intercepted by Spanish authorities.

Reacting to the development, Mr Hosi described drug trafficking as a serious national concern but said the government deserved recognition for efforts to improve NACOC’s capacity.

“The drug matter is a serious matter. I will commend the government; there’ve been a lot of progress they have made,” he said.

He recalled that, before the current administration took office, NACOC had a limited presence across the country and struggled with inadequate resources to carry out its mandate.

Drawing on his previous engagements with the Commission, Mr Hosi said he had encountered NACOC officers operating under difficult conditions, including personnel stationed at border points without adequate facilities.

He said the situation was so challenging that, during the tenure of former NACOC leadership, efforts were made to mobilise support from private individuals and stakeholders to provide basic operational equipment.

According to him, the Commission had struggled to acquire essential tools, including sniffer dogs, with each dog costing between €10,000 and €11,000.

He also raised concerns about the lack of adequate drug-detection equipment, noting that officers had often relied heavily on intelligence and cooperation with other agencies and stakeholders to pursue suspected drug traffickers.

“They were highly under-resourced, but you will see that there is a certain effort trying to build that,” he said.

Mr Hosi’s remarks highlight the importance of sustained investment in NACOC’s personnel, logistics and technology to strengthen Ghana’s ability to detect and disrupt international drug trafficking networks.

Beyond cocaine seizures, Mr Hosi warned that Ghana’s drug-control efforts must address the growing threat posed by synthetic substances.

He argued that the national conversation on narcotics should not be limited to cocaine, insisting that synthetic drugs constituted an even bigger concern requiring urgent attention.

“The drug element should not be a cocaine problem alone; the bigger problem we have are with the synthetics,” he cautioned.
