Prosecutors hold Iran’s agents responsible for the assaults.

World.title: Ukraine’s Starshield Access Is Being Restricted Again, Zelensky Says
World.content:
Ukrainian military operations were disrupted again this week along the front lines because of restrictions on Starshield, the satellite internet system developed by Elon Musk’s SpaceX and controlled by the U.S. government, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Friday.

Mr. Zelensky told reporters that speed limits of about 100 miles per hour were being enforced for Ukrainian devices connected to the system. It would be the second time in recent weeks that Ukraine’s Starshield connectivity had been throttled. The previous restrictions caused Ukrainian drones to lose their connection to the system if they flew above certain speeds.

Mr. Zelensky said that the latest speed limits took effect on Monday and were being enforced over Russian-occupied territories, not over all of Ukraine. That hurts Ukraine’s ability to strike Russian troops with drones in those territories.

Imposing restrictions on occupied territories is “very dangerous, because it already has political implications,” Mr. Zelensky said. “If you impose restrictions there, you are already partially recognizing the temporarily occupied territories as not ours,” he added.

World.title: Trump’s Oil Grab in Venezuela Is Testing the Country’s National Identity
World.content:
Like generations before him, Leonardo Silva grew up steeped in beliefs about the extraordinarily abundant resource that made Venezuela special. All the oil under their feet was theirs, they felt. Virtually free gasoline was a birthright. To be born atop this bounty was like winning the lottery.

Mr. Silva, 38, said his generation viewed oil as a cornerstone of the country’s national identity, when a booming economy allowed Venezuela to occupy a privileged tier in the global order. His children, he said, have a far less rosy view.

“To them oil isn’t important, it’s secondary,” said Mr. Silva, who works at a foundation in Caracas helping people with disabilities. “They don’t have that culture of us being a rich country. They just know that if you don’t work, you don’t eat.”

Oil has shaped Venezuela to an extent that is rare outside the Middle East for more than a century, becoming a defining feature of the social fabric like baseball, beauty pageants or the veneration of the liberation hero Simón Bolívar.

World.title: South Sudan’s National Election, Its First, Will Be Delayed
World.content:
The upcoming election was supposed to underwrite that agreement. But the peace deal has unraveled since March 2025, when Mr. Machar was placed under house arrest in the capital, Juba, and charged with treason. In recent months, the government has replaced opposition lawmakers with its own supporters and dissolved the unity government.

With Mr. Machar effectively sidelined, there are no credible challengers to Mr. Kiir, who is widely expected to win the presidential election. He has a broad national following, and his party controls state institutions and the news media.

The election faces stark logistical challenges. Civil servants have not been paid in more than a year, and parts of the country are controlled by armed groups, including Mr. Machar’s forces. Thousands of people have died in fighting and attacks on civilians. In March, more than 200 people were killed in a massacre in Unity State near the border with Sudan, according to human rights groups.

World.title: US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says
World.content:
US negotiators have touted the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for Nato membership, Volodymyr Zelensky has said.

The US has not confirmed the Ukrainian president's comments. A US official told the BBC "many ideas continue to be discussed but any final deal will have to be agreed to by both parties".

Zelensky's remarks came after US envoys met him and Russian President Vladimir Putin as part of US efforts to end the war between their two countries.

Kyiv has long sought membership of the military alliance, but this has previously been opposed by the US and others, while Russia has said another Nato member on its border was unacceptable.

Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 and currently controls most of the industrial Donbas region. Zelensky has consistently said Ukraine was unwilling to give up sovereign territory.

"The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," Zelensky said in remarks released by his office on Saturday.

He went on to say that if he received a specific proposal that contained security guarantees, no constraints on Ukraine's military and funds to rebuild the country, he would put it to a referendum.

US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff travelled to the Irish capital, Dublin, on Thursday to meet Zelensky, after a round of talks with Putin in Moscow.

Comments by both Putin and Kremlin officials suggest that Russia's position on the war has not shifted. It has previously proposed limits on the size of Ukraine's military, territorial concessions and Kyiv's guaranteed neutrality as conditions of a peace deal.

Ukraine has rejected these suggestions, arguing that such constraints would hamper its ability to stave off any future invasion.

World.title: Copper wire upgrade behind US flight suspension, transport secretary says
World.content:
A nationwide US ground stop that caused thousands of flight cancellations and prompted travel chaos was caused by a technical issue following a copper wire upgrade, the transport secretary has said.

Sean Duffy told a news conference that the government was trying to find out whether the problem that led to air traffic controllers suspending take-offs for four hours on Friday had been caused by "incompetence" on the part of the company doing the upgrades or faulty equipment.

Though the ground stop was lifted on Friday evening, it had a knock-on effect on air travel on Saturday as airlines attempted to clear a backlog of flights.

Officials including Duffy had previously attributed the issue to outdated equipment.

Maintenance on US air traffic control systems was being carried out to switch from copper wire to fibre-optic cable by a contractor called L3Harris, a technology provider, Duffy said.

The US had "an incredibly old telecommunications system", he said, adding: "It was such an old wire that it was being discontinued."

World.title: Pope Leo speaks of community 'suffering' on visit to remote Andes town
World.content:
Cajamarca has lost the highest number of people to internal migration, with 729,000 people born there now living elsewhere in Peru.

In his sermon, Pope Leo thanked those who had made the journey to him and emphasised the importance of never losing heart, despite life's difficulties.

Santa Cruz is within the Diocese of Chiclayo, where Pope Leo served as bishop from 2015 to 2023. During his tenure, he visited Santa Cruz several times a year to minister to the town's rural population.

On Saturday he returned by helicopter, where he was greeted by singing and cheering. He later did a tour in a popemobile, where he waved to people who had travelled from across the region to see him.

Speaking at a local parish on Saturday, the Pope said he felt "joy" at being able to visit the small town once again.

"It is like a very big dream that the Lord has allowed this servant to come here," he said.

Rev. Kevin Noriega, who was ordained in 2018 by the then-bishop, told Reuters the visit had brought "enormous hope and emotion" to Santa Cruz.

He said: "People are eager to experience this Holy Mass ... because after so much time they will be able to see their bishop - 'Father Robert,' as they used to call him - now as the Holy Father."

World.title: Judge temporarily blocks Trump from closing Washington DC golf course for renovation
World.content:
A federal judge has temporarily blocked the US government's closure of a historic golf course and park in Washington DC.

US District Judge Ana Reyes has been overseeing a months-long challenge to the president's plans for East Potomac Golf Links, which he said would be closed from 15 November for extensive renovations.

Reyes has said Donald Trump cannot close the park or its golf course, but added that his administration was not required to actively manage either.

Trump, an avid golfer, has said his plans to upgrade the 106-year-old course will create "one of the Best and Most Spectacular Golf Courses anywhere in the World". The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.

Declaring the current course "Trash Island", he announced in October it would be renovated over 15 months to create a space that "will be open to the Public while, at the same time, designed to the Highest Level of Golf and able to hold World Class Tournaments" - despite the ongoing litigation.

In a 30-page decision issued on Saturday, Reyes said the Trump administration's justifications for the proposed course closures were pretextual, and that the government violated at least two federal laws "to meet an arbitrary deadline."

"The Government proposes to close a historic park, daily enjoyed by Washingtonians of all stripes, indefinitely," Reyes wrote.

She said the closure "runs counter to the public interest in utilising national parkland", adding that the government had not "plausibly identified any harm it would suffer from a temporary restraining order that preserves the status quo pending further proceedings".

Her order will last until the 28 November.

World.title: Italy fines Meta €805m over accessing users' photos
World.content:
Italian regulators have fined social media giant Meta â¬805m (Â£670m; $887m) for accessing Android users' photos without their specific consent.

Italy's Data Protection Authority said Meta did not properly inform about 20 million smartphone users that it had access to their photos and videos via a feature of the Facebook app.

It has given Meta 60 days to disable the feature by default and seek users' consent separately.

The fine is among the largest an Italian authority has ever imposed on a tech giant.

A Meta spokesperson told the BBC that it planned to appeal.

The charge is related to a feature which suggests photos and videos from a user's phone gallery as ideas for posts.

Facebook requested access to users' photo galleries through a single app-wide authorisation. According to the Italian regulator, a preceding notice did not make clear that this would also allow Facebook to generate suggestions based on photos in their gallery.

The regulator said it took into account "the high number of people affected" and the fact it is "still ongoing for those who have not updated the app and for those who have already given their consent to the system".

It also cited "Meta's lack of co-operation".

Meta told the BBC: "We strongly disagree with the [regulator's] assessment of the facts, its application of the law, and the disproportionate level of the fine.

"This is a straightforward feature which helps people post photos and videos to Facebook. People must give permission on their device before it can operate, and they can change this permission at any time via their settings."

Last month, Meta, which is also behind Instagram and WhatsApp, was hit with its largest fine ever for its business practices.

A US judge in New Mexico ordered the company to pay $25bn (Â£18.6bn) after it found that found it had spent years lying to the public about how it handled Facebook user data.

World.title: 'Can you believe it?': SpaceX catches part of its Starship rocket on return to Earth
World.content:
SpaceX has successfully caught the top part of its huge Starship rocket on its return to Earth for the first time.

"Can you believe it?," a commentator said as large crowds cheered at the launch site in Texas.

The company had hoped to catch both the bottom and upper stages of the rocket using mechanical arms - nicknamed chopsticks - on its launch tower.

But the first catch of the rocket's booster was aborted a few minutes after the launch on Friday. The booster was diverted to the ocean, bursting into flames just above the sea.

The top part, known as the Ship, returned to Earth a few minutes behind schedule at around 15:20 local time (21:20 GMT) on Saturday, in the first-ever successful catch attempt.

World.title: Philippines wins first Eurovision Song Contest Asia
World.content:
The Philippines have won the very first Eurovision Song Contest Asia, hosted in Bangkok and with 11 countries vying for the title.

Nineteen-year-old singer Carmelle was always a front runner with her women's empowerment anthem Sobra-Sobra, complete with its catchy rap section.

She earned 211 points in total - 93 from the jury and 118 from the public vote - ahead of Thailand's MANG x DAOU in second place with 170 points.

There was a joyous atmosphere at the One Bangkok Arena as the crowd cheered the contestants and celebrated the popular winner.

World.title: Sotheby's auction of $180m Van Gogh challenged over claims it was 'sold under duress'
World.content:
Auction house Sotheby's says it is working to resolve a dispute over the intended sale of a painting by Vincent van Gogh.

ChÃ¢taigniers en Fleurs, which carries an estimate of $180m (Â£136m), is due to go under the hammer in New York on Wednesday.

But representatives acting for heirs of the Fischer family - earlier German owners of the work - say it may have been sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis.

Sotheby's say its own "extensive research" has not established this, but say they will work with the family to try and reach a solution.

"Sotheby's takes provenance and restitution matters extremely seriously and has undertaken extensive research into the ownership history of ChÃ¢taigniers en fleurs," Sotheby's told the BBC in a statement.

"We are aware of the concerns recently raised by representatives of the Fischer heirs and have been in dialogue with them regarding the painting's history.

"While our research to date has not established that the painting was sold under duress, we recognize the importance of engaging thoughtfully and constructively with the family and are committed to working toward a mutually satisfactory resolution."

The painting - whose name translates as Blossoming Chestnut Trees - is being sold as part of a set called the Blaquier-Arrieta Collection.

Sotheby's website details the provenance of the oil painting and how it has researched the artwork changing hands since 1890.

It says Samuel Fischer - a famous German publisher - acquired it 1909 before it was passed down in his family after his death in 1934.

The painting was deposited with Paul Cassirer in Amsterdam in 1932 or 1933 before it went to Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in Paris in 1936, Sotherby's says.

Four other owners have had it since before it was put up for auction this year.

Fischer family heirs have instructed a lawyer who, according to the New York Times, external, has written to Sotherby's.

He is said to have told the auction house the painting was sold in Amsterdam before World War Two because of financial losses the Fischer family's publishing company suffered under the Nazis.

The BBC has contacted the lawyer for comment.

World.title: SPECIAL REPORT: 2027 polls and rising tide of violence, hate speech
World.content:
On Thursday, 12 November, thugs attacked supporters of the opposition Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) during a town hall meeting in Oregun area of Ikeja, Lagos State, leaving several people injured and propertiesr destroyed, including vehicles belonging to party members.

The hoodlums, armed with cutlasses and stones, invaded the venue of the meeting, disrupted it and chased away the party’s supporters.

Before the attack, many of the supporters, dressed in the party’s colours, were dancing and singing at the gathering. But the disruption triggered panic as party supporters scampered for safety. Police officers later arrived at the scene to restore order and defuse the tension.

Although Peter Obi, the NDC presidential candidate, and his running mate, Rabiu Kwankwaso, a former governor of Kano State, were not at the venue when the incident occurred, some suggest they were the target of the attack, not necessarily to harm them but to frustrate their campaign efforts.

Mr Obi, a former governor of Anambra State, is seeking the presidency for the second time. He first ran for the nation’s highest political office in 2023 under the Labour Party, finishing third in the election. In that election, he won Lagos State, a stronghold of the All Progressives Congress (APC) and its candidate, Bola Tinubu, with 582,354 votes.

Earlier in 2019, the former governor had paired with former Vice President Atiku Abubakar on the ticket of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP). Atiku has since defected to the African Democratic Congress (ADC), where he is running for president in the 2027 election, while Mr Obi left the LP for the ADC and subsequently for the NDC.

Both Messrs Atiku and Obi are among the 18 presidential candidates cleared by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) for the 16 January 2027 election.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Some of the other presidential hopefuls include President Bola Tinubu of the All Progressives Congress (APC), who is seeking a second term, Oyo State Governor Seyi Makinde of the Allied Peoples Movement (APM), Sandy Onor (PDP), Omoyele Sowore (AAC), former Cross River Governor Donald Duke (PRP), and Adewole Adebayo (SDP).

The commission also cleared governorship candidates for 28 of the nation’s 36 states where governorship elections will be taking place on 6 February 2027. It also approved candidates for the National Assembly and State Houses of Assembly elections.

Consequently, in line with the election timetable and schedule of activities for the 2027 polls, it mandated the candidates for the elections to commence campaigns.

While the presidential and National Assembly candidates began their campaigns on 19 August, those of the governorship and State Houses of Assembly started a month later.

However, since the campaigns commenced, the nation has witnessed violent attacks launched on campaign rallies, town hall meetings and other political events organised by parties in their quest for the mandate of the people.

In the build-up to the polls, political activities across the country are increasingly being accompanied by reports of violence, intimidation and threats.

Campaign activities associated with presidential candidates and opposition parties have encountered security challenges in different parts of the country, including attacks on convoys, disruptions of political gatherings and confrontations involving party supporters.

In some instances, presidential candidates have alleged that their lives or those of their supporters were endangered. In others, political gatherings have been disrupted, vehicles damaged and participants injured or killed.

Other incidents

On 13 September, unknown gunmen attacked and disrupted a state-wide monthly ward meeting of the NDC in Ihuani Awkunanaw, Enugu State, the hometown of the party’s governorship candidate, Christian Ohaa. At least eight party members were injured, while several party materials, canopies and plastic chairs at the venue were destroyed.

Sampson Ukwu, media aide to the NDC governorship candidate, identified the victims as Onovo Donald Ekene, Ngene Godwin Madueke, Ogbodo Gloria, Onovo Victor, Maduabuchi Ugwu, Nnaemeka Nelson, Chinonso Nwagbara and Obinna Daniel Owo.

On 18 September, suspected political thugs disrupted a mobilisation rally involving supporters of Mr Obi and his running mate, Mr Kwankwaso, in Warri, Delta State.

Esther Umoh, a photographer associated with Mr Obi, alleged that the attackers opened fire on members of the campaign team, including the entourage of the party’s Delta State governorship candidate.

Although the circumstances surrounding the incident were not independently established, the police did not deny that an attack occurred.

The incident raised concerns about the security arrangements for opposition campaign activities and the ability of political candidates to move freely during electioneering.

In a similar incident on 10 October, gunmen invaded an NDC political gathering in Afa, Udi Local Government Area of Enugu State, killing a young man identified as Ifeanyi Nwolie.

After the incident, Mr Obi, the party’s presidential candidate, pledged financial support to the mother of the slain supporter.

On 30 October, the presidential candidate of the African Action Congress (AAC), Omoyele Sowore, alleged that he and members of his team were attacked in Ado-Ekiti, Ekiti State.

The incident occurred at Tawakalitu Restaurant in the Dalimore area of the capital city, after Mr Sowore had attended an interview at MIDAS FM.

The presidential hopeful alleged that armed men attacked him and members of his team with sticks and machetes. He also reported that communication devices were stolen, vehicle tyres were slashed and other property was damaged.

Mr Sowore further described the incident as an assassination attempt and demanded an independent investigation. But the police characterised the incident as an altercation and announced the arrest of 11 suspects.

The activist cum politician questioned the police’s account and demanded that relevant electronic evidence, including CCTV footage, be preserved.

Nevertheless, the suspects were arraigned on several charges, including conspiracy and assault occasioning harm.

They were granted bail, while the case was adjourned until 4 December.

The disagreement between the candidate and the police over the characterisation of the incident raises concerns about the transparency and credibility of investigations into attacks involving political figures.

While the arrests represent a step in the investigation, the evidence presented in court and the outcome of the proceedings will be important in establishing what happened and who was responsible.

Up North, in Sokoto State, another violent incident was reportedly recorded on 31 October. The governorship candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Manir Dan’iya, was attacked near the city’s airport.

The party alleged that personnel of the Sokoto Marshal and the state Community Guard blocked his convoy, fired gunshots and damaged vehicles.

It also alleged that two State Security Service (SSS) operatives accompanying the candidate were detained during the incident.

But the Sokoto State APC chairman, Haruna Adiya, denied reports of the attack, describing them as fabricated claims intended to discredit the state government run by the party.

According to Mr Adiya, the security deployment was connected to preparations for a traditional title conferment ceremony and was not intended to obstruct the ADC’s political activities.

However, the state police command confirmed it was aware of the incident and that it had initiated investigations. On its part, apart from confirming the attack, the SSS said its operatives evacuated Mr Dan’iya to safety and that two of its personnel were injured while protecting him.

Atiku, the ADC’s presidential candidate, condemned the incident, describing it as troubling.

The incident is particularly significant because it involves allegations against state-linked security personnel. It, therefore, raises questions about the neutrality of security officials during political campaigns and the responsibility of state authorities to protect candidates, regardless of their political affiliations.

On 4 November, Mr Obi’s convoy was attacked around Watt Market Roundabout in Calabar, Cross River State.

The incident occurred as he was returning from the palace of the Obong of Calabar to the Metropolitan Hotel, where a presidential town hall meeting was scheduled to be held.

Suspected hoodlums reportedly attacked vehicles in the convoy with sticks and machetes, smashing some of their windscreens.

According to reports, the attackers emerged from the Calabar Road and Clerks Alley areas, damaging the windscreens of vehicles in the convoy.

The Cross River State Police Command confirmed the incident and announced the arrest of a 27-year-old suspect, Victor Duke.

The police, however, cautioned that the arrest did not establish the suspect’s guilt, adding that investigations were ongoing.

Mr Obi accused APC supporters of being responsible for the attack. However, the police said it had not established the political affiliations of the attackers or whether any political organisation sponsored them.

A separate confrontation also occurred between supporters of the NDC and APC near the Metropolitan Hotel in the city. The police described the incident as an encounter between two groups whose routes converged but had not established whether the confrontation was connected to the convoy attack.

On 7 November, a political procession organised by supporters of the NDC and the Obidient Movement along Nnebisi Road in Asaba, Delta State, turned violent, leaving one person dead and five others injured.

The Delta State Police Command confirmed the attack, saying it had earlier warned the party and the Obidient Movement against holding an open-road rally after receiving intelligence suggesting a likelihood of violence during the procession.

The police said they advised the organisers to hold the rally at a designated venue instead. However, the organisers reportedly rejected the advice and proceeded with the procession, which later turned violent. The command subsequently criticised the party and the movement for disregarding its warning.

On 11 November, armed thugs attacked the campaign convoy of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) governorship candidate in Gombe State, Isa Pantami, along Jekadafari Road in Gombe town.

The attackers barricaded the highway with tyres, set them ablaze and smashed the windscreens of several vehicles in the convoy, bringing traffic along the road to a standstill.

Human rights organisation Amnesty International condemned the attack, saying its preliminary findings suggested that the suspected attackers were working for the ruling APC. The allegation, however, has not been independently established.

The National Peace Committee, chaired by former Head of State Abdulsalami Abubakar, recently reported 109 breaches of the National Peace Accord across 26 states and the Federal Capital Territory during a monitoring period covering 19 August to 27 October.

The report identified political violence and thuggery as the largest category of violations, accounting for 33 incidents.

Separately, the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data project (ACLED), an organisation that monitors political violence and conflict, reported more than 30 attacks targeting political campaigns, candidates, supporters, convoys and gatherings since the presidential and National Assembly campaigns began on 19 August.

According to ACLED, the incidents resulted in more than 10 deaths and several injuries.

On its part, the African Centre for Security, Governance and Development (CentreSGD) reported 70 physical election-related attacks across 19 states and the Federal Capital Territory between 1 January and 27 October 2026. It said 27 people were killed in 20 of the incidents.

Hate, divisive outbursts

Beyond physical attacks, statements attributed to some political officeholders and party officials have heightened concerns about the atmosphere in which Nigerians will be expected to exercise their democratic rights.

Some politicians have thrown caution to the wind by expressing divisive sentiments that force people to ponder if politics and governance is not about service.

For instance, in Edo State, the Chairman of the ruling APC, Jarrett Tenebe, was quoted as invoking ‘AK-47 fire’ against anyone who might obstruct the party’s plan to secure 2.5 million votes for President Tinubu in 2027.

In the Federal Capital Territory, the Chairman of Kuje Area Council, Samuel Shekwolo, was seen in a viral video in August telling residents that they must support the APC or leave the area.

Similarly, in Borno State, the Commissioner for Youth and Sports Development, Sainna Buba, was seen in another viral video threatening that people who refused to support the APC in the 2027 elections would be flogged. He made the statement during a campaign inauguration organised by the Tinubu City Boy Movement, a political support group campaigning for Mr Tinubu’s re-election, in Maiduguri.

Although the commissioner later apologised, the incident illustrates the blurred line between political mobilisation and the coercion of citizens by public officials.

The threats came on the heels of the controversial one by the senator for Osun East Senatorial District, Francis Fadahunsi, before the state off-cycle governorship election in August.

Mr Fadahunsi, a member of the APC, was heard in a viral video threatening members of the opposition Accord Party.

He subsequently clarified that his statement referred to defeating the opposition politically, not physically killing its members.

Also, in Edo State, the Chairman of Esan West Local Government Area, Blessing Ebhodaghe, was reported to have directed commercial drivers to wear APC caps or risk being removed from motor parks.

Global Rights also documented a threat by the chairman of Ibi Local Government Area in Taraba State, an APC member, against civil servants who might vote for candidates other than his preferred choice.

These incidents are occurring against a backdrop of concerns among election observers about the security of political campaigns and the possibility that intimidation could undermine citizens’ participation in the electoral process.

They also raise concerns about whether political parties can campaign freely across the country, whether security agencies are adequately protecting political actors and whether Nigerians can support candidates of their choice without fear of intimidation.

Security agencies and accountability

The responses of security agencies to the reported incidents will be central to determining whether the government is adequately protecting political activities and holding perpetrators accountable.

In Calabar, where Mr Obi’s convoy was attacked, the police announced an arrest and said investigations were continuing.

The police arrested 11 suspects in Ekiti following Mr Sowore’s allegation. However, the AAC candidate questioned the police’s account and called for an independent investigation.

In Sokoto, the SSS said its operatives protected the ADC governorship candidate and that two SSS officials were injured in the attack. The police also confirmed that they were investigating the incident.

In Delta, where the Asaba violence left one person dead and five others injured, the police said they were investigating the clash.

These responses indicate that security agencies have taken some investigative steps. However, arrests and announcements of investigations do not necessarily translate into accountability.

Legal framework

Nigeria’s electoral legal framework prohibits the use of violence and threats to compel citizens to support or reject a political party or candidate.

Section 97(1) of the Electoral Act 2026 prohibits a political party, candidate, aspirant or individual from directly or indirectly threatening anyone with force or violence to compel or prevent political support.

The provision is particularly relevant to threats against citizens over their political affiliations and voting preferences.

Global Rights has also drawn attention to this provision in its monitoring of the 2027 electoral environment.

Section 40 of the Nigerian Constitution guarantees citizens the right to assemble freely and associate with other persons, including forming or belonging to political parties. Section 39 protects freedom of expression, while Section 14(2)(b) identifies the security and welfare of the people as the primary purpose of government.

Concerns and condemnations

The rising cases of attacks and hate speech have attracted condemnations from groups and individuals who fear that they could jeopardise the nation’s democratic journey.

The Presidential Campaign Council of the APC, the party whose supporters have been accused of being behind some of the attacks, has condemned the spate of violence targeting political gatherings across the country.

In a recent statement issued by its spokesperson, Dele Alake, the council urged security agencies to identify, arrest and prosecute those responsible for the attacks on political gatherings, irrespective of their political affiliations.

Nigerian lawmakers are equally worried about the spate of violence. Last Thursday, the House of Representatives resolved to investigate the incidents of violence during political campaign activities across Nigeria, following reports of attacks, injuries, deaths and disruption of political gatherings in several states.

President Tinubu has also expressed worries over the rising incidents of violence. In a statement issued by his media aide, Bayo Onanuga, the president warned politicians and their supporters against violence, saying his administration would not tolerate conduct capable of undermining public order during the electioneering period.

“As the leader of this country, I commit myself to a peaceful, free, and fair election, and I urge political leaders and supporters across party lines to conduct themselves responsibly.

“I have said that being in different political parties or pursuing different ambitions does not make us enemies,” he said.

President Tinubu gave a marching order to the security agencies to clamp down on thugs and other anti-democratic activities.

“Security agencies are therefore authorised to confront thuggery and other anti-social and anti-democratic activities with full force,” he stated.

But Human Rights lawyer, Femi Falana, says the government must go beyond arresting suspected political thugs and hold accountable those who recruit, finance and arm them.

“I am suggesting that INEC should have a prosecution unit with a view to getting reports from the police and other security agencies about electoral offences and then take them to court,” he said.

He also criticised the National Assembly for failing to implement the recommendation for an Electoral Offences Commission, arguing that the absence of an effective prosecution mechanism had allowed politicians involved in electoral violence to escape accountability.

Speaking on the issues, the President of the Campaign for Democracy (CD), Ifeanyi Odili, recommended that security authorities establish who organised the attacks, whether political actors were involved, whether weapons were used, and whether anyone provided financial or logistical support.

Mr Odili also argued that investigations should examine whether adequate security arrangements were made for political gatherings and whether warnings issued by security agencies were acted upon appropriately.

Kazeem Odekunle, the spokesperson for the Campaign for Peace, a non-governmental organisation promoting peaceful coexistence among political parties, said political parties had a major responsibility to ensure their supporters did not resort to violence or intimidation.

“Political parties also have a responsibility to ensure that their supporters do not resort to violence or intimidation. The APC, as the ruling party, should explain what measures it has taken to address threats attributed to its officials and members.

“The opposition parties, meanwhile, should be asked whether their own supporters have been involved in violence, intimidation or attacks on rival political activities. This is necessary to ensure that investigations examine political violence across party lines rather than attributing responsibility without evidence,” he told PREMIUM TIMES.

What Nigerians may lose

Aside from political rivalry, these incidents have serious implications for ordinary citizens and the credibility of the electoral process.

Political campaigns provide some of the most visible opportunities for citizens to engage with candidates, hear their programmes, question their records and publicly express support for their preferred parties.

When violence disrupts these activities, the consequences extend beyond candidates and party officials.

Supporters may become reluctant to attend rallies, residents may avoid political gatherings, and community members may become afraid to publicly identify with opposition parties. Such an atmosphere of fear can weaken citizens’ participation in the electoral process, particularly in communities where political intimidation is common.

It can also restrict the ability of candidates, especially those from opposition parties, to reach voters, communicate their policies and compete on equal terms.

Ultimately, an election cannot be considered genuinely free and competitive if citizens are intimidated into silence or prevented from supporting candidates of their choice.

The responsibility for preventing such an outcome rests not only with security agencies but also with political parties, candidates and public officials, whose conduct can either strengthen democratic participation or undermine it.

World.title: 2027: Udeh unveils ATM support group for Tinubu, Mbah, APC candidates
World.content:
Minister of Innovation, Science and Technology, Dr Kingsley Udeh, on Saturday officially inaugurated a political support group, As Tinubu and Mbah Move (ATM), to mobilise support for the re-election of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, Enugu State Governor Peter Mbah and other All Progressives Congress (APC) candidates in the 2027 general elections.

The group, which is anchored on technology and innovation, is expected to deploy digital tools to mobilise voters, monitor grassroots engagement and track its membership and electoral mobilisation activities across the 4,145 polling units in Enugu State.

Speaking at the inauguration, Governor Mbah commended Udeh for the initiative, describing its technological approach and grassroots mobilisation strategy as important complements to the existing political structures of the APC in the state.

Mbah, who expressed excitement over the large turnout at the event, urged members of the group to extend the enthusiasm generated by the inauguration to communities, villages, kindreds, families and polling units across the state.

He said the support group’s effectiveness would be measured not by the crowd at its inauguration but by its ability to translate the energy into grassroots mobilisation and electoral support.

“ATM, this heat, this energy must go beyond this inauguration hall. You must take this energy to our streets, villages, polling units, kindreds and families,” he said.

The governor urged members to convince voters through visible development projects and the achievements of his administration, including Smart Green Schools, the International Conference Centre, Presidential Hotel, International Hospital and other infrastructure projects.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

On President Tinubu’s re-election bid, Mbah described the President as a unifier, arguing that his administration’s economic reforms and infrastructure investments had laid the foundation for national growth and shared prosperity.

He said the President’s decision to remove fuel subsidy and unify the foreign exchange regime demonstrated the political courage required to address longstanding structural challenges in the Nigerian economy.

According to him, although the reforms initially imposed difficulties on citizens, they were necessary to restore macroeconomic stability, rebuild confidence in the economy and attract private capital and foreign investment.

Mbah argued that sustained economic reforms were necessary to translate the emerging growth trajectory into employment opportunities and improved living conditions for Nigerians.

He also highlighted the Federal Government’s infrastructure interventions in the South-East, particularly the improved Enugu-Onitsha highway, the ongoing Enugu-Port Harcourt Expressway project and the concessioning of the Akanu Ibiam International Airport.

The governor said the airport concession would strengthen the South-East’s economic competitiveness, particularly with the planned commencement of cargo operations and direct flights between Enugu and Guangzhou, China, before the end of the first quarter of 2027.

He maintained that the region stood to benefit significantly from the expansion of its aviation and cargo-handling capacity, given the volume of goods currently transported by road from Lagos to the South-East.

On the political implications of the 2027 elections, Mbah urged the people of the South-East to adopt a strategic approach to national politics, stressing the importance of building political alliances beyond the region.

He recalled the political alignments of the First and Second Republics, particularly the alliances involving Dr Nnamdi Azikiwe and Dr Michael Okpara, as examples of how political cooperation across regional boundaries could advance the interests of the Igbo.

The governor argued that supporting Tinubu’s re-election would provide the South-East with an opportunity to strengthen its political relevance and deepen its participation in national governance.

He cautioned APC members against complacency, despite the party’s dominance of the state’s political structures, urging them to campaign vigorously as though they were the underdogs.

Mbah disclosed that the group would complement the party’s existing structures across the state’s 4,145 polling units, adding that its digital monitoring platform would provide a verifiable picture of grassroots mobilisation.

He also urged eligible voters who had yet to collect their Permanent Voter Cards (PVCs) to do so and mobilise for the January 16, 2027, presidential and National Assembly elections, as well as the February 6, 2027, governorship and State Assembly polls.

The governor, however, stressed that the administration’s development agenda remained a work in progress, noting that the presence of poverty, inadequate electricity supply, water challenges and unpaved roads in some communities meant that more work was required.

Earlier, the convener of ATM, Dr Udeh, said the support group was different from conventional political organisations because of its reliance on technology, innovation and a data-driven approach to electoral mobilisation.

He disclosed that the group had established an innovation situation room and digital dashboard to monitor membership registration, grassroots activities and voter mobilisation across polling units.

According to him, membership registration would be tied to the possession of a PVC and the submission of voters’ identification details through a dedicated online portal, while the platform would also track referrals and recruitment of new members.

Udeh said the initiative was designed to replace unverified membership claims with a credible database that would enable the group to measure its performance and provide verifiable reports.

He added that Governor Mbah would have direct access to the dashboard to monitor activities, verify membership figures and assess the group’s progress.

Describing the initiative as an expression of appreciation and loyalty to the governor, Udeh said the relationship between the group and Mbah went beyond the 2027 electioneering season.

He pledged that ATM would deliver measurable results in support of APC candidates at all elective levels, particularly President Tinubu.

Also speaking, the APC National Vice Chairman, South-East Zone, Dr Ijeomah Arodiogbu, commended Governor Mbah for his developmental strides in Enugu State and his efforts in coordinating the party’s presidential campaign activities in the South-East.

Arodiogbu also praised Udeh for establishing the support group and his contributions to the Federal Ministry of Innovation, Science and Technology.

He called on the people of the South-East to support Tinubu’s re-election, while urging the people of Enugu State to vote for Mbah and all APC candidates in the 2027 elections.

Using an apprenticeship analogy, the APC chieftain said no responsible father would send his son to learn a trade under a master who would not settle him after completing his apprenticeship.

He argued that the South-East should support Tinubu because, according to him, the President understood the importance of rewarding loyalty and political support.

Also speaking, the Enugu State Coordinator of ATM, Ugwuoke Onyebuchi, said the group comprised largely individuals who had previously been active in civil society rather than partisan politics.

He said their decision to mobilise support for Mbah and Tinubu was informed by the confidence reposed in Udeh and their conviction that they could contribute to the state’s political and developmental direction.

Ugwuoke said members would embark on grassroots mobilisation, voter education and engagement to persuade residents to support the APC candidates in the forthcoming elections.

He added that the group would deploy technology and data-driven strategies to identify, classify and engage voters across communities, insisting that its activities and results would be measurable.

The highlight of the event was the swearing-in of ATM members and executives at the state and local government levels by the Enugu State Commissioner for Youth and Sports, Barr. Lloyd Ekweremadu.

The event was attended by the APC National Vice Chairman, South-East Zone, Dr Ijeomah Arodiogbu; former members of the House of Representatives, Hon U.S.A Igwesi, who is also the Enugu State Coordinator of Renewed Hope Ambassadors of Nigeria, and Hon Ogbuefi Ozomgbachi, Deputy Coordinator of the Presidential Campaign Council in the South-East.

Others included the Chairman of the Enugu State Traditional Rulers Council, HRM Igwe Ikechukwu Asadu; local government chairmen; members of the Enugu State Executive Council; the state Chairman of the APC, Dr Martin Chukwunwike; and the APC South-East Women Leader, Dr Oby Ajih.

World.title: Rights group hails DSS Director General, Ajayi, over The Sun ‘Courage in Leadership Award’
World.content:
The Centre for Public Integrity (CPI) has extended its warmest felicitations to the Director-General of the Department of State Services (DSS), Mr Oluwatosin Ajayi, following his prestigious conferment with The Sun ‘Courage in Leadership Award.’

In a statement issued in Abuja on Saturday and signed by its Executive Director, Comrade Job Samuel Danfulani, the organization described the honour as a fitting national validation of Mr Ajayi’s ongoing institutional reforms, which have redefined secret service operations in Nigeria through strict adherence to constitutionalism, professionalism, and democratic accountability.

According to the Centre, the award underscores a pivotal paradigm shift within the nation’s premier domestic intelligence agency since President Bola Tinubu appointed Mr Ajayi as DG.

“This recognition by The Sun is not merely ceremonial; it is an objective verdict on a leader who has demonstrated the rare courage to modernize a critical security institution from within, and President Tinubu’s penchant for appointing the right people,” the statement read.

“Mr Ajayi has successfully steered the DSS away from traditional strong-arm perceptions toward a sophisticated, intelligence-driven, and citizen-respecting agency.”

Highlighting the hallmarks of the current administration, the CPI noted that the DSS has recorded remarkable operational milestones in neutralizing complex security threats, dismantling transnational arms syndicates, and preempting asymmetric attacks through covert, surgical intelligence gathering.

More importantly, the group applauded the Service’s unprecedented respect for the rule of law and judicial authority—a development it described as a watershed moment in Nigeria’s democratic evolution.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“For the first time in recent memory, Nigerians are witnessing a secret police leadership that actively submits its operations to the crucible of legal due process,” the group stated.

“Under Mr Ajayi’s watch, the Service has not only secured a string of landmark judicial victories through diligent, evidence-based prosecution, but has also exhibited remarkable institutional maturity by obeying court orders, reviewing past operational excesses, and ensuring the payment of court-mandated compensations to citizens previously affected by wrongful arrests or prolonged detention.”

The Centre emphasized that pairing ruthless efficiency against enemies of the state with genuine empathy and restitution for innocent citizens represents the gold standard of modern intelligence leadership. By strengthening inter-agency synergy, opening constructive channels with civil society and the media, and prioritizing personnel welfare, the DG has elevated the DSS into a formidable pillar of national stability.

While urging Mr Ajayi to view the accolade as an inspiration for greater national service, the Centre called on

other heads of security and law enforcement agencies to emulate his template of transparent, accountable, and rights-based leadership.

“We congratulate the Director-General on this well-deserved feather in his cap. As Nigeria navigates complex security challenges, the nation requires precisely this brand of courageous, cerebral, and law-abiding stewardship to safeguard our sovereignty and democracy,” the statement concluded.

World.title: Reopening Africa’s wounds, waiting for gangrene to set in, By Owei Lakemfa
World.content:
A tragedy engineered by Morocco, watered by Western Europe and the United States (US) with the connivance of the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) is unfolding in Africa. War has become inevitable on the continent with the UNSC reversing the peace process in Western Sahara and abolishing the United Nations Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO).

Africa had experienced colonialism but all 55 countries had become independent. However, a sister country, Morocco had tried to recolonise the Sahara Arab Democratic Republic, SDAR better known as Western Sahara. Africa had put its foot down. On 22 February, 1982, the Organisation of African Unity, now, the African Union (AU) recognised the independence of Western Sahara and admitted it as its full Member. A gluttonous Moroccan monarchy would not accept the decision of the African people and on 12 November, 1984, worked away.

After 33 years of wandering about and being rejected by the European Union, it returned on 31 January, 2017 like a prodigal son. Unfortunately the AU did not sufficiently interrogate Morocco but simply accepted it as a lost son. Now, that Morocco has repudiated the peace agreement and wants to colonise Western Sahara by force of arms, it is clear that the Moroccan establishment, had ulterior motives.

Also, Africa had not been critical of the United Nations, believing that its offer of peace which led to the establishment of MINURSO was genuine. The UN which is now pretending to be working for peace, has repudiated one of its basic principles in order to pamper Morocco and its Western backers. The UN Resolution 1514 of 1960 had proclaimed that: “All peoples have the right to self-determination; by virtue of that right they freely determine their political status and freely pursue their economic, social and cultural development.”

In line with this, the UNSC on 9 April 1991, passed Resolution 690 directing that a referendum be held in Western Sahara. Today, 35 years later with Morocco refusing to allow the referendum, the UNSC has rather than uphold its resolution, cancelled the referendum and, decided that only Morocco’s dubious plan in which Western Sahara will be ruled by King Mohammed VI, would prevail. This leaves our Sahrawi brothers and sisters with little or no alternative but to return to armed struggle.

On the other hand, this has sent the Moroccan establishment into celebratory mood. The Moroccan Monarchy celebrated with what it called “Unity Day” It declared that: “A 35-year chapter has now come to a close. Rooted in an anachronistic and outdated context, this Mission (MINUSO) has long served as a tool for internationalising the regional dispute concerning the Kingdom of Morocco’s legitimate recovery of its Saharan provinces.”

On the other hand, Western Sahara warned that it is willing to completely abandon the peace negotiations. The Representative of the Polisario Front to the UN, Sidi Mohamed Omar warned that if the UN draft is: “approved without substantial and significant modifications, the Polisario Front will have no choice but to withdraw from the entire peace process.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Ambassador Mike Waltz, US Representative to the UN in endorsing the end of the UN peace mission asked: “each of the concerned parties to negotiate a lasting peace.” He added: “Under President Trump’s leadership, the United States has done more for peace in Western Sahara this year than in decades.”

China had warned the UNSC against what it considered a one-sided approach to the Western Sahara issue.

Algeria which has for decades given political, moral and material support to the Sahrawi including granting them shelter in its Tindouf region, pointed out that the: “tragedy being endured by the Sahrawi people has oddly been diluted to the concept of refugee populations” It pointed out the well known fact that the Polisario Front is the legitimate representative of the Sahrawi and decried the: “failure of this Security Council”.

The UN Secretary-General António Guterres in his usual double speak, said ending the peace mission: “does not abrogate” the Saharawi people’s “inalienable right to self-determination” He called on all parties: “to respect and promote the rights of the people of Western Sahara.” The question is why has this not been respected for the nine years he has been in office? With the planned departure of MINURSO, he asked all: “to respect and promote the rights of the people of Western Sahara.” So, why is it that even with MINURSO, those rights are not respected. How does he expect King Mohammed IV who rules by decree even over Moroccans, to respect the fundamental rights of the Saharawi?

Tragically, the African Union whose founding Member is about being recolonised, has kept mute. If war breaks out again between Morocco and the Saharawi people, it is Africa that will suffer. So, why are African leaders quiet?

The move against the Saharawi is just one more step being taken by Western Europe and the US who amongst them, still own over sixty colonies. They are working for a world that would accept colonialism as normal. As part of this plan, the US in October asked the UN to end the mandate of its Special Committee on De-colonisation. It claims the UN Hearings on decolonisation are a waste of resources.

The US which once proclaimed that all men are equal and advertises a statute of Liberty does not want to end colonialism. Neither does it want the colonized to have a voice, not even at a UN Committee level.

If colonialism were to become normal as the West wants, it would not be long before they begin to campaign for the recolonisation of free countries. So, in fighting for the people of Western Sahara against Moroccan colonialism, we in the underdeveloped countries like Nigeria and South Africa would actually be fighting for our freedom.

Owei Lakemfa, a former secretary general of African workers, is a human rights activist, journalist and author.

World.title: Re: Obasanjo: Why debt is an instrument of leverage for purposeful governance, By ‘Tope Fasua
World.content:
On the contrary though, I posit that debt can build generations. In fact debt has built generations. All the countries that matter borrowed by leveraging their cash flows to get where they are. My earlier argument in the article stands. The Western world has only played with peanuts in Africa and we are not monkeys. One could argue that the recent engagements with China have been more promising and beneficial to Africa, and Nigeria in particular because we see the tangibles – roads, rail lines, airports etc.

The tragedy of our times is that there is so much ignorance in the age of information; so much illiteracy in a time when people are educated. The challenge for all is to speak up and keep repeating facts in the hope that somehow facts begin to sink in where they now seem bereft. The times present new challenges. Economies are not what they used to be. And we cannot solve the problems of today by using the same thinking that created them. These are my initial thoughts as I attempt a necessary riposte to the vehement political statements of former President Obasanjo. I call it political even though it is meant to be an economic subject – Nigeria’s debt. But the reasoning and delivery are so well-timed to do damage that the field of economics has to reject what was stated as fact and dump them in the trashcan of chicanery.

First, it is apposite to look at today’s national economies. There is a race for development and no nation wants to be left behind; not even North Korea, perhaps the most isolated country on earth. Every government is working to improve the lives of their people, build infrastructure, or at least create a legacy. In this development superhighway, nobody is slowing down for anyone. What is even more likely to happen is for those who can, to slow down those who are not wary of geopolitics. I wrote an article some months back where I charged that indeed the world has underinvested in Africa and that Africa (especially Nigeria) is certainly not over-borrowed. That conviction still stands.

In today’s world, we cannot run an economy without proper treasury management – which means leveraging our resources and cash flows for the future in order to grow bigger, provide better for our people and obtain the assets we need today for a greater future, such as tangible infrastructure. I wagered in my article that the smart nations of the world – most of them western – have ensured that they collected real leverage and have become where we all troop to for everything under the sun – education, health, tourism, technology, knowledge, information, skills and everything in between. I urged African nations to wake up!

It’s therefore a wonder why Obasanjo will make such a statement. I can only put this down to his political support for Peter Obi (who he probably hopes to use like dough in his hands), and age-long opposition to President Bola Tinubu who has naturally proved to be a tough cookie for anyone to gobble up and who certainly possesses a strong mind of his own.

History of National Debts

This is a fine opportunity to trace the history of national debts. Why do countries borrow? Do countries have to borrow? What happens if they do, or if they don’t? When we are stumped for answers it is always inevitable to look back to determine how we got to where we are. Making statements in reaction to immediate events is a mindset we should leave for the unwise. I was recently addressing a gathering where secondary school students were and I realised that we are raising them to be angry because almost all of them are not rooted in Nigerianism.

The only way our children can be invested in Nigeria is if they understand the history of Nigeria. Who founded Nigeria. What is colonialism and slavery? Why were the northern and southern territories merged? Who got us our independence? What caused political breakdown during the parliamentary government? What caused the first coup? Who died? And the second coup? And subsequent ones? Who were/are the key players of Nigeria’s First, Second, Third and Fourth Republics? What were their legacies? How have we managed our diversity so far? These questions and the answers to them are what will enable us to build our nation. We shouldn’t shy away from them.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

And on the matter of debt, we need history too. Below is what I found in a simple Internet search:

Ancient and Medieval Eras: Rulers in ancient Mesopotamia and the Roman world borrowed money for wars and public works, occasionally enacting “debt jubilees” or forgiveness decrees when obligations became unsustainable. In medieval Europe, tally sticks (notched wooden pieces split between the crown and creditor) tracked royal debts.

Rulers in ancient Mesopotamia and the Roman world borrowed money for wars and public works, occasionally enacting “debt jubilees” or forgiveness decrees when obligations became unsustainable. In medieval Europe, tally sticks (notched wooden pieces split between the crown and creditor) tracked royal debts. The 17th-Century Shift: The Dutch Republic revolutionised state borrowing by issuing long-term public bonds to citizens to fund its war of independence.

The Dutch Republic revolutionised state borrowing by issuing long-term public bonds to citizens to fund its war of independence. The history of the British national debt can be traced back to the reign of William III (a Dutchman, otherwise called William of Orange, who became King of England, Scotland and Ireland from 1689 to 1702), who engaged a syndicate of City traders and merchants to offer for an issue of government debt, which evolved into the Bank of England.

The Bank of England (1694): Britain adopted and formalised this framework with the establishment of the Bank of England, turning national debt into a permanent, tradable financial instrument, rather than a sign of royal bankruptcy.

Britain adopted and formalised this framework with the establishment of the Bank of England, turning national debt into a permanent, tradable financial instrument, rather than a sign of royal bankruptcy. Wartime Spikes: Throughout the 18th and 19th centuries, major conflicts (such as the Napoleonic Wars and the American Revolutionary War) were the primary drivers of debt. British debt-to-GDP surpassed 200 per cent following the Napoleonic Wars.

Throughout the 18th and 19th centuries, major conflicts (such as the Napoleonic Wars and the American Revolutionary War) were the primary drivers of debt. British debt-to-GDP surpassed 200 per cent following the Napoleonic Wars. World Wars I and II: Global conflict pushed debt to historic heights. US and British debt-to-GDP ratios peaked around or above 240 per cent–250 per cent by the end of World War II in 1945.

So, from the get go, we can see that nations borrow for projects. And the most important projects in the beginning, as humans gathered and cooperated in large civilisations, were wars. The first national borrowing by rulers were therefore for war – whether it was in Dutchland, England or America. In China, the Emperors viewed borrowing from people to fight wars as beneath their imperial dignity, so they resorted to fines and taxes when such events presented themselves. There is a second critical reason behind national debts and government borrowings, and that is because it secured the commitment and loyalty of the monied class behind their societies or nations.

When you give money to the King for a war, you stay behind that money and ensure your society survives. It could be argued that post-colonial nations like Nigeria never had that organic opportunity to secure the loyalty and commitment of the monied class and their people in this same manner, as we were quickly introduced to borrowing through global structures and foreign banks. But in general, borrowing is essential in today’s economy because national economies must now be managed with the prowess of bank treasurers. And the first principle at that level is never to sit on cash or fail to leverage in order to achieve more – especially as populations explode.

The idea is not to borrow recklessly. But Nigeria’s debt-to-GDP ratio at a mere 35 per cent is one of the lowest in the world today. An astute financier will wonder whether we had no need for money – no infrastructure to build, no population to take care of, no children to send to school, no old people to help with healthcare. Therefore, saying debts are worse than leprosy or that they are bad for a national economy, is a very careless fallacy to utter.

The Andrew Jackson Experience: Paying Down National Debts

And the world has learnt lessons around national debts. In the medieval times referenced above, a king borrows to fight wars, and when he dies, the debts die with him. In time, through the establishment of national banks or central banks, debts to nations were tracked beyond the death of specific monarchs. And some leaders have also tried to pay down debts because they believed that debts were bad.

One of such presidents was US President Andrew Jackson – who hated debts of any kind – and decided to square off and repay the national debt of that country (about $75 million in 1835). Jackson was a Tennessee landowner and land speculator who had lost money and fallen into debt himself before becoming president. He therefore abhorred the idea of borrowing money for anything. But his decision proved the distinction between running a household, company or government, because it resulted in a disaster for the US economy. When he paid down the debts by selling of federal lands, this is what happened:

Distribution of the Surplus: With the debt eliminated and money still flowing in from federal land sales and tariffs, the government accumulated a large cash surplus. Congress passed the Deposit Act of 1836, which distributed these surplus federal funds to the states.

With the debt eliminated and money still flowing in from federal land sales and tariffs, the government accumulated a large cash surplus. Congress passed the Deposit Act of 1836, which distributed these surplus federal funds to the states. Wildcat Banking and Speculation: Jackson had dismantled the Second Bank of the United States, removing central banking controls. The surplus funds sent to state banks (“pet banks”) led to a massive expansion of paper money and uncontrolled lending, fueling a frantic western land-speculation bubble.

Jackson had dismantled the Second Bank of the United States, removing central banking controls. The surplus funds sent to state banks (“pet banks”) led to a massive expansion of paper money and uncontrolled lending, fueling a frantic western land-speculation bubble. The Specie Circular: To curb land speculation and paper money inflation, Jackson issued the Specie Circular in July 1836, an executive order requiring buyers to pay for federal public lands only in hard currency (gold or silver).

To curb land speculation and paper money inflation, Jackson issued the Specie Circular in July 1836, an executive order requiring buyers to pay for federal public lands only in hard currency (gold or silver). The Panic of 1837: The sudden demand for hard coin drained banks of their reserves, burst the speculative bubble, and triggered the Panic of 1837. This led to bank failures, widespread unemployment, and a deep depression that lasted nearly seven years.

The sudden demand for hard coin drained banks of their reserves, burst the speculative bubble, and triggered the Panic of 1837. This led to bank failures, widespread unemployment, and a deep depression that lasted nearly seven years. Return of the Debt: The debt-free status lasted only about a year; the economic crash dried up government revenues, forcing the US government to resume borrowing.

From the above, the US could only maintain the debt-free status for just one year but suffered a seven-year recession. Historians say that if the US had maintained a debt-free status it would have ended up as a mere agrarian state, because the ability to borrow for ventures has positive effect on creativity and expansion whether for government, businesses or individuals. He equivalent of the meltdown that happened post-1835 in the US economy, today is that if Nigeria wakes up and fully repays its loans, then we can only grow our economy in tandem with what the government is able to raise as taxes, duties, rates and fines. This means the government will put the people under immense pressure. The economy will shrink into a recession, meaning poverty rates, crime, and unemployment will spike.

The idea is not to borrow recklessly. But Nigeria’s debt-to-GDP ratio at a mere 35 per cent is one of the lowest in the world today. An astute financier will wonder whether we had no need for money – no infrastructure to build, no population to take care of, no children to send to school, no old people to help with healthcare. Therefore, saying debts are worse than leprosy or that they are bad for a national economy, is a very careless fallacy to utter.

With infrastructure buildup at the level of Dwight Eisenhower’s National System of Interstate and Defense Highways, an addition of $10 billion to total debt stock should certainly not attract statements from President Obasanjo to the effect that ‘debt is worse than leprosy’. One can only put such statement down to politics; President Obasanjo is rooting for Peter Obi, a man he believes he can control, and a man who has not put down any progressive initiative for Nigeria apart from rabble rousing.

The Obasanjo Debt Repayment

We learnt about the Debt Trap in every Economics class pre-2006. It was the story of how Africa, Asian and some South American mismanaged debt, or were sometimes coaxed or arm-twisted by much smarter lenders categorised into the London and Paris Club. Precisely, affected countries were categorised into Heavily Indebted Poor Countries (HIPCs) and those that were deemed rather capable of paying at least some of their debts. Nigeria fell into the latter group and was made to pay the sum of $12 billion in exchange for the write-off of $18 billion. Some prominent Nigerians, notable ex-Governor Tunde Fashola, expressed their opinion that Nigeria oughtn’t have reached such an expensive deal. Of course, 33 African countries, benefitted from the 2006 arrangement named the G8’s Multilateral Debt Relief Initiative (MDRI), which cancelled 100 per cent of eligible multilateral debts for many of the world’s poorest nations.

Following the 1970s oil shocks and collapsing commodity prices in the 1980s, 39 to 42 low-income countries became trapped in unpayable external debt owed primarily to Western governments, the IMF, and the World Bank. To qualify for the World Bank’s HIPC Initiative, these nations had to prove their debt burdens were unsustainable even after traditional debt-relief mechanisms. In Sub-Saharan Africa these countries include: Benin, Burkina Faso, Burundi, Cameroon, Central African Republic, Chad, Comoros, Côte d’Ivoire, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Eritrea, Ethiopia, The Gambia, Ghana, Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, Liberia, Madagascar, Malawi, Mali, Mauritania, Mozambique, Niger, Republic of the Congo, Rwanda, São Tomé and Príncipe, Senegal, Sierra Leone, Somalia, Sudan, Tanzania, Togo, Uganda, and Zambia. In Latin America, and the Caribbeans, Bolivia, Guyana, Haiti, Honduras, and Nicaragua. While in Asia, Afghanistan benefited from 100 per cent write-off from IMF, World Bank and others. (Laos, Myanmar, and Vietnam had appeared on early pre-2006 HIPC assessments but were dropped, like Nigeria and Kenya).

It is however noteworthy that by the end of President Obasanjo’s government, Nigeria was back in debt. Domestic debt stood at ₦2.05 trillion, while Foreign Debts stayed at $3.35 billion. The naira converted at ₦124 to $1, taking Nigeria’s total national debt to $19.8 billion at the time that President Yar’Adua took over. Nigeria’s debt rose to $45 billion as at 29 May, 2011 and $63.8 billion as at 29 May 2015 when President Buhari took over. The Tinubu administration inherited $113.42 billion in total debt (including the CBN Ways and Means figure). Today, the number stands at $123 billion. This rundown is important to debunk the false claim and false alarm going round that President Tinubu has been overborrowing. He has only been responsible, borrowing only when absolutely necessary. But as an ambitious government, the total turnaround that Mr President has embarked upon certainly requires funding.

With infrastructure buildup at the level of Dwight Eisenhower’s National System of Interstate and Defense Highways, an addition of $10 billion to total debt stock should certainly not attract statements from President Obasanjo to the effect that ‘debt is worse than leprosy’. One can only put such statement down to politics; President Obasanjo is rooting for Peter Obi, a man he believes he can control, and a man who has not put down any progressive initiative for Nigeria apart from rabble rousing. The statement also reeks of hypocrisy, given that Obasanjo struck what some call a terrible deal with the World Bank – with the whooping $12 billion repayment plus commissions everywhere.

Indeed one should add that Obasanjo contradicted himself. He was chums with the Bretton Woods Institutions in his time. But now he disparages them, when he spoke about mere bachelors and spinsters coming here to dictate policy to African countries; policies that, he said, lead to our ruination. He said “These brilliant boys will package everything very well academically. They tell us, and we take it, lock, stock, and barrel, and we use it. For a country of 250 million people, it is boys and girls who are not even married, let alone manage a home, who will tell us what we will do to manage our people, our country, and we swallow it, and we destroy ourselves… World Bank and IMF were not designed for us. They were not built by us. They were built before we became independent, and that’s the people who will determine what we do… (British Prime Minister James Callaghan received four euros per year for every sheep on his farm while the World Bank and IMF barred African nations from subsidising their own farmers).., debt is worse than leprosy because leprosy destroys only one person. Debt destroys generations.”

On the contrary though, I posit that debt can build generations. In fact debt has built generations. All the countries that matter borrowed by leveraging their cash flows to get where they are. My earlier argument in the article stands. The Western world has only played with peanuts in Africa and we are not monkeys. One could argue that the recent engagements with China have been more promising and beneficial to Africa, and Nigeria in particular because we see the tangibles – roads, rail lines, airports etc. For more than three decades most African countries have not seen finances for tangibles but only for soft matters such as gender violence, job acceleration, business-enabling reforms, etc.

To cap it, there is a video circulating online where President Obasanjo spoke about a certain Mrs Kruger, a World Bank/IMF executive who demanded a presidential welcome during his presidency. He spoke about how he sent her report to his then Economic Adviser, Professor Soludo (who always rejected ALL their recommendations), and Mrs Okonjo-Iweala (who always supported ALL their recommendations, given that she made a career in those institutions). He said he would then blend both positions and strike a midpoint, and that he warned Soludo to never show that he was against those institutions else ‘they will rub his nose in the dirt’ (his exact words).

So, President Obasanjo is very aware of what is going on and he knows that we are much smarter today. He is only playing politics… and that is unfortunate given where this country is today. I would have thought he should put his age-long political differences aside and support progress for Nigeria – on the back of reforms that no president was able to pull through. Why is he trying to pull back the hand of the clock for Nigeria by trying to smuggle a puppet in by means fair or foul?

‘Tope Fasua is the special adviser to the President on Economic Matters.

World.title: UN secretary-general marks last climate summit with call to make polluters pay
World.content:
António Guterres, the United Nations secretary-general, has renewed his call to hold fossil fuel companies accountable by making them pay for the harm their actions have done to poorer countries through climate change, marking a defining moment of his last UN climate summit in office.

Mr Guterres gave his final press conference at the 31st Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31) in Antalya, Turkey, as the head of the organisation.

The former prime minister of Portugal has led the UN since January 2017 and exits the role on 31 December, when his second five-year term ends.

Mr Guterres addressed representatives of civil society groups, who gathered Friday to bid him farewell and recognised him with an award for using the UN’s platform to confront the world’s most powerful industries.

“You have given a voice to this injustice like no other leader,” Louise Hutchins, convener of the Make Polluters Pay International Coalition, said.

The session was filled with chants of “make polluters pay”, and speakers asked him to return to a future climate summit wearing an NGO badge.

Mr Guterres told the gathering that the UN’s loss and damage fund now exists but was “funded at a ridiculous level”.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“Those who pollute the least are those who are paying the highest price,” he said.

He urged civil society to apply the counter-pressure needed to help governments understand that things must change.

The UN chief’s final address to a COP leaders’ summit on Wednesday urged governments to levy a tax on oil companies’ windfall profits and use the money to help vulnerable countries recover.

He also proposed a climate justice compact to help countries shift away from fossil fuels, noting that the climate crisis is outrunning the world.

Mr Guterres told the leaders he will no longer be secretary-general from next year, but said, “I will not stop telling the truth.”

At Friday’s press conference, he demanded an immediate and drastic cut in emissions by big emitters.

“You cannot build peace on a burning planet,” he said.

Mr Guterres’ successor has not been announced. The new secretary-general will take office on 1 January 2027 and will lead the UN into the next climate summit (COP32) in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, later that year.

World.title: Tanzania vs Nigeria: Injury knocks Lookman out of next crucial test
World.content:
Ademola Lookman will miss Nigeria’s 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifier against Tanzania in Zanzibar on Tuesday. He sustained a knee ligament sprain, which also casts doubt on his availability for Atlético Madrid’s upcoming fixtures.

A scan confirmed the injury on Saturday, following the Super Eagles’ 3-1 victory over Tanzania at the Godswill Akpabio International Stadium in Uyo on Friday.

The team’s media officer, Promise Efoghe, announced that the forward would be unavailable for the return fixture.

“Scan has revealed Ademola Lookman suffered a sprain in his knee ligament during yesterday’s match. This rules him out of Nigeria’s next AFCON qualifier versus Tanzania in Zanzibar on Tuesday,” Mr Efoghe said.

Lookman was forced off late in the first half in Uyo and was replaced by Moses Simon.
