Before his withdrawal, the Atlético Madrid forward had provided the assist for Alhassan Yusuf’s second-minute opener, giving Nigeria an early advantage.

However, Tanzania drew level in the 32nd minute through Alphonce Msanga, who scored with the visitors’ first shot on target.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The teams went into the break at 1-1. Still, Super Eagles coach Éric Chelle introduced Tolu Arokodare in the second half, and the striker responded with two goals to secure Nigeria’s victory.

The result revived Nigeria’s qualifying campaign following their disappointing 3-0 defeat to Guinea-Bissau in September. The Super Eagles now have six points from three matches in Group L, one behind leaders Guinea-Bissau.

Atlético fixtures in doubt

Lookman’s injury comes at a difficult time for the forward, who was not used in Atlético Madrid’s 2-1 defeat to Barcelona in their LaLiga encounter on 8 November.

The Nigerian remained on the bench throughout the match despite his club seeking a late equaliser.

He now faces a race against time to recover for Atlético’s next two matches after the international break.

Diego Simeone’s side are scheduled to visit Getafe in a LaLiga fixture on 22 November before hosting Norwegian club Viking FK in the Champions League three days later.

The Getafe encounter will take place at the Coliseum, while the European fixture is scheduled for the Riyadh Air Metropolitano in Madrid.

Lookman’s availability for either match will depend on his recovery from the knee injury. Atlético will be keen to assess his condition before deciding when he can return to action.

For Nigeria, his absence is a setback as Chelle’s men prepare for Tuesday’s return fixture at the Amaan Stadium in Zanzibar, where they will seek another victory to strengthen their position in Group L.

World.title: Nigeria, South Africa trade words over exclusion from diplomatic ceremony livestream
World.content:
In the last 24 hours, the Nigerian and South African governments have been trading words over the exclusion of Nigerian High Commissioner to South Africa Femi Fani-Kayode’s speech from the live stream of a diplomatic ceremony in Pretoria.

In its latest response to South African presidential spokesperson Vincent Magwenya, the Nigerian High Commission in Pretoria said Mr Fani-Kayode was treated with contempt and disdain, and that this, by extension, is mistreatment of Nigeria.

The commission, through its official X handle, called Mr Magwenya a “liar” and a “disgrace.”

“Outside of that, your insolence and ignorance know no bounds. You are bringing your nation into disrepute and willfully and purposely burning the bridge of peace and reconciliation. That is a matter of concern to us. The only thing that is inappropriate is the shameful way that you and your team behaved,” the commission said.

The comment was a response to Mr Magwenya’s X post, which was directed toward Mr Fani-Kayode.

The Nigerian High Commissioner, on Friday, accused the South African presidency of cutting off the live stream during his speech at the Sefako Makgatho Presidential Guest House in Pretoria, where he presented his credentials to President Cyril Ramaphosa.

PREMIUM TIMES reported that Mr Fani-Kayode, also accredited to Lesotho and Eswatini, said he was the only one of the 15 ambassadors given the stage to speak whose live stream was cut off.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“To be clear, we were the ONLY ones that were left out. Clearly, some elements in South Africa do not want to hear what we have to say or see our faces, but we are here to stay as long as we are welcome and have the confidence of President Ramaphosa, which I am sure we do,” he said.

The South African presidential spokesperson responded to Mr Fani-Kayode, stating that the event was livestreamed by the South African Broadcasting Corporation (SABC), whose operations are not controlled by the presidency.

Mr Magwenya said the SABC is a public broadcaster, and that the “President does not interfere with its operations or intervene in its editorial processes.”

He accused Mr Fani-Kayode of misrepresenting the facts.

He also said, “I would encourage you, as you start your tenure in South Africa, to meet with SABC to forge a mutually beneficial, respectful and professional relationship.”

However, hours after Fani-Kayode’s allegations, the SABC uploaded a separate video featuring his speech on its website.

Joining the diplomatic spat, the Nigerian High Commission accused Mr Magwenya of trying to heighten diplomatic tension between the states by “adding fuel to the fire.”

“A few months ago you, as spokesman to the President of the Republic of South Africa, described our President and the President of Ghana as peddlers of fake news after they expressed their deep and legitimate concerns about Afrophobia and Xenophobia in your country.

“We let that one go and ignored you. Today, you are calling our newly accredited Ambassador to your country a liar, barely a few hours after he presented his letters of credence.

“You also claim that he has disgraced our country simply because he complained to your President about a slight which your media team subjected him and our nation to.

“We also have the full video clip of the proceedings after the pictures were taken which, if and when we are given the go-ahead to do so, we shall release,” the High Commission said.

Relations between Nigeria and South Africa grew tense after a new wave of xenophobic violence broke out in April and has since been linked to the death of at least 12 Nigerians.

Mr Fani-Kayode, first deployed to Germany as ambassador, said he asked to be redeployed to South Africa because it was more “proximate to my political thinking when it comes to foreign affairs and a pan-African vision.”

World.title: Meet 2 African countries to ever break into top five FIFA World Ranking
World.content:
Only two African countries have ever reached the top five of the FIFA Men’s World Ranking, with Nigeria and Morocco achieving the historic feat more than three decades apart.

The Super Eagles of Nigeria were the first African team to break into the world’s top five, reaching fifth place in April 1994.

The achievement came during one of the most memorable periods in Nigerian football history, following the country’s victory at the 1994 Africa Cup of Nations in Tunisia.

Nigeria, coached by Clemens Westerhof, had a talented generation featuring Rashidi Yekini, Daniel Amokachi, Emmanuel Amunike, Finidi George, Sunday Oliseh and Austin Jay-Jay Okocha.

The Super Eagles also made their debut at the 1994 FIFA World Cup in the United States, where they topped their group before being eliminated by Italy in the round of 16.

For 32 years, Nigeria’s fifth-place ranking remained the highest position ever achieved by an African national team.

However, Morocco joined the exclusive list in September 2026 after climbing to fifth in the FIFA Men’s World Ranking.

The Atlas Lions’ rise followed a period of impressive performances, including their historic run to the quarter-finals of the 2026 FIFA World Cup.

Morocco had also made history at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar, becoming the first African country to reach the semi-finals of the competition.

Their latest achievement saw them equal Nigeria’s record, making them the second African country to reach fifth place in the global ranking.

According to FIFA, Morocco’s achievement matched the highest position ever attained by an African national team, a record Nigeria had held since April 1994.

The two African countries are:

Nigeria: Fifth place in April 1994. Morocco: Fifth place in September 2026.

The two countries have therefore written their names into African football history, becoming the only representatives of the continent to reach the top five of the FIFA Men’s World Ranking.

World.title: Mbappe available for clash with Turkey – Zidane
World.content:
France’s forward #10 Kylian Mbappe reacts to his team’s defeat at the end of the 2026 World Cup football tournament semi-final match between France and Spain at the Dallas Stadium in Arlington on July 14, 2026. (Photo by RONALDO SCHEMIDT / AFP)

Kylian Mbappe is available to play in France’s final Nations League group fixture against Turkey, coach Zinedine Zidane said on Saturday, as Les Bleus seek a spot in the quarter-finals.

Real Madrid forward Mbappe missed Thursday’s defeat to Group A1 leaders Italy with a hamstring problem, but Zidane confirmed: “He will be with us tomorrow (Sunday).

Mbappe, who has netted 17 goals in all competitions for his club this season, was back in the France squad for this international break after missing his country’s previous three matches through injury.

Zidane said Mbappe’s return “changes everything”, adding: “I’d rather have him with us than not.”

The 54-year-old, a World Cup winner with France in 1998 and European champion two years later, denied any tensions with Mbappe and said his relationship with his star striker was going “perfectly”.

“I can’t stop people saying what they’re saying, but it’s nonsense and quite irritating,” said Zidane.

France are second in Group A1, level on 10 points with Italy, and need just a draw against Turkey in Bordeaux to secure qualification for the Nations League quarter-finals.

World.title: Nigeria’s mission in S/Africa urges calm in row over Ramaphosa spokesman’s remarks
World.content:
The Nigerian High Commission in South Africa has urged restraint and reconciliation after remarks by President Cyril Ramaphosa’s spokesman, Vincent Magwenya, about Nigeria’s High Commissioner, Mr Femi Fani-Kayode.

The Mission said on its verified X handle that it wants cordial relations between both countries preserved.

The row followed a disruption of the South African Presidency’s YouTube livestream when Fani-Kayode was due to present his letters of credence to Ramaphosa in Tshwane.

The broadcast was restored while Ramaphosa was addressing the ambassadors.

Magwenya had then accused Fani-Kayode of of lying about Ramaphosa intervening in the controversy surrounding his diplomatic credentials.

The Mission said Fani-Kayode, one of the last diplomats to present credentials, complained that his speech had been deliberately omitted.

It said he raised the matter with Ramaphosa, who apologised and assured him all was well.

It said the disagreement should have been handled through diplomatic channels and urged Magwenya to show restraint.

The Mission described Magwenya’s conduct as provocative and diplomatically inappropriate.

It said its post was meant to reject what it called his attempt to portray Fani-Kayode as dishonest and to damage Nigeria’s image.

“To us this matter is closed, but if you wish to escalate it you are welcome to do so and we are up to the task. A word is enough for the wise,” the Mission said.

It commended Ramaphosa for intervening.

“Thankfully your President had the decency and presence of mind to put out the fire and direct you and your state broadcaster to do the right thing. He literally saved the day,” it said.

World.title: My subjects are very loyal — HRM Albert Akpomudje (SAN), the Ohworode of Olomu Kingdom
World.content:
By Akpokona Omafuaire

The Ohworode of Olomu, HRM Albert Akpomudje, SAN, FCIArb, Eyavwien-Alaka I, is marking his first year coronation anniversary. In this interview, Akpomuje bares his mind on his experience as a traditional ruler, Chairman, Body of Benchers and a practising lawyer. Excerpts:

Your Majesty, it’s been one year since you ascended the throne. What has been your experience as the traditional ruler of ancient Olomu Kingdom?



Well, I must say it’s been a very exciting one year. First of all, I must commend my subjects on the fact that since after the coronation on the 15th of November, 2025, they have been very, very loyal. After the coronation I decided to go round the 15 communities under Olomu Kingdom, and the excitement of the people during the time gave me a very positive and commendable impression of the people; it was like they were seeing their king for the first time visiting their communities, which had not happened before. They did everything to make the occasion memorable. That encouraged me to say I have loyal subjects in Olomu Kingdom.

How have you been coping with your legal practice and also continuing your role as the Chairman of Body of Benchers?



Well, it’s not been easy. But I want to thank God who has given me the strength and good health to be able to manage three things or four together. One, I still go to my office to do what I’m used to. What I don’t do frequently now is maybe going to court, but I’m on ground. I’m still in charge of the office, and I have very able juniors. Then, of course, the Body of Benchers, I have to be on ground in Abuja for meetings and so many other things and then you have to come back to the traditional set up. But I want to thank God that I’ve been coping well. It is exciting. I know that it is not too easy. It’s not something you can say it’s exhausting, but, at the same time, I’m enjoying it because these are three different things which I have to cope with. But I’ve enjoyed every bit of it. I’ve coped very well with the Body of Benchers to the extent that I have been dining with students in almost all the campuses. I go to the campus to dine with them, the statutory dining terms, and at the home front I am on ground, so I’m not lacking in anything.

One year down the lane, do you regret your decision to accept being the Ohworode of Olomu Kingdom?



I can never regret it. I think it is God’s divine arrangements you know, it is God’s favour on me; even though it’s not something I thought of before in my life. And the reason why I’m enjoying it is that I’m having cooperation from my people. So far, there are no issues. I don’t have issues with them. They rely on me. They respect me, and they do everything to show to me that they are ready to do anything as far as the kingdom is concerned, once it comes from me.



Well, I think from the beginning that was a major obstacle. My second-in-command, who is supposed to be the Otota, there were disputes about who was to occupy the position, and they were in court. We did all we could to try and have an amicable settlement, but we thank God that not too long ago the matters were withdrawn, and we had to swear-in the Otota. So at least I have somebody who can deputize for me at any point in time, so I’m so happy that it was resolved. But we are still left with the issue of Akpile. We are doing our best to see that these matters are resolved amicably. We don’t want a situation where we go to court and a decision is taken. Only one party will be happy, but the way we are going about it, we want to make full reconciliation, and we have a full complement of the principal traditional title holders in Olomu who will be helping me out to be able to rule our people effectively and peacefully.

What has been your most challenging experiences?



The challenge is that people give us respect but they also expect so many things from us. Unfortunately, we don’t have the finances with which to execute some of the projects my people want in the kingdom. For example, we have the issue of telephone network. So when I’m there, it’s like I’m cut off from the rest of the world. But we are doing everything possible to see that we get some of these service providers to come and put their masts so that we can be receiving signals to operate our phones. Then also the herders’ issue is another one. Our people are suffering from the destruction of their crops, their farm produce; they think that we shouldn’t allow open grazing in the kingdom. The law is there, but the problem is that it’s not easy to implement. A cow destroys your crops, are you going to arrest a cow? It’s not something that you can get the police to do. And then, of course, those who take them round, they are just workers, you don’t have their identity. If you go and arrest them, you get no result. So that’s a problem I want to tackle with the government. Let us know the owners of these cattle, so that when there is destruction of crops, the victims should be compensated. Good compensation that you know will assuage whatever has been destroyed in their farms. That’s a major problem. Then we also have parts of our roads giving way. And most importantly, we need a good hospital in Olomu, a full-fledged hospital, and, of course, a higher institution that will bring development to the area. These are some of the things we need. Once we are able to put them in place, we don’t want our people to be traveling so far before they attend to their health problems. So these are the problems we have. But we want to see how we can persuade government to at least put some things in place to make the people feel that there’s a government looking after their interest.

Lastly, can what has been your relationship with the state government since emerging as a traditional ruler?



Well, our relationship has been fine. I was appointed a member of the Delta States Traditional Council just a few weeks after I got the staff of office, and the governor has been to a very large extent shown a good interest in our kingdom. Once in a while we talk, but I’m proposing to pay a courtesy call on him with my people, where we can tell him, face-to-face, you know, the problems we want him to solve for us.

World.title: Bamidele: The quiet general selling Tinubu in Ekiti
World.content:
By Rotimi Ojomoyela

In the rolling hills of Ekiti, where politics is played in markets, churches, palaces and town halls, a quiet storm is gathering ahead of 2027 and at its eye stands one man, Senator Opeyemi Bamidele.



The Senate Leader and representative of Ekiti Central Senatorial District has emerged as the central figure coordinating mobilisation for President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s second term campaign in the state, not with noise, but with work that people can see, touch and ride on.



For Bamidele, already a two term senator and an earned ticket for another term, the assignment is not just about party loyalty. It is about consolidating a political partnership that has defined Ekiti’s place in national politics since 2023 and proving that alignment with the centre pays

The bridge between Abuja and Ado-Ekiti



Bamidele is no stranger to the Tinubu political family. As a former aide, commissioner and long-standing ally of the President, he understands the President’s vision and speaks with authority on it.



That proximity has made him the natural bridge between Abuja and Ekiti. While other leaders talk about 2027 in hushed tones, Bamidele has taken the conversation to town halls, party meetings, professional groups and community gatherings.



Party sources say his approach is deliberate; unite first, mobilise second and win convincingly third.

Where projects speak louder than promises



What sets Bamidele’s mobilisation apart is that it is anchored on visible projects, not just promises. In Ekiti Central, constituents point to roads, schools, water, light and empowerment as evidence that the Tinubu era is working.



Across Ekiti West, Efon-Alaaye, Ijero, Irepodun/Ifelodun and Ado-Ekiti, his interventions have focused on basic amenities that touch daily life.



Dozens of motorised solar-powered boreholes have been installed in communities like Aramoko, Iyin, Ijero and Ado-Ekiti to reduce reliance on unsafe water sources.



Solar-powered street lights have also been installed across major roads and communities from Aramoko to Ikogosi and Iyin-Ekiti, improving security, nightlife commerce and reducing accidents, while transformers have been provided to boost electricity supply.



The most quoted scorecard of his stewardship is in road infrastructure. Reports on his record put the number at over 50 roads rehabilitated and constructed across his district, alongside 12 mini-stadiums, thousands of solar streetlights, ICU facilities at five hospitals and new ambulances donated to health centres across Ekiti State.



In Iyin-Ekiti alone, constituents have cited the construction of the Iyin-Ilawe road, the road network within the community, installation of solar lights and construction of market stalls with modern facilities. For canvassers of Tinubu’s second term, those roads are walking billboards.

A University rises in Iyin



At the heart of Bamidele’s legacy project is the Federal University of Technology and Environmental Sciences, Iyin-Ekiti, FUTESI.



He sponsored the bill establishing the Federal University of Medical and Environmental Sciences, Iyin-Ekiti, which was passed by the Senate, and later secured federal funding to establish the Federal University of Technology and Environmental Sciences in Iyin-Ekiti, giving his community a tertiary institution it did not previously have, a development that has brought federal presence, jobs, students and economic activity to Ekiti Central.



To protect the interest of secondary school students sharing the same site with the new university, Bamidele personally undertook the renovation of Government Science College, Iyin-Ekiti, at a cost of over N200 million, covering the boys’ hostel, administrative and classroom blocks, girls’ hostel, dining hall and kitchen, while he also presented a brand-new bus to the school and another to FUTESI.



In his words, “The essence of investing in schools is to create an environment where children could acquire the knowledge, skills and character needed to become better and greater leaders of tomorrow.



“My hope and prayer is that this is the home of tomorrow’s engineers, medical doctors, physicists, pharmacists and in the leadership sector future governors, future senators, commissioners and other leaders”.

Hands that empower, voices that mobilise



Beyond infrastructure, Bamidele’s record shows a strong emphasis on skills acquisition and economic empowerment, with thousands of constituents benefiting from training in entrepreneurship, vocational skills, agriculture and technical services.

His mega empowerment programmes distributed tools and equipment aimed at boosting small businesses and agriculture, with beneficiaries receiving sewing machines, grinding machines, motorcycles, tricycles and minibuses.



In a state where elections are often won in markets and motor parks, those empowerment items have become powerful testimonials for the Tinubu campaign.



His interventions have also included day care centres for the elderly in Aramoko and Iyin-Ekiti, and in Ado-Ekiti, he established an ultra-modern ICT centre and library, reflecting a forward-looking approach to education and digital literacy.



Commending the Senate Leader for his consistent mobilisation, empowerment and grassroots engagement, Governor Biodun Oyebanji noted that such efforts have continued to strengthen the APC’s popularity in Ekiti and position the party to deliver over 90% votes for President Tinubu in 2027.



According to Oyebanji, “Senator Opeyemi Bamidele is one of the pillars holding the APC together in Ekiti. His leadership, his loyalty, and his constant engagement with our people have made our party stronger, more united and more popular across the 16 local governments.



“When you talk about the popularity of the APC in Ekiti today, you cannot talk about it without mentioning Senator Bamidele. He has been consistent in mobilization, in empowerment, and in defending the party at the national level.”

Women at the heart of the campaign



At the 2026 Law Week of the International Federation of Women Lawyers, FIDA, Ekiti State Chapter, in Ado-Ekiti, Bamidele used the platform to connect the Tinubu administration’s reforms to the lives of women and children.



Speaking on the theme, “Justice in a Changing World: Responding to New Challenges Affecting Women and Children”, he said the 10th National Assembly was committed to breaking barriers limiting women’s participation in governance.



He disclosed that a proposed constitutional amendment would create special seats for women, designed to address persistent underrepresentation and ensure adequate participation in decisions affecting the country.



“A democracy that systematically excludes over half of its population from the decision-making tables that determine their future is, at best, a flawed democracy and, at worst, a veiled oligarchy.



“The law is only as good as its implementation. Hold us accountable. Demand that the Special Seats Bill becomes law. Demand that appropriations for child protection and women’s health are not just passed, but released and utilised”.



He linked the federal government’s reforms to tangible benefits for Ekiti families, pointing to the four Tax Reform Acts of 2025, which exempted sanitary products, baby diapers and other essential products for women and children from Value Added Tax.

One party, one voice, one mission



Beyond FIDA, Bamidele has been engaging traditional rulers, youth groups, artisans, traders, students and professional associations across the 16 local government areas of the state, with one consistent message, Ekiti must remain in the mainstream of national politics.



Within the All Progressives Congress, APC, in Ekiti, his mobilisation has helped to calm frayed nerves and prevent the kind of internal rivalry that often weakens ruling parties ahead of elections, working closely with Governor Biodun Oyebanji and other leaders to preach unity, discipline and collective ownership of the Tinubu project.



His pitch for Tinubu’s second term rests on continuity. He argues that the reforms of the first term, however painful, need a second term to mature and deliver prosperity and that protecting women and children is not merely a humanitarian responsibility but a constitutional obligation and a critical investment in national development.



As the presidential election draws closer, Bamidele’s mobilisation is expected to intensify, with ward-to-ward tours, stakeholder summits and strategic endorsements across Ekiti and if early signals are anything to go by, Ekiti may once again prove to be one of the President’s strongest bases, because in Ekiti Central, the campaign is not just being preached, it is being seen in roads, a university, schools and empowerment.

World.title: 2027: Shagari urges politicians to shun character attacks
World.content:
Former Minister of Water Resources, Mukhtar Shehu Shagari, has urged politicians across the country to focus on issue-based campaigns and responsible political engagement ahead of the 2027 general elections.

Shagari warned that personal attacks, derogatory remarks and inflammatory political statements could heighten tensions, undermine national unity and affect the peaceful conduct of the elections.

The former minister made the appeal in a statement issued by his Media Aide, Musa Ubandawaki, expressing concern over what he described as the increasingly hostile tone of political discourse as activities ahead of the 2027 elections gather momentum.

He urged political leaders and their supporters to make policies, leadership credentials and development programmes the focus of their campaigns rather than resorting to personal attacks and attempts to discredit political opponents.

According to him, political differences should not degenerate into hostility capable of creating divisions among communities or worsening ethnic and religious tensions.

“Politicians must learn to play the game with decorum, maturity and a high sense of responsibility. Democracy thrives on constructive engagement, healthy competition and the presentation of alternative ideas, not on derogatory statements, character assassination and deliberate attempts to malign political opponents,” he said.

Shagari also cautioned political figures against making statements capable of provoking supporters and escalating tensions, stressing that the consequences of irresponsible political communication could extend beyond electoral contests.

He called on political parties, candidates, campaign organisations and their spokespersons to centre their campaigns on issues affecting Nigerians, including governance, economic recovery, security, education, healthcare, infrastructure and employment.

The former minister maintained that political contests should not be allowed to undermine the country’s collective interests, noting that Nigeria’s unity and stability should take precedence over individual political ambitions.

He reminded politicians that elections were temporary contests, while the country remained a common heritage that required the commitment of citizens, irrespective of their political, ethnic or religious affiliations.

Shagari, who also chaired the Governing Board of the National Inland Waterways Authority (NIWA), appealed to political stakeholders to promote mutual respect, tolerance and responsible communication.

He stressed that political ambition should not come at the expense of the country’s peace and unity, urging those seeking public office to demonstrate restraint and respect for democratic values throughout the electioneering period.

World.title: Iliasu vows to reclaim Kwara senatorial mandate in court
World.content:
By Demola Akinyemi, Ilorin

Former Kwara State Commissioner for Works, Engineer Rotimi Iliasu, has vowed to pursue his legal challenge over the outcome of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) senatorial primary election in Kwara North, insisting that he remains committed to reclaiming his mandate through the court.

Iliasu, who recently defected from the All Progressives Congress (APC) to the PDP, said his decision to join the opposition party in March was informed by his dissatisfaction with developments in his former party.

He spoke on Saturday during the News Keg Engagement Series organised by the Correspondents’ Chapel of the Nigeria Union of Journalists (NUJ) in Ilorin.

The former commissioner said his senatorial ambition was driven by his desire to promote equal opportunities and encourage wider political participation, particularly among people from communities he believes have been underrepresented in elective positions.

He disclosed that he had approached the Federal High Court over the outcome of the party’s senatorial primary, expressing confidence that the judicial process would address his grievances.

“I will reclaim my mandate at the Federal High Court. The case is already there. I do not believe that the candidate who won the primary election cannot win the 2027 election,” he said.

Iliasu said he had invested considerable personal resources in his political ambition, including the purchase and branding of campaign vehicles and grassroots mobilisation across communities in Kwara North Senatorial District.

He described his emergence in the primary election as a potential political milestone for Moro Local Government Area, which, according to him, had not produced a member of the National Assembly or recorded a victory in the direct primary election of a major political party since 1999.

The former commissioner urged people of integrity and good character to participate actively in politics, saying credible individuals should not abandon the political space.

He attributed his political experience and grassroots acceptance to years of engagement with communities across Kwara North.

Recalling his political activities in Lafiagi, Edu Local Government Area, Iliasu said residents only became aware of his Moro origin about two weeks before the 2018 APC senatorial primary.

He said the support he received despite the late awareness helped him secure approximately 45 per cent of the total votes cast in the primary.

Iliasu also spoke about his record in public service, noting that he had served in different capacities, including Works, Transport and Housing, under the APC-led administration in Kwara State.

He described Lafiagi, particularly Bagwako community in Lafiagi Ward 4, as his home, saying he had maintained cordial relationships with residents over the years.

The PDP chieftain reaffirmed his commitment to the party and expressed optimism about its prospects ahead of the 2027 general elections, urging members in Kwara North to remain united.

World.title: State police, resource control top Makinde’s ‘Reset Agenda’
World.content:
By Dapo Akinrefon

The presidential candidate of the Allied Peoples Movement (APM) in the 2027 general elections and Governor of Oyo State, Seyi Makinde, has unveiled an ambitious plan to restructure Nigeria’s governance and economy, promising to dismantle institutional bottlenecks, devolve more powers to states, strengthen security and redirect public resources towards productive sectors if elected president.



Under his proposed Reset Agenda, entitled: ‘Reset Nigeria: A governing programme for a productive, secure, capable and accountable federation’ Makinde is offering Nigerians a governing programme built around what he describes as the need to rebuild the relationship between government and citizens, restore the country’s federal balance and establish an economic system capable of translating Nigeria’s human and natural resources into better living standards.



The governor argues that Nigeria’s development challenges are rooted not simply in a shortage of resources or the absence of economic policies, but in institutional failures, excessive concentration of authority at the centre, poor coordination among government agencies and the inability of successive administrations to translate policy announcements into tangible improvements in people’s lives.



His proposal, therefore, goes beyond promising new infrastructure, social interventions and economic programmes. It seeks to alter the structure through which the government makes decisions, allocates resources and delivers public services.

Makinde’s argument is that Nigeria cannot achieve sustainable economic growth under a system in which the Federal Government retains excessive control over critical responsibilities while state governments and communities bear much of the consequences of policy failures.



He traces some of the country’s present difficulties to the centralisation of authority during military rule, arguing that the return to democracy did not sufficiently restore the federal balance envisaged by Nigeria’s founding fathers.



According to him, the country must return to a system in which different levels of government have the authority, resources and institutional capacity to address problems within their jurisdictions, while remaining accountable for their performance.

“Reset Nigeria means correcting that course and building a federation capable of making our unity work,” he declared in presenting the programme.



The proposal comes against the background of widespread public dissatisfaction over the cost of living, insecurity, unemployment, unreliable electricity, poor infrastructure and the declining purchasing power of households.



Makinde acknowledges that Nigerians are experiencing the consequences of rising food, transportation, energy and housing costs, arguing that the government must move beyond explaining why economic reforms require time and demonstrate how those reforms improve the lives of citizens.



He maintains that although rebuilding institutions cannot happen overnight, the time required for reform should not become an excuse for inaction or institutional failure.



Economic restructuring and productivity



At the centre of the Economic Reset is a promise to reorganise the country’s economic priorities around productivity, domestic production, employment and the reduction of avoidable costs.



The APM candidate opines that Nigeria’s economic difficulties are compounded by the failure to connect agriculture, transportation, energy, manufacturing, finance and security into a coordinated production system.



He cites the difficulties farmers encounter in moving produce to markets, the high cost of electricity for manufacturers, the recurring expenditure on government-owned refineries and the delays businesses experience in dealing with public institutions as examples of a system that increases production costs and transfers the burden to consumers.



Rather than introduce a new policy for every problem, he proposes an integrated economic framework that would identify the country’s most important productive sectors and remove the obstacles preventing them from expanding.



His approach will be guided by five principles: establishing the true cost of government interventions, assigning responsibility for results, connecting related policies, setting measurable delivery deadlines and discontinuing arrangements that repeatedly consume public funds without delivering value.



One of his major proposals is to prioritise federal road construction around economically important corridors connecting farms, industrial clusters, ports, markets and border communities.



He holds the view that road construction should not be measured simply by the number of kilometres awarded or the amount of money released, but by the economic opportunities created through improved transportation.



Under the proposed Federal-State Road Compact, states undertaking projects on federal roads would have clearly defined agreements with the Federal Government on financing, reimbursement, construction standards, supervision and maintenance.

This, he believes, would end the uncertainty surrounding situations in which states spend substantial resources repairing federal infrastructure without knowing who will ultimately bear the financial responsibility.



Agriculture is another major component of the economic restructuring plan.



Makinde proposes a national food-production strategy that will bring farming, security, storage, processing, transportation and market access under coordinated delivery arrangements.



The initial priority commodities identified in the programme are rice, maize, cassava, beans and tomatoes, subject to further assessment of production capacity, household consumption and regional suitability.



Rather than attempting to run farms or processing businesses, the Federal Government would coordinate national standards, provide shared infrastructure, facilitate financing and address constraints that cut across state boundaries.



The governor’s argument is that increasing agricultural production alone will not bring down food prices if farmers cannot safely access their farms, preserve harvested produce or transport it to consumers.



He also proposes the development of selected industrial value chains, including food and agro-processing, textiles and apparel, pharmaceuticals and medical supplies, and construction materials derived from locally available minerals.



The Federal Government, under his leadership, would work with states and private investors to identify infrastructure, energy, skills, financing and regulatory requirements for each selected sector.



Besides, the objective is to create an environment in which local businesses can expand production, generate employment and compete in domestic and international markets.

Refinery, electricity and fiscal reforms



On energy, the APM candidate promises to end what he describes as the cycle of public expenditure on government-owned refineries that fail to operate reliably.



He proposes an independent technical, financial, environmental and asset assessment of all government-owned refineries within the first six months of his administration.



Within 12 months, each refinery would be assigned one of three options: a partnership with a technically qualified private operator, conversion into a commercially viable petroleum, petrochemical, storage or logistics facility, or an orderly decommissioning process.



He proposes concluding viable transactions within 18 months and enforcing production or conversion milestones by the end of the third year.



The underlying principle is that government ownership should serve a demonstrable public interest and should not become a permanent excuse for financing commercially unsustainable operations.



On electricity, he proposes a targeted protection arrangement for low-income households, under which qualifying metered households would receive their first 50 kilowatt-hours monthly at a protected rate.



The arrangement would be funded through verified electricity delivered rather than estimated consumption, with priority metering for qualifying unmetered households.



He also proposes support for qualifying off-grid households through competitively procured solar-home-system and mini-grid connections.



On macroeconomic management, thenOyo State governor promises fiscal discipline, monetary stability and a transparent foreign-exchange market.



He noted that the Central Bank would retain operational independence in pursuing price stability, while the Federal Government would support monetary policy through responsible borrowing, improved revenue administration and measures to expand domestic production.



He rejects the defence of artificial exchange rates and preferential foreign-exchange arrangements that reward access rather than productivity.



His proposed fiscal framework would also restrict routine monetary financing of federal deficits, while requiring major borrowing proposals to disclose their purpose, repayment sources, foreign-exchange exposure and expected economic or social returns.

Foreign-currency borrowing, he says, should be exceptional and restricted to projects with identifiable foreign-currency earnings or concessional financing whose overall costs are demonstrably lower than domestic alternatives.



The proposals suggest an attempt to combine market-based economic management with targeted social protection, although their implementation would depend on the country’s fiscal capacity, the availability of reliable data and the cooperation of relevant institutions.



State police and decentralisation of security



Perhaps one of the most politically consequential proposals in the Reset Agenda is the planned decentralisation of policing.

Makinde argues that Nigeria’s security architecture places excessive operational authority at the centre while expecting governors and communities to respond to threats over which they have limited lawful control.



He believes the country’s security challenges cannot be adequately addressed through the deployment of more personnel, weapons and vehicles alone without improving intelligence gathering, local knowledge, communication and operational accountability.



His proposal is to complete and implement the constitutional, legal, financial and operational arrangements for state policing.

Under the framework, states seeking to establish their police services would be required to demonstrate sustainable funding, transparent recruitment, professional training and independent disciplinary and complaints mechanisms.



State police would concentrate principally on public safety and crimes within their respective jurisdictions, while federal security agencies would retain responsibility for terrorism, border security, organised crime and offences that cross state or national boundaries.



The two levels of policing would operate through interoperable communication systems, shared intelligence and common criminal records.



Governor Makinde, however, recognises the danger of transferring excessive security powers to state governors without adequate safeguards.



He proposes national standards governing the use of force, detention, investigation, firearms and human rights, alongside independent oversight and judicial review to prevent the abuse of state police for political, ethnic or religious purposes.



He also proposes a common Threat-to-Action Standard across security agencies, under which every credible security warning would have an identified lead agency, supporting institutions, a responsible command structure and a traceable response.



Serious security incidents would trigger operational reviews to determine what authorities knew, what action they took and where institutional failures occurred.



Beyond policing, he wants security operations connected to economic recovery in affected communities.



Under his proposed Security and Economic Recovery Plans, protection of farming communities, transport routes, schools, markets and health facilities would be linked to efforts to restore legitimate economic activities.



He argues that security should not be measured by the number of checkpoints established, vehicles purchased or arrests announced, but by reductions in attacks and abductions, the safe return of farmers to their land and the restoration of economic activities.



Devolution, resource control and a new federal arrangement



Makinde’s proposed Federal Responsibilities Review is another major plank of the governance reset.



Within his first year, he promised to examine the responsibilities currently exercised by the Federal Government and determine which should remain exclusively federal, which require national standards but state-level implementation, and which should be transferred principally to states or local governments.



The review would produce proposals for constitutional amendments, legislation, fiscal adjustments and transition arrangements.

His position is that transferring responsibilities without corresponding financial resources, personnel, assets and accountability would merely relocate existing institutional failures.



The proposal has particular implications for resource control and the management of solid minerals.



Under the present constitutional arrangement, the Federal Government retains primary control over mineral resources, including licensing, while states contend with many of the environmental, security and social consequences of mining activities within their territories.



Makinde proposes giving state governments a greater role in decisions concerning the exploration and exploitation of solid minerals within their territories.



Although the Federal Government would continue issuing mining licences under the existing constitutional framework, states would be formally involved in the process and allowed to raise concerns about land use, environmental protection, community interests and public safety.



He also proposes publicly accessible registers of mining licences and beneficial ownership, stronger cooperation between federal and state regulators and improved mechanisms for tackling illegal and dangerous mining.



The broader implication is that states would have greater influence over the economic activities and natural resources within their territories, although the precise extent of this devolution would require constitutional and legislative changes.



For Makinde, the objective is not to weaken the federation but to make federalism more functional by ensuring that decisions are taken at the level best equipped to deliver results.



Education, healthcare and social protection



The proposed reset also places considerable emphasis on human capital development.



In education, Makinde wants the country to move away from measuring success primarily through school enrolment, the construction of buildings and the number of certificates awarded.



He proposes a National Foundational Learning Guarantee under which every child should acquire basic literacy and numeracy by the end of Primary Three.



Working with state governments, his administration would target at least 50 per cent of Primary Three pupils meeting the national minimum proficiency standard in literacy and 65 per cent in numeracy within three years.



The programme would include teacher training, classroom support, regular assessment and additional instruction for children who have fallen behind.



He also proposes stronger links between technical education, vocational training, apprenticeships and industry requirements, arguing that public investment in skills development should be judged by whether beneficiaries acquire recognised competencies and secure employment or establish businesses.



At the tertiary level, he wants universities and other institutions to place greater emphasis on practical experience, research and the application of knowledge to Nigeria’s development challenges.



His healthcare proposal is to strengthen existing reforms, particularly primary healthcare, and establish a clear guarantee of essential services in participating states.



Federal health funding would increasingly be linked to verified service delivery rather than the existence of buildings or the submission of administrative documents.



The administration would also strengthen health insurance coverage for poor and vulnerable Nigerians, prioritising maternal healthcare, childhood immunisation, emergency stabilisation and treatment of diseases responsible for preventable deaths.



On social protection, Makinde proposes an accountable gateway connecting existing federal and state systems, including the National Social Register and cash-transfer programmes.



The objective would be to establish transparent eligibility requirements, traceable payments and an appeals mechanism for people wrongly excluded from assistance.



He says the system should be capable of responding to poverty, disability, displacement and sudden economic or climate-related shocks without creating new emergency lists whenever a crisis occurs.



Public accountability and rebuilding citizens’ confidence



A central theme running through the Reset Agenda is the demand for greater accountability in public administration.

Makinde believes Nigerians have become accustomed to government announcements that are not followed by clearly identifiable results.



To address this, he proposes that every major government commitment should have an identifiable lead institution, a delivery timetable, measurable targets and an officer responsible for reporting progress.



Within the first 100 days, his administration would publish a consolidated Reset Delivery Plan identifying the responsibilities of ministries, departments and agencies, the legal and administrative steps required, funding arrangements and three-year implementation milestones.



He also proposes extending what he calls the ‘Tell Government Once’ principle across public services, allowing government agencies to obtain verified information already held by other institutions instead of repeatedly demanding the same documents from citizens.



Procurement plans, awarded contracts, beneficial ownership and implementation records would be published in accessible formats, subject to legitimate national security and privacy restrictions.



He promises to strengthen professional standards in the civil service, protect judicial and prosecutorial independence and ensure that public appointments and promotions increasingly reflect competence, performance and integrity.



On democratic governance, he supports reforms to improve transparency in electronic accreditation and transmission of election results, political financing and the appointment of electoral officials.



He also pledges to protect peaceful protests, journalists, civic organisations and political opponents, arguing that criticism should not be treated as disloyalty to the country.



The Oyo experience and the presidential test



Makinde’s justification for offering Nigerians the Reset Agenda rests partly on his experience as governor of Oyo State since 2019.

The programme cites interventions in agriculture, infrastructure, education, healthcare and security as evidence of what he believes can be achieved through better planning and institutional coordination.



Among the examples highlighted is the Fasola Agribusiness Industrial Hub, which the document credits with attracting private investment and supporting youth training.



It also cites the rehabilitation and upgrading of healthcare centres, improved health-insurance enrolment and the restoration of academic activities and accreditation in state-owned educational institutions.



In security, the document points to reductions in selected crime categories during his first term and the establishment of a toll-free emergency response number.

World.title: Tinubu Seeks Forgiveness from Plateau, Promises Decisive Action Against Insecurity
World.content:
•Vows to return IDPs to their ancestral homes

• Gov Mutfwang: Tinubu met Nigeria in intensive care unit

• Massive turnout reflects North-Central’s confidence in Tinubu’s leadership, says information minister

Deji Elumoye, Adedayo Akinwale in Abuja and Yemi Kosoko in Jos



President Bola Tinubu yesterday asked families affected by the deadly attacks in Anguwan Rukuba in Jos North Local Government Area (LGA) of Plateau State that left many killed and several injured in March 2026, to forgive him for not visiting the communities.

He stated that his administration was taking stern security measures against those carrying out the dastardly acts in the state.

This is just as Governor Caleb Mutfwang of Plateau State said President Tinubu met Nigeria in an intensive care unit when he assumed office but has gradually moved the country into recovery through his administration’s policies.

Meanwhile, the Minister of Information and National Orientation, Mohammed Idris, has attributed the large turnout of party faithful and supporters at yesterday’s rally of the All Progressives Congress (APC) in Jos to what he described as growing public appreciation of the achievements of President Tinubu’s administration by the North-Central over the past three years.

Speaking at the ruling APC presidential campaign rally in Jos, Tinubu said too many lives had been lost to attacks in Plateau since 2001.

“When I last visited the other time, I was limited to the airport. Forgive me if you didn’t see me in the hinterland. But I saw the devastation; I got the report from the governor. I saw horror in the faces of our people.

“But since then, that has changed; we are forging together,” he explained.

He, however, assured residents that their communities would be rebuilt for those displaced to return home.

Tinubu pledged the reconstruction of conflict-ravaged communities, the return of internally displaced persons (IDPs) to their ancestral homes and accelerated economic development across the region.

Recalling his previous visits to the state, the president said the state had suffered years of violent attacks that resulted in loss of lives, destruction of homes and displacement of thousands of residents.

He expressed sympathy to victims of violence and IDPs, pledging that the federal government would rebuild affected communities and support their safe return to their ancestral homes.

He said the government had intensified security measures to tackle insecurity, including training 1,000 forest guards and deploying surveillance technology to strengthen intelligence gathering and rapid response capabilities.

“Crises and attacks have inflicted deep wounds on Plateau. Too many lives have been lost, homes destroyed, communities displaced.

“To every bereaved family, every survivor and everyone unable to return home, I offer my heartfelt condolences for your loss and pray that only God will console you.

“We are one single family created by the same God Almighty. We are just living in different rooms, speaking different languages and behaving in different ways, but living in different rooms and speaking different languages does not make us enemies of one another.

“We have to live together. We have to farm together. We have to build this Plateau and this country together. It is our responsibility to behave as brothers and sisters”, he further said.

The president promised that the 2027 general election would be peaceful, warning individuals and groups plotting to unleash violence or intimidate voters that his administration would not tolerate any attempt to undermine the democratic process.

He also appealed for electoral support for APC candidates at all levels, encouraging voters to support the party in the presidential, governorship, National Assembly and state House of Assembly elections.

Tinubu said he had directed security agencies to intensify operations against those responsible for violent attacks and ensure lasting peace across Plateau State.

“What we should be getting is prosperity, not havoc, not crisis. Our government is not elected to inflict wounds on one another or to bury people. We have to lift people from adversity to prosperity”, he added.

The president said the security arrangements would target threats facing rural communities, where farmers and other residents had been forced to abandon their homes and livelihoods.

“Crises and attacks have inflicted deep wounds on the state. Too many lives have been lost, homes destroyed, communities displaced.

“To every bereaved family, every survivor and everyone unable to return home, I offer my heartfelt condolences for your loss and pray that only God will console you”, he said.

He urged Plateau residents to embrace peaceful coexistence and resist attempts to exploit their ethnic, religious or political differences.

“We are one single family created by the same God Almighty. We are just living in different rooms, speaking different languages and behaving in different ways, but living in different rooms and speaking different languages do not make us enemies of one another.

“We have to live together. We have to farm together. We have to build this Plateau and this country together. It is our responsibility to behave as brothers and sisters”, he declared.

On economic development, Tinubu announced plans to collaborate with the Plateau State Government to transform the Jos airport into an agro-cargo hub that can facilitate the direct export of agricultural produce to international markets.

He said the proposed project would enable farmers in Plateau and surrounding states to export vegetables, potatoes, and other agricultural commodities, expanding market access, creating economic opportunities, and improving farmers’ incomes.

“From that, you will be able to export vegetables and potatoes abroad directly. The economy will improve. Development and prosperity will grow this economy”, he said.

He urged Nigerians to obtain and safeguard their Permanent Voter Cards ahead of the 2027 elections, describing the PVC as a vital instrument for democratic participation and prosperity.

Gov Mutfwang: Tinubu Met Nigeria in Intensive Care Unit

In his welcome address, Governor Mutfwang said President Tinubu met Nigeria in an intensive care unit when he assumed office but had moved the country into recovery through his administration’s policies.

The governor pledged Plateau State’s support for Tinubu ahead of the 2027 presidential election.

The governor said, “You met Nigeria in the intensive care unit, and through the policies you have administered, like a drug, you have been able to bring Nigeria out of the intensive care unit. We are now in recovery.”

“We are confident that if you continue, we will not only recover but prosper as well. That is why we are determined that in the 2027 election, there is no alternative for us. We will stick with you and go with you.”

He described Tinubu as a friend of Plateau State and the North-Central region, citing the federal government’s interventions in road infrastructure, education and healthcare.

According to him, students in tertiary institutions across the state had benefited from the Nigerian Education Loan Fund scheme, while strategic federal road projects had improved connectivity and economic prospects.

The governor pledged overwhelming support for Tinubu in the 2027 election, insisting that the people of Plateau had resolved to reciprocate what he described as the President’s goodwill towards the state.

Earlier, the Director-General of the APC Presidential Campaign Council, Senator Abdul’Aziz Yari Abubakar, declared that Plateau and the North-central zone remained firmly behind Tinubu’s re-election bid.

Yari said the administration’s achievements in security, infrastructure and economic management had strengthened public confidence in the APC government, adding that the President had demonstrated commitment to fulfilling the party’s manifesto.

Yilwatda Charges North-central Governors, Candidates to Unite for Tinubu’s Victory

Speaking at the event, the National Chairman of APC, Prof. Nentawe Yilwatda, urged the party’s governors and governorship candidates in the North-central to unite all stakeholders in their states and mobilise massive support for President Tinubu.

He also urged Plateau people to translate the rally’s enthusiasm into votes, insisting the state must deliver a record-breaking victory for Tinubu.

The chairman described Tinubu as a promise-keeper who has fulfilled his commitments to Plateau State, saying the administration’s record of delivery provides a strong basis for renewed public confidence.

“All political leaders in Plateau State are now united, 100 per cent, behind the President,” Yilwatda said, assuring Tinubu that the ballot box would reflect the people’s overwhelming support.

Yilwatda specifically charged governors, candidates and leaders across the region to close ranks, bring every stakeholder on board and establish a united front behind Tinubu.

The chairman emphasised that the North-Central must approach the elections with a common purpose, stressing that personal interests and political differences must give way to the collective objective of securing victory for the APC.

Massive Turnout Reflects North-Central’s Confidence in Tinubu’s Leadership, Says Information Minister

Meanwhile, the Minister of Information and National Orientation, Idris, has attributed the large turnout of party faithful to what he described as growing public appreciation of the achievements of President Tinubu’s administration by the North-Central over the past three years.

Speaking at the rally, the minister said the enthusiastic participation of party faithful and supporters reflected, in his assessment, confidence in the administration’s reform agenda and its efforts to reposition the country for sustainable economic growth and development.

“The turnout we are witnessing here today is a clear demonstration of the confidence Nigerians have in President Bola Ahmed Tinubu and the direction his administration is taking the country. The people can see the efforts being made to address longstanding challenges, strengthen the economy and create a better future for our country,” Idris said.

Idris said the administration remained focused on consolidating the gains of its reforms and ensuring that their benefits translated into tangible improvements in the lives of citizens across the country.

“President Tinubu remains committed to staying the course and ensuring that the decisions being taken today deliver lasting benefits for Nigerians. What is important is that we continue to build on the progress made and work towards a stronger, more prosperous nation,” he said.

The minister also urged opposition political parties to embrace issue-based campaigns and demonstrate greater organisational preparedness rather than relying on political rhetoric and criticism of the government.

He maintained that Nigeria’s democratic process would be better served by constructive political engagement, credible alternatives and robust debates on policies and programmes that directly affect the welfare of Nigerians.

Idris further emphasised the importance of responsible political conduct as the country approaches the 2027 general elections, noting that political parties have a collective responsibility to promote peaceful participation and strengthen public confidence in the democratic process.

Also speaking at the rally, the Minister of Solid Minerals Development, Dele Alake, underscored the strategic importance of the North-Central geopolitical zone to Nigeria’s political stability, economic growth and national development.

He highlighted the region’s enormous potential, particularly in solid minerals and other productive sectors, and stressed its significance to the country’s broader economic transformation.

World.title: Amaechi: 13 North-east, North-west States Backing ADC in 2027 Elections
World.content:
• I’ll restore fuel subsidy, tackle insecurity if elected, Atiku vows

•Promises to continue Kolmani oil exploration in Bauchi

Segun Awofadeji in Bauchi

The vice-presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Mr. Rotimi Amaechi, has claimed that 13 states in the North-east and North-west backed the opposition party in the forthcoming 2027 elections, and expressed confidence that the party would defeat President Bola Tinubu and the All Progressives Congress (APC).

This comes as the ADC presidential candidate and former Vice President, Atiku Abubakar, has reiterated his determination to restore fuel subsidy and tackle insecurity if elected president.

Atiku also promised to continue oil exploration activities at the Kolmani Oil Field in Bauchi State

Speaking yesterday during the ADC presidential campaign rally in Bauchi State, Amaechi said the ADC would also challenge the APC in the South-south and North-central regions, predicting victories for the opposition party in Niger, Kogi and Nasarawa states.

The former Rivers State governor vowed that the party would not accept a repeat of what he alleged happened during the 2023 general election.

“Because these people will do what they did in 2023. This time, we shall not agree. Do you understand? We will not do what?” he said.

Amaechi argued that the ADC had a stronger regional presence, citing the 13 states in the North-east and North-west.

“We are the only party that comes with 13 states. The whole of North-east, the whole of North-west, that is 13, right? Let the president tell us how many states he comes with. He comes with only five in the South-West,” he added.

He further claimed that the APC would lose a sixth state in the South-west to the Allied Peoples Movement (APM).

“And the sixth state in the South-west will vote APM, whether he likes it or not,” he added.

Amaechi said the ADC would also compete strongly against the ruling party in the South-South and North-Central, expressing confidence that Atiku would secure Niger, Kogi and Nasarawa states.

“We will fight with him in South-South. We will fight with him in North-Central. And be sure, be rest assured, Niger, Kogi, Nasarawa will be in ours easily,” he said.

Amaechi also predicted that Tinubu would not make significant electoral gains in the South-east, insisting that the ADC would win the presidential election.

“He will not go to South-east at all. Be assured, we will win. We will win. Things will get better,” he said.

I’ll Restore Fuel Subsidy, Tackle Insecurity If Elected, Atiku Vows

Speaking at the rally, Atiku reiterated his determination to restore the fuel subsidy and tackle insecurity and urged voters to vote for the party’s candidates in all elective positions.

“I have already promised all Nigerians that I will restore petroleum subsidy. Not only that, but I will also restore subsidy in electricity,” he said.

Atiku also pledged to address insecurity in the North-east and other parts of the country, while promising to expand petroleum exploration in the Kolmani area to generate additional revenue.

He called on Nigerians to support the ADC, urging voters in Bauchi to elect the party’s candidates from the presidency to the councillorship positions.

The former vice-president thanked the people of the state for their previous support, saying Bauchi had consistently given him substantial votes in past elections.

He urged residents to turn out in large numbers during the 2027 polls and ensure their votes were protected and counted.

“I want you to make sure you come out in your thousands. You vote for ADC. You defend the vote. You ensure that the votes are counted, and results are transmitted before you leave the polling booth,” Atiku said.

President Bola Tinubu announced the removal of petrol subsidy during his inauguration on May 29, 2023.

Tinubu said the funds would instead be redirected to infrastructure, education, healthcare and job creation.

The subsidy removal has inflicted hardship on Nigerians, and Atiku repeatedly promised to restore it if elected in 2027.

The former vice president had questioned how the savings from its removal had been spent.

Uncertainty has surrounded the ADC’s leadership following a November 5 judgment by the Federal High Court in Abuja, which sacked the Senator Mark-led National Working Committee (NWC) and invalidated decisions taken under it, including the process that produced Atiku as its presidential candidate.

Justice Peter Lifu also ordered the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) not to recognise decisions taken at the party’s 99th National Executive Committee meeting held on July 27, 2025.

But the ADC rejected the judgment and said it would challenge the decision in court.

The party also continued its activities and preparations for the 2027 elections.

World.title: Tegbe: Over 15,000 MVA Capacity Added to Grid in Three Years, Eyes N19bn Private Investments
World.content:
•FG spends over N10tn on power supply in 13 years, says Anuwe

Emmanuel Addeh in Abuja

The Minister of Power, Mr. Joseph Tegbe, has disclosed that more than 15,000 megavolt-amperes (MVA) of additional transmission capacity was added to the national electricity grid between 2023 and 2026.

This is just as the Managing Director of FGN Power Company Limited, Mr. Kenny Anuwe, revealed that the federal government invested more than N10trillion in Nigeria’s Electricity Supply Industry (NESI) since the privatisation of the sector in 2013.

FGN Power is the Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) set up by the Nigerian government to implement the Presidential Power Initiative (PPI), the flagship programme conceived in 2018 to tackle Nigeria’s long-standing electricity challenges.

Speaking at the Sixth Edition of the Power Correspondents Association of Nigeria (PCAN) Conference in Abuja, Tegbe added that the federal government had taken steps to address longstanding financial and infrastructure challenges in the electricity sector as part of efforts to support President Bola Tinubu’s ambition of building a $1 trillion economy.

The minister said the president had approved a plan to settle verified legacy debts owed to generating companies, reiterating that the initiative had raised N1.2 trillion to ease financial pressure on the companies and improve their capacity to pay for gas and maintain their plants.

He disclosed that more than 2.8 million customers had been metered under the Presidential Metering Initiative (PMI).

At the same time, the Rural Electrification Agency (REA) had continued to connect universities, hospitals and rural communities to solar power.

Tegbe also said construction had commenced on a new National Grid Control Centre in Osogbo to replace the existing facility built more than 60 years ago.

He added that more than 15,000MVA of additional transmission capacity had been added to the national grid between 2023 and 2026.

According to him, newly installed substation equipment commissioned across several locations in the country had added more than 1,300 MVA to Nigeria’s transmission capacity, making additional electricity available to distribution companies.

The minister, represented by his Special Adviser on Administration and Projects, Martins Olajide, identified grid stabilisation, sector liquidity and sustainability, asset optimisation, and grid expansion and enhancement as the four priorities of the government’s roadmap for addressing the sector’s challenges.

He said the plan would adopt a corridor-based approach to prioritise major economic centres for reliable, round-the-clock electricity supply.

FG Spends over N10tn on Power Supply in 13 years

Meanwhile, delivering a keynote address at the PCAN conference, themed: “$1tn Economy: Nigeria’s Roadmap to Reliable and Affordable Power Supply,” the Managing Director of FGN Power Company Limited, Mr. Anuwe, revealed that the federal government invested more than N10 trillion on power supply since 2013.

Anuwe said that government funding had helped sustain the electricity industry despite its challenges.

He pointed out that public funding has remained insufficient to meet the country’s power needs, stressing that the company had secured a $1 billion commitment from the Africa Finance Corporation (AFC). In comparison, other financiers were expected to commit $18 billion to the sector.

Anuwe, however, argued that the scale of investment required to support Nigeria’s ambition of building a $1 trillion economy could not be achieved through public funding alone.

“The government has invested over N10 trillion in the electricity sector since the advent of privatisation. But is it enough? How much money is enough?” he asked.

According to him, the industry would not have remained operational without the government’s financial interventions.

He stated the country must adopt new investment models capable of attracting substantial private capital.

Anuwe said the federal government accounted for more than 95 per cent of new infrastructure investment in the sector, a development he described as inconsistent with the objectives of privatisation.

“That’s not why we privatised,” he said, urging stakeholders to move beyond excuses and develop practical solutions to the sector’s financing and infrastructure challenges.

He maintained that the government should focus on providing the policy, regulatory and infrastructure conditions that would enable public and private capital to operate effectively.

“The government can provide the enablers, provide infrastructure, delivery, and market conditions under which public and private capital can perform effectively,” he argued.

The FGN Power chief said Nigeria needed between 10,000 megawatts and 30,000 megawatts of electricity to support the growth of a $1trillion economy, stressing that achieving the target would require a different approach to power sector planning and implementation.

He identified integrated resource planning, coordinated policy interventions, reliable technology, financial discipline and stronger private sector participation as essential to expanding electricity supply.

Anuwe also called for simpler institutional and regulatory arrangements, noting that the complexity of the electricity market, involving generation and distribution companies, transmission operators, regulators, government agencies, financiers and gas suppliers, could discourage potential investors.

He said clearer responsibilities, predictable regulation, bankable projects, faster decisions and measurable delivery would improve investor confidence and accelerate infrastructure development.

Anuwe disclosed that the company had structured commercial arrangements with original equipment manufacturers and engineering, procurement and construction firms, with the federal government providing 15 per cent equity in the financing arrangements.

According to him, the company’s transmission substation and line projects were progressing, with most of the ongoing Phase One projects expected to be completed in the first quarter of 2027.

He added that the second batch of Siemens substations, comprising 12 facilities, was being prepared for implementation, subject to the necessary financing approvals, with commencement targeted for the fourth quarter of 2026.

Anuwe said the projects, alongside the Omotosho substation project, were expected to deliver a combined capacity of just under 3,400 megawatts.

The company, he said, was targeting an additional 5,540 megawatts by 2029, alongside an improvement of at least 60 per cent in grid reliability.

Anuwe said the planned improvements could also enable at least 2,000 industries to return to the national grid, with households and businesses expected to benefit from more reliable electricity supply.

He said FGN Power Company was working toward a $2.3 billion project financing package, comprising $1.3 billion from Europe and $1 billion from China.

On his part, the Managing Director of the Nigerian Electricity Management Services Agency (NEMSA), Olusegun Adesayo, restated the organisation’s commitment to ensuring that electrical installations, equipment and networks across the country comply with prescribed technical standards and regulations.

Adesayo explained that beyond infrastructure, safety remains critical, since unsafe installations that do not comply with regulations cannot serve the people effectively.

Earlier in his welcome address, the Chairman of PCAN, Obas Esiedesa, said the association’s annual conference had evolved into an important platform for engagement among policymakers, regulators, operators, investors, industry experts and journalists since its inaugural edition in November 2021.

Esiedesa called for urgent attention to the recurring seasonal decline in electricity generation, particularly between November and March, when reduced water inflows into hydroelectric power stations and gas supply constraints to thermal plants often affected electricity output.

World.title: Decline in Loan Impairment Charges of Eight Banks By  46.9% Lifts Profit Before Tax to N4.8tn
World.content:
Kayode Tokede

Eight Nigerian banks reported a 46.9 per cent decline in loan impairment charges to N1.01 trillion in the nine months ended September 2026, compared with N1.91 trillion in the corresponding period of 2025.

Loan impairment charges, often referred to as credit losses, are provisions banks make to cover potential defaults and deterioration in the value of their financial assets.

The substantial decline in impairment charges helped lift the eight banks’ combined profit before tax (PBT) by 12.2 per cent to N4.8 trillion, from N4.3 trillion in the corresponding period of 2025.

The eight banks are Jaiz Bank Plc, Zenith Bank Plc, Ecobank Transnational Incorporated, First HoldCo Plc, Guaranty Trust Holding Company (GTCO) Plc, Access Holdings Plc, Wema Bank Plc and Sterling Financial Holdings Plc.

THISDAY gathered that lower impairment charges at GTCO, Access Holdings, Zenith Bank and First HoldCo supported their combined profitability, although earnings growth sources varied across the groups.

Access Holdings recorded the largest percentage reduction in impairment charges, which fell by 73.5 per cent to N92.91 billion in the nine months ended September 2026, from N349.99 billion in the corresponding period of 2025. Its PBT rose by 8.3 per cent to N667.36 billion.

Zenith Bank recorded the second-largest percentage reduction, with impairment charges declining by 70.5 per cent to N230.77 billion, from N782.76 billion.

Its PBT rose 1.2 per cent to N928.80 billion, from N917.41 billion, suggesting lower credit-loss provisions helped offset weaker income from other activities.

Together, Zenith Bank and Access Holdings accounted for approximately N809 billion of the reported N906 billion reductions in impairment charges across the eight groups.

GTCO also benefited from approximately N39.6 billion in lower impairment charges, although its PBT declined by 2.3 per cent to N879.90 billion.

The results show that lower impairment charges can materially support earnings but do not automatically translate into higher profits when other income sources weaken or expenses rise.
