On the question of selecting a joint presidential candidate, Gachagua revealed that differences remained over the appropriate timing, with Wiper leader Kalonzo Musyoka proposing that the flagbearer be identified before December, while Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna favoured February and Narc Kenya leader Martha Karua suggested May.

Gachagua, however, argued that selecting a candidate too early could expose the individual to political pressure and possible frustration from the government.

He proposed April next year as a more suitable time, maintaining that the coalition was united on the principle of having one candidate even if its leaders differed on the timing.

The DCP leader also dismissed arguments that academic qualifications, experience or political credentials should determine who becomes the coalition's presidential candidate, insisting that electoral numbers and the support of ordinary Kenyans would ultimately decide.

“As others say they have experience and an agenda in the Opposition, the deciding factor is the numbers. I'm with the people. You say you have capacity, but the person to decide is the voter,” he said.

He added: “Akili nyingi ni nzuri, but bila kura unaweza kaa nayo nyumbani.”

World.title: Mudavadi urges Western Kenya to unite, says region cannot remain on sidelines
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Prime CS Musalia Mudavadi. [File, Standard]

Prime Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi has urged Western Kenya to unite ahead of the 2027 General Election, saying the region must strengthen its political representation to have a greater say in national decision-making.

Speaking during a UDA delegates' meeting in Shitoto village, Mumias East, Kakamega County, he said Western Kenya could not afford to remain on the sidelines while decisions affecting the country were being made.

"2027 is the moment we must change the narrative. We must make sure that we are at the table where decisions are made. We cannot afford to remain spectators when the future of our country and our region is being determined," he said.

Mudavadi said parliamentary influence depended on numbers, arguing that electing more MPs would give the region a stronger voice in key parliamentary committees, including the Budget Committee.

"Parliament exercises authority in its own right. We want more MPs so that we can have a say in the Budget Committee and other important committees. These positions are secured through numbers, and numbers matter when decisions affecting the country are being made," he said.

Turning to the opposition, Mudavadi described its leaders as divided and challenged them to present clear manifestos outlining what they would offer Kenyans.

He said the divisions within the opposition would work in President William Ruto's favour as he seeks re-election in 2027, expressing confidence that he would win in the first round.

"We want Ruto to win without a petition. We want to thrash them in the first round," he said.

World.title: Middle East aims to targets 100 million tourists by 2030 – Egypt leads the growth
World.content:
As the Arab region prepares for an exceptional winter season, the latest ATM Travel Trends Report 2026 revealed that 77 percent of travelers considering a visit to the Middle East prioritize “luxury” when making booking – a figure significantly higher than the 51 percent of travelers looking at other destinations.

The report, released on November 9, notes that “luxury” is no longer confined to five-star hotels – it now encompasses a desire for authentic cultural experiences, interactions with local residents, and attendance at heritage and religious events—a clear shift that is reshaping the landscape of regional demand.

The report arrives at a highly significant moment: the global market is recovering faster than anticipated, and the Middle East is transitioning from a mere transit hub into a primary, standalone destination.

According to the report, 55 percent of visitors to the region seek to attend cultural events, compared to 42 percent for other destinations, placing Egypt in a strong competitive position within the region, bolstered by its unique civilizational heritage and the state-of-the-art Grand Egyptian Museum (GEM).

Egypt amongst fastest-growing tourism destinations

Amidst these shifts, Egypt has emerged as one of the fastest-growing tourism destinations in the world.

In statements made on Monday, Minister of Tourism and Antiquities Sherif Fathy announced that Egypt had welcomed approximately 16.2 million tourists by the end of October.

He projected that the total would reach 20 million by the end of this year- with a further increase to 22 million next year.

These figures are bolstered by a record 20 percent growth in visitor numbers, the highest tourism growth rate in the Middle East, according to a regional report by the United Nations World Tourism Organization.

The surge is not limited to visitor numbers alone; the sector generated US$ 18.4 billion in revenue during the 2025–2026 fiscal year, a 10.3 percent year-on-year increase, according to data from the Central Bank of Egypt.

The government aims to reach 30 million tourists annually by 2030, with projected revenues ranging between $ 36 billion and $40 billion.

Hitting this target requires the addition of 240,000 to 250,000 new hotel rooms, an expansion of airport capacity, and the development of tourism-related transport systems and logistics services.

While these figures reflect a tangible improvement in the sector’s indicators, they also reveal a gap between current ambitions and existing infrastructure.

Although Egypt possesses immense competitive advantages, accommodating 30 million tourists necessitates substantial investments in accommodation, transportation, and services, an area the government is currently addressing by offering incentives to investors and streamlining licensing procedures.

The new ATM report reflects a deeper shift in traveler behavior: with 55 percent of visitors to the region seeking to attend cultural events, Egypt has emerged as an ideal destination for this type of experience, thanks to its unique cultural heritage and a modern, world-class museum.

Optimistic outlook

Data from the World Tourism Organization indicates that Egypt recorded a 16 percent increase in tourist numbers during the first quarter of 2026, surpassing both regional and global averages, even as tourism slowed in some neighboring countries.

Globally, the outlook is even more optimistic; a joint report by World Travel Market (WTM) and Tourism Economics, released on November 3, reveals that international tourism is on track to reach 1.57 billion tourist arrivals and $1.8 trillion in spending by 2026, with a clear transition from mass tourism toward experience-based and sustainable travel.

The report’s projections indicate that the Middle East aims to welcome approximately 100 million tourists by 2030, an ambitious goal that requires doubling hotel capacity, as well as developing airports and air connectivity.

Egypt lies at the heart of this figure, due to its population size, geographical diversity, and its strategic location serving as a gateway between Europe, Asia, and Africa.

World.title: US Air Force responds to suspected drone activity over UK airbase
World.content:
Reuters — US Air Force personnel at the RAF Lakenheath base in Britain responded to “suspected unauthorized drone activity” on Friday evening, although no personnel, aircraft or infrastructure were affected, a US Air Force spokesperson said.

“We continue to work closely with our host nation counterparts to ensure the safety and security of our US service members, US and host nation civilians, contractors, and all of our families,” the spokesperson said by email.

Britain’s Ministry of Defence said US Air Force Security Forces personnel had responded to reports of unauthorized drone activity and that the situation had been resolved.

“We are working closely with them to establish the facts. We will provide updates in due course,” a ministry spokesperson said in an emailed statement.

The US has in recent weeks moved bombers that had been used to strike Iran out of Britain, and relocated huge refueling aircraft from Britain to Germany. A news report later said there had been a threat from Iran.

The bombers left RAF Fairford on security grounds after a group of men approached ​the base in white vans in the middle of the night on September 27.

Two men ​were charged last month in relation to ⁠that incident, with prosecutors alleging one of them had tried to assist Iranian intelligence in Britain. The US Justice Department said this week that a member of an Iran-backed militia had plotted to attack the Fairford air base while detained in the US on criminal charges.

The Wall Street Journal has reported that the refueling aircraft were moved due to a threat from Iran.

Britain’s domestic spy ‌chief said in October that Iran had stepped up attempts to hit ​harder targets such as military sites in Britain.

Tehran has rejected accusations of involvement in the Fairford incident or any other accusations of malign activity in Britain, where the authorities have ​for a number of years accused it of being involved in plots and attempted assassinations against dissidents and Israeli and Jewish targets.

Germany has blamed Russia for an attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport in August after airport workers found a drone laden with explosives and a detonator at the airport, an important civilian freight and NATO logistics hub in eastern Germany that is also a base for several giant Ukrainian Antonov An-124 cargo planes.

World.title: The Trump administration is diverting billions in health funding away from low-income countries, defying Congress’ plans
World.content:
The Trump administration plans to redirect or withhold nearly all funding that Congress had slated for international family planning aid this year – about $605 million – according to an internal US State Department budget report and a memo to lawmakers that were obtained by CNN.

The budget plans also involve an effort to move nearly a billion dollars into a global health innovation fund benefiting US corporations, while sharply cutting global health funding for low- and middle-income countries.

The actions have drawn criticism from nonprofit organizations and lawmakers who argue it represents overreach by the administration, given that Congress holds the power to decide how money is spent.

A copy of the budget report – called the preliminary Fiscal Year 2026 allocation – reveals plans to divert or repurpose almost all of the $607.5 million in funding that Congress had allocated to supply contraception and other reproductive health services to women overseas.

Tens of millions of that funding will be diverted to support the “energy security needs” of US partners facing market disruptions amid the wars in Iran and Ukraine, according to a separate memo signed by Secretary of State Marco Rubio in September. The memo offered few additional details on how that money would be spent.

For decades, US family planning aid has provided millions of women overseas with modern contraceptives to give them the ability to prevent or space out pregnancies, which research shows improves maternal mortality rates, family incomes and babies’ health.

In fiscal year 2024 – before Trump came back to office – US investment in global family planning is estimated to have prevented 34,000 maternal deaths, according to the Guttmacher Institute.

The budget plans also reveal steep reductions in US health assistance for most countries when compared to 2024 funding levels, according to an analysis of the leaked budget document conducted by Public Citizen, a nonprofit consumer advocacy organization. Their analysis, which was shared exclusively with CNN ahead of its publication Saturday, was conducted in conjunction with the nonprofit organizations Partners In Health (PIH) and PAI, a reproductive rights advocacy organization.

The countries with the largest funding decreases for health programs are South Africa, Tanzania and Zimbabwe, which have all been hit with more than $100 million in cuts. Eight countries – Afghanistan, Central African Republic, Gambia, South Africa, Somalia, Sudan, Timor-Leste and Yemen – have had their health funding cut to zero since 2024.

Asked about the funding diversions, a State Department spokesman told CNN that “the administration is consistently evaluating the use of foreign assistance to ensure it is used to meet critical needs, including unanticipated contingencies such as the current global energy crisis, within the context of its annual appropriated budget and the authorities available to the president and the secretary.”

Asked about the department’s diversions of family planning funding, the spokesman said: “Our focus is on implementing life-saving care, including in HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, malaria, and maternal and child health, through new, landmark bilateral global health MOUs (memoranda of understanding).”

A mother holds her child while waiting for treatment in February 2025 at Hossainpur Upazila Health Complex in Bangladesh, as information about contraception services backed by USAID can be seen in the background. Piyas Biswas/SOPA Images/LightRocket/Getty Images

Vincent Lin, associate director of health policy and advocacy at PIH, told CNN that the latest budget moves are “counter to what Congress has put in the appropriations bills.”

“To see dollars that have been fought for and written into the law by Congress moved away or siphoned away to energy security needs, or to US private companies with a profit margin, or out of really important public health programs … I think it is devastating to see that happen,” Lin said.

“The executive branch is flagrantly not spending the money that Congress has written into law for a very specific purpose,” Lin told CNN. “On the family planning side … this is the clearest situation of the executive branch ignoring and or violating the Congressional will.”

In the last two years, the State Department has made several efforts to assume more control over US global health funding and make spending reductions, including by not transferring certain funds to the Centers for Disease Control. CNN has also previously reported on the administration’s redirection of $1.35 billion in funding intended for global health programs to cover the cost of closing the US Agency for International Development (USAID).

Many of those changes have lacked public announcements or transparency.

Public Citizen has sued the State Department in an effort to force the release of records surrounding those bilateral global health agreements, which the administration has largely kept confidential. That lawsuit is ongoing in federal court, but some of the documents have been released following Freedom of Information Act requests by watchdog groups.

Congresswoman Lois Frankel (D-FL), who serves on the House Appropriations Committee, said: “The Trump administration’s refusal to spend Congressionally-appropriated funds for international family planning, as required by law, is shameful and dangerous.”

“These decisions have real, life-changing consequences for women’s health, economic security, and opportunities, as well as the well-being of their families and communities,” Frankel said in a statement to CNN.

Family planning aid diverted for ‘energy security needs’

In a memo to Congress signed by Secretary of State Rubio – which was obtained by CNN and first reported on by The New York Times – he said he authorized the redirection of up to $125 million in foreign aid to support “energy security needs.”

More than $48 million of that would be taken from family planning aid, according to the memo.

The memo also spelled out multi-million-dollar diversions away from other US programs, including peacebuilding initiatives between Palestinians and Israelis and overseas assistance for civilian victims of war.

In the memo, Rubio invoked a law that allows the government to use existing foreign assistance funds to address unanticipated crises, saying that funding would be used to “support exigent energy security needs for partners facing coercive supply cutoffs, market disruptions, and inflated costs – particularly due to the deliberate, extortionary actions of Russia, China, and Iran.”

It comes as the war in Iran has disrupted energy markets and led to a huge increase in global oil prices.

The State Department memo didn’t give further details on how the money diverted for energy security would be spent.

A Democratic Congressional aide told CNN the funding diversion is “an authority that they do have, but it is unlike it’s ever been used before.”

Separately, the State Department budget document shows that another $32 million originally allocated for the United Nations Population Fund is also being diverted into other health programs.

And a further $524 million in family planning aid is being withheld without a justification given, according to the analysis by Public Citizen, PIH and PAI. That funding is listed in the State Department budget document as “To Be Programmed.” Other publicly available budget documents list that sum as “unallocated,” which analysts said suggests the funds have not been made available for spending.

“This decision is not consistent with the congressional history of bipartisan support for family planning and reproductive health care,” said Nabeeha Kazi Hutchins, president and chief executive of PAI. “It is Congress that holds the power of the purse, and the actions of this administration and the statements of this administration raise very serious concerns about whether the executive branch is exceeding its constitutional authority.”

“For us, this is not just an isolated budgetary decision,” she told CNN. “This is part of a much broader policy direction that’s increasingly restricting women’s health and wellbeing.”

It’s not the first time the Trump administration has indicated it does not plan to spend money on family planning or reproductive health aid, despite the bipartisan allocations made by Congress. Last year, Rubio said in his testimony before the House Committee on Appropriations that with regards to family planning programs, “we’re not going to be in that business globally.”

The Trump administration has also previously conflated certain kinds of contraception with abortion – something that medical professionals have refuted.

Shifting money into ‘innovation fund’ as foreign countries hit with aid cuts

The 2026 budget document also showed plans to move $888 million of global health funding into an “innovation fund” that backs US companies working in science, technology and medicine.

At the same time, more than $1.6 billion is being cut from global health funding for foreign countries, according to the analysis by Public Citizen, PIH and PAI.

The move comes after the Trump administration last year launched an overhaul of the way the United States provides health assistance throughout the world, called the “America First Global Health Strategy.” The stated goal of the strategy is to have aid recipient countries further develop their own health systems – and the US decrease its assistance spending.

But Public Citizen, PIH and PAI argue that in reality, the funding cuts and diversions are making it more difficult for countries to bolster their own health systems.

“The administration’s cuts to country level programming takes away resources that support local health systems and services that deliver care and stop diseases from spreading. The simultaneous increase in resources for the innovation fund prioritizes commercial interests over these fundamental global health objectives,” the three organizations said in their analysis.

The administration’s justification of the new “America first” strategy was that NGOs were wasting money and it should go directly to foreign governments instead, according to Peter Maybarduk, who directs Public Citizen’s initiative on access to medicines. “But the reality is, we’re going to take money from the governments and the NGOs and give it to big corporations,” he said.

Public Citizen’s report also raised concerns about a lack of transparency regarding how government contracts will be awarded through the “innovation fund” of $888 million, which is far more money than when the fund was first created in 2025.

The administration originally set aside $60 million for the innovation fund, according to FY 2025 budget documents.

“The State Department has not clarified how it will solicit and review awards under the (innovation) fund,” wrote Public Citizen, PIH and PAI in their report, which also criticized the department for “increasingly relying on non-competitive sole-source awards.”

The State Department spokesman told CNN: “The Trump administration is continuing to explore ways to identify and leverage American innovations to save lives, and to do so more cost-effectively while working with Congress.”

The department did not respond to CNN’s question regarding the specific process for awarding contracts through the innovation fund.

CNN has previously reported on the Trump administration’s use of no-bid contracts in other areas of government, particularly surrounding the renovation and construction projects in Washington, DC.

There has been little public information about the specific projects and companies that the global health innovation fund will go towards. However, the State Department has recently announced some partnerships that it says promote American innovation, including contracts with the drone delivery company Zipline, the pharmaceutical company Gilead Sciences and SC Johnson.

“Without a transparent and accountable process for new awards, funding could flow not to those with the best proposals for public health impact, but to those with direct, private access to the administration,” the Public Citizen report said. “Moreover, new technologies are not a substitute for direct support to countries.”

World.title: Yemen’s Houthis hold mass funeral as they call for action to protect civilians
World.content:
A mass funeral procession was held in the Yemeni capital Sanaa on Wednesday for at least 43 people allegedly killed in an airstrike by the Saudi-led coalition, according to Saba news agency, which is run by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels.

The victims were killed in a strike Saturday on six homes in Al-Shariya, a Yemeni village east of Sanaa, Saba said. Among the dead are 21 children and 10 women, the agency reported.

Footage aired on the Houthi-run Masirah TV showed large crowds gathered at a graveyard. Men carrying rifles were seen digging graves.

Ahead of the funeral, Masirah TV published graphic images showing children lying motionless, whom Houthi authorities said had been killed in the strike. The attack involved three consecutive raids that also hit ambulance crews and rescue workers, it said.

CNN has reached out to the Saudi government as well as the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen for comment.

Fighting between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition reignited in July, shattering a 2022 UN-brokered ceasefire that had brought years of relative calm, after Saudi-backed forces struck Sanaa Airport in an attempt to block a Houthi plane arriving from Iran.

Houthi forces retaliated by launching an offensive and captured territory along Yemen’s western coast and near the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a key trade route.

Saturday’s attack comes as casualties surge in Yemen, where the years long conflict has dragged the country into a severe humanitarian crisis.

The World Health Organization (WHO) reported on Tuesday that at least 2,025 people were killed or wounded between Oct. 31 and Nov. 8, including 163 deaths in the strategic northern city of Marib alone.

In response to the worsening conflict, the UN Security Council on Thursday voted unanimously to renew its Yemen sanctions regime for another year, extending targeted asset freezes and travel bans until November 2027 amid the escalating violence.

The UK-drafted resolution — which strongly condemns the Houthis’ military offensive as well as their missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia and Red Sea shipping — also expands a UN monitoring panel to include maritime security experts and affirms that arbitrarily detaining UN and humanitarian workers is grounds for sanctions.

An administrative building belonging to Aramco that was damaged in a Houthi attack, in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia on Tuesday. Saudi Press Agency/Reuters

On Wednesday, Yemen’s Houthi-controlled parliament appealed to United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres to intervene amid the intensifying fighting. The parliament claimed that hundreds of Saudi airstrikes over the previous five days had killed or wounded more than 300 people, most of them children, women and elderly people. CNN hasn’t independently verified the figure.

The Houthi-run Health Ministry also said Wednesday that at least 359 civilians had been killed and 780 wounded in what it described as the latest Saudi escalation. The ministry said most were women and children.

The Houthi armed forces said Tuesday that Saudi Arabia had carried out 93 airstrikes and missile attacks over the previous 24 hours, targeting sites including civilian and energy infrastructure across Houthi-controlled areas.

The rebel group, in turn, continues to target Saudi infrastructure, including the King Khalid International Airport in the capital Riyadh, and oil facilities. In October, back-to-back attacks on the airport killed at least 20 people and wounded hundreds of others.

On Wednesday, the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted two drones over Mecca, Islam’s holiest city. On Thursday, it intercepted another over Riyadh.

The Houthis denied targeting Mecca, calling the coalition’s claim “another lie.”

Over the weekend, a building belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco in the financial district of Riyadh was damaged in a missile attack.

Correction: This story has been corrected to say 2,025 people were killed or wounded in Yemen between Oct. 31 and Nov. 8, according to the World Health Organization.

World.title: Massive Microsoft outage disrupts businesses, schools and governments around the world
World.content:
A massive Microsoft outage that has left people around the world without access to Outlook email, Teams meeting tools and other staples of modern office life is nearly fixed, according to the latest word from the company.

Microsoft has apologized for the outage, which could end up costing billions in lost productivity. Microsoft said the outage was caused by a “technical issue” rather than any cybersecurity breach. “The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change,” the company said.

The company reported that queues of emails waiting to be delivered are “significantly reduced and approaching normal levels.”

Problems started midday Thursday on the US East Coast, and quickly spread around the globe. As many as 430 million users were reportedly affected at some point.

In the United States, some companies’ frustrated workers went home early on Thursday. In Australia, businesses couldn’t print invoices and some schools couldn’t hold online classes on Friday.

And there was no quick fix. As of 10:30 p.m. ET on Thursday, the outage was still widespread, affecting untold millions of people.

“We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners,” Microsoft said in a post on X around 1 p.m. ET on Friday. “We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services.”

“We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions,” the company added. “Given the scale of demand, we restored services gradually, validating stability at each stage. While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration.”

The disruption has caused a wide range of reactions. Some US office workers celebrated the email blackout and joked that they could start the weekend early. Others barely missed a beat, connecting with colleagues via Slack, phone and even the old-fashioned way: in-person.

But small businesses scrambled for Microsoft alternatives to communicate. Local governments alerted constituents to call instead of email.

The outage could cost $7 billion in lost productivity, according to an estimate by Anderson Economic Group, a Michigan-based think tank. Patrick Anderson, the firm’s president, said that perhaps as many as 26 million users on Thursday and 51 million users on Friday have actually seen their operations disrupted in a way that caused an economic loss. And he said the cost will likely increase beyond this initial estimate.

In Australia, Friday began with a realization that the Microsoft cloud was unresponsive. The outage took out live feeds from courts, and schools texted parents to phone in any absences until email systems were restored.

Australia’s national broadcaster, ABC, reported people missing job interviews because they couldn’t connect to virtual meetings, and even some supply issues with distribution centers stocking supermarkets due to the outage.

At first, Microsoft said the connection issues were happening “in the Americas,” but over time, it became clear the troubles were global.

Downdetector showed a peak of 130,000 reports about Outlook outages, but that figure understated the scope of the problem, since most people do not report their experiences.

World.title: Expert explains Finance Ministry allocating state-owned land on the Red Sea to reduce public debt
World.content:
Economist Fakhri al-Fiqi explained that the decision to allocate 112 million square meters of state-owned land in the Red Sea governorate to Finance Ministry for investment purposes does not entail selling the land or transferring its ownership.

During a phone interview with the “Modern MTI” television channel on Friday, Fiqi noted that this allocation is not a new development – it was enacted via a presidential decree as part of the state’s broader strategy to leverage its assets for economic gain.

The decision authorizes the Finance Ministry to grant usufruct rights to the land or to utilize it as an in-kind asset for economic development, he explained.

The proceeds generated would then be directed toward servicing the public debt and reducing its burden, while the state retains the underlying ownership.

Usufruct rights

The economic expert emphasized the necessity of distinguishing between allocating land under a “usufruct” (right-of-use) arrangement and selling land to transfer its ownership.

Fiqi’s remarks came in response to questions regarding whether the government intends to sell state-owned land to generate financial resources to help repay public debt.

He clarified that the announced measure concerns the management and economic utilization of assets through usufruct rights, rather than the relinquishment of ownership.

Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi had issued a presidential decree allocating over 112 million square meters of state-owned land in the Red Sea Governorate to Finance Ministry.

The decree was published in the Egyptian Gazette on Wednesday.

This land is to be used for the purpose of reducing public debt and issuing sovereign “Sukuk” (Islamic financial certificates)—a move aimed at leveraging state assets to lower the national debt burden.

World.title: Egypt, UN showcase results of EU-Funded Joint Program Supporting Refugees
World.content:
Assistant Minister of Foreign Affairs for Migration, Ambassador Neveen Elhussein, United Nations (UN) Resident Coordinator in Egypt Gianluca Rampolla del Tindaro and representatives from the European Union (EU) led a high-level field visit Thursday, 11 November 2026.

The visit brought together senior Government officials, representatives of United Nations agencies and heads of Cooperation from partner missions to observe firsthand the results of the EU-funded UN Joint Program on Refugees, Migrants and Host Communities. It demonstrated how coordinated and institutionalized international cooperation can translate into meaningful improvements in the lives of refugees, asylum seekers, migrants and members of host communities.

The delegation visited education and health facilities in 6th of October City and Omraneya rehabilitated through the Program, reflecting that supporting refugees and migrants must go hand in hand with strengthening national systems and public services. The delegation reaffirmed its support for the Joint Program and commended the results achieved through the close partnership with the Ministry of Health and Population and the Ministry of Education and Technical Education.

Egypt has consistently shouldered its responsibilities in hosting refugees and asylum-seekers. Today, it hosts 1.1 million registered refugees and asylum seekers alongside several million migrants, including millions of migrants in vulnerable situations.

Launched in 2024 under the Joint Platform for Migrants and Refugees, the Program is a flagship partnership between the Government of Egypt, the United Nations and development partners. Implemented by UNHCR, IOM, WHO, UNICEF and WFP, the Program supports Egypt’s national response to migrants and refugees, as well as the Egyptian communities hosting them.

Since its inception, the Program has reached more than half a million people. It has supported 120 schools, helping create more inclusive learning environments, and strengthened 56 public health facilities. The Program has provided education services to over 162,000 students, trained more than 2,500 health professionals, and supported efforts to raise nutrition awareness and improve maternal and child nutrition and food security. It has also delivered protection services to 85,200 individuals and promoted social cohesion among children and adults refugees, migrants and host communities. Through these integrated interventions, the Program is expanding access to essential education, health and protection services across Egypt.

“The visit demonstrates the importance of translating international solidarity into tangible investments that benefit both refugees and migrants and the community hosting them. The obligation of responsibility sharing must go beyond humanitarian assistance to include sustained support to strengthen national systems and public services to enhance the resilience of host community,” said the Assistant Minister of Foreign Affairs for Migration.

“What we have seen demonstrates the power of partnership. Working together, the Government, the United Nations and development partners are delivering tangible results for the most vulnerable. At a time of growing needs and increasing pressure on national systems, enhanced international responsibility-sharing is essential to build on these results, and reinforce Egypt’s capacity to provide inclusive services for all,” said the UN Resident Coordinator in Egypt.

“The EU remains deeply committed to supporting Egypt’s efforts to address complex migration challenges in an increasingly volatile regional context. Through this Joint Program, we are supporting Egyptian authorities in building resilient local systems that benefit both vulnerable populations and the host communities that generously welcome them,” said Sebastien Lorion, Team Leader, Delegation of the EU to Egypt.

The visit underscored the importance of continued international solidarity and investment in Egypt’s national systems to scale up access to services for refugees, migrants in vulnerable situations and host communities, while contributing to social cohesion and sustainable development.

World.title: Egypt, Morocco discuss public administration reform cooperation
World.content:
Head of the Central Agency for Organization and Administration (CAOA) Hatem Nabil discussed with Moroccan Minister Delegate to the Minister of Artificial Intelligence, Digital Transformation and Administrative Reform, in charge of Administrative Reform Aisha Kelaa, ways to enhance cooperation and exchange experiences between the two countries.

Discussions took place during a bilateral meeting held by the two sides in the Moroccan capital, Rabat, on the sidelines of the meetings of the Executive Council of the Arab Organization for Administrative Development, in the presence of the Egyptian Ambassador to Morocco, Ahmed Nihad Abdel Latif.

Talks focused on developing public administration and improving the efficiency of the administrative apparatus.

Nabil stressed Egypt’s keenness on strengthening relations with Morocco, pointing to the experiences that both countries possess that can be built upon to support institutional development efforts and modernization of public administration.

He reviewed the areas of work of the Arab Administrative Development Organization (ARADO) and its role in the state’s efforts to qualify leaders, improve the human resources management system and build capacities, enhance the efficiency of government performance, in addition to modernizing work systems and administrative procedures.

For her part, Kelaa stressed the importance of exchanging experiences between the two sides and benefiting from successful experiences in the field of public administration development, in order to support the priorities of administrative reform in Morocco.

The meeting addressed a number of proposed areas of cooperation, most notably the exchange of experiences in institutional development and restructuring, modernization of human resources management systems and capacity building and training.

The two sides affirmed their desire to continue coordination, communication, and working to identify priority areas of cooperation.

World.title: Liberia: Grassroots Petition Urges Morlu’s Return To CDC
World.content:
Former chairman, who quit in 2024 after a long rift with Weah, is asked to help rebuild the party for 2029

MONROVIA – A group calling itself the “Concerned Partisans, Grassroots Mobilizers, and Supporters” of the Congress for Democratic Change (CDC) on Saturday sent a formal petition to former National Chairman Mulbah K. Morlu, Jr. It asks him to “reconsider your departure” and come back to the party he left more than two years ago.

By Rodney D. Sieh



The petition is dated November 14, 2026 and carries the theme “Experienced, Trusted, Vibrant, Capable, and No-Nonsense Leadership Ahead of the 2029 Elections.” It says its backers come from all 15 counties. No individual signs it.

“We want you back! Not tomorrow. Not someday. Now! Today!” the document says. It ends with the chant “Morlu Must Return!”

What the petitioners want

The petition makes five requests. Morlu should return to the CDC, reconnect with ordinary partisans, lead reconciliation between rival factions, help rebuild the party and work with others to restore its “electoral competitiveness.”

It does not say outright that he should get his old job back. But FrontPageAfrica reported last week that his supporters, organized across Bong, Margibi, Grand Bassa and Montserrado counties, want him back in the party’s top post. As that report noted, a supporters’ petition cannot hand anyone the chairmanship; any change has to go through the CDC’s constitutional and electoral procedures.

The petitioners point to the 2023 result to argue that the party can still win. In the presidential runoff, Joseph Nyuma Boakai of the Unity Party received 814,481 votes and George Manneh Weah received 793,914, a margin of 20,567. The CDC also won 25 of the 73 House seats, the largest bloc held by any single party.

The document lists Morlu’s posts since 2005. They include chairman of the CDC-aligned Progressive Action for Change, vice chairman for operations from 2012 to 2018, deputy campaign manager in 2017 and national chairman from 2018 to 2024. It credits him with leading the 2012 internal campaign that removed then-Standard Bearer Cllr. Winston Tubman and restored Weah as standard bearer. It also says that in 2013 he led 11 members of the Executive Committee in defending Weah’s Senate candidacy, at a time when Robert Sirleaf, son of then-President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, was being promoted as an alternative.

Without naming anyone, the petition says it is not trying to “reopen old wounds, assign blame, or revisit past disagreements.”

Those old wounds

Those disagreements were mostly with Weah himself.

Morlu took over the party when Weah became president in 2018, and even that was disputed. Then-chairman Nathaniel McGill said that after consulting party leaders he would step aside and let Morlu, the vice chair for operations, act as chair until the convention. But a statement signed by then-Secretary General Janga A. Kowo denied that the national chairman had been replaced. Kowo now leads the party.

Morlu went on to win the chairmanship on a white ballot at the CDC’s 7th national convention, and he also chaired the wider Coalition for Democratic Change until he resigned.

The relationship with Weah broke down in December 2019, when an audio recording leaked in which Morlu made disparaging remarks about the president’s personal life. Morlu told this newspaper the remarks were “mere liquor talk,” said out of frustration and anger during the party’s internal crisis. Weah played it down in public: “everyone can get angry and talk,” he said. He saved his anger for whoever made the recording. By then Morlu had been publicly pressing the government to reshuffle the cabinet and dismiss officials who were not performing.

The two sides announced a reconciliation, but it did not last. As the 2023 elections approached, Morlu spoke less and less, mostly through written statements, and he was barely seen or heard during the campaign.

After the defeat, Morlu tried to take charge of the rebuilding. He announced a “CDC Comeback Retreat” to plan the road to 2029. Weah stopped it. He suspended all of Morlu’s plans for a retreat in Grand Bassa County, saying he had not been informed.

Morlu resigned as chairman on February 27, 2024. He blamed the shrinking room for him to do the job effectively and wrote: “I hold no resentment towards anyone for these difficulties, and I do not desire conflict.” FrontPageAfrica learned at the time that Weah had been marginalizing him since the leaked audio. In the letter, Morlu said his disagreements with Weah were “driven solely by my principles and love for the party.”

He promised to remain a lifelong member, but within months he had gone. He left the party and gave up his membership, saying he had been chosen as chairman and lead advocate of Solidarity and Trust for a New Day (STAND).

After that, he attacked Weah openly. In mid-2024 he accused the former president of failing to prosecute Sirleaf-era officials over alleged looting, which he called a criminal conspiracy, and he described it as the “biggest economic crime conspiracy against Liberia”. In August 2025, when Senator Saah Joseph quit the CDC, he claimed party insiders had targeted Morlu and that Morlu had been drugged and beaten. Morlu flatly denied it.

From party boss to street leader

As head of STAND, Morlu has become one of the loudest critics of the Boakai government. He has accused it of police brutality, presiding over a worsening economy, widespread corruption and “political witch hunts” against opposition figures. After the December 17, 2025 “Lead or Leave” protest, police charged Morlu and his deputy, Rev. Festus R. B. Logan, and sent the case to court. The Independent National Commission on Human Rights said a follow-up demonstration on July 17, 2026 drew more than 1,500 people and was largely peaceful.

The movement has also caused friction in the opposition. The Liberian People’s Party distanced itself, accusing STAND of political opportunism and of links to the CDC.

Where the CDC stands now

Kowo has led the party since Morlu left, first as acting chairman. In May, the party said it would begin preparing for an extraordinary national convention to reposition itself. Meanwhile, allies have already started mobilizing for a Weah comeback in 2029.

As of November 8, Morlu had not confirmed any response to the campaign. The CDC leadership has not said in public whether it would welcome him back.

The petitioners say they are ready. “Come back and help rebuild the house you helped construct,” the petition says.

World.title: Liberia: Mulbah Morlu Announces Return to CDC, Says He Is Not Seeking Party Leadership
World.content:
CONGO TOWN– Congress for Democratic Change (CDC) Former National Chairman Mulbah K. Morlu Jr. has announced his return to the opposition party, accepting a petition from grassroots supporters calling for the restoration of his membership.

By Jaheim T. Tumu- [email protected]

Morlu made the announcement on Saturday while responding to a group of CDC supporters who presented a petition urging him to rejoin the party, following his resignation as national chairman in June 2024.



In his response, Morlu made it clear that his return would be as an ordinary member and should not be interpreted as an attempt to reclaim the party’s chairmanship or compete for another leadership position.

Said Morlu, “In response to your petition, my statement makes today represent those who have felt lukewarm about the party and will return. “I hereby restore my membership in the CDC.”

“I am not coming because I desire office,” Morlu said, recalling that he resigned from the chairmanship with six years remaining in his tenure.

He explained that his resignation was motivated by his desire to prevent internal divisions from plunging the CDC into a prolonged political crisis following its defeat in the 2023 presidential election.

According to Morlu, he stepped aside because he believed the party’s survival was more important than holding on to leadership.

He said he was proud that his resignation helped create a period of peace and stability within the CDC.

Morlu also warned that the party must overcome internal disagreements and unite ahead of the 2029 general and presidential elections.

“If I should come back, I can be very relevant even as a full member of the party. I don’t need a title to be effective. I don’t need a title to serve,” he declared.

He further challenged the party’s future leadership to embrace inclusiveness, arguing that a chairman must be capable of bringing together supporters of different factions, including those who may disagree with his leadership.

A successful leader is one that brings people together to form a team, even those that don’t support his leadership,” Morlu said.

Beyond his return to the CDC, Morlu used the occasion to launch a strong criticism of President Joseph Nyuma Boakai’s administration, accusing it of targeting opposition figures through what he described as politically motivated prosecutions and selective justice.

He also called on the CDC to abandon what he termed its policy of constructive engagement with the government and adopt a more confrontational political approach.

Morlu while in the civil society community did not abandon his principles or political independence, maintained that his return would not mean exempt him from being Chairman of the Solidarity Trust for a New Day (STAND)

“I am an accomplished revolutionary. I cannot be bought. I cannot be compromised,” he declared.

He also acknowledged that his decision to return could affect some personal relationships, particularly with individuals who may disagree with his political position.

Despite those concerns, Morlu insisted that political differences should not destroy personal friendships, throwing jabs and alleging that House of Representatives Deputy Speaker, Thomas Fallah refused to allow him entrance to his house after news that he was returning to the CDC as chairman.

He described the CDC as one of Liberia’s most significant political institutions and said its survival must go beyond the ambitions and interests of individual leaders.

“CDC, whether I accept your petition or not, is the future, and CDC must survive or outlive all of us,” he said.

His return comes at a critical moment for the opposition party as it seeks to rebuild its political strength and position itself for the 2029 elections.

World.title: House Agriculture Committee Lauded for Intervention in Contentious Executive Order 166
World.content:
Monrovia, November 13, 2026 – A prominent rubber planter has commended the House of Representatives, through its Committee on Agriculture, for taking a bold step to bring all stakeholders together to examine the controversial Executive Order 166.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

Mr. Charles Bamakpeh, Chief Executive Officer of Meawon Liberia Incorporated, said the Committee’s decision to convene series of roundtable discussions was a welcome intervention that could pave the way for better understanding and a recommendation to the President for a positive reversal of the order.



Since the issuance of Executive Order 166, local rubber farmers across the country have cried foul, arguing that the order disadvantages them while giving leverage to bigger farmers and concessionaires. Many smallholder farmers have expressed frustration on ground that the policy has made it difficult for them to compete and survive in the sector.

Bamakpeh indicated that the House’s intervention is timely and shows that lawmakers are listening to the plight of local farmers.

“This is a bold step by the House of Representatives. Bringing all stakeholders to one table to ascertain the facts surrounding Executive Order 166 is the right thing to do. It will lead to better conversation and a recommendation to the President,” Bamakpeh told legislative reporters at the Capitol Building.

The latest meeting, however, ended prematurely due to the absence of several key stakeholders, including representatives of big concession companies, regulatory authorities, and the Ministry of Agriculture.

According to Committee, the hearing could not properly proceed because of the absences and other irregularities observed. The Committee said it does not want to keep pushing the matter down without proper verification and stressed the need for all relevant parties to be present to ensure a fair and transparent process.

A new date for the hearing is expected to be announced once all parties have been duly notified.

Despite the postponement, Bamakpeh is somewhat excited for the step taken by the House.

“This action should be lauded, though it’s the first step forward.”

He called on the august body to exert further and speedy action to bring the situation to a successful and conclusive end.

“As I said, we appreciate the House for starting this process. We now call on them to act swiftly so that this matter can be brought to a successful and conclusive end for the benefit of all Liberian rubber farmers,” he added.

President Joseph Nyuma Boakai signed Executive Order No. 166 on June 24, 2026, banning the export of unprocessed natural rubber indefinitely, effective July 1, 2026. The order defines unprocessed rubber broadly such as natural latex, coagulum, cup lump, tree lace, bark scrap, ground scrap, and any rubber not subjected to industrial processing.

The government pointed out that the ban is intended to strengthen local processing, create employment, increase domestic value addition, and ensure Liberian rubber farmers benefit more directly from the industry.

But this has somewhat proven indifference, as local farmers believe that it’s an unjust way of taking them from the industry.

World.title: AfDB, World Bank Urge Liberia to Strengthen Institutions to Unlock More Development Financing
World.content:
CPIA workshop identifies weak governance and unreliable data as key barriers, as YEIB-MANCO CEO calls for establishment of National Data Center

By Charles G. Lamadine

Monrovia- The African Development Bank (AfDB) and the World Bank have called for stronger institutional performance, improved governance and reliable national data as critical measures to help Liberia secure increased concessional development financing.



The call was made during a one-day high-level Country Policy and Institutional Assessment (CPIA) workshop hosted on Wednesday by the AfDB Liberia Country Office in collaboration with the World Bank Liberia Office.

The workshop brought together deputy ministers from the Ministry of Finance and Development Planning, Ministry of Agriculture and Ministry of Public Works, alongside senior officials of the Central Bank of Liberia (CBL), technical representatives of both development institutions, the Youth Entrepreneurship Investment Bank Management Company (YEIB-MANCO), and other government institutions and development partners.

The meeting focused on helping government officials understand the CPIA assessment process, examine Liberia’s current performance and identify reforms needed to improve the country’s ratings and access to concessional financing.

The workshop was moderated by AfDB Senior International Consultant, Dr. James Francis Davis, who described the CPIA as an important instrument for measuring the quality of a country’s policies and institutions in promoting economic growth and reducing poverty.

Dr. Davis explained that the assessment forms the foundation of the AfDB’s Performance-Based Allocation (PBA) system, which determines how a significant portion of the African Development Fund’s (ADF) concessional resources is distributed among 37 eligible African countries.

He noted that countries with stronger policies and institutions generally receive greater access to concessional financing, making the CPIA more than a technical assessment exercise.

According to him, Liberia’s performance under the assessment directly influences the volume of development financing it can access and also serves as an important reference for bilateral donors and international development partners.

Liberia’s CPIA Performance Under Review

Presentations during the workshop highlighted the differences and similarities between the AfDB and World Bank assessment frameworks.

While both institutions use nearly identical CPIA methodologies, they independently assess countries to determine their respective concessional financing allocations.

The AfDB presented its assessment methodology and recent scores for Liberia, explaining the relationship between the country’s performance and its allocation under the ADF.

The World Bank, meanwhile, outlined its assessment framework and explained how the ratings influence financing available to Liberia through the International Development Association (IDA).

The CPIA measures the quality of a country’s policies and institutions on a scale of one to six, with one representing the lowest performance and six the highest.

The AfDB framework comprises six clusters and 18 criteria, including an additional cluster on Regional Integration. Unlike the World Bank, which conducts its assessment annually, the AfDB carries out its CPIA assessment every two years.

Data presented at the workshop showed improvements in Liberia’s economic management, particularly in monetary policy, whose AfDB score increased from 3.5 in 2020 to 5.0 in 2025. Fiscal policy maintained a score of 4.0.

However, governance and other institutional performance indicators remain below regional averages, requiring further reforms and sustained government attention.

The World Bank’s assessment placed Liberia’s overall CPIA score at 3.0, with Public Sector Management and Governance recording the weakest performance at 2.6, compared with 3.3 for Economic Management.

Presenters emphasized the financial implications of these ratings, noting that a 0.1-point improvement in Liberia’s overall CPIA score could increase the country’s IDA allocation by approximately 10 to 13 percent.

The workshop also highlighted developments in Liberia’s Debt Sustainability Assessment (DSA), which has indicated an improvement in the country’s debt-carrying capacity from weak to medium.

However, participants were informed that two consecutive positive assessments are required before the improvement can be formally confirmed.

Workshop Recommends Inter-Ministerial Committee

To improve Liberia’s performance, the workshop recommended the establishment of an Inter-Ministerial Committee to coordinate and lead the national CPIA process.

It also called for the preparation of a detailed action matrix covering each CPIA cluster, with measurable targets, clearly assigned institutional responsibilities and implementation timelines.

The proposed committee would be required to report progress monthly or every two months to the Minister of Finance and Development Planning.

Another major recommendation was increased investment in institutions responsible for producing national statistics and ensuring that reliable, up-to-date information is accessible through official government websites.

Participants identified weak data collection, documentation and accessibility as significant obstacles to Liberia’s performance in international assessments.

Rwanda was cited as an example of a country that has made the CPIA an integral part of routine government performance management, contributing to stronger institutional ratings.

YEIB-MANCO CEO Calls for National Data Center

Meanwhile, the Chief Executive Officer of the Youth Entrepreneurship Investment Bank Management Company (YEIB-MANCO), Joseph Fatorma Sando, has called for the establishment of a National Data Center to strengthen Liberia’s data collection, verification and management systems.

Delivering the institution’s statement, Mr. Sando urged the AfDB and World Bank to support the Government of Liberia in establishing a coordinated national data management system that would improve the timely collection and accessibility of credible information across ministries, agencies and public institutions.

He argued that the absence of reliable and verifiable data could negatively affect Liberia’s performance in international institutional assessments, regardless of the progress being made by government institutions.

“A Data Center Coordinator in every ministry, agency and parastatal will minimise the challenges currently affecting the country’s rating, which has a significant impact on economic decisions and investors’ attraction,” Sando stated.

He explained that a coordinated data management system would help Liberia improve its institutional ratings, strengthen its eligibility for concessional financing from the ADF and IDA, and build a stronger investment profile.

“Liberia is doing a lot, but if what we are doing is not documented, verified and made accessible in a timely manner, it will not count in these assessments,” he emphasized.

Sando further maintained that improved data management would strengthen government accountability and provide development partners and investors with credible evidence of the country’s progress.

Why the CPIA Matters to YEIB-MANCO

The workshop also holds strategic importance for YEIB-MANCO, which receives financing from the AfDB under the Program for Advancing Youth Entrepreneurship Investment (PAYEI).

According to the institution, improved CPIA performance could create greater opportunities for development financing and support the expansion of its three principal funding windows: the Investment Fund, Credit Guarantee Fund and Technical Assistance Fund.

YEIB-MANCO also noted that its institutional performance, particularly in procurement, disbursement, auditing and governance, contributes to the broader assessment of Liberia’s AfDB-supported development portfolio.

The institution said its growing database, which includes 1,124 applicants, information on women-owned businesses, financing requirements and employment creation, could provide useful evidence of progress in the country’s youth entrepreneurship sector.

It further highlighted its contribution to regional integration through support for businesses engaged in cross-border trade.

As a non-bank financial institution licensed by the Central Bank of Liberia, YEIB-MANCO said it recognizes the importance of maintaining strong standards of transparency, accountability and fund management.

YEIB-MANCO Pledges Support for Government Reform Efforts

Speaking at the close of the workshop, Sando reaffirmed the institution’s commitment to strengthening its internal governance, operational performance and data management systems to support Liberia’s broader development objectives.

“The CPIA shows clearly that the strength of our institutions determines how much development Liberia can attract. At YEIB, we will continue to strengthen our governance, delivery and data systems so that we contribute to better scores and unlock more financing for young Liberian entrepreneurs,” he said.

He also expressed YEIB-MANCO’s readiness to support any government-led CPIA coordination initiative, including serving as a pilot institution and data partner for private-sector and youth entrepreneurship indicators.

About YEIB-MANCO

The Youth Entrepreneurship Investment Bank Management Company (YEIB-MANCO) is a non-bank development finance institution licensed by the Central Bank of Liberia and financed by the African Development Bank.

Through its Investment Fund, Credit Guarantee Fund and Technical Assistance Fund, the institution provides financing and business development support to youth-led micro, small and medium-sized enterprises across Liberia, with a stated target of reaching 30,000 young entrepreneurs.

World.title: Liberia: Kemayah, Co-Defendants Appeal 10-Year Prison Sentences to Supreme Court
World.content:
As Criminal Court ‘C’ Denies Motion for New Trial Before Sentencing Convicted Officials in US$500,000 Saudi Rice Case

By: Willie N. Tokpah

Monrovia-Foreign Affairs Minister Dee-Maxwell Saah Kemayah and other defendants convicted in Liberia’s controversial US$500,000 Saudi Rice case have announced an appeal to the Supreme Court of Liberia following Criminal Court ‘C’s denial of their motion for a new trial and subsequent imposition of prison sentences.



The announcement of the appeal came Friday, November 13, 2026, shortly after Criminal Court ‘C’, presided over by Judge Ousman Feika, denied the defense’s request for a new trial and proceeded to sentence the convicted defendants at the Temple of Justice in Monrovia.

Kemayah and some of his co-defendants were sentenced to 10 years in prison, while other convicted defendants received five-year prison terms, according to information from the court proceedings.

The decision marks another significant development in one of the most closely watched corruption-related prosecutions arising from the administration of former President George Manneh Weah.

With the motion for a new trial rejected and sentences imposed, the defense has now turned to the Supreme Court, seeking appellate review of the convictions and the proceedings that resulted in the guilty verdicts.

Defense Takes Fight to Supreme Court

The defense team’s decision to appeal follows its unsuccessful attempt to persuade Criminal Court ‘C’ to set aside the October 9 jury verdicts and order a fresh trial.

The motion for a new trial, which was heard on November 6, challenged the outcome of the proceedings involving 13 defendants accused of various offenses connected to the alleged diversion of humanitarian rice donated to Liberia by the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.

The defense had maintained that the jury’s findings were inconsistent with the weight of evidence presented during the trial, which lasted more than 40 days.

However, Criminal Court ‘C’ declined to grant the requested relief, clearing the way for the court to proceed with sentencing.

The defense has now announced its intention to pursue an appeal before the Supreme Court, Liberia’s highest judicial authority.

The appeal is expected to place the trial proceedings, the jury’s findings, the denial of the new-trial motion, and the resulting sentences under further judicial scrutiny.

For Kemayah and his co-defendants, the Supreme Court represents the next available judicial avenue to challenge the outcome of the prosecution.

From Jury Verdict to Prison Sentences

The latest development follows the October 9, jury verdict, which produced mixed outcomes among the 13 defendants.

Eight defendants were found guilty, three were acquitted, while the jury failed to reach unanimous verdicts on two others.

Among those convicted were Kemayah, former Internal Affairs Minister Varney A. Sirleaf, and other former government officials.

The convictions arose from allegations involving the handling and distribution of 29,412 bags of 25-kilogram rice donated by the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Center in April 2023.

The donation was intended to assist disaster victims and vulnerable communities in Liberia.

Prosecutors alleged that 25,054 bags of the donated rice, valued at approximately US$425,918, were diverted from their intended humanitarian purpose.

The defendants faced charges including theft of property, economic sabotage, misuse of public office, criminal conspiracy, and misapplication of entrusted property.

The prosecution argued that the humanitarian donation was improperly handled, while the defense consistently challenged the allegations and the evidentiary basis of the case.

The October 9 verdicts subsequently resulted in the sentencing proceedings now being challenged before the Supreme Court.

Supreme Court Review Could Become Another Major Legal Battle

The announcement of an appeal introduces another important phase in the Saudi Rice prosecution.

Under Liberia’s criminal justice framework, defendants convicted of criminal offenses have the right to seek appellate review of their convictions and sentences in accordance with applicable law and procedural requirements.

The Supreme Court will be expected to examine the issues properly raised in the appeal and determine whether the proceedings complied with the applicable legal standards.

Among the questions that could arise are whether the trial court properly applied the law, whether the evidence supported the jury’s findings, whether any prejudicial procedural errors occurred, and whether the denial of the motion for a new trial was legally justified.

The appellate proceedings will also provide an opportunity for the defense to formally present its objections to the convictions and sentences.

Depending on the arguments and the court’s findings, the Supreme Court may affirm the lower court’s decision, reverse all or part of the judgment, or grant another legally appropriate remedy.

However, the filing or announcement of an appeal does not automatically invalidate the convictions or sentences.

The defendants must pursue the appeal through the prescribed judicial process.

For the Asset Recovery and Property Retrieval Taskforce, AREPT, and the Ministry of Justice, the convictions and sentencing represent a significant stage in the prosecution’s pursuit of accountability.

For Kemayah and his co-defendants, however, the rejection of their motion for a new trial has made an appeal to the Supreme Court their next major legal undertaking.

The three defendants acquitted by the jury remained distinct from those convicted and sentenced, while the two defendants against whom the jury could not reach unanimous verdicts remain subject to separate judicial proceedings.

As the matter moves toward the Supreme Court, the central legal question will no longer be limited to the prosecution’s allegations but will also encompass whether the convictions and sentences can withstand appellate scrutiny.

The Supreme Court’s eventual determination could have implications for the defendants and the broader administration of criminal justice in Liberia.

The Saudi Rice case, therefore, enters a new chapter, from the jury’s guilty verdicts, through the denial of a new trial and prison sentencing, to an impending appeal before the Supreme Court of Liberia.
