World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Trump renews tariff threats as Sheinbaum prepares for China
World.content:
Listen to this article

The second week of November started with news of the arrest of the CJNG operator known as “R2” following a shootout in Guadalajara on Sunday. The focus quickly turned to the economy on Monday, as President Sheinbaum announced a new record for formal employment levels in Mexico and sought to calm worries about the rollout of Mexico’s new Digital Economy Law, designed to phase out some cash payments.

U.S. President Donald Trump threatened Thursday to double tariffs on Mexican goods unless Mexico stops a migrant caravan heading north from Chiapas. The warning came as Mexico seeks lower U.S. duties on steel, aluminum and vehicles. President Claudia Sheinbaum replied that no caravan has reached the northern border during Trump’s second term.

The same trade talks frame her trip to China next week, where she will address APEC business leaders in Shenzhen and meet Xi Jinping. She says the meeting should not complicate negotiations with Washington.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Mexico-U.S. relations: Tariff threat and a wanted ex-prosecutor test bilateral ties

New revelations this week shed light on CIA operations in Chihuahua. The operations, which Mexican authorities call a sovereignty violation, came to light in April and have since been the focus of numerous government investigations.

The New York Times reported Tuesday that Guillermo Zuany Portillo, a former Chihuahua special prosecutor, helped the CIA operate in Mexico in exchange for a U.S. visa. On Wednesday, Sheinbaum called the report “very interesting” and said the CIA’s participation in an April drug lab raid in Chihuahua violated the National Security Law. Former Chihuahua attorney general César Jáuregui was detained last month on a treason charge tied to that raid. Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said federal and state prosecutors hold outstanding warrants for Zuany.

On Thursday, Trump threatened to double tariffs in a Truth Social post, two days after a group of over 1,000 migrants left Tapachula heading north. The tariffs that could be affected include those on Mexican steel, aluminum and vehicles. Sheinbaum said Mexico will not use force against migrants, noting that no caravan has reached the northern border during Trump’s second term in office.

On Friday, after the Times reported that Zuany had fled to the U.S. and is under U.S. government protection, Sheinbaum said she would ask the Security Cabinet for more information. She called his alleged collaboration “very significant, even for the bilateral relationship,” but said she expects no friction because the matter has been discussed with the U.S. government.

China: Sheinbaum’s APEC pitch and a Yucatán research deal

As tensions with the U.S. simmer, Mexico continues to strengthen its relationship with China. On Nov. 6, Mexico’s Culture Ministry and INAH formalized a Maya archaeology project with Shandong University. The project grew out of residents’ objections to a quarry, which INAH sided with before the quarry proposal was quashed. Yucatán Governor Joaquín Díaz Mena then presented it to the Chinese Embassy, citing his aim of expanding Yucatecan exports to China.

At Thursday’s mañanera, Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard said Sheinbaum will be in Shenzhen Nov. 17-19. She will be the main speaker at an APEC Business Advisory Council event, where only she and Xi will address the plenary. She will pitch Plan México to investors and will not meet Trump in China, though she said she will “probably” meet him at the G20 summit in Florida in December. The stakes are tied to USMCA: the Trump administration decided in July not to renew it for 16 years, and U.S. concerns include Mexico’s trade relationship with China.

Economy: Record jobs and solar permits, rising inflation

Economic signals were positive throughout the week. On Monday, Sheinbaum said formal employment reached a record 23,088,353 at the end of October. The same day, inflation rose to 3.75%, above the 3.65% median forecast in a Bloomberg survey and a third straight monthly increase. The previous week, Banxico cut its benchmark rate by 25 basis points to 6.25%. Sheinbaum credited the cut to the economy’s “good performance,” while the central bank said risks to its inflation outlook remain tilted to the upside.

The president also addressed the Digital Economy Law, which gives the Finance Ministry power to designate sectors where only digital payments are accepted. Openbank México CEO Juan José Galnares said it could cut cash use by up to 50% by widening access to credit, but warned against moving too aggressively. Sheinbaum said cash will not be phased out, though gas stations will go cash-free to curb fuel theft.

The MND Sheinbaum Index reflected the economy’s strength. It reached 71.5 for September, its highest score to date, driven by growth and employment data. Business confidence, at 48.4, remained below the 50 neutral benchmark.

In industry, the National Energy Commission approved six solar permits worth US $750 million, adding 649 MW from 2028. Only six of 57 applications met all criteria. Auto parts production hit a record US $11.118 billion in August, though U.S. imports of Mexican parts fell 1% in value in the first eight months. Parts enter the U.S. tariff-free if they comply with USMCA rules.

Tourism: Record totals, slower growth and fewer air arrivals

New data showed that visitation is up across the country, with new records in both arrivals and spending in September. Growth, however, has slowed compared to past years: spending rose 1.4%, against 6.1% a year earlier. Air arrivals, which account for 80% of tourism foreign exchange, have fallen two years running, and Cancún, Los Cabos and Puerto Vallarta airports handled 1.9 million fewer international passengers through October. Private-sector analysts cite the lack of promotion and a 17.8% Non-Resident Tax increase in January.

Mexico City expects 65.9 million tourist arrivals in 2026, up from 61.2 million in 2025. Officials credit concerts, sporting events and cultural activities.

A record-breaking year for sargassum is finally drawing to a close. Quintana Roo declared sargassum season over, a month later than in 2025, with over 150,000 tonnes of seaweed collected.

The influx of stinky algae weighed on Caribbean beach tourism this year, but failed to sink international visitation. Tourism Minister Josefina Rodríguez told the ITB Americas trade show in Guadalajara that culture was the main draw: About 36.3% of visitors came for it, more than double the 15%-16% who came for beaches.

Security: Arrests, an abduction and a homicide data gap

The weekend featured two dramatic security incidents. On Saturday, armed men abducted Río Bravo Mayor Miguel Ángel Almaraz on a highway between Zacatecas and San Luis Potosí. He was found Sunday at a Coahuila police checkpoint and said he escaped.

Also Sunday, the Navy arrested CJNG cell leader Rafael Álvarez Ayala, “R2,” and 19 others in Guadalajara after a shootout. García Harfuch said DEA intelligence helped locate him. He is the brother of the alleged mastermind of Uruapan Mayor Carlos Manzo’s 2025 assassination.

On Monday, García Harfuch announced a 900-million-peso (US $48.2 million) package for Sinaloa, where 22,667 troops are deployed amid a rise in violence that has centered on the resort town of Mazatlán in recent months. Sinaloa’s homicides fell 18.8% in the first 10 months of 2026, yet it ranks fourth in total homicides nationwide.

Then, INEGI reported 29,488 homicides in 2025, 5,140 more than the federal count and the largest gap in more than a decade. INEGI shows a 12.1% decline from 2024; federal data show 21.2%. The Security Ministry says the sources use different methods but show the same trend. On Friday, Sheinbaum said a working group is reviewing the gap.

Good news: Young inventors, robotics wins and a World Cup bid

Looking ahead

At home, Mexicans are hitting their favorite stores as Buen Fin, the annual shopping discount extravaganza, kicks off.

President Claudia Sheinbaum travels to Shenzhen next week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum, where she will court investors and strengthen ties with Asian leaders, including Chinese President Xi Jinping. A meeting with Trump is not on the agenda, leaving Mexico-China relations in the spotlight. However, Sheinbaum plans to meet the U.S. president in December at the G20 summit in Miami. Unresolved tariff and USMCA issues are likely to be on the table when they do.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: From the archive: The joy of having things made in Mexico
World.content:
The goal of our “From the archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article — originally published in January 2025 — explores Mexico’s unique DIY economy, where virtually anything can be made to order.

It’s not that I’m embarrassed, but I do feel a little sheepish writing it: I have, apparently, abnormally large calves. At least for Mexico.

And let me tell you, that makes me pretty sad. I don’t know much about fashion — most currently fashionable clothing looks so silly to me — but I do love a sexy knee-high boot (no heels, please).

Alas, almost every knee-high boot I try on stops zipping up as soon as it hits my calf; they’re just not wide enough. And it’s heartbreaking, because I have seen some really cute boots out there.

But wait! It’s not the end!

Not too far from where I live is a town called Naolinco, famous for its leather products, mainly boots and belts. And if I decide to make a trip up to Naolinco, I can have a pair of boots made just for me! The style, the fit, the color — I can get exactly what I want with exactly the right fit.

Have I done this? Well, no. It’s a little pricey, yes, though not prohibitively expensive. The main thing is that you’ve got to make a day of it. It’s a bit of a drive, and then it’s figuring out exactly what you want and finding someone to make it for you. Then you’ve got to go back to pick them up. Mexico being Mexico, you’re definitely going to want to call and confirm they’re ready ahead of time, even if you’ve got a promised ready-by date.

But I could do it, and that’s the important thing.

And shoes aren’t all you can have made. The sky really kind of is the limit!

Having things made in Mexico: from plush carrots to custom furniture

When my daughter wanted “carrots” for her stuffed rabbit one Christmas, we had little stuffed carrots made. When she wanted “number blocks” from her favorite YouTube math singers, we had those made. And when her tastes became decidedly creepier, we had a bloodied “Canelita” from the “Animal Crossing: New Horizons” crossover made, complete with a detachable Velcro gun. She was over the moon. Oh, dear.

What else can you do? Well, there’s a seamstress a few blocks from my house, for example, who can “clone” clothing items. Just pick out the material, give her the original, and voilà! I’ve got a favorite dress and a favorite pair of pants that will be getting that treatment soon. After last year’s hellishly hot spring season and drought conditions, I’m going to be prepared for this one with the thinnest, lightest clothing I can find!

Speaking of drought, a water catchment system is another thing that you can have fitted to your home. This is something I’m personally dying to do; but alas, I rent. But aside from actual companies that can install these systems, it’s possible to find individuals who can do so, as well.

But the category of things I’ve had made the most of by far is furniture.

The importance of finding a good carpenter

It’s not the easiest thing in the world finding a good, reliable carpenter. So when you find one, hold on to this person for dear life! Because especially in a country where storage can be sparse, it’s important to be able to create options for yourself.

My favorite most recent carpenter-made piece of furniture is my standing desk. I bought the electrical base on Amazon, but skipped their overpriced desktops. Instead, I designed exactly the desktop I wanted, and a carpenter made it for me! We’ve also had a TV stand/bookshelf made to fit a tight living room, and a toy chest that I had fun painting once it was done. In the last house we lived in, I had a loft bed with built-in drawers and a desk made for my daughter. She loved the height and the cave-like feel underneath.

Why, you can even have beer made, a service my partner has provided. Got a restaurant or bar and want a special house recipe? There are people who can design and produce them for you. And of course, food, party favors and decorations for parties of any size can always be found. Themed t-shirts for the parents at birthday parties are currently a big thing in my city, actually. This is overkill if you ask me, but people seem to really get excited about it!

Will your own bespoke designs hit the nail on the head every time? Well, no. I found out a couple of times, for example, that my furniture-designing skills weren’t quite as professional as I thought they were. Fortunately, there are people who know much more about the things they make than we do. Trust them as guides.

The main trouble with having anything made, of course, is finding the right person or business. If you’re new in town or have limited Spanish skills, this can be tough. But if you have friends or at least know some people whose opinion you trust, then that’s your in. This is a country where everybody “knows a guy.” Ask around, and you’re sure to find someone!

And when in doubt or truly at a loss, take a look around Facebook or Instagram; many will have pages that display examples of their work.

So remember: there’s legwork, but it’s fun legwork. Think of it as an adventure and a chance to meet some cool new people. You might get your custom-made stuff and a new friend!

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, sarahedevries.substack.com.

World.title: The death of the night out? How Mexico City’s youth are socializing
World.content:
What if the problem isn’t that young people have stopped going out, but that we’ve been getting the night out wrong all along?

For decades, the formula seemed pretty straightforward: Friday night meant getting dressed up, meeting friends, drinking too much, dancing until the early hours and spending Saturday recovering. Going out was practically a weekend obligation.

But for a growing number of young people, getting wasted is losing its appeal. And the traditional clubbing experience is no longer the default way to socialize.

Instead, think dinner with friends, a long walk, a fitness class, a coffee that turns into a three-hour conversation, or a night at someone’s apartment. Alcohol hasn’t disappeared, and neither has the desire to have fun. But the priorities seem to be shifting.

So, is the night out dying? Or are we simply learning to have a good time differently? In Mexico City, where nightlife has long been part of the city’s appeal, I wanted to find out.

Is Gen Z drinking less?

There is evidence that young people are drinking less in several countries, although the trend isn’t universal. According to the European School Survey Project on Alcohol and Other Drugs, the proportion of European students who reported drinking alcohol in the previous month fell from 55% in 1995 to 43% in 2024. The figures concern school students across participating European countries, not all young adults worldwide.

Mexico offers another interesting example. The country’s 2025 National Survey on Drug, Alcohol and Tobacco Consumption (ENCODAT) found that the percentage of adolescents aged 12 to 17 who had consumed alcohol in the previous month fell from 16.1% in 2016 to 7.5% in 2025. That’s a substantial decline among teenagers, although it doesn’t tell us exactly how much Mexico City’s 20-somethings are drinking.

So, what’s behind the change?

Health consciousness is an obvious place to start. Fitness has become part of everyday life for many young adults, from Pilates and running clubs to strength training and early morning workouts. When your Saturday plans involve a long run rather than nursing a hangover, Friday night suddenly looks different.

There’s also a growing awareness of alcohol’s health risks. We know more about its relationship with sleep, physical performance and long-term health, including cancer. And when social media is full of people sharing their workouts, wellness routines and carefully curated lives, waking up feeling terrible can seem like a particularly bad trade-off.

But there’s a contradiction: The same social media that encourages us to go to bed early also makes us feel as though we should be doing something worth posting about. The perfect workout, the perfect job, the perfect group of friends and the perfect weekend have become another set of expectations to keep up with.

I still tell my friends to send me pictures when they travel. Increasingly, though, they would tell me they can’t wait to see my stories when it’s my turn to go somewhere. Sometimes it feels as if an experience isn’t quite complete until you’ve posted about it.

Could the pandemic have played a part, too? Young people who spent months isolated during formative years may have developed different social habits. But it would be too easy to blame COVID for an entire generation’s changing relationship with nightlife. Technology, money, work, wellness culture and shifting social norms may all be part of the picture.

And there’s another question worth asking: If drinking less is becoming more acceptable, does that mean we’re becoming less social, or simply less dependent on alcohol to socialize?

Everything in moderation

I’ve been doing Dry January for four years. Back in 2022, only one of my friends had even heard of it. She was the one who introduced me to the idea.

At the time, not drinking seemed strange unless you were taking antibiotics. How could you possibly go out and not drink? Every January, I’d find myself explaining why I was doing it and why taking a break from alcohol appealed to me. Most people weren’t particularly interested. They only wanted me to have a glass in my hand.

This year was different. By the end of January, I realized I didn’t really feel like drinking. I didn’t miss it at all, and when the month ended, I didn’t see a reason to start again.

I’d already been going out less, drinking fewer cocktails and mostly having wine when I went to restaurants. My first alcoholic drink of the year eventually came in May, at a friend’s wedding. I had a few cocktails, enjoyed myself and moved on.

What surprised me most wasn’t how easy it was to say no to alcohol. It was how much I enjoyed the mornings afterwards. Waking up after a fun evening with no hangover, enough energy to exercise, go for a walk or visit a museum felt like getting an extra day back.

Mexico City has also made it easier to experiment. There are bars and restaurants where alcohol-free drinks feel like a genuine part of the menu rather than an afterthought. A good mocktail can be just as enjoyable as a cocktail, without the alcohol.

Still, I don’t think everyone needs to give up drinking. If I go to Italy with my best friends, I’ll be more than happy to have a Spritz. At Christmas, I’ll gladly share a bottle of wine with my family.

For me, the shift has been about choice rather than restriction. I don’t want to drink just because everyone else is drinking, or because I’ve convinced myself that a night out requires alcohol. And I don’t think there’s anything wrong with someone who feels differently.

Perhaps that’s the real change: Not that drinking has become unacceptable, but that not drinking is becoming less of a big deal.

What do young people actually want from a night out?

To understand what’s happening in Mexico City, I asked young people about their habits, what they do instead of going out, and what would make them want to go out more often.

In my survey, 55% said they go out less frequently than they did three years ago. Respondents also described drinking less when they do go out. Their explanations were revealing.

Several said their friends simply weren’t interested in going clubbing as often. Instead, they preferred daytime plans, relaxed dinners or meeting at someone’s home. These gatherings felt more intimate and made it easier to catch up, have proper conversations and spend time together without feeling rushed.

Sports and wellness came up, too. For young adults juggling work, studies and other responsibilities, a weekend workout or an early start the next morning can take priority over a late night.

What stood out in my conversations was that the issue wasn’t always a lack of desire to socialize. It was a lack of enthusiasm for the available ways of doing it.

In my survey, respondents talked about wanting clubs closer to home, shorter queues and friends who were more willing to go out. Some described asking their friends to make plans and feeling as though they were begging.

That last detail stayed with me. Imagine wanting to go dancing, getting a group together and feeling as though you’re asking everyone for a favor.

But we should be careful not to confuse a preference for smaller gatherings with a rejection of nightlife altogether. People can want fewer nights out without wanting nightlife to disappear. They may simply be more selective about when they go, who they go with and what makes the evening worthwhile.

In fact, 65% of respondents in my survey said they still went to bars, clubs or parties at least once a week. That complicates the idea of a dying night out. Going out less often doesn’t necessarily mean giving it up.

Are bars noticing the shift?

If young people are changing their habits, what does that mean for the places where they spend their evenings?

I spoke to young people about what they drink and to bar and club owners in La Roma about what they have noticed since the pandemic.

In my survey, respondents described drinking less hard liquor and fewer cocktails, such as gin and tonics or rum and Coke. Beer and wine remained popular, while some said they alternated alcoholic drinks with water or delayed their first drink until later in the evening.

Others admitted that they didn’t particularly enjoy the taste of alcohol. For them, drinking was more about loosening up, feeling more sociable and having fun with friends.

Alcohol-free options therefore have an obvious appeal. But mocktails aren’t a complete replacement for the drinking experience: Some respondents said they found it boring to spend an entire evening drinking sodas or alcohol-free cocktails, particularly when everyone else was drinking.

The message isn’t necessarily that young people want bars without alcohol. They want more choice, a good atmosphere and a reason to stay.

The owner of a bar in La Roma that also serves food offered another perspective on the experience of running a venue where people can eat, drink and socialize. His observations, alongside those of a local club owner, suggest that the relationship between nightlife and the pandemic deserves a closer look.

The club owner described a shift after COVID, with fewer young people going out, while holidays and days off could still bring busy nights, including crowds of international visitors.

These are individual observations, not proof of a citywide decline. But they raise an interesting question for Mexico City’s nightlife industry: If people still want to meet friends, what kind of venues and experiences will persuade them to leave home?

The answer might not be another club with louder music and more expensive cocktails. It could be a place where the music is good but conversation is still possible, where food is as important as the drinks, or where people can spend an entire evening without feeling pressured to keep ordering alcohol.

What does the perfect night out look like now?

For many of the young people I spoke to, the ideal evening sounded surprisingly simple: dinner and drinks with friends, either at a restaurant or at someone’s home. Good food, music they actually like, an intimate atmosphere and, crucially, music that isn’t so loud they have to shout to hear one another.

They still enjoy dancing, meeting new people and discovering new places. But they also want to talk, catch up and feel comfortable.

Perhaps the problem with the traditional night out is that it sometimes asks us to choose between the things we want from socializing. We want music, but we also want conversation. We want to meet new people, but we also want to feel safe. We want spontaneity, but we don’t necessarily want to spend hours queuing or traveling across the city.

And Mexico City has no shortage of alternatives.

The night isn’t dead; it’s simply being redefined.

What if the best place to read were also the last place you’d expect to find a book?

From Tokyo to Amsterdam, book raves have been bringing reading into clubs and cultural venues, turning it into a collective experience. The idea is simple: a book, some music and the pleasure of being together, without the pressure to talk. Less noise, more pages. Silence, too, can bring people together.

Mexico City has its own version of this quieter pleasure. The city’s audioramas, including those in Parque México and Chapultepec, offer spaces where people can sit among the trees and listen to music. I discovered them recently and was fascinated by the idea of spending an afternoon there reading or even learning Italian, as I did on my last visit. Just watch out for the person beside you who might have decided to take a nap and start snoring…

Then there are running clubs, which have turned exercise into a social activity in its own right. From themed runs and coffee meet-ups to longer races that bring strangers together, the possibilities go well beyond a night at the club.

These activities aren’t necessarily replacements for nightlife. They’re reminders that socializing doesn’t have to revolve around alcohol, a late bedtime or a particular kind of venue.

Think about your own life for a moment. When you meet your friends, does it always involve drinking? Could it be a museum, a fitness class, a walk through Chapultepec, dinner somewhere new or a Sunday morning spent running and getting coffee afterwards?

None of these plans is inherently better than going dancing until sunrise. And there’s no reason we can’t enjoy both.

Maybe the death of the night out is really the death of the idea that there’s only one way to have a good time.

Young people still want connection, excitement, music, romance and stories to tell the next morning. They just seem increasingly willing to decide for themselves what those things look like.

So, no, I don’t think the night out is dead.

But perhaps the best night out is no longer the one you barely remember. It’s the one that leaves you with a good story, people you feel closer to and a Saturday morning you’re actually excited about.

And you? What’s your perfect night out?

Marta Delgado is a Spanish writer and marketing professional from Galicia, Spain, currently based in Mexico City. She writes about culture, lifestyle, and what it means to build a life abroad, drawing from her own time living in different countries.

World.title: I grew up watching Mexican stereotypes. Hollywood hasn’t changed much
World.content:
William Nericcio, like most of the roughly 500 million residents living in Mexico, the United States and Canada, grew up watching popular television shows and consuming major media outlets.

As a Chicano raised in Laredo, Texas — one of the most densely populated Latino cities in the U.S. — Nericcio regularly saw himself and his community reflected in popular media. Often, however, those portrayals weren’t very accurate or authentic, instead relying on repetitive tropes and one-dimensional stereotypes that Hollywood has been recycling for generations.

#NewProfilePic https://t.co/lbCa4WKiVl — William Nericcio (@eyegiene) July 6, 2026

Nowadays, as a professor of English and comparative literature at San Diego State University and co-author of “Talking #browntv: Latinas and Latinos on the Screen,” Nericcio’s work largely focuses on the historical depictions and evolving complexities of his community on the screen.

Predictable stereotypes

“There are particularly demented representations of your average Mexican (as being) violent, dirty, lazy,” Nericcio tells Mexico News Daily. “If they’re a woman, they like good sex. They’re gonna take things from you. They’re a spitfire. Temptresses (who) carry daggers. That’s the signifier of our violent deviance as Mexicans.”

While Nericcio admits that he likes shows such as “Breaking Bad” and “Narcos” — two popular series featuring prominent Latino characters — he says that representations of Latin Americans have largely remained stagnant and predictable.

“I watched ‘Better Call Saul’ (the ‘Breaking Bad’ spinoff) and after that, even I would cross the street (after seeing a Mexican person in public),” he jokes. “They don’t just kill. They kill with the artistic vision of Salvador Dalí. It’s killing cubed, masterful.”

Century-old tropes still being used

Of course, those kinds of derogatory character oversimplifications have existed for more than a century, going back to 1894, when the short film “Mexican Knife Duel” premiered, marking one of the earliest known forms of Mexican protagonists in U.S. media.

Quoting the scholar Gary D. Keller, the Library of Congress notes that “These films villainized Mexican men and sexualized Mexican women, a pattern that would recur all throughout the 20th century.”

My childhood through Hollywood’s Mexican lens

As a California-raised Mexican American myself, who came of age in the 1990s and 2000s, I can relate. For decades, Mexican characters have too often been minimized in U.S. media, flattened into binary archetypes. Think Speedy Gonzales, who’s portrayed as charming, quick-witted and brave, or his familial counterpart, Slowpoke Rodriguez, slow but cunning and dangerous.

Some of my earliest memories of action flicks are films like “Desperado” with Antonio Banderas and Salma Hayek. In it, Banderas plays El Mariachi, a stone-cold assassin who packs firearms in his guitar case. Hayek’s Carolina, meanwhile, causes car accidents when crossing the street because of gawking men.

Like Nericcio, however, I’ll admit that “Desperado” was one of my favorite movies growing up.

I can also recall films like “The Sandlot,” which featured the character Benny “The Jet” Rodriguez, a baseball-loving kid who, in retrospect, is arguably one of the most fleshed-out Chicano characters ever portrayed. Rather than focusing on his cultural differences or moral deficiencies, Benny is just a regular kid who dreams of making the big leagues. It felt relatable to me back then, and in many ways still does. Benny’s heritage is neither a strength nor a weakness, and besides the name on the back of his jersey, his latinidad was never a factor.

A.C. Slater, played by Mario Lopez in the popular TV series “Saved by the Bell,” was similarly down-to-earth in the ’90s.

Profit over authentic representation

But those examples of wholesome, fully dimensional Chicano and Chicana figures were hard to come by, in my memory.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Paul Shipper 🎨 (@paulshipper)

“It’s called show business, not show ethnography,” Nericcio says. “It demands a profit. What gets a profit? What has worked before. Hollywood is about rebroadcasting images that are tried and true: the criminality of the Mexican.”

Nericcio goes on to say, “It’s how Trump blasted his way into office. He hoodwinked Latinos by saying he’s good for the economy (and fueling media stereotypes about the threat of Mexican immigrants). Folks fall for this.”

In that sense, what’s shown on the screen has real-world consequences and larger implications. It’s not simply about wanting to see more diverse representations of Chicanos and Chicanas in popular media; it’s about how, by not diversifying characters, beliefs can be formed and popularized to negative ends.

Amongst this deluge of negative portrayals, there have been several authentic representations that, unlike A.C. Slater or Benny Rodriguez, also reflect on the lived experiences of Latin populations.

Nericcio points to two of his favorite examples: 2006’s “Children of Men” and 2008’s “Sleep Dealer.”

Both films are set against a dystopian backdrop, allowing social commentary about immigration, exploitation and labor to be at the core of the films’ messaging.

Perhaps more importantly, though, each film was directed by Latinos, with Alfonso Cuarón helming “Children of Men” and Alex Rivera crafting “Sleep Dealer.”

View this post on Instagram A post shared by CALÓ News Arizona (@calonewsaz)

“It’s sci-fi about the future,” Nericcio says of “Sleep Dealer.” “It follows a cyber-bracero who plugs into the matrix and sells his labor by staying in Mexico. The film broadcasts corporate America’s biggest wet dream. Labor without the Mexicans. We don’t want their bodies; we want their food and their labor … we don’t want to hear them speaking. The film is a brilliant portrayal of Mexican subjectivity on the border in its complexity.”

The push for change in writers’ rooms

Those films, though, don’t often generate as much box office success. “Children of Men” was considered a commercial disappointment and was unable to recover its production budget during its theater run. This, despite receiving fairly critical acclaim and a cult following, including three Academy Award nominations, while being retroactively lauded as one of the best thrillers of its time.

“Latino filmmakers are making stories that feature Latino and Mexican actors, but with storylines that aren’t ripped from the tabloid headlines,” Nericcio says. “But most people don’t watch. The progress that will come, if it will come, will come from numbers. Are more Chicanos in film school? Are more of them breaking into creative spaces? The key is the writers’ rooms.”

In that case, the present and future look as grim as the past.

Under-representation in the film industry

In 2021, the Los Angeles Times reported that “Latino representation among film writers is even worse than Latino representation on screen: Since 2008, Latinos have never constituted more than 5% of employed Writers Guild of America (WGA) film writers, according to the available data.”

Earlier this year, the University of California, Los Angeles shared statistics from the LA Times’ De Los, which found that “in 2024, only 1% of leading roles went to Latinos; less than 5% of directors were Latino; and approximately 2% of writers were Latino. Latinos make up nearly 20% of the U.S. population.”

Same old Hollywood

In 2015, Nericcio attempted to do his part by developing his own show, “Mextasy,” that sought to “rewrite televised borders, rethink televisual borders or fronteras, revealing the pulsing, growing body of Latin America alive and thriving within and outside of Uncle Sam’s unknowing body to celebrate the Latino experience throughout the world.”

The show never took off. But the concept — and the intent — remains as urgent today as it did more than 10 years ago, when Nericcio pitched his idea to networks.

“I’m a Chicano from Laredo, Texas, who thinks I’m Anthony Bourdain,” Nericcio jokes. “But it didn’t get picked up. Hollywood will crush your soul.”

As ever, it’s up to consumers to dictate, through our wallets and watching power, what we do or don’t want to see.

It’s something I think about whenever I have the urge to watch the latest hit show or visit a theater (rare for me as the dad of a toddler, but still). Putting our money behind genuine creatives in the communities we’re from is one of the only ways we have to shift the tides.

Until then, Hollywood will continue Hollywood-ing when it comes to its interpretations of Mexican and Mexican Americans.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: What exactly is the ‘real’ Mexico? A perspective from our CEO
World.content:
Last week we published an article written by Sarah Devries asking the question: “Is the beach the real Mexico?” It resonated with me for a number of reasons.

To begin with, I think Mexico has some of the best beaches in the world and have frequented many of them now for over 30 years. I even convinced my wife to get married on one of them (near Playa del Carmen) many moons ago in a wild Indian/Mexican/American cultural mashup. It was a wonderful experience to see our guests, who were from all over the world, falling in love with the beaches in the same way we had years earlier. I have always told people that when you take into account the sheer beauty, variety and atmosphere of Mexico’s beaches, no other country can come close to competing.

Where else can one find the raw beauty of the beaches of Baja — from Playa Balandra to Todos Santos to those of the Bahía Concepción near Mulegé? The party atmosphere of beaches in Acapulco, Puerto Vallarta, Mazatlán and Manzanillo? The crystal clear waters of beaches in Cancún, Playa del Carmen and Tulum? The incredible nature of the beaches in Oaxaca? And all in one country!

So it resonated with me when Sarah took a bit of offence to her friends and family questioning if the beach was, in fact, “the real Mexico.” I have been told by many foreigners that it is not, despite nearly 10% of the Mexican population living on or near the nearly 7,000 miles of coastline in the country. Going back as far as our wedding, people remarked that they had the time of their lives, but that Playa del Carmen and Tulum aren’t “the real Mexico.” I have heard people raving about their vacations to places as diverse as Cancún, Acapulco, Puerto Vallarta and Los Cabos — only to feel the need to confirm to me that those places, in their opinion, aren’t the “real Mexico.”

I have found myself in a similar situation far from the beach, in my adopted hometown of San Miguel de Allende. Well over a hundred friends and family members have come to visit us over the past few years, and without exception, they have a great time. At some point of their visit, however, a comment is always made that, “You guys aren’t really living in the ‘real Mexico.'” They have told me that I live in a “Mexican Disneyland” or a “Mexican Epcot Center.” It frustrates me, as I am pretty sure that the 200,000 Mexicans living here consider themselves “real Mexicans” who really live in Mexico. It seems like most foreigners seem to consider the places in Mexico that they visit to be somehow less “real.” How weird.

The whole “real Mexico” concept really hit home with me again in just the past few weeks. Two weeks ago, my wife, some friends, and I did the Camino Copalita hike in the mountains of rural Oaxaca. (I will be writing more about this incredible experience soon — stay tuned!)

For five days and nights, we lived off the grid. No electricity, no internet or cell phone signal, no running water (except rivers), sleeping outside, eating what was grown or raised within a few hundred meters of where we slept, and just being in the awesomeness of nearly undisturbed nature along with the few hundred residents that make up the towns along the trail.

Then, immediately after the hike, we spent a week in Mexico City, mostly in the Polanco neighborhood, where my wife was having an art exhibit. Polanco is just about as far from rural Oaxaca as you can get: fancy hotels, international cuisine, high-end boutiques, and both residents and tourists from around the world. As you might imagine, such a quick change in environment was intense — quite jarring actually.

But it brings me back to the “real Mexico” question. Was our time in the rural Oaxacan mountains the “real Mexico”? Was our time in posh Polanco the “real Mexico”? Was neither? Were both? Before answering, think about how you would answer the question in your home country. In the United States, for example, what is “the real U.S.”? I would contend that there is no such thing, that it’s an impossible question, as each state and even each city has such tremendous diversity in its nature, food, people, culture and architecture.

So my answer to the “real Mexico” question is that ALL of it is the real Mexico. The beaches, the colonial mountain towns, the rural south and the big cities. We foreigners need to stop thinking about the country in terms of what is “real” and what is “not real”. The country has an incredible diversity and each place, in its own way, ultimately makes up the fabric of the “real Mexico.” I am thrilled to see an increasing number of travelers venture out from a few tourist areas and start to see for themselves firsthand what the “real Mexico” really means. I am certain that they will find it to be incredibly rewarding.

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.title: Ready to host another World Cup? Mexico-US-Costa Rica-Jamaica joint bid for 2031 women’s tournament likely
World.content:
Mexico appears set to host another World Cup in less than five years after FIFA green lighted a joint hosting bid of which the Mexican Soccer Federation is a part.

FIFA, soccer’s international governing body, announced on Wednesday that the bid to host the 2031 Women’s World Cup submitted jointly by Mexico, the United States, Jamaica and Costa Rica “has a strong foundation” and will be voted on at the Extraordinary FIFA Congress on Nov. 23.

If approved (as the lone bid, it is expected to pass with little difficulty), it would mark the second FWWC to be hosted jointly after Australia and New Zealand co-hosted the 2023 tournament.

The Congress will also be considering the joint bid to host the 2035 FIFA Women’s World Cup (FWWC) submitted by England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

Next year’s FWWC is to be hosted by Brazil and will feature 32 teams and 64 matches. The 2031 tournament will be expanded to include 48 teams and 104 games.

The joint 2031 bid proposes 20 host stadiums across the four countries, with 14 in the United States, four in Mexico and one each in Jamaica and Costa Rica. Mexico’s proposed host cities are Mexico City (Estadio Azteca), Guadalajara (Estadio Akron), Monterrey (Estadio BBVA-Bancomer) and Torreón, Coahuila (Estadio Corona).

Following a thorough assessment of the proposal, including inspection visits to the prospective host countries, FIFA published an evaluation report indicating that the bid exceeded its minimum requirements.

“While certain commitments require further engagement, there is a sound basis for confidence that continued dialogue and collaboration with the relevant government agencies should support the successful organization and delivery of the tournament,” FIFA said.

In endorsing the bid, FIFA acknowledged the success of this year’s men’s World Cup which Mexico and the U.S. co-hosted alongside Canada.

FIFA also praised Mexico’s “longstanding record as a FIFA host, having staged the FIFA World Cup in 1970 and 1986, the FIFA Confederations Cup in 1999 and multiple youth competitions, including the FIFA U-20 World Cup 1983 and FIFA U-17 World Cup 2011.”

The technical evaluation focused on “defined priority areas, including the event vision, infrastructure, services and commercial considerations” as well as FIFA Fan Festival sites, while the risk assessment considered “safety and security, sustainability, human rights and environmental protection.”

As co-host, Mexico’s women’s team would be participating in its fourth FWWC after qualifying for the 1999, 2011 and 2015 tournaments. The El Tri Femenil also participated in the unofficial 1971 Women’s World Cup hosted by Mexico. The first FWWC was held in 1991.

With reports from Reuters, Fox Sports, FIFA and ESPN

03

What to See & Do

SUNDAY IN SÃO PAULO

TODAY’S PICK — ART ON AND AROUND PAULISTA MASP in the afternoon, Japan House to follow Start at MASP on Avenida Paulista, in Bela Vista. It opens at 10am and closes at 6pm on Sundays, and entry is R$85. Go in the early afternoon, once the park walk is done. If rain arrives, you are already under cover. Japan House São Paulo is also on Avenida Paulista. It is free and open until 7pm on weekends, which makes it a good second stop. Take the metro and pay R$5.40 per single journey. Paulista is easy to reach by metro from most central neighbourhoods. If you want one museum only, choose MASP. If the price puts you off, Japan House costs nothing.

OUTDOORS — IBIRAPUERA BEFORE LUNCH Parque Ibirapuera, in Ibirapuera, is open from 5am to midnight and is free. Go in the morning, before any afternoon showers. MAC USP, the modern art museum, is also in Ibirapuera. It opens 10am to 6pm and is free, so it works as a dry fallback.

COFFEE & WHERE TO WORK — PAULISTA AND VILA MADALENA Do your laptop work early and keep the afternoon for museums. If you must work, pick a café near Avenida Paulista and confirm its wifi and Sunday hours before you travel.

THE CONTRASTING PLAY — CENTRO AT A SLOWER PACE Head to Centro for the Mercado Municipal (Mercadão), which is open Sunday from 6am to 4pm. Entry is free. Then walk to the Pinacoteca de São Paulo, in Luz, open 10am to 6pm for R$40. The Museu da Língua Portuguesa, also in Luz, admits visitors until 4:30pm on Sundays.

TONIGHT, AFTER 7 PM The safe evening call is Vila Madalena. Beco do Batman is an open-air street, always open and free. Walk it early in the evening, then pick a bar nearby.

ALSO ON TODAY MASP — Avenida Paulista, Bela Vista — 10am–6pm, R$85, the city’s flagship art museum Pinacoteca de São Paulo — Luz, Centro — 10am–6pm, R$40, Brazilian art in a historic building Japan House São Paulo — Avenida Paulista, Bela Vista — 10am–7pm, free Sesc Pompeia — Pompeia — a cultural centre in a converted factory Museu do Ipiranga — Ipiranga — 10am–5pm, the history museum Farol Santander — Centro — 9am–8pm, R$45, a city viewpoint

04

Getting Around

TRANSPORT

The single metro journey costs R$5.40. No Metrô, CPTM or ride-app disruption has been confirmed for Sunday.

There is no rodízio restriction on Sunday, so no plates are restricted. It resumes on weekdays, so check the plate rules before driving on Monday 16.

05

Where to Eat

LUNCH & DINNER

Lunch: Try the Mercado Municipal (Mercadão) in Centro, open until 4pm on Sundays, and arrive before the afternoon rush. Budget for a sandwich-and-drink lunch rather than a full sit-down meal.

Dinner: Eat in Vila Madalena, around Beco do Batman, where bars and restaurants cluster within a short walk.

06

Practical Info

GOOD TO KNOW

Carry a card and a little cash. Pix is widely used, but a visitor without a Brazilian bank account should rely on a card.

MASP costs R$85 on Sundays, so it is worth arriving early in the afternoon. Keep your phone out of sight on the street, especially around Centro in the evening, and use a ride app after dark.

07

Community & Lifestyle

FOR NEWCOMERS

Sesc Pompeia, a cultural centre run by the Sesc social-services network, is a good place to meet people; check its Sunday hours first. Newcomers can plug in by joining the crowd at Parque Ibirapuera in the morning, when many runners and walkers are out.

08

Game Day

THE WEEKEND ROUND

No kickoff time for a São Paulo club match on Sunday has been confirmed, so no fixture or bar is named here. If a Corinthians, Palmeiras, São Paulo FC or Santos match is on, check the club’s official page for kickoff in BRT.

09

Business & Markets

WEEK IN FIGURES

Friday’s close was mixed. Brazilian stocks rose, while Wall Street ended lower and tech shares led the fall.

The dollar firmed against the real and the Colombian peso, and Argentine stocks fell. The Business & Markets / WEEK IN FIGURES board carries every figure.

Markets are shut at weekends, so the next move comes at Monday’s open.

10

Plan Ahead

THE WEEK

THE DAYS AHEAD SUN 15 — Ibirapuera in the morning, MASP (R$85) or Japan House (free) after lunch MON 16 — Pinacoteca, Luz, open 10am–6pm for R$40; rodízio resumes on weekdays TUE 17 — MASP is free all day (book online); the Pinacoteca is closed WED 18 — Museu do Ipiranga, Ipiranga, free on Wednesdays, 10am–5pm THU 19 — Japan House, Avenida Paulista, free, open 10am–6pm

FAQ

QUICK ANSWERS

What is open in São Paulo on a Sunday?

MASP, the Pinacoteca, Japan House, Sesc Pompeia and the Museu do Ipiranga are all open. Parque Ibirapuera is open from 5am to midnight. The Mercadão closes at 4pm on Sundays, so go for lunch.

How much is the metro?

A single journey costs R$5.40. The metro is the quickest way to reach Avenida Paulista.

Is there a rodízio today?

No. The rodízio does not apply on Sunday. It resumes on weekdays, so check the plate rules before driving on Monday 16.

In plain English Mexico and Jamaica are playing two matches against each other, and the combined score (the aggregate) decides who moves on. Jamaica won the first one away from home, so Mexico must now win the second in front of its own fans.

Published Saturday, November 14, 10:58 p.m. ET (9:58 p.m. Monterrey) · Source: Concacaf, Mexican Football Federation, official match data

Mexico spent an hour in Kingston chasing a match that was already slipping away, then almost clawed it back. Jamaica won the first leg 3-2 on Saturday night in the quarterfinal of the Concacaf Nations League, the national-team tournament of North and Central America and the Caribbean, in the Mexico vs Jamaica tie that now swings on Tuesday in Monterrey.

Mexico trailed 3-0 before two late goals cut the gap to one. It was the first official match for coach Rafael Márquez, the former Barcelona defender, as we reported in our preview of the first leg.

Gilberto Mora, an 18-year-old Mexico midfielder, pulled one back in the 70th minute with a shot from outside the box. It made the score 3-1.

Eleven minutes later, Mexico’s Julián Quiñones converted a penalty in the 81st minute. The spot kick came after Jamaica’s Ronaldo Webster fouled Mexico substitute Santiago Sandoval inside the area, and it made the score 3-2.

The second leg is on Tuesday, November 17, at 9:30 p.m. ET (8:30 p.m. in Monterrey) at Estadio BBVA. Jamaica leads the tie 3-2 on aggregate, the combined score over both matches, so Mexico trail by one goal.

The winner of the tie goes to the Nations League Finals in March 2027 at SoFi Stadium, the NFL arena in Los Angeles, and to the 2027 Gold Cup, the region’s continental championship. The loser drops into the Gold Cup preliminary round.

World.content:
File photo from 2015: Ramy Bensebaini in training at Montpellier. Photo: 34 super héros, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Africa · Football

Published Saturday, Nov. 14, 7:46 p.m. ET (1:46 a.m. Sunday, Algiers) · Source: Rio Times match desk, two independent match reports, Polymarket

Togo held Algeria goalless for 75 minutes, and then one cross settled the night. Captain Ramy Bensebaini headed in the winner in the 76th minute, and Algeria beat Togo 1-0 on Saturday evening, Nov. 14, in Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) qualifying.

In plain English The Africa Cup of Nations is the continent’s national-team championship, and teams must qualify in four-team groups first. The top two in each group go to the finals, which Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda host from June 19 to July 17, 2027.

A Stubborn Togo, Then One Cross

The first half finished goalless, and Togo kept Algeria out for more than an hour. Then Anis Hadj Moussa, an Algeria attacker, whipped in a cross and Bensebaini met it with his head.

Bensebaini is a defender who captains the team, so the winner came from the back line. The match was played at the Hocine Aït Ahmed Stadium in Tizi Ouzou, a city in the Kabylie mountains east of Algiers.

File photo: the Great Mosque of Algiers, in the capital. It was not taken at the match.

What the Win Does to Group I

Algeria now have seven points from three games, three more than Zambia in second place. They opened the campaign with a 3-1 win over Zambia in Tizi Ouzou and have not lost since.

Only the top two teams in each group qualify, so three points on Saturday matter more than the scoreline suggests. Each team plays six games, which leaves the group at its halfway point.

Tuesday’s Return Match in Lomé

Algeria travel to Togo for the return fixture at the Stade de Kégué in Lomé on Tuesday, Nov. 17. A second win would lift Algeria to 10 points with two games left.

Togo, nicknamed the Éperviers, or Sparrowhawks, will need points at home to stay in the race. We could not confirm a kickoff time for that match.

Polymarket, a prediction market where people trade real money on outcomes, priced Algeria at 10.5% to win the whole 2027 tournament as of 7:46 p.m. ET on Nov. 14, on US$22,515 traded. Morocco led that market at 32.5%, followed by Senegal at 19.4% and Ivory Coast at 12.3%.

We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What It Means for US Readers

Algeria are two-time African champions, winning in 1990 and 2019, and a strong qualifying run keeps them on course for the 2027 finals. The tournament runs from June 19 to July 17, 2027.

No source we reviewed gave the kickoff time, the attendance or the full line-ups. The reports also label the group differently, Group I in most and Group Nine in one, and we use Group I.

We found no match report from the Confederation of African Football, the sport’s governing body in Africa, at the time of writing. The points tally for Togo and Burundi was not confirmed to our standard, so we do not print it.

World.title: Mexican Singer Gabito Ballesteros Detained
World.content:
Mexico’s federal prosecutors, the Attorney General’s Office (FGR), have opened an investigation into singer Gabito Ballesteros after state police detained him in Querétaro following a fair concert that was cut short.

Gabito Ballesteros, a 27-year-old Mexican singer of corridos tumbados, was detained at 04:00 on Saturday 14 November 2026 in Santiago de Querétaro, central Mexico. Corridos tumbados is a young style of regional Mexican music, often with lyrics about narco-culture, the world of drug trafficking.

The case matters beyond Mexico because a concert at a public fair ended with a federal firearms investigation. It also puts a dispute over an approved song list at the centre of the night.

Key Facts —Who. Gabito Ballesteros, 27, singer of corridos tumbados, a young Mexican regional music style. —What. Detained by Querétaro state police; Mexico’s federal Attorney General’s Office (FGR) opened an investigation. —Where. Santiago de Querétaro, central Mexico, after a show at the Querétaro International Livestock Fair. —When. Detained at 04:00 on Saturday 14 November 2026; legal status due “in the coming hours”. —Status. As of 15 November 2026, 00:30 GMT

What We Know

The National Detentions Registry (RND), the federal public register of arrests, lists Ballesteros as detained by the Querétaro state police at 04:00 on Saturday 14 November 2026. It says he was placed at the disposal of the Ministerio Público, the public prosecutor, and was presented before the Ministerio Público of the FGR, according to the registry entry.

The registry does not state the alleged offence, but the FGR, Mexico’s federal Attorney General’s Office, said it opened an investigation. It covers alleged carrying of a firearm for exclusive use of the armed forces, and “disobedience and resistance by private individuals”.

The FGR said on 14 November that the investigation covers Ballesteros and four other people, five in total. It said one pistol, two magazines and 34 cartridges were found in a vehicle, and that it will determine whether the group held the permits.

Latin America Power Index · November 2026 edition Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 with 70.8 points. Strongest pillar: economic relationships (90); weakest: state capacity & security (46). Alignment group: Hedging. Watch21 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.7 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The FGR said the legal status of all five would be decided “in the coming hours”. Until then, all five are suspects and presumed innocent, not convicted.

Ballesteros’s real name is Gabriel Ballesteros Abril, and he was born on 23 July 1999 in Cumpas, in the northern state of Sonora. He is known for “AMG”, a song recorded with fellow singers Natanael Cano and Peso Pluma.

File photo: the aqueduct in the city of Querétaro, Mexico.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Querétaro (Mexico) Email address Follow

What the Organisers and the Singer Say

Ballesteros performed on the night of Friday 13 November at the Feria Internacional Ganadera de Querétaro, the Querétaro International Livestock Fair. The show was on the fair’s Teatro del Pueblo (People’s Theatre) stage, and the organising committee says the repertoire had been reviewed beforehand.

The committee says he breached the approved repertoire twice. It says inspectors from El Marqués, the municipality hosting the fair, took him off stage after the first.

According to the committee, he returned and played “AMG”, and the show was then cancelled and the sound cut. Authorities described this as possible “apología del delito”, meaning public glorification of crime.

Local rules against shows that glorify crime, as reported by the authorities on 14 November, allow fines of up to 10,000 UMAs. A UMA is Mexico’s inflation-linked unit for fines and fees, and no fine has been confirmed.

Ballesteros gave a different account in a livestream on 14 November, which authorities have not confirmed. He said he had been given restricted song titles and that “AMG” was not among them.

He said he had been told he could sing “AMG”. He also said police held his security team, disarmed his escorts and used gas to make him leave his car.

He asked in the livestream: “What was my crime?” His claim that he was cleared to sing “AMG” is the strongest counter-view to the organisers’ account that he went beyond the approved list.

What Is Not Known

The registry lists only Ballesteros, while the FGR names five people, while one early report counted six people and two firearms. The FGR has not said who owned the pistol.

It is not known whether charges will be filed, or what the permit check will find. It is also not known whether Ballesteros has been released, or how the FGR links “AMG” to the case.

The FGR gave no date for its next step, only the phrase “in the coming hours”. That leaves no scheduled checkpoint to follow.

What It Means for Fans and Travellers

The dispute turns on a simple clash of accounts. The organisers say an approved list applied, while he says he was cleared to sing “AMG”.

In this case, municipal inspectors enforced a set list on the night, according to the organisers. Whether that was done fairly is exactly what the two accounts dispute.

The case also tests where the line sits between a song and a crime. Authorities have called the show possible “apología del delito”, but the FGR’s announced investigation names a firearm and disobedience, not that offence.

The prosecutors’ decision on the five suspects will show whether the case moves to court. More coverage is in our Mexico section.

More: Mexico news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Gabito Ballesteros?

Gabriel Ballesteros Abril, 27, was born on 23 July 1999 in Cumpas, Sonora. He sings corridos tumbados, a young Mexican regional style, and is known for the song “AMG” with fellow singers Natanael Cano and Peso Pluma.

Why was Gabito Ballesteros detained?

The National Detentions Registry shows Querétaro state police detained him at 04:00 on Saturday 14 November 2026 but does not state the offence. The FGR is investigating alleged firearm carrying and disobedience.

What does Ballesteros say happened?

In a livestream on 14 November he said “AMG” was not among his restricted titles and that he had been told he could sing it. Authorities have not confirmed his account.

Has Gabito Ballesteros been charged?

Not as of 15 November 2026, 00:30 GMT. The FGR said the legal status of all five suspects would be decided “in the coming hours”, and all are presumed innocent.

World.title: Lesotho Bank Runs World Cup Card Contest
World.content:
A road junction in Maseru, Lesotho’s capital. File photo.

LESOTHO · BANKING

FNB Lesotho (First National Bank of Lesotho), part of South Africa’s FirstRand financial group, and Visa, the global payments company, ran a prize contest for customers who paid by card around the 2026 FIFA World Cup. The bank says the aim was to move shoppers from cash to digital payments.

The contest terms published by the bank say it closed on 31 July 2026. Press reports say weekly prize draws started on 1 June 2026 and listed monthly prizes, including a three-month salary payout.

Key Facts Contest “Get In The Game with Effortless Payments”: FNB Lesotho Visa debit card users were entered automatically.

Weekly prizes From 1 June 2026, press reports say: petrol, paraffin (kerosene) vouchers and cash.

Monthly prizes Press reports list a three-month salary payout, grocery vouchers and cash.

Open We found no published entry numbers, winners or total prize value.

A South African-owned bank in Lesotho used football fever to push card payments.

Rio Times membership Read everything we publish for US$1 in the first month. Then US$8.99 a month. Cancel anytime. Start for US$1

How the Contest Worked

Customers who swiped, tapped or paid online with their FNB Lesotho Visa debit cards were entered automatically if eligible, according to the contest terms. Winners were drawn at random from customers who paid by card at least three times a week, the terms say.

Press reports listed the weekly prizes as petrol vouchers, paraffin vouchers and cash, starting on 1 June 2026, and the monthly prizes as a three-month salary payout, grocery vouchers and cash. The terms themselves name cash, petrol, grocery and paraffin prizes.

A street in central Maseru, Lesotho’s capital. File photo. Photo: Ymblanter, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on World Cup 2026 Email address Follow

What the Bank Said

Delekazi Mokebe, chief executive of FNB Lesotho, said the contest was launched as excitement built for the World Cup. Nthabeleng Khoali, the bank’s head of retail, said the bank wanted to encourage “effortless and secure payments” while rewarding customers weekly and monthly.

FNB also urged local businesses to take up FNB Speed Points, its card payment terminals, so that they could accept card payments. A cashless shift needs shops that take cards as well as customers who carry them.

Why It Matters

The contest rewarded small everyday purchases, such as groceries or fuel, with a chance of a prize. Visa supplied the prizes, according to press reports.

For FNB, the contest builds card activity and more shops that accept cards. Our Lesotho explainer gives the wider economic background.

See also our report on Lesotho’s road rebuild.

What Is Not Known

The number of entries, the winners and the total prize value have not been published, as far as we found. Press reports gave end dates of 3 July and 31 July 2026, and the contest terms confirm 31 July.

The terms give a start of 1 March 2026, earlier than the 30 April in press reports, and they set no date for the weekly draws. We make no claim about how much cash is still used in Lesotho.

Frequently Asked Questions

What was the FNB Lesotho and Visa contest?

It was a prize contest for customers who paid with FNB Lesotho Visa debit cards around the 2026 World Cup. Press reports list vouchers, cash and a three-month salary payout as prizes.

When did the contest run?

The contest terms say it closed on 31 July 2026. Press reports say weekly prize draws started on 1 June 2026.

Who is FNB Lesotho?

FNB Lesotho is First National Bank of Lesotho, the Lesotho bank of South Africa’s FirstRand group, which is listed on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange.

World.title: Lesotho Farmers Told to Prepare for El Niño
World.content:
Kingsway Road in central Maseru, Lesotho. File photo. Photo: Paramente Phamotse, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

LESOTHO · AGRICULTURE

Lesotho’s farmers were told in August to prepare early for El Niño, the warm Pacific weather pattern that can bring drought to southern Africa. Standard Lesotho Bank, part of South Africa’s Standard Bank Group, hosted the forum in the capital, Maseru, where the UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and the national weather service also spoke.

The forum heard that November to April is the critical period for Lesotho, so the advice is relevant to the current season. The bank’s chief executive pointed to crop insurance as one way to limit weather losses.

Host Standard Lesotho Bank, with the FAO and Lesotho Meteorological Services.

Season The forum heard that November to April is the critical period for Lesotho.

Forecast Lesotho Meteorological Services says El Niño could be strong but relatively short.

Open No new bank product or fund was announced.

A bank, a UN agency and forecasters asked Lesotho’s farmers to turn weather warnings into early action.

What the Speakers Said

Mokitinyane Nthimo, an FAO representative, urged farmers to act early on water management and to ask whether plans exist to harvest and store water. Nthimo also advised farmers to use climate information when choosing planting dates and seed varieties.

Samuel Seboka, chief executive of Standard Lesotho Bank, said farmers, government, development partners and financial institutions must work together to withstand climate shocks. He said forecasts should be translated into practical action, not just received as information.

Houses on the edge of Maseru below Qoaling mountain, Lesotho. File photo.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Lesotho Email address Follow

The Forecast

Rammolenyane Lethaha, a forecaster and spokesperson for Lesotho Meteorological Services, said many farmers lack clear climate information. Lethaha said the service is developing a weather application to make it simpler.

Lethaha also said the El Niño could be strong but relatively short, with a possible shift back to La Niña, its cooler opposite, by February. August, Lethaha added, was a key month for improving rainfall projections for the coming season.

Why It Matters

The forum heard that the critical period for Lesotho runs from November to April, which is the season now under way. Seboka named crop insurance as one way to manage weather losses.

For readers following Southern African banks, the event shows a lender positioning itself on climate risk rather than announcing a product. Related reading: Burundi’s El Niño needs and our Lesotho explainer.

What Is Not Known

The forum reports describe no new Standard Lesotho Bank product, fund or lending target. We could not find a statement from the bank itself on the event, so this account rests on the speakers’ remarks as reported on 12 and 14 August 2026.

How strong the El Niño will be in Lesotho, and when it will end, remains a forecast that Lesotho Meteorological Services is still refining.

What was the El Niño forum in Maseru?

The Agribusiness Drought Proofing Stakeholder Forum was held in Maseru in August 2026 and hosted by Standard Lesotho Bank. The FAO and Lesotho Meteorological Services also spoke.

Which months are critical for Lesotho’s farmers?

The forum heard that the critical period for Lesotho runs from November to April.

Did Standard Lesotho Bank launch a new product?

No new product, fund or commitment was reported. Its chief executive, Samuel Seboka, highlighted crop insurance as a way to manage weather losses.

World.title: Costa Rica Banks Pay as Little as 436 Colones per Dollar – Here’s How to Get More
World.content:
If you are changing dollars into colones, where you do it matters more than ever. With the dollar at a record low, Costa Rica’s banks closed Friday buying dollars for between ₡436 and ₡440 each, according to Central Bank of Costa Rica (BCCR) data compiled by El Observador. On $1,000, the gap between the best and worst of those rates is ₡4,000, or about $9.

The dollar closed Friday at a weighted average of ₡446.10 on Monex, the foreign exchange market run by the BCCR, a new record low and the lowest level since Monex began operating in 2006. It was the eighth straight session of declines and broke the previous record of ₡446.80, set on Sept. 17. The dollar has lost 10.3% of its value against the Costa Rican currency so far this year, according to El Observador.

Bank counter rates, as reported to the BCCR on Friday, varied by up to ₡4 per dollar. Banco Cathay offered the most, buying dollars at ₡440 and selling them at ₡452.50. Banco Nacional and BAC bought at ₡439 and sold at ₡453. Banco de Costa Rica (BCR) and Banco Popular bought at ₡438 and sold at ₡452. BCT paid the least, buying at ₡436 and selling at ₡454. The BCCR’s official reference rate in effect for the weekend is ₡442.56 for buying and ₡448.34 for selling.

Every bank pays less than the market rate when you sell it dollars. At BCT’s ₡436, changing $1,000 brings in ₡10,100 less than the Monex average, about $23. For a retiree converting a $2,000 monthly pension, choosing the best counter rate over the worst is worth about ₡8,000 a month. Changing money twice costs even more. At Banco Nacional’s rates, converting dollars to colones and back again loses ₡14 on every dollar, or roughly $31 on $1,000.

The BCCR publishes the buying and selling rate of every bank and exchange house each business day on its website, so you can compare before you go. Rates posted on Friday afternoon generally carry through the weekend, but they will move again when Monex reopens on Monday. If you already bank in Costa Rica, ask whether your bank applies a different rate to conversions made through online banking than at the teller window.

If you are paying with a foreign card, choose colones when a card terminal or ATM offers to charge you in dollars instead. That on-the-spot conversion, known as dynamic currency conversion, usually uses a less favorable rate than your card network applies. Shops, restaurants and tour operators that accept cash dollars set their own exchange rate, so it is worth checking it against the bank rate before you pay.

The Central Bank has been buying heavily without stopping the slide. On Friday it bought $41.8 million, or 84.8% of the $49.3 million traded on Monex, including $32.3 million in purchases meant to stabilize the market, according to El Observador. Its stabilization purchases total $1.39 billion so far in 2026, with no stabilization sales recorded. Specialists have said the dollar’s decline tends to deepen toward the end of the year, particularly in November, as companies pay year-end aguinaldo bonuses and taxes in colones.

For residents whose income arrives in dollars, including retirees, remote workers and landlords who charge rent in dollars, the slide has meant a steady loss of purchasing power. By early November, each $1,000 bought 46,810 fewer colones than in January, and the weak dollar has also hit businesses that earn in foreign currency, from exporters to Costa Rica’s medical tourism industry. With no sign yet that the slide is ending, the few colones you gain by shopping around for a rate are among the only savings within your control.

World.title: Costa Rica Moves to Demolish Narco Airstrips Without a Conviction
World.content:
Costa Rican authorities could destroy clandestine airstrips used by criminal groups without waiting for a final court ruling, under a bill that cleared a key legislative committee this week with unanimous support.

The Security and Narcotrafficking Committee approved the bill on Thursday. It is titled the Law to Sanction and Disable Clandestine and Unauthorized Airstrips and Allow the Confiscation of Assets Linked to Illicit Activities. The bill now goes to the full Legislative Assembly for a first-round vote and is not yet law.

President Laura Fernández submitted the measure in June as one of six bills in her administration’s package against organized crime. It is the fourth of the six to clear the committee. Under the bill, the Civil Aviation Directorate (DGAC) would declare an airstrip, airfield or helipad clandestine or illegal through a reasoned administrative resolution. Owners, tenants and administrators would first get a 10-business-day hearing to present evidence.

Once that resolution is final, the Public Security Ministry’s Air Surveillance Service could disable, demolish or destroy the site, with help from other agencies and municipalities. The rules would cover facilities used for drug trafficking, money laundering, human trafficking and organized crime.

Prosecutors could also ask a criminal judge to freeze the property in the National Registry, which would block its sale, donation, transfer or mortgage while the measure is in force. Machinery, vehicles and aircraft used to build or operate the strips could be seized and later permanently forfeited. The Costa Rican Drug Institute (ICD) would administer them.

The bill raises the prison sentence for building, enabling, facilitating or allowing a clandestine airstrip from the current three to eight years to five to 10 years. Owners, tenants or administrators who rebuild, rehabilitate or reuse a strip that authorities have already closed or destroyed would face 10 to 15 years.

Fines for operating aircraft at unauthorized facilities would double, from 20 to 40 base salaries. Deputy Kattia Calvo of the governing Pueblo Soberano party said changes were added to guarantee due process, including a way for property owners to present evidence of their innocence. Social Christian Unity Party deputy Abril Gordienko backed the bill, noting that clandestine strips can also enable crimes beyond drug trafficking.

Frente Amplio caucus leader José María Villalta said it was the first bill the committee had discussed that could truly hit organized crime, because it targets the assets criminal groups use to operate. He also raised procedural concerns. He warned that a separate bill on tourist airparks could create conflicting rules on air surveillance.

Costa Rica already allows the Air Surveillance Service to identify, declare illegal and disable clandestine strips under Law 9902, in force since 2020. According to the new bill’s statement of purpose, that law has no specific tools to act on the assets used to build or maintain the strips.

How many strips exist is unclear because they are built to go unnoticed. Fernández has said there are close to 200. The Public Security Ministry’s last official figure, from 2020, put the number of identified unauthorized strips at more than 140, and at least 20 were reported destroyed between the law’s entry into force and the end of 2024.

Some legal analysts have questioned whether the property freeze adds much to existing organized crime and registry security laws. They have also warned that a landowner may not know a strip is operating on their land. The bill now awaits a first-round vote in the full Assembly.

World.title: Italian Wanted in 2021 Santa Cruz Killing Extradited to France
World.content:
Costa Rica extradited two men to France on Thursday afternoon. One of them is an Italian national investigated in connection with the 2021 shooting death of a French citizen in Santa Cruz, Guanacaste. The Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) identified the men as Gianni Marco Basile, 68, and Iván Javier Pablot Martínez, 48, a Colombian-born naturalized Costa Rican.

French authorities want them in separate cases. Basile is sought on suspicion of aggravated homicide and extortion, and Pablot on international drug trafficking charges. Agents from the OIJ’s Special Tactical Response Service (SERT) escorted both men from La Reforma prison to Juan Santamaría International Airport in Alajuela. There they were handed to French officials and flown on a commercial flight to Charles de Gaulle Airport in Paris.

INTERPOL’s National Central Bureau in San José coordinated the transfer, and the Public Prosecutor’s Office directed the case. Attorney General Carlo Díaz said the extraditions are part of the international judicial cooperation mechanisms through which Costa Rica responds to requests from other countries.

According to the OIJ, Basile is investigated for his alleged role in the killing of Pierre Claude Gazel, a French citizen who died on Oct. 5, 2021. The agency said Gazel was shot in front of his home in Santa Cruz at around 6:40 a.m., and the gunman fled on a motorcycle with another person.

The OIJ said French investigators identified prior conflicts and communications between Basile and Gazel. Because the victim was French, authorities in France chose to prosecute the case there. A judicial authority in Paris issued an international arrest warrant for Basile on Feb. 14, 2025.

OIJ INTERPOL agents tracked Basile for about two months before finding that he lived in Escazú, west of San José. They arrested him on Nov. 7, 2025, while he was driving in Curridabat. A criminal court in San José’s Third Judicial Circuit authorized his extradition on June 3, 2026. Pablot was detained in September 2025 by OIJ agents who specialize in organized crime. French authorities allege he belonged to a network that shipped drugs from Colombia to France and other European countries.

The case dates to Nov. 22, 2011, when French customs officers in Marseille arrested two Colombians carrying 29 kilograms (64 pounds) of cocaine. Investigators found the group allegedly used a company that sold wooden houses as cover for moving drugs into Europe. French authorities linked Pablot to the group, where he allegedly worked with a man known as “El Viejo.”

Case documents cited in local reports indicate that a criminal court in Marseille sentenced Pablot to nine years in prison on drug trafficking charges. A San José criminal court authorized his extradition on in April and an appeals court later upheld the decision. The OIJ described Pablot’s case as one of the first extradition proceedings coordinated with France over international drug trafficking. A second man detained with Pablot and named in the same French case, Hamilton Fernando Restrepo Osorio, has not yet been extradited.

Both cases now pass to the French courts. The transfers add to a growing number of extraditions out of Costa Rica this year, as the country handles more requests from abroad tied to violent crime and drug trafficking.

World.title: The Local Pharmacy and the Surprises of Costa Rica Life
World.content:
Your local neighborhood pharmacy is a one-stop-for-all-your-health-needs institution. Last year, a law passed requiring a doctor’s prescription for many types of antibiotics and other stronger drugs.
