Before that, you could self-medicate with your choice of uppers, downers, painkillers and plain old antibiotics if you knew which pharmacy to frequent.

I knew a guy who walked into one with the word ‘clonazepam’ written on a piece of paper and told the person at the counter that he was a truck driver in the states, and this was prescribed it for his insomnia, and wouldn’t you know it, he was suffering from the same sleep issue here and could anyone help? They could. A few minutes after a brief consultation with the pharmacist, he walked out with a bottle of high potency valium.

My first experience with a pharmacy took place in a back room. I knew I wasn’t in the US anymore when the pharmacist led me behind the counter, closed the door, instructed me to drop my trousers, and injected me in the thigh with a shot of epinephrine ( better known as adrenaline).

The reason for the shot was that I had been hit with asthma so severe that every breath sounded like I had just tried to run to the top of Chirripo. I’d spent a sleepless Saturday night seated in a rocking chair as I was unable to breathe lying down. It was rainy season and I was living in a half finished cabina that provided little protection from the elements. A tropical front had arrived, the rain came down in torrents, wind howled off the nearby Fila Tinamastes, and I was no match for the elements.

Sunday morning I was driven to a pharmacy half an hour away. Every shallow wheezing breath felt like it could be the last. The jab of the pharmacist’s needle brought instant relief. I had received this same injection as a teen, for the same reason. There it was done by a doctor, and I still remembered the doctor’s instruction to remain seated for several minutes after the injection as there is risk of a sudden drop in blood pressure.

The pharmacist here gave me no such instruction. He was not a medical doctor after all, just a guy who could measure out the proper dosage and give an injection. I stayed put in the back room, puzzling the pharmacist. Many pharmacies now have a doctor on duty during business hours, in order to write the antibiotic or clonazepam prescription that is no longer available over the counter. Still, I am always surprised by what is available without a doctor.

A while back I pinched a nerve in my upper back and the pain ran from my neck down to the fingers on my left hand. I was about to leave for a visit stateside and needed relief. My stepson is an RN in the local hospital and he gave me a list for purchase from the pharmacy. I bought a syringe and several ampules of painkiller. My stepson injected me at home. No doctor or prescription necessary.

There remain smaller mom and pop pharmacies in Costa Rica that don’t have a doctor on duty but will prescribe medication based on your symptoms. They are worth finding if you trust your self-diagnoses and don’t feel the need for a middleman with MD after the last name. And those back rooms? They are still open if an injection is necessary.

World.title: Costa Rica Falls 2-0 to Ecuador in Quito as the Bryan Ruiz Era Begins
World.content:
Costa Rica opened the Bryan Ruiz era with a 2-0 loss to Ecuador on Friday night in Quito. The team finished the friendly with 10 men and lost a defender to a knee injury, four days before it faces Argentina. Jordy Caicedo put Ecuador ahead in the first half. Moisés Caicedo, the Chelsea midfielder and Ecuador captain, sealed it from the penalty spot late in the second half at Estadio Olímpico Atahualpa, which sits about 2,850 meters (9,350 feet) above sea level.

The result gave Argentine coach Marcelo Gallardo his first win in charge of Ecuador. It was Ruiz’s first match as Costa Rica’s permanent head coach. The former national team captain won both of his games as interim coach, against Nicaragua and Haiti in the Concacaf Nations League, before the Costa Rican Football Federation gave him the job.

Costa Rica set the early tempo. The visitors pressed high and won the ball back quickly in the opening minutes. Striker Manfred Ugalde, back with the squad after serving a suspension, forced a save from Ecuador goalkeeper Hernán Galíndez around the ninth minute. Ecuador struck midway through the half. Jordy Caicedo, who plays for Argentine club Huracán, ran onto a long ball from Piero Hincapié. He went around goalkeeper Patrick Sequeira and finished with his left foot for his fifth international goal.

Costa Rica came closest to an equalizer early in the second half. Andrey Soto shot after a pass from Carlos Mora, and Ecuador defender Jackson Porozo cleared the ball off the line. Ruiz made four changes shortly before the hour mark. Alexis Gamboa, Celso Borges, Josimar Méndez and Kenyel Michel came on for Francisco Calvo, Roan Wilson, Soto and Josimar Alcócer. The changes quickly turned costly.

Gamboa went down after a collision with Ecuador’s John Yeboah a few minutes after coming on and was carried off on a stretcher. The federation said he has a left knee injury and will return to Costa Rica on Saturday for further tests, which rules him out against Argentina. Diego Mesén replaced Gamboa around the 65th minute in his first appearance for the national team. He was sent off a few minutes later for a foul on Jordy Caicedo.

Playing a man down at altitude, Costa Rica could not hold on. Ecuador was awarded a penalty for a foul on Yeboah in the box, and Moisés Caicedo converted with less than 10 minutes left. Ruiz said after the match that he left Quito satisfied with what he saw. He said many of the things the coaching staff asked for were carried out and the team showed personality, and he called the result secondary to what the squad learned. He also acknowledged that the game became an uphill battle and said the team’s style of play still needs fine-tuning.

Gallardo said Ecuador grew into the match after an uncomfortable start and called it a constructive performance. He added that the win was a good way to reconnect with the home crowd. The loss extended Costa Rica’s winless run against Ecuador, which dates back to 1992. Ecuador has now won six straight meetings, including a 3-0 win at the 2006 World Cup in Germany and a 3-1 friendly win in Chester, Pennsylvania, in June 2023.

Costa Rica plays Argentina, the 2026 World Cup runner-up, on Tuesday, Nov. 17, at Estadio Mario Alberto Kempes in Córdoba. It is the team’s last match of the year. The federation tried to call up Kendall Waston as cover, but Saprissa said the veteran defender is still recovering from an injury and will not travel.

For a team rebuilding after missing this year’s World Cup, the night in Quito showed what Ruiz has to work with. There were early signs of the aggressive approach he wants, but also how quickly a thin squad can come apart. Tuesday’s game against the world’s runner-up will show how much of that can be fixed in four days.

World.title: Monteverde Went From 25 Dry Days a Year to Nearly 120, BBC Reports
World.content:
Costa Rica’s best known cloud forest is in the international spotlight this week after the BBC published a lengthy feature on Monteverde, reporting that the clouds that define the forest are pulling away from it and changing the life inside. The piece appeared on November 12 on BBC Future, the British broadcaster’s science and environment section. It was written by journalist Jocelyn Timperley, who reported from the Children’s Eternal Rainforest and other reserves around Monteverde.

The central message will be familiar to anyone who has followed the science here. The BBC reports that the fog bank that once sat on the forest almost year-round is rising with warmer temperatures, leaving the canopy exposed to sun and dry air for much of the dry season.

It leans on the long running records of Alan Pounds, resident scientist at the Monteverde Cloud Forest Biological Preserve, who has counted the days when neither rain nor mist reaches his gauge. There were about 25 a year in the 1970s. His latest figures, which the BBC describes as preliminary, put the recent average near 119.

Much of the feature is devoted to the epiphytes, the orchids, mosses, bromeliads and ferns that cover Monteverde’s trees and drink directly from the mist. The BBC follows ecologists Nalini Nadkarni of the University of Utah and Sybil Gotsch of the University of Kentucky, along with Costa Rican scientist Elenter Cubero Campos, whose experiments are designed to show what the forest loses as those hanging gardens dry out.

The feature also revisits the golden toad, the Monteverde species that vanished after 1989 and is widely cited as one of the first extinctions linked to a warming climate. It also describes the newcomers now arriving from the lowlands, including toucans, terciopelo snakes and bats that were once kept out by the cold.

Local voices get a share of the space. The BBC speaks with members of the Monteverde Institute, the Costa Rican Conservation Foundation and the community group CorClima about tree planting, biological corridors and whether ecotourism, long credited with saving the forest from cattle pasture, is approaching its limits as new hotels go up.

Little of this is new to Costa Rica as reseasrchers here have reported on Monteverde’s rising dry day count for years. What is different is the scale of the audience. Monteverde is one of our signature protected areas and a place known by name around the world, and a prominent BBC feature puts its troubles in front of millions of readers and potential donors.

That attention cuts both ways. Coverage of this kind can bring research funding and support for conservation groups working on the mountain. It can also change how the world sees a place whose identity is built on mist and dripping moss. For now the forest remains green, the quetzals still nest and the reserves are open. But the BBC’s reporting makes plain that the scientists who know Monteverde best believe it is becoming a different kind of forest, and that the rest of the world is now watching it happen.

World.title: Blocked Estuary May Explain Playa Langosta Fish Die-Off
World.content:
Sand blocking an estuary’s connection to the ocean, combined with reduced freshwater flow during a period of little rain, may explain the mass fish deaths at Playa Langosta, according to National University (UNA) biologist Teresita Ulate. Ulate said the interruption of water exchange between the mangrove and the sea could have reduced the oxygen available to aquatic animals. Her assessment offers a possible explanation, but the cause has not been confirmed.

The deaths occurred at the San Francisco Estuary in Playa Langosta. The Ministry of Environment and Energy (MINAE) opened an investigation after images showed dead fish, rays and other animals along the shoreline and in the water, including two bull sharks found dead in the estuary.

The ministry said the analysis, led by the National System of Conservation Areas (SINAC), would examine the blocked outlet, water quality and possible effects of El Niño, including warmer Pacific waters and changing coastal conditions. Authorities cautioned that assigning a cause before a technical evaluation would be premature.

Ulate explained that reduced rainfall meant less freshwater was reaching the mangrove while accumulated sand restricted its connection to the sea. She said El Niño had contributed to that drop in rainfall, part of the dry conditions now straining water supplies across Guanacaste, and that the episode could have been anticipated given the lower rain forecast.

Decomposing organic matter can add pressure because bacteria consume oxygen as they break it down, leaving less available for fish. Ulate said water testing she carried out in the San Francisco mangrove in June had already found low oxygen levels, which she described as a warning sign for the ecosystem. She added that daily monitoring would be needed to produce precise data.

The animals were reported dead on Nov. 4. Local lifeguards urged people not to collect or eat them because they were decomposing, and asked residents to stay away from the estuary, warning that the loss of fish could draw crocodiles closer to shore. The environment ministry also asked residents not to alter the estuary’s mouth without authorization.

Eduardo Vargas, director of the Tamarindo Integral Development Association, said strong seasonal tides had carried sand from other stretches of coast and sealed the opening. He said residents initially tried to clear it with shovels before bringing in heavy machinery, that the work had the necessary permits and that subsequent heavy rain helped widen the opening.

Vargas described the reopening as a stopgap rather than a fix, saying a lasting solution would require managing the mangrove from the surrounding watershed. Restoring that connection does not establish what killed the animals. Ulate cautioned that human activity could not yet be ruled out as a contributing factor and that SINAC’s analysis would be needed to better understand the episode.

World.title: US Ground Stop Canceled 15 Costa Rica Flights. Here’s What to Expect Today
World.content:
Updated Saturday afternoon with the cause of the outage, Saturday’s cancellations and when flights should be back to normal.

The nationwide US ground stop that froze flights on Friday afternoon is over, but if you are flying between Costa Rica and the United States this weekend, you may still feel it. Fifteen flights were canceled on Friday at Costa Rica’s two main international airports, 10 at Juan Santamaría International Airport and five at Guanacaste Airport in Liberia, and US airlines were still canceling thousands of flights early Saturday as planes and crews worked their way back into position.

The backlog should clear soon. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said on Saturday he expected air travel to return to normal levels by Sunday. Saturday was still rough, with more than 5,000 US flights canceled, according to FlightAware, more than the FAA had forecast. If you fly Sunday or later, your flight is much more likely to run as scheduled, but check it before you leave for the airport anyway.

Aeris, which runs the airport outside San José, said 23 flights there were affected on Friday, 12 departures and 11 arrivals. Six departures and four arrivals were canceled. The other 13 flights were moved to overnight and early Saturday morning slots.

The Federal Aviation Administration lifted the order at about 8 p.m. Eastern time on Friday, or 7 p.m. in Costa Rica, after more than four hours. That made it the second-longest nationwide ground stop on record, behind the shutdown that followed the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks. When it began, it was only the third nationwide US ground stop ever.

Aeris said operations will return to normal gradually, depending on each airline’s schedule. Guanacaste Airport in Liberia canceled five departures on Friday, flights to Dallas, Toronto and Ottawa carrying 473 passengers, who were left waiting for new itineraries. Airport officials there had said on Friday afternoon that 23 flights were scheduled for Saturday.

The knock-on effects are what matter today. The flight-tracking service FlightAware counted more than 9,100 cancellations and more than 24,500 delays in the United States on Friday, and more than 3,000 additional cancellations by early Saturday. Many US airlines fly a plane into Costa Rica and send the same jet straight back, so a canceled flight in Miami, Houston or Atlanta can mean a canceled departure here.

Check your flight in your airline’s app before you leave for the airport. App and text alerts usually update before departure boards do. Copa Airlines said the US disruption could cause delays and cancellations on its flights to and from the United States and asked passengers to confirm their status on its website or app. United and JetBlue both said they would cancel most of their remaining Friday night flights, a fresh strain for JetBlue’s Costa Rica routes.

If your flight was canceled or you want to move your trip, look for a travel waiver on your airline’s website. American and other US airlines said they would change tickets affected by the outage with no fee and no fare difference, which is often faster than waiting in a rebooking line. If you decide not to travel at all, US rules entitle you to a cash refund, even when the cause is out of the airline’s control. Airlines do not have to cover hotels or meals in that case, so keep your receipts if your travel insurance covers delays.

If you are connecting through a US hub, rebook through the airline that sold you the ticket rather than each carrier separately. And if you are heading north, remember that every passenger flying to the United States must now sign a new form, which can slow check-in on a day when lines are already long.

US officials said the outage was not a cyberattack. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Saturday that it began while contractor L3Harris Technologies was switching telecommunications lines from copper wire to fiber at a remote FAA site. When one router was switched over, he said, it flooded other routers in the air traffic control network with more than 1,000 connection attempts about every five seconds, disrupting radio communications and radar feeds at the Air Route Traffic Control Centers, the facilities that guide planes between airports. The FAA has not yet determined the root cause. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no evidence of a hostile attack. Duffy said he had asked Congress on Thursday for $30.1 billion to modernize the air traffic control system.

The disruption was the second to hit air travel at Juan Santamaría airport in less than a month, after a power failure affected its control tower in October. Costa Rica relies on US gateways for much of its air traffic, and the busy high season is just weeks away, so even a few hours of trouble in US airspace can strand travelers here for a day or more.

World.title: International News: Small Island nations demand urgent Climate action at UN summit
World.content:
International News: Small Island nations demand urgent Climate action at UN summit

By Zoila Palma: Leaders of small island nations are calling for urgent global action to address climate change, warning that rising sea levels and increasingly severe weather events threaten the survival of their countries.

The appeal was made Thursday during the United Nations climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, where world leaders are discussing ways to reduce emissions and support vulnerable nations.

Seychelles Vice President Alix Sebastien Pillay said climate change is already causing millions of dollars in damage to his country, a 115-island archipelago in the Indian Ocean, despite its minimal contribution to global warming. He urged governments to move beyond discussions and strengthen funding mechanisms to help vulnerable countries recover from climate-related disasters without accumulating unsustainable debt.

A report released during the conference by the independent Climate Action Tracker warned that global progress in reducing warming has stalled over the past five years. It found that even if countries fulfill their existing climate commitments, global temperatures could rise by approximately 2.6 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels by the end of the century, exceeding the 1.5-degree target established under the 2015 Paris Agreement.

Leaders from vulnerable countries also highlighted the growing financial and human costs of climate disasters. Niue Prime Minister Dalton Tagelagi warned that unusually high Pacific Ocean temperatures signal worsening conditions, while Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif called for greater international cooperation and financing, noting that no country can confront the climate crisis alone. Climate activist Greta Thunberg also criticized world leaders for failing to take sufficient action.

Meanwhile, the United Kingdom announced the appointment of Madeleine Alessandri as its first special envoy for climate security risks, citing concerns that environmental damage could threaten food supplies, increase migration and contribute to conflict.

World.title: International News: Pope Leo celebrates mass before 500,000 faithful in former Peruvian Diocese
World.content:
International News: Pope Leo celebrates mass before 500,000 faithful in former Peruvian Diocese

By Zoila Palma: An estimated 500,000 people gathered on Friday, November 13, to attend a Mass celebrated by Pope Leo in Chiclayo, Peru, where he previously served as bishop for eight years.

The large outdoor celebration took place at the Pampas de Pimentel grounds, drawing pilgrims from across Peru and abroad for the pontiff’s return to the northern city.

Vatican figures cited by EWTN News Español placed attendance at approximately half a million people, despite temperatures reaching 90 degrees Fahrenheit.

Worshippers began arriving on Thursday night, with many spending hours waiting to secure a place at the celebration.

During his homily, Pope Leo expressed his joy at returning to the community where he served from 2015 to 2023, before Pope Francis called him to Rome for new responsibilities at the Vatican. “What a joy to return to Chiclayo! It is a blessing for me to be with you again,” he told the congregation.

The pontiff also thanked the faithful for their affection, support and prayers, particularly as he continues recovering from recent medical difficulties. Representatives of the Diocese of Chiclayo welcomed his return and recognized his eight years of service to the local Catholic community.

In his message, Pope Leo emphasized that sharing the Catholic faith should go beyond religious teaching and be demonstrated through personal example, solidarity and commitment to helping those in need. He also highlighted the importance of respecting freedom of conscience while warning against religious indifference, materialism and selfishness.

The Mass formed part of the Pope’s visit to Peru, the final stop on his South American tour, which began on November 6 and also included Uruguay and Argentina.

World.title: International News: Powerful El Niño could bring flooding risks across parts of North America
World.content:
International News: Powerful El Niño could bring flooding risks across parts of North America

By Zoila Palma: A developing El Niño phenomenon is continuing to strengthen and could significantly influence weather patterns across North America during the 2026-2027 autumn and winter seasons, BBC reports.

The event is already showing signs of becoming one of the strongest recorded, with the United States National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) reporting a strong-to-very strong El Niño is likely to persist through early 2027.

El Niño is a naturally occurring climate phenomenon that develops when trade winds over the Pacific Ocean weaken or reverse, allowing warmer ocean waters to shift eastward.

This releases additional heat into the atmosphere and influences global weather patterns, affecting rainfall, temperatures and storm activity in different regions.

NOAA’s November 12 assessment indicated approximately a 60% chance that the event could reach historic strength, exceeding previous El Niño events recorded since 1950 under one measurement.

For the United States, forecasts suggest increased rainfall across much of California, the Southwest, Central and Southern Plains, the Southeast and parts of the eastern seaboard. Florida and other southeastern states could experience particularly wet conditions, raising concerns about flooding. California may also face increased risks of heavy rainfall, flooding and mudslides, particularly in areas affected by previous wildfires. However, the intensity and location of rainfall will vary.

Meanwhile, warmer-than-average winter temperatures are expected across parts of Alaska, the western United States and northern regions, while below-average precipitation is forecast for areas including the Northern Rockies and parts of the Great Lakes.

El Niño can also influence snowfall patterns, increasing the possibility of heavier snowfall in some southern mountain ranges while reducing snow chances in certain northern areas. Scientists are also monitoring possible disruptions to the stratospheric polar vortex, which can sometimes allow Arctic air to move farther south.

World.title: Belizean Pride: British Royal Army Medical Service welcomes Cayo-native Indira Greig
World.content:
Belizean Pride: British Royal Army Medical Service welcomes Cayo-native Indira Greig

By Zoila Palma: Indira Greig from San Ignacio, Cayo District, has completed basic military training in the United Kingdom and officially joined the British Army’s Royal Army Medical Service (RAMS). Private Indira Greig marked the milestone after successfully completing her training at the Army Training Centre (ATC) Pirbright.

Pte Greig proudly marched off the parade square during a ceremony celebrating the completion of her basic training.

The Royal Army Medical Service is a specialist corps established on November 15, 2024, providing medical, nursing and dental support to British Army personnel during both peacetime and military operations.

Her achievement was celebrated by family members, including her father, Robert Greig, his partner, Susan, and her brother, Gunner Gordon Greig, who serves with the Royal Artillery.

Her grandparents also travelled all the way from Belize to witness the special occasion.

Several members of the British Army were present to welcome Greig into the medical corps, including Sergeant J. Tablada of 1 Medical Regiment and Belizean Network Ambassador Warrant Officer Class One (Regimental Sergeant Major) Heredia.

The milestone marks an important step in Greig’s military career and a proud moment for her family, community and country.

World.title: International News: France sees 5th consecutive Saturday of nationwide protests
World.content:
International News: France sees 5th consecutive Saturday of nationwide protests

By Zoila Palma: Today, thousands of demonstrators took to the streets across France marking the fifth consecutive weekend of nationwide protests.

The demonstrations brought together members of the Yellow Vest movement, students, education unions and other advocacy groups expressing frustration over the rising cost of living, education funding, child protection and proposed changes to police powers, euronews reports.

In Paris, demonstrators gathered at Place de la République before marching toward Place de la Nation. According to France’s Interior Ministry, approximately 106,000 people participated in demonstrations nationwide, including 24,000 in Paris.

Organizers, however, estimated the turnout at 200,000, with nearly 100,000 in the capital. The turnout was lower than the previous weekend, when authorities recorded 146,000 demonstrators nationwide.

Protesters also opposed a proposed police bill that would provide officers and gendarmes with additional legal protection when using firearms in the line of duty. Supporters argue that the measure would protect law enforcement officers from automatically being presumed guilty when using their weapons, while critics have described it as a “license to kill,” warning that it could weaken accountability for alleged police violence.

Demonstrators also called for better protection of children and teenagers and improved funding for public education.

The protests come after more than a month of school blockades and demonstrations over economic and social concerns.

World.title: Mopan Technical High School wins Gold at ExpoCiencias Nuevo León 2026 in Mexico
World.content:
Mopan Technical High School wins Gold at ExpoCiencias Nuevo León 2026 in Mexico

By Zoila Palma: Mopan Technical High School has made history after securing first-place Gold award at ExpoCiencias Nuevo León 2026 in Monterrey, Mexico.

The school’s delegation proudly represented Belize as the only participating school from the country, earning top honours in the Social Sciences category for its project titled “Supporting Multilingual Learners!”

The achievement marks the first time Mopan Technical High School has secured a first-place award at an international competition.

Students Karoly and Jasiely were recognized for their dedication, creativity and hard work in developing the project, which earned them international recognition and brought home the gold medal for Belize.

The school also credited the achievement to the guidance of their coach, Marcelo Torres, and mentors Casiana Sagastume and Karen Figueroa.

Appreciation was also extended to the school’s administration, staff, wider school community and sponsors whose support helped make the international participation possible.

Mopan Technical High School celebrated the victory as more than just a medal, highlighting the importance of investing in young people and creating opportunities for students to showcase their talents internationally.

Mopan Tech says that the achievement is a proud moment for Benque Viejo del Carmen and Belize, as its students made their mark on the international stage.

World.title: Belize’s Maya-led Climate adaptation project highlighted at COP31 in Türkiye
World.content:
Belize’s Maya-led Climate adaptation project highlighted at COP31 in Türkiye

By Zoila Palma: Belize’s Indigenous leadership took centre stage on November 11 during the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye.

The Caribbean Community Climate Change Centre (CCCCC) and Belize’s Julian Cho Society hosted a side event at the CARICOM Pavilion titled “Project Q’anil: A Maya-Led Pathway to Green Climate Fund Adaptation Finance,” highlighting the importance of placing Indigenous communities at the centre of climate adaptation efforts.

The discussion explored Maya principles, including “Aj ral Ch’och” (people of the land), “Loq’la Tzuul Taq’a,” which recognizes the sacred relationship between the land, forests, animals and the spirit world, and “Komonil,” which emphasizes mutual support, collective work and commitment.

The Julian Cho Society works to advance Indigenous rights and environmental conservation in southern Belize. The event highlighted how traditional knowledge, community leadership and partnerships can help Indigenous communities access climate financing and develop solutions that reflect their needs and priorities.

Elishah St. Luce, Social Inclusion and Gender Specialist at the CCCCC, emphasized the importance of ensuring that Maya communities lead efforts shaping their future. “It is our responsibility to take the future the Maya people have dreamt and place that in a project ensuring that the Maya-led aspect dominates,” she stated.

COP31 is being held from November 9 to 20, 2026, bringing together world leaders, governments, Indigenous representatives and climate advocates to advance global climate action.

World.title: Belize brings Kulcha to International stage in Mexico
World.content:
Belize brings Kulcha to International stage in Mexico

By Zoila Palma: The Mopan Technical High School delegation brought a taste of Belizean culture to the international stage during ExpoCiencias 2026 in Monterrey, Nuevo León, Mexico.

Beyond showcasing scientific knowledge and innovation, the international science fair also provided an opportunity for participating countries to celebrate their cultural identities, traditions and talents.

During a cultural presentation, Belize was represented through a dance celebrating Creole culture, accompanied by music from Belizean cultural icon Leela Vernon. The performance highlighted Belize’s rich cultural heritage and gave international audiences an opportunity to experience a piece of the country’s music and traditions.

Among those participating were students Karoly and Jasiely, alongside Mopan Technical High School Principal Katie Jones, who also made a special appearance in the cultural presentation. The delegation proudly showcased their talents and represented Belize with enthusiasm and national pride.

Mopan Tech noted that experiences such as ExpoCiencias go beyond classroom learning by encouraging cultural exchange, building friendships and allowing students to discover different perspectives.

From sharing scientific innovations to celebrating Belizean culture, the Mopan delegation continues to represent the country in Monterrey, Mexico.

World.title: Reggae Boyz stun Mexico 3-2 in Nations League quarterfinal first-leg
World.content:
Reggae Boyz (from left) Richard King, Tyreece Campbell and Karoy Anderson celebrate after winning the FIFA World Cup qualifiers semi-final play-off match against New Caledonia at Akron Stadium in Zapopan, Mexico, on March 26, 2026.Photo: AFP

KINGSTON, Jamaica – Jamaica’s Reggae Boyz pulled off a 3-2 upset victory over Mexico in their first-leg Concacaf Nations League quarterfinal, despite almost surrendering a commanding three-goal advantage in Kingston on Saturday.

Having established what appeared to be an unassailable lead, the Boyz were left clinging desperately to their advantage as El Tri mounted a late fightback, scoring twice to set up a nervy finish.

Jamaica went into the lead in the 28th minute when a period of sustained pressure led to an own goal off a corner.

Renaldo Cephas doubled the advantage at the start of the second half with a beautiful solo effort that saw him curl the ball into the net after a cut back that left his defender for dead.

Richard King scored a 63d minute penalty after Kaheim Dixon was judged to be fouled in the box following a lengthy VAR review, opening up what appeared to be an insurmountable lead for the Boyz at home.

However, the Mexicans charged back and reduced the deficit in the 70th minute through a Gilberta Mora strike from outside the 18-yard box.

Julian Quinones then converted a penalty in the 81st minute to set up the nervy ending.

However, the Reggae Boyz held on to clinch a memorable victory and set up an intriguing second leg in Mexico.

World.title: Finally!
World.content:
The entrance to Cornwall Regional Hospital’s newly opened Accident and Emergency department (Photo: Anthony Lewis)

MOUNT SALEM, St James — The opening of the refurbished Accident and Emergency (A&E) department at Cornwall Regional Hospital (CRH) on Friday was accompanied by an apology from Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness to the people of western Jamaica for the prolonged delay in completing the facility’s $23.5-billion rehabilitation.

Holness acknowledged that the near-decade-long undertaking to rehabilitate the 52-year-old, 10-storey hospital might have been completed more quickly had the Government opted to demolish the structure and build a new facility from the ground up.

“In retrospect, it may have been a quicker operation to have torn down the building and just built it anew. But politically, we’re not certain whether or not the public would have appreciated that. But I can tell you, going forward, the economics is that it is better to just tear down those old buildings and build brand new,” said Holness.

The hospital officially opened on May 10, 1974, following the start of construction in 1968 at a cost of approximately US$12 million and another US$5 million to equip it, through a grant from Canada. Holness argued that in today’s terms, that type of work, plus land acquisition and other expenses, would cost approximately $40 billion.

He said the 25.9-acre campus on which the upgraded CRH and the under-construction Western Child and Adolescent Hospital (WCAH) sit will be renamed in honour of former chairman of the Jamaica Labour Party and Minister of Health Dr Herbert Eldemire. He also reiterated that the WCAH will bear the name of former Prime Minister Portia Simpson Miller, who was instrumental in securing funds from the Chinese for that project.

During his address, the prime minister acknowledge the hardship faced by residents in western Jamaica as the work on CRH dragged on.

“I must, first of all, apologise to the people of the region who have been without their hospital, and for the suffering that it has caused. No doubt, the absence of the hospital would have caused suffering, particularly during COVID. I toured during COVID and I saw the difficulties being experienced both by the service providers and the patients in cramped quarters, in difficult circumstances,” stated Holness.

Pointing out that a large percentage of the 24 hospitals across Jamaica were built before the country’s Independence from Britain in 1962, Holness said he views the Government of Jamaica’s ability to execute major projects like the CRH upgrade as a symbol of the country’s independence.

According to him, all the other sections of CRH will be open to the public by March 2027.

“I leaned over to Minister Tufton to inquire, ‘When will we finally open this hospital fully?’ And he was hesitant in committing to me. But he did say to me that by the end of the fiscal year they would be in a good position to open,” said the prime minister.

Clinical coordinator for the Western Regional Health Authority Dr Delroy Fray expressed delight at the completion and opening of the A&E department.

“Look at what stands before you now: A first-class accident and emergency department. We are handing over a state-of-the-art facility designed for dignity, speed, and comfort. From the moment you present with an emergency, you are seamlessly triaged in a high-efficiency environment,” stated Dr Fray.

The newly renovated facility boasts advanced diagnostic stations and cutting-edge operating theatres for immediate surgical intervention.

“This is not just health care; this is First-World medicine at the absolute highest level — the first of its kind in Jamaica and the entire English-speaking Caribbean,” Dr Fray said.

World.title: 1,446 new homes for St James
World.content:
Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness (seated, third left) participates in a Grange Pen Housing Development contract signing at the Housing Agency of Jamaica (HAJ) corporate office in St Andrew on Thursday. Also taking part are (seated, from left) China Harbour Engineering Company (CHEC) Project Manager Hoinan Wong; CHEC Country Manager Dangran Bi; permanent secretary in the Ministry of Economic Growth and Job Creation Arlene Williams; HAJ Chairman Norman Brown; and HAJ Managing Director Doreen Prendergast. Looking on are (standing, from left) CHEC Legal Counsel Colleen Franklin; HAJ Senior Manager and Legal Services Peta-Gaye Ellington; Minister of Tourism Edmund Bartlett’ and permanent secretary in the Ministry of Tourism Jennifer Griffith.Photo: Karl Mclarty

A $24-billion housing development that will deliver 1,446 new units in Grange Pen, St James, and expand housing opportunities in the busy tourism parish has been welcomed by Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness as a significant step forward following Thursday’s signing of a construction agreement.

Under the deal signed by the Housing Agency of Jamaica (HAJ) and China Harbour Engineering Company (CHEC), at least 20 per cent of the units will be reserved for tourism workers as the Government moves to tackle housing shortages in areas experiencing rapid tourism-related growth.

Speaking at the signing ceremony at the HAJ’s St Andrew corporate office, Holness said the development also forms part of a wider push by the Government to keep pace with employment opportunities, particularly along the north coast, where informal settlements tend to develop due to insufficient housing solutions.

“The idea is to ensure that we are positioning the housing stock where people work. That’s very important. A large part of the informal and insecure settlements that we have was that the jobs came first and the housing lagged behind. The jobs came first and there was no proper transportation system for people to leave where they lived to get to work. And so, people had to make do to live where the land was in proximity to where they work,” reasoned the prime minister.

Holness added that the Government has insisted that all new hotels provide housing for their workers, while he has directed the HAJ, and the National Housing Trust (NHT) to dedicate more housing solutions to the tourism sector.

“So, we are trying to get ahead of the curve and I would want to say that in the next 10 years we should not have this problem of informal settlements popping up because people just simply don’t have anywhere to live in proximity to where the jobs are,” added Holness.

He pointed out that the contract between HAJ and CHEC requires at least 60 per cent of the workforce on the housing development to be Jamaicans.

“In every project that we have done, we have put in place this requirement that there is a certain percentage of Jamaicans who must hold the jobs. On the north coast, where we’re doing the Montego Bay Perimeter Road, not only have we put in a quota for Jamaicans, we have put in place a system of training where the Jamaicans who are participating there are also certified at the end of their duty on that project. So we are ensuring that at the end of these large projects the Jamaicans who are trained, their skills are certified,” Holness said.

Thursday’s proceedings also included the signing of an HAJ contract to add 301 units to the existing 1,506 homes under the fifth phase of the Catherine Estate development in St Catherine.

Holness, who described Catherine Estate as one of the agency’s most successful housing developments, welcomed the increase, noting the demand for housing in the area.

“I’m saying it’s the most successful to date because of the size of it, but also because it has managed to maintain a price point. I was told that for the 1,000 units they have more than 20,000 applications,” he noted.

Meanwhile, Tourism Minister Edmund Bartlett pointed to earlier investments in the Grange Pen area, where he said more than $1 billion had been spent on the regularisation of existing settlements and the provision of community infrastructure.

According to Bartlett, the initial component of that development is now 90 per cent complete and included work on roads, water, electricity, and sewage systems.

“The prime minister is about ready to hand over 535 titles to 535 families who otherwise would have been called squatters or, to be more pedantic, informal settlers.

“Today, they are homeowners with tenure on a property that belong to them and they can leave [it] to their great, great grandchildren. So the brownfield was done. And we hope that with the development that CHEC is involved with us, we will see the full completion of that,” said Bartlett.

He added that discussions were under way with a mortgage provider to introduce a financing arrangement that would allow tourism workers to repay housing loans over periods of 30 to 40 years.

Bartlett said the proposed arrangement, which he described as a “patient mortgage”, is intended to make homeownership more accessible by reducing the monthly repayment burden on workers.

“This is an innovation that the Government of Jamaica, led by Prime Minister Andrew Holness, has been driving, and it’s our part in making sure that we don’t only have housing solutions, but affordable solutions,” added Bartlett.

World.title: Craigy T readies new music
World.content:
Craigy T.

On the heels of the success of his debut solo album, Ascension: Out of Many… 1, which topped the iTunes Reggae Albums global chart and earned Grammy consideration, international dancehall artiste Craigy T is preparing to release new music.

The entertainer has joined forces with producer KickRaux for his upcoming single, Music Within Me, slated for release in late November.

For Craigy T, the song carries a deeply personal message, reflecting the passion and resilience that have sustained him throughout his nearly three-decade musical career.

“Music Within Me kinda defines my very essence in its lyrics. It verbalises what keeps me going when times are tough. It was written several years ago and has chosen now to reveal itself,” he said.

The collaboration developed after the two connected through Instagram, with KickRaux expressing an interest in working with Craigy T after listening to Ascension.

“I did some research into his work and was equally impressed. Skip, skip, skip, and here we are,” Craigy T recalled.

Although their creative partnership is relatively new, the artiste said they have already established a productive working relationship, particularly when navigating their unconventional musical ideas.

“Both of us tend to have way-out, unorthodox ideas. Whenever one wanders too far, the other provides grounding for the project, and we interchange those roles throughout the process,” he explained.

For KickRaux, the objective was to create something distinctive without sacrificing the musical appeal that allows listeners to connect with a song.

“We live in an impersonal, digital world where trends and algorithms run our lives. As soon as something catches a hype, everyone starts copying it. Craigy T and I didn’t know where our collaboration would land, but the one rule was ‘Don’t blend in,’ ” he said.

“I used organic sounds to paint the musical backdrop. I wanted the music to be creative and forward-thinking, but not so left field that you couldn’t just put it on, hold a vibe, and enjoy yourself,” the producer added.

KickRaux said he was particularly impressed by Craigy T’s willingness to experiment and the vulnerability reflected in his solo material.

“Working with Craigy T feels like working with a new artiste, because he’s so open to trying new sounds. But at the same time, he’s reggae and dancehall royalty. A hitmaker who knows what people want to hear,” he said.

“You can really hear his classical training in the way he approaches harmonies. He’s always coming up with ideas you wouldn’t expect. We kept finding new ways to approach the music,” he continued.

Released on August 7, the 17-track Ascension: Out of Many… 1 showcased Craigy T’s versatility, blending dancehall, reggae, and soul influences. The project also attracted international radio spins and play list placements in territories including the United Kingdom, Japan, Latin America, and Africa.

While the album introduced audiences to a more personal dimension of his artistry, Craigy T believes his forthcoming single will take listeners even further into his creative world.

“I think Music Within Me is an evolution of the material in Ascension, not a departure. So, not different, but diving deeper into my mind,” he explained.

Meanwhile, the entertainer’s evolving solo journey has earned praise from international radio personality DJ GQ, who recently interviewed him on

Dancehall Cyaan Done, aired on SiriusXM’s Bob Marley Tuff Gong Radio.

Describing Ascension as a masterpiece, DJ GQ said the project represents a long-awaited opportunity for audiences to experience Craigy T’s individual creativity.

“Massive! This type of energy, vibe, and expression was long overdue. Definitely a masterpiece,” he said.

Having known the entertainer for more than 30 years, DJ GQ said one of the highlights of their recent conversation was discovering that he had unknowingly influenced Craigy T’s early career through a childhood stage show featuring Spragga Benz.

The radio personality also underscored the importance of providing platforms for established entertainers who continue to contribute to the evolution of Jamaican music.

“Veteran dancehall artistes don’t just guide and influence the new generation of music; they are literally the role models and legends for the genre!” he said.

As he prepares for the release of Music Within Me, Craigy T remains appreciative of the support he continues to receive while embracing new creative opportunities.

“I am truly grateful to be able to continue sharing my gift with my tribe. Every day is a new day with new experiences or sometimes similar experiences from a new perspective. I welcome life’s changes and new directions. It excites me,” he expressed.

Fans can also anticipate additional material from the partnership, with KickRaux confirming that more collaborations are on the horizon.

“Definitely look out for more from us,” Craigy T added.

World.title: US grounds all flights, sparking travel chaos
World.content:
MIAMI, United States — Passengers wait in the terminal of Miami International Airport on November 13, 2026. US aviation regulators issued an extremely rare ground stop of all flights across the country after a major communications outage which the Department of Homeland Security said did not appear to be the result of any “nefarious attack”. (Photo: AFP)

NEW YORK, United States (AFP) — All flights in the US were grounded Friday, sparking travel chaos across the vast country, after what government officials said was a major communications outage, insisting it was not the result of any “nefarious attack”.



The nationwide stop left tens of thousands of passengers in limbo, with some pulled off planes moments before departure by airline staff who appeared in the dark about unfolding events.

The incident marked only the second time such an alert was given in US airspace since the 9/11 attacks.

“So supposedly, nobody’s flying, but they haven’t told the public yet,” said an exasperated Joseph Anderson, 72, who was trying to fly from Las Vegas to Oakland, California.

“We’re trying to debate whether or not we need to reschedule or drive or what, but if the whole country is stopped, that means the highways are going to be jammed too.”

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) “issued a nationwide ground stop for all US airports following a communication issue impacting all air route traffic control centres,” the agency said. “FAA technicians are investigating the issue.”

In a subsequent message on X, the agency described the problem as “a temporary telecommunications outage” and said it was acting “out of an abundance of caution”.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no sign of a threat to the United States.

“This isn’t another 9/11,” he said.

“There was no indication, as of yet, that this was a nefarious attack against us, it’s just a telecommunication outage, as of right now,“” Mullin said, adding officials were “not ruling out anything at this point”.

There was a short nationwide stop in January 2023 when a pilot notification system failed, but the only other national stop happened in the wake of the 9/11 attacks, when no aircraft took to the skies for days.

Friday’s FAA order came a day after US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy formally asked Congress for US$30 billion to upgrade and modernise the US Air Traffic Control System.

“This investment is critical to complete the modernization of our national airspace — delivering a resilient telecommunications backbone for air traffic controllers, modern hardware and software, state-of-the-art control towers, and world-class airport infrastructure,” Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought wrote in a letter to lawmakers.

It also came the same day that Microsoft apologised for a global outage that wreaked havoc for millions of users, public services and businesses worldwide.

The company ruled out any malicious “cyber or AI” activity as the cause of the disruption, which affected several Microsoft products from Thursday. Most operations had resumed by late Friday.

World.title: MEXICAN STAND-OFF
World.content:
Jamaica Reggae Boyz squad members go through their paces during their final training session on Friday ahead of the Concacaf Nations League quarter-final, first-leg football match against Mexico at the National Stadium on Saturday. (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

Mexico are usually favourites heading into most matches in Concacaf competitions, but Jamaica Reggae Boyz interim Head Coach Rudolph Speid says his players are undaunted and confident of pulling off a major upset to put themselves in a strong position.

The national senior football men’s will take on the Mexicans this evening at 8:00 pm at the National Stadium in the first leg of the Concacaf Nations League quarter-finals.

Since the competition’s inception in 2019, Jamaica have only qualified for the semi-finals once in their history, back in the 2023/24 season when they beat Canada in the last eight.

They will now have one of their toughest tests yet as they take on the mighty Mexicans who soared to 10th in the FIFA Rankings following their Round-of-16 finish in last summer’s FIFA World Cup.

The Reggae Boyz have struggled against Mexico, winning just four of their 32 meetings. Their last victory came in the 2017 Concacaf Gold Cup semi-final, with the team winless in their last six encounters since.

Speid, though, says the team is eager to prove their worth against one of the world’s best.

“It’s surreal to be playing against such a good team twice but there’s a reason why the game is played. It’s because the result is not guaranteed by anyone,” he said. “These are the times that you trained for as a player, these are the games you want to play if you’re really a good player and ambitious, and these are the games that a coach would like to coach against some of the top coaches, so it’s all good.”

“This is a part of our development. It’s a rebuilding squad, and we have to be forged in fire if we want to go forward in the future.”

Jamaica, who finished runners-up behind Guatemala in the group stage last month, completed their fourth and final training session on Friday morning at Stadium East field. Speid believes the extended time together has been beneficial.

“Familiarity helps, it is good. We were able to just continue what we were doing [from the last window] and add a few surprises; so I think the team is more prepared than they would have been in the qualifying rounds.”

With Mexico boasting considerable attacking firepower, including Gilberto Mora, Julián Quiñones and Santiago Giménez, Speid will have to navigate the tie without goalkeeper and Captain Andre Blake, who is sidelined with a groin injury.

“He’s probably one of the best goalkeeper in Concacaf, if not the best, so it’s a big miss for us. We’re just hoping that he’s well though and he’ll join us later on when we go further in the competition,” said Speid.

The interim boss has also had to contend with several other injury concerns and withdrawals from the squad. However, he insists those setbacks will not serve as an excuse for his team not to compete.

“I always believe that whenever players get injured or for some reason they can’t turn up, Jamaica is a big enough country,” said Speid “We give a lot of other players opportunities, we’re still in a rebuilding phase, so it’s good for some of the youngsters to get a run out and new players to get a call-up. So we don’t really think about it a lot, we just move on with business.”

One player who has benefited from the injury list is striker Ricky Jade-Jones who earned his first call-up to the national team.

The 24 year old, who currently plays for FC St Pauli in Germany’s second division, says he’s hoping to make a good impression.

“Obviously I’m really excited and I couldn’t wait to just get started. The training’s been good, I feel good in myself. The team feels good, we’ve got a good bond. We’ve only been here for a couple of days and I feel really part of it already, so I’m looking forward to the game,” he said.

New Mexico boss Rafael Marquez, who took over from Javier Aguirre following the World Cup, has yet to get off the mark, going winless in his first four games.

Speid is an admirer of the former star defender but has no intentions of taking him lightly.

“I’m just as hungry as he is to win a game. Every game is new, we have to start all over. He was a wonderful player when he used to play for Barcelona, he definitely has some characteristics that we studied very well, so I’m hoping to beat him,” he said.

“I’ve seen them play a lot, pull off extraordinary victories, especially in the World Cup just recently. We know they’re ranked number 10, we know what they bring. They easily are the best team over the years in Concacaf but the teams from the Caribbean have improved a bit and we expect for that to come on show in the tie,” Speid added.

Jamaica, who conceded four goals in four games during the Nations League group stage, will have to be wary with the introduction of the away goal rule.

Both teams will be looking for the advantage ahead of Tuesday’s return leg at the Estadio BBVA.

World.title: JFF president confident win over Mexico will put Jamaica on the football map
World.content:
Michael Ricketts, president of the Jamaica Football FederationPhoto: Garfield Robinson

Jamaica Football Federation (JFF) President Michael Ricketts believes a win for Jamaica against Mexico could play a significant role in boosting the country’s football and commercial profile.



The Reggae Boyz host Mexico in their Concacaf Nations League quarter-final first leg today at the National Stadium, starting at 8 pm.

The national senior men’s team are coming off a successful group stage campaign where they finished second in Group B with their only loss from four games coming against Honduras.

However, they are now one of the region’s and world’s best in Mexico who have made the final of every Nations League since the competition’s inception in 2019.

After Jamaica’s historic third-place finish in 2023/2024 season, they crashed out in the quarter-final stage in the 2024/2025, losing to the USA 5-2 on aggregate.

That disappointment was compounded by a group-stage exit at the Concacaf Gold Cup last summer and their failure to automatically qualify for the FIFA World Cup last November.

Ricketts, though, is hoping that the players will show a better fight this time around.

“It’s going to be tough but we have to ensure that our players are mentally prepared and that’s key and probably that’s what we’ve been lacking over the last few years,” he told the Jamaica Observer.

“We have not been able to execute very well on the field of play but we’re looking forward to moulding a set of young players that will represent us well.”

Mexico are coming off an impressive FIFA World Cup campaign, where they served as hosts, after advancing to the round of 16 and narrowly losing to eventual third-place finishers England.

The Mexicans, ranked number 10 in the world, have an incredible record against Jamaica with 23 wins from 32 games.

Ricketts believes victory could put the world on notice that Jamaica intend to end their World Cup drought ahead of the 2030 edition.

“We are bracing ourselves for that and a good result against Mexico would certainly send a message around the world that we are on a path of recovery and we are on a path of recruiting young players that are committed to the process of getting us to the World Cup by the next edition in 2030,” the JFF boss said.

“To beat Mexico certainly would send a strong signal, would send a strong message and we not just want to beat Mexico but we want to do very well, we want, of course, to be into the Gold Cup when that time comes around.”

The JFF missed out on nearly $2 billion after missing last summer’s World Cup. Ricketts isn’t expecting any major financial gain from the Nations League but believes it can be the start of their recovery path.

“We are hopeful that we will be able to get things right at the latter part of this year so that next year financially and from a commercial perspective, we would be in a better position than we have been in the last few months,” he said. “We would have invested heavily in probably six World Cup qualifying tournaments and that would have cost us hundreds of millions of dollars. We must now try to recoup some of those lost funds.”

“Next year I’m pretty certain that things will be a lot better from a commercial standpoint. We, of course, maintain our main sponsor adidas and there are some local sponsors who have always been there for us and with us. As we get back into the marketplace for a new year, we are very optimistic and hopeful that we on the field of play will do enough so that we can attract some of these new business partners that will help us to grow the sport.”

— Daniel Blake

World.title: FAA grounds all flights across US amid communications problem
World.content:
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has issued a nationwide ground stop, grounding all flights across the United States (US) until further notice because of what it described as extraordinary circumstances and safety concerns.

According to CNN, the FAA said a communications problem affecting Air Route Traffic Control Centres, which manage flights travelling across the country, prompted the disruption.

The cause of the problem was not immediately known. However, preliminary reports from two law enforcement officials indicated that it was not a cyberattack, CNN reported.

The nationwide ground stop is a rare occurrence. The last time such a measure was implemented was in January 2023, when a pilot notification system went down. Before that, a nationwide ground stop was issued following the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks.

World.title: Ukraine claims thousands of Russian casualties and a slowing Kremlin advance
World.content:
Russian casualties are rising, according to the commander and to NATO officials.

“In the past few months, Russia has been losing more than 40,000 troops — killed or seriously wounded — every month. The United States in 14 years, in Vietnam, lost 56,000. Here in one month, Russia, dead or seriously wounded, 40,000. And in October, early reporting indicates this number may have climbed to over 50,000,” NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said this week.

Neither Ukraine nor Russia publishes their exact military losses.

The Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies this summer estimated that Russian forces had suffered about 1.4 million casualties, including 400,000 to 450,000 fatalities, from the start of the full-scale invasion through June 2026. It estimated Ukrainian casualties at 525,000 to 625,000, including 125,000 to 150,000 fatalities, over the same period.

Despite rising casualties, the Russian military continues to press forward but is making few lasting gains, Apostol said. He estimated that Ukrainian forces had retaken more than 800 square kilometers from Russian forces this year as the result of two local counteroffensive operations.

Ukraine’s offensives have both a military and a political meaning as they show Kyiv is successfully resisting Russian pressure, Apostol said.

World.title: EU reiterates ‘grave concern’ over Gaza humanitarian crisis as winter approaches
World.content:
Kallas also called on Israel to comply with international law and allow the United Nations and humanitarian organizations unimpeded access and to reopen all border crossings into Gaza. | Nicolas Tucat/ AFP via Getty Images

The bloc’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has called on Israel to allow more humanitarian aid into Gaza as weather worsens living conditions.

Europe’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has called on Israel to protect civilians in Gaza as severe flooding batters the enclave, saying an airstrike on the Nasser Hospital on Thursday was “deeply alarming.”

“The severe flooding and winter conditions that have struck Gaza are further aggravating the living conditions of an already exhausted population, exacerbating unsafe conditions and human suffering,” Kallas said in a statement Saturday.

Kallas also called on Israel to comply with international law and allow the United Nations and humanitarian organizations unimpeded access and to reopen all border crossings into Gaza.

World.title: Italy hits Meta with €805m fine over privacy law violation
World.content:
The investigation, launched in 2025, established that access to a user's camera roll is requested with a single permission for the entire app, which the authority said covers multiple features with different needs. The authorization request was preceded by a generic warning that didn't allow users to understand that they were authorizing picture and video suggestions, the authority said.

"If granted in full, this type of permission allows the app to read the device's entire photo archive, usually permanently, without the user or the authorities being able to verify which information is actually being used,” the statement reads.

The authority also said it "rejected the objection of lack of jurisdiction raised by the company in favor of the Irish authority, because the ePrivacy regulation does not provide for the 'one-stop-shop' mechanism."

Meta has 60 days to get consent separately and specifically for the feature, clearly explain what it does and how it can be disabled, the authority said. It also must be disabled by default, including for those who have already authorized it.

Meta didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. It has the right to appeal the decision.

World.title: Nearly €20m in cash found buried, hidden in Hungary corruption case
World.content:
The money — more than 5 billion forints, €2.6 million and €1.2 million — was found across locations in Budapest, Pest, Békés and Nógrád counties, the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office, an anti-corruption body, said in a statement.

“This officially marks the end for the Fidesz-KDNP mafia!” Magyar posted on Facebook, originally in Hungarian, in reference to Orbán’s government.

It took 12 Treasury staff eight hours to tally the cash using 5 counting machines, Finance Minister Kármán András said.

The announcement comes after Hungarian authorities detained Aron Orbán, the former prime minister’s brother, as part of an investigation into people smuggling. The former prime minister said on social media that the move, announced by Magyar on Monday, was part of a “political witch-hunt” to get him.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk reacted wryly to the latest announcement, referring to the arrest of Orbán’s brother and the cash discovery on X.

“Dear Victor, I’ve always been an admirer of your creativity, but now I must say I’m impressed as never before,” he wrote.

World.title: US suggested Ukraine could give up Donbas for NATO membership, Zelenskyy says
World.content:
Giving up Donbas has long been part of the proposals put forward by U.S. President Donald Trump's administration, including the 28-part plan for a peace agreement proposed by the White House in 2025. Russian President Vladimir Putin has previously demanded that Ukraine abandon its efforts to join NATO and accept strict limits on the size of its military.

“I have said repeatedly: Ukraine is not retreating and is not giving up its land to terrorists,” Zelenskyy told reporters.

The White House and U.S. State Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Zelenskyy said he was discussing a “comprehensive security package” with partners that would include specific guarantees from NATO and the EU, a strong Ukrainian army with adequate troops, weapons and financial support for a set period and a recovery plan with clear funding attached.

“If the American side confirms precisely this to us, together with other NATO partners, then I will ask our Ukrainian society what it thinks: do we accept it or not? I have no right to make that decision on my own,” Zelenskyy said. "Of course, this would be without any recognition of the occupied territories as Russian," he added.

“But we need specifics, and we don't have them yet. All of this is still under discussion,” the president said.

Veronika Melkozerova contributed to this report.

World.title: Finland rejects reported Russian demand to leave NATO as part of peace talks
World.content:
Russia proposed withdrawing its nuclear weapons from Belarus and refraining from stationing intermediate-range missiles there in exchange, Bild reported.

But it remains unclear which proposals Russian President Vladimir Putin would support after discussions between intermediaries, according to the report.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a new security framework for Europe for after the war raised by the Americans “can be dangerous."

“Russia certainly cannot make decisions on behalf of all the societies that are members of NATO,” he told reporters on Friday.

Zelenskyy’s comments were not in direct response to the demands reported by Bild, but came after a meeting between Zelenskyy and U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner on Thursday in Dublin.

“Putin's desire to change borders in Europe is a fact. I am sure this is part of his concept of revising security guarantees in Europe. This is dangerous because, in my view, it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations,” Zelenskyy said.

World.title: EU deal on Ukraine talks overshadows AI-focused summit in Dublin
World.content:
Ireland, which holds the EU’s rotating presidency and hosted the informal gathering, had billed the meeting as a rare chance for a high-level discussion on how to develop artificial intelligence in accordance with European values.

But the question of how to secure peace in Ukraine — and who should negotiate on Europe’s behalf — quickly dominated discussions, as leaders sparred over the format of future peace negotiations and warned about the risks of a potential deal brokered between Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Indeed, a meeting next week between the U.S. and Russian leaders has set Europe on edge, prompting warnings about a possible Yalta-type agreement in which superpowers would decide on European security questions over the heads of countries directly concerned, reminiscent of talks toward the end of World War II that divided Europe up between the four allied powers.

UAE’s Foreign Minister Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al-Nahyan, members of the Ukrainian and Russian delegations hold talks mediated by U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff Jared Kushner in Abu Dhabi on November 10, 2026. | Pool photo by Altaf Qadri/AFP via Getty Images

“That is why I want to make our message to the U.S. very clear: Please, no surprises!” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said regarding the Trump-Putin meeting, scheduled to take place during an APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 18-19. “Continue to play on Team Europe and on the same team as Ukraine. And let’s work together for genuine peace in Ukraine.”

The question of who should represent Europe in future discussions about Ukraine and the post-conflict security order was added to the summit’s agenda at the last minute, following a request from Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni.

Earlier in the day, Merz had voiced preference for a narrower group made up of officials from Berlin, Paris and London, while Kaja Kallas, the EU’s chief diplomat, argued that she was best placed to lead discussions.

World.title: Why Europe failed to find a superhero to take on Putin
World.content:
The push to identify one representative to speak for Europe was understandable. The appeal of having a single, respected leader taking the reins is largely based on a desire to project European strength and unity — as well as an interest in making negotiations with Russia, the U.S. and Ukraine efficient and effective.

Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy himself said this week he wanted Europe to identify within days who will take its place in the talks, and suggested he’d prefer it was one person (he even indicated that he had a preference, though would not reveal a name).



He didn’t get his way. Instead, leaders at a summit in Dublin on Friday, decided that the “E5” made up four big EU countries ― Germany, France, Poland and Italy ― and the U.K., plus officials from the European Commission and Council, would take the work forward as a team.

Technical discussions

The search for a top representative to fill Europe’s seat at the negotiating table at the next round of peace talks had become a political obsession in Brussels that missed at least two big points.

Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy takes part in a press conference at Government Buildings in Dublin on November 11, 2026. | Paul Faith/AFP via Getty Images

The first is that the leadership level is not currently where the negotiations are at. Talks this week in Abu Dhabi were technical discussions between senior officials. The big political players like Putin and Zelenskyy were not there, never mind Trump. Russia sent a Kremlin aide to lead its team and Ukraine tasked its intelligence chief with making its case.

If these officials make progress toward a deal, leaders will no doubt want to get involved. Ultimately, it will be leaders who sign any peace agreements that follow — and there’s no limit on the number of EU presidents or prime ministers who could join such a meeting as signatories or guarantors of the final deal.

The next thing that needs to happen, according to both Ukraine and the U.S. envoys mediating the talks, is for Europe to join the discussion with Russia — at this technical level.

World.title: Zelenskyy questions SpaceX over reported Starshield speed restrictions
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has reportedly accused Elon Musk's SpaceX of misleading Kyiv over speed restrictions to its Starshield network.

 

Zelenskyy said on Thursday that Ukrainian forces were facing restrictions to the service, with terminals limited to a maximum speed of 161 kilometres per hour in areas occupied by Vladimir Putin's invading forces.

"The restrictions have now been in place for five days," the Ukrainian leader said in comments released on Saturday and reported by multiple outlets. "They say it is some kind of technical issue. We do not believe that is the case."

The restrictions have been directly affecting Ukraine's ability to intercept Russian jet-powered attack drones, Zelenskyy said in an address at the European Political Community summit in Dublin earlier this week.

"If someone in America is making decisions that basically treat Ukrainian territory as if it is not Ukrainian, then this tells us where things are going," he told the summit.

On Friday, he added that Kyiv had received "no clear explanations" for the curbs.

"I instructed Ukraine’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Minister of Defense to step up contacts with the U.S. Department of State, the Pentagon, and SpaceX to obtain clarification and resolve the situation," he wrote in a post on social media.

Starshield has proved critical to Ukraine's military operations against Russian forces, providing resilient internet and communications over the battlefield.

It came as Zelenskyy said Washington had proposed the idea of Ukraine ceding land to Russia in exchange for NATO membership as efforts to accelerate peace talks continue.

"The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," Zelenskyy told reporters on Friday in comments embargoed until Saturday, per the AFP news agency.

Zelenskyy added that Ukraine was discussing "specific security guarantees" from NATO and the European Union and that he would ask Ukrainians if they accepted the terms should Western nations confirm.

"I have no right to make that decision on my own," he said.

World.title: Judo: double gold for Canada on day 2 at Zagreb Grand Prix
World.content:
It's Day 2 of the Zagreb Grand Prix, hosted at the Arena Zagreb, here in the heart of Croatia. The event was officially opened with a local Kata performance followed by speeches -from Secretary General of the International Judo Federation, Dr Lisa Allan_,_ and President of the Croatian Judo Federation, Dr Sanda Corak. Day two brought world class judo, putting fans right up close to all the action. At -63kg, former world champion Jessica KLIMKAIT of Canada was up against Slovenia's Kaja KAJZER ZABKAR. With just seconds to go, a Waza-ari score from KLIMKAIT was enough to take the victory. It’s been super nice. The last time I was here was 2019 so it’s been quite a long time. It’s nice to come back and have a little bit of that nostalgia feeling and see the crowd, see Zagreb again. It’s always been really nice here. Jessica KLIMKAIT Canadian judoka Dr Krešimir ŠAMIJA, Croatia Prime Minister Representative, awarded the medals. Georgia's Giorgi LOLADZE and Joshua GREEN of Ireland were both competing in their first ever Grand Prix final. In a close battle, just a Yuko score would crown LOLADZE the -73Kg champion. I'm really happy with my performance. There were so many people, and the atmosphere was full of emotion. I can't really describe how I feel right now. I'm just so happy.

Giorgi LOLADZE Georgian judoka Ambassador of Georgia to Croatia, His Excellency Mr Zaal GOGSADZE awarded the medals. At -70kg, Nauana SILVA of Brazil met Poland’s Aleksandra KOWALEWSKA in the final. SILVA has 4 Grand Prix medals to her name, but never taken gold. A relentless drive from the Brazilian earned her that elusive first title! Mr Krešimir MAKVIĆ, City of Zagreb Mayor Representative, awarded the medals. It was a great day for the Canadian team with François GAUTHIER DRAPEAU at -81Kg providing a fantastic footsweep in golden score, to take Canada’s second gold medal. The medals were awarded by Ms Tina TRSTENJAK, International Judo Federation Referee Director. A sensational bronze medal for Croatia’s Iva OBERAN and unstoppable local judo action gave the home crowd plenty to cheer for throughout the day. We’ll see you tomorrow for the heavyweights on Day 3.

World.title: Hope springs eternal in award-winning photos showcasing nature’s resilience
World.content:
From wildfire-scorched forests to algae-choked lakes, humans are leaving increasingly indelible marks on nature.

 

Carbon emissions from the burning of fossil fuels are pushing global warming towards and beyond the 1.5°C limit, resulting in ever worsening weather extremes.

Mass consumption is strewing coastlines with waste and polluting waterways with chemicals.

Europe is the world’s fastest-warming continent, and the European Environment Agency’s (EEA) latest state of the environment report found more than 80 per cent of protected habitats in poor or bad condition.

With the UN’s COP31 summit now in full swing, world leaders are coming together to get climate action back on track. Hot on the heels of the COP17 biodiversity talks, which ended on 31 October with a new roadmap but a UN report showing the world is falling behind on its 2030 nature goals, the intersection between nature and climate has been thrown into the spotlight.

It’s a relationship Europeans were invited to explore for this year’s EEA ‘Resilient by Nature’ photo competition.

Photographers from 35 countries set out to capture nature in states of harmony, disruption or renewal. From almost 2,800 entries, an external jury chose a winner in each category, as well as awarding a youth prize. The images were also put to a public online vote for the public choice award.

‘Sanctuary’ by Ali Aslan captures the branching roots of the ancient delta ecosystem of Dalyan, Muğla. Ali Aslan, Resilient by Nature / EEA

Harmony: Humans and nature find balance in Türkiye’s ancient delta

Türkiye’s Dalyan Delta has for decades stood strong against tourism development, with strict environmental protections helping to fight off resorts and other human activity.

Designated as a Special Environmental Protection Area in the 1980s, the ecologically vital wetland ecosystem is home to over 150 bird species and rare, endemic Turkish sweetgum forests.

Vulnerable loggerhead sea turtles nest on İztuzu Beach, where seasonal night closures and a ban on pets are in place to protect hatchlings.
