Two years later, he described purchasing Italian equipment as the most cost-effective option. However, the plans never materialised.

From one landfill to another

In 2018, the landfill in the Mayak neighbourhood was finally closed. However, the problem did not disappear – it was simply relocated. Waste from the capital began to be transported daily to a landfill in the village of Shashakuara, in Gali district, 72km away, resulting in significant costs and wear and tear on vehicles.

“The Sukhum landfill contains hundreds of thousands of cubic metres of waste. But most of that volume is air. Only 15% consists of solid and liquid waste, while 85% is air. So these trucks keep driving back and forth, transporting air and burning fuel,” Russian hydraulic engineer Alexander Tsekhovoy explained to specialists in Sukhum in 2019.

According to his calculations, rather than endlessly transporting waste between landfills, each district should establish special compaction stations capable of compressing waste four- to fivefold. This would reduce the number of trips to the central landfill to just four truckloads a day.

However, instead of introducing these technologies, the authorities have continued simply transporting waste from one district to another.

Costly and pointless landfill in Katsikyt

A new waste management complex in the village of Katsikyt, in Gulripshi district, was supposed to provide a breakthrough solution to the waste problem.

The 5.5-hectare site was equipped with a waste disposal pit featuring a multilayer insulating base, treatment facilities and a conveyor belt for sorting waste. Construction proved extremely challenging, both technically and financially, with the project costing more than 150m roubles [$1.81m].

However, by the time the facility was nearly complete, it turned out that nobody wanted it.

Sukhum refused to use the complex, while the authorities in Gulripshi district were also reluctant to take responsibility for it. Security personnel were soon withdrawn from the site, which has since been effectively abandoned and remains unused.

Waste processing complex in the village of Katsikyt

The landfill in the village of Katsikyt was intended to be a financially sustainable facility. During its construction, Timur Agrba, then head of the Capital Construction Department and now mayor of Sukhum, said the facility could become self-financing by sorting, compacting and selling recyclable materials, including plastic, paper and metal.

According to Agrba, if properly managed, the facility could not only cover its operating costs but also generate revenue for further development.

However, in practice, the main obstacle is the tariff for household waste disposal.

“The current tariff policy does not reflect the realities or the costs incurred by our companies. International practice shows that waste collection and transportation should be funded through payments made by the residents who generate that waste,” Beslan Eshba, then head of the Sukhum city administration, explained back in 2014.

He promised that city authorities would seek to introduce relevant amendments to a new housing code. However, 12 years later, the new code has still not been adopted.

The current waste collection fee in Abkhazia is 27 roubles [$0.33] per person per month, a relatively modest amount. Yet most urban residents do not even pay this, as there is no clearly established system for collecting utility payments.

To obtain an objective assessment of the situation, Abkhazia’s Public Chamber held a series of meetings with Russian specialists, local environmental experts and representatives of district administrations.

As a result, an expert report was drawn up, providing a comprehensive assessment of the entire household waste management system. The report has already been submitted to the president, parliament, executive authorities and the Institute of Ecology.

For now, however, it represents little more than another faint glimmer of hope on the horizon. No tangible progress has been made towards resolving the problem.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Проблема мусора в Абхази

World.title: Special forces officers convicted of assaulting protesters jailed for five years each
World.content:
Special forces officers jailed for assaults

A court has sentenced special forces officers convicted of physically assaulting journalist Guram Rogava and protester Zviad Maisashvili during demonstrations in November and December 2024 to five years in prison each.

The special forces officer convicted of assaulting Guram Rogava, a journalist with Formula TV, was also banned from professional duties for three years. Lasha Gamkrelidze, the new prosecutor in the case, informed the journalist of the verdict by telephone.

According to Formula, Rogava had expected to testify as a victim during the trial. However, the prosecutor explained that his testimony was unnecessary because the court and the defence had accepted the charges as undisputed. Rogava himself believes that the person who directly assaulted him remains at large.

Two other special forces officers arrested in connection with the assault on Zviad Maisashvili were each sentenced to five years in prison. Lawyer Dimitri Mchedlishvili confirmed the information to Tabula.

On 30 November 2024, at around 06:30, special forces officers kicked Zviad Maisashvili in the face during a protest on Rustaveli Avenue, causing him to lose consciousness. Footage of the assault circulated on social media.

On 7 May 2026, Georgia’s Prosecutor’s Office announced that it had identified and detained five people in connection with assaults on Rogava, Maisashvili and opposition politician Levan Khabeishvili.

According to the Prosecutor’s Office, four of those detained were current or former special forces officers, while the fifth was a serving officer with the Interior Ministry’s Security Police Department. Two of the suspects were already serving prison sentences at the time of their arrest.

Prosecutors said that on 29 November 2024, during a protest on Rustaveli Avenue, an officer from the Interior Ministry’s Special Tasks Department assaulted Guram Rogava while the journalist was carrying out his professional duties.

The detainees were charged under Article 333(3) of the Criminal Code with abuse of official powers involving violence. The officer detained in connection with the assault on Rogava also faced an additional charge of unlawfully obstructing a journalist’s professional activities.

According to the Prosecutor’s Office’s initial statement, the charges carried prison sentences of five to eight years.

Maisashvili said both special forces officers detained over the assault on him had admitted their guilt and apologised to him.

Guram Rogava and Zviad Maisashvili

Background

The assaults on Guram Rogava and Zviad Maisashvili were among several high-profile incidents of police violence during pro-European protests in Tbilisi in November and December 2024.

The protests began on 28 November 2024, after Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze announced that the government would take the issue of opening EU accession talks off the agenda until the end of 2028.

In the following days, law enforcement officers used water cannon, tear gas and other crowd-control measures against protesters on Rustaveli Avenue and near the parliament building. Numerous incidents of physical violence against demonstrators, journalists and human rights defenders were documented.

Both protesters and members of the media sustained injuries during the demonstrations. The assault on journalist Guram Rogava attracted particular attention. On 29 November 2024, a special forces officer attacked Rogava while he was reporting live from Rustaveli Avenue, leaving him seriously injured.

Media representatives and human rights organisations called for investigations into these incidents. On 30 November 2024, the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR) said the police’s use of water cannon, pepper spray and batons, including against peaceful demonstrators and journalists, had been disproportionate.

According to Georgia’s Public Defender’s 2024 report, the ombudsman and his representatives visited 624 people who had been detained or injured during protests between 15 April 2024 and 1 March 2025. Of those, 360 reported ill-treatment.

The report also noted that no police officers had been held accountable for violence committed by law enforcement personnel during that period.

According to the Prosecutor’s Office statement of 7 May 2026, more than 550 witnesses were questioned and thousands of investigative and procedural actions were carried out as part of the investigations into the cases involving Zviad Maisashvili, Levan Khabeishvili and Guram Rogava.

The Prosecutor’s Office said the investigations would continue to identify other possible perpetrators and bring them to justice.

World.title: Azerbaijan's non-oil sector share in budget revenues set to approach 61% in 2027
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 15. The share of the non-oil and gas sector in Azerbaijan's state budget revenues is projected to increase to 60.6% in 2027, while the share of oil and gas revenues is expected to decline to 39.4%, according to the opinion issued by the Chamber of Accounts on the draft law "On the state budget of the Republic of Azerbaijan for 2027."

According to the document, Azerbaijan's nominal gross domestic product (GDP) is expected to increase by 6.9 billion manat ($4.06 billion), or 5.1%, compared to the current year, reaching 141 billion manat ($82.95 billion) in 2027. GDP in the non-oil and gas sector is projected to grow by 7.4 billion manat ($4.35 billion), or 7.2%, to 109.1 billion manat ($64.16 billion).

According to the Chamber of Accounts' analysis, the higher growth rate of economic activity in the non-oil and gas sector will also positively affect state budget revenues from this sector.

Specifically, state budget revenues are projected to reach 39.25 billion manat ($23.09 billion) in 2027, up 645 million manat ($379.4 million), or 1.7%, compared to the 2026 forecast.

The role of non-oil and gas sources in the revenue structure is expected to increase. Non-oil and gas revenues are projected to amount to 23.77 billion manat ($13.98 billion), up 1.6 billion manat ($941.2 million), or 7.2%, compared to this year's forecast. As a result, their share of total state budget revenues is expected to rise from 57.4% in 2026 to 60.6% in 2027.

Meanwhile, oil and gas revenues are projected to decline. In 2027, state budget receipts from this source are expected to amount to 15.48 billion manat ($9.11 billion), down 955 million manat ($561.8 million), or 5.8%, compared to the 2026 forecast. Consequently, their share in total state budget revenues is expected to fall from 42.6% to 39.4%.

The Chamber of Accounts attributed one of the main reasons for the decline in oil and gas revenues to lower projected transfers from the State Oil Fund of Azerbaijan to the state budget compared to the previous year.

State budget revenues as a share of GDP to decline

Another point highlighted in the opinion is the projected decline in the ratio of state budget revenues to GDP.

Specifically, the share of state budget revenues in GDP is projected to decrease by 1 percentage point compared to the current year, reaching 27.8% in 2027. The main reason is that nominal GDP is expected to grow faster than state budget revenues.

For comparison, while GDP is projected to increase by 5.1% in 2027, state budget revenues are expected to grow by 1.7%.

At the same time, non-oil and gas revenues as a share of GDP in the respective sector are projected to remain stable at 21.8%.

According to the report, state budget revenues amounted to 35.24 billion manat ($20.73 billion) in 2023, 37.16 billion manat ($21.86 billion) in 2024, and 39.18 billion manat ($23.05 billion) in 2025. This figure is projected at 38.61 billion manat ($22.71 billion) for 2026 and 39.25 billion manat ($23.09 billion) for 2027.

Meanwhile, GDP in the non-oil and gas sector is expected to increase from 77.66 billion manat ($45.68 billion) in 2023 to 109.1 billion manat ($64.16 billion) in 2027.

The 2027 projections indicate that the non-oil and gas sector will play an increasingly significant role in generating state budget revenues, while the share of oil and gas revenues in total budget receipts is expected to decline.

World.title: President Ilham Aliyev congratulates President of State of Palestine
World.content:
Photo: Press Service of the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 15. President of the Republic of Azerbaijan, Ilham Aliyev, sent a congratulatory letter to Mahmoud Abbas, President of the State of Palestine.

The text of the letter was published on the official website of the President of Azerbaijan.

"Dear Mr. President,

On the occasion of the National Day of the State of Palestine, I extend my most sincere congratulations to you and, through you, to your entire people, on my own behalf and on behalf of the people of Azerbaijan.

We attach great importance to relations between Azerbaijan and Palestine, which are based on the principles of friendship and mutual respect.

Azerbaijan has always demonstrated solidarity with regard to the Palestinian issue and supports its resolution based on the two-state principle, in accordance with the relevant resolutions and decisions of the United Nations, through the establishment of an independent State of Palestine with East Jerusalem as its capital.

We will continue to provide humanitarian assistance to the brotherly Palestinian people.

Taking this opportunity, I also congratulate you on your birthday and wish you robust health, happiness, and success in your efforts to ensure peace and prosperity for the brotherly Palestinian people," the letter reads.

World.title: Homophobic graffiti sprayed on Sydney MP's office under investigation
World.content:
Homophobic graffiti sprayed on the outside walls and windows of Sydney MP Alex Greenwich's office is under investigation by NSW Police.

Mr Greenwich told the ABC that the vandalism was unprecedented.

"I've got lots of written threats, phone abuse, social media, but never anything like this," he said.

Alex Greenwich says he has never experienced this level of attack before. (ABC News: Keana Naughton)

Reports of the attack at the Oxford Street premises in the inner-east Sydney suburb of Surry Hills were received by police on Sunday at about 12pm.

"A crime scene has been established, and investigators are reviewing CCTV and conducting inquiries to identify the people involved," police said in a statement.

In a post on social media, Mr Greenwich said the incident was "deeply distressing" for both his staff and himself.

"No-one should face this kind of hatred in their workplace, especially on the 9th anniversary of Australia’s marriage equality YES vote," the post said.

"If the intention was to intimidate me, it has had the opposite effect. I’m more determined than ever to make Sydney and NSW safer, fairer and more equal for our community."

The incident has been condemned as "vile". (Supplied)

Allegra Spender, the federal member for Wentworth, condemned the incident as "vile", saying she was "disgusted and appalled".

"There is no place for homophobia or hate in our community, and certainly not in Australian politics," she said.

"Words matter, and this kind of attack is designed to intimidate and harm."

She added that her electorate was "sending you all our love and support".

Focus on violence against politicians

The vandalism comes after growing awareness and discussion on violence against politicians, after the shocking car attack on Victorian Independent MP Helen Haines, which led to both her legs being amputated.

NSW MP Jodie Harrison told the ABC last month that the attack on Ms Haines had resurfaced memories of nine years ago when two envelopes containing death threats were slipped under the door.

Threats to MPs linked to political debate AFP Commissioner Krissy Barrett on the correlation between heated moments of political discourse and the number of threats reported against politicians.

"It made me feel physically sick," she said.

"One of the downsides of public life is that people who might not like us know that we can actually easily be found, because we're public people."

Recently, AFP Commissioner Krissy Barrett told the ABC's Insider programme that there was a direct link between inflammatory political discourse and threats against parliamentarians.

"It does have a direct correlation to what we see in terms of threats and abuse, and sometimes it's very immediate," she said.

"I would challenge any Australian to read some of these threats and some of the abuse that is reported to us from federal parliamentarians and for anyone to argue that that is free speech or political discourse."

Police are urging anyone with information to contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000 or Surry Hills Police Area Command.

World.title: Jillaroos' World Cup win is more of the same old story
World.content:
Right from the start, the women's Rugby League World Cup final was yet another version of the same old story.

Australia's 34-10 win over New Zealand was the latest procession for the Jillaroos, who cruised to victory on the back of a brilliant and brutal beginning from which the Kiwi Ferns never recovered.

Against the second-best team in the world, the Jillaroos still looked several classes above. By the time New Zealand completed its first set it was already down 12-0.

Rugby League World Cup finals live: Follow all the action in our blog.

Jillaroos win Rugby League World Cup A dominant first-half performance and a Jaime Chapman hat-trick has fired the Jillaroos to a 34-10 victory over New Zealand in the Rugby League World Cup final.

The Australians fell short of beating the clock in the first half but with a 34-6 lead at the break they went pretty close.

Jess Skinner's side has the greatest collection of talent the women's game has ever seen and it was typified by the likes of Jamie Chapman and Jess Sergis, who both turned one-out runs into long range tries.

Chapman was particularly exceptional. Her first-half hat-trick displayed the full dimensions of her athleticism: the strength of her first try, the graceful finish for her second and the speed she showed for her third earned her player-of-the-match honours.

A repeat of the 2022 final, which Australia won by 50, looked to be on the cards before a meandering second half in the thick Brisbane humidity and by the end, the match was falling over the line.

It was far from their greatest performance but the Jillaroos are the kind of team who would be good enough on a bad day and New Zealand, like everyone else who's run into the Jillaroos through this World Cup, was helpless to stop what was coming.

You might as well ask them to stop the tide coming in or stop the sun rising in the morning.

The Kiwi Ferns did a better job of it in the second half but the contest was already gone. Winning the second half is little consolation if it's a World Cup final and what long felt inevitable came to pass when Isabelle Kelly lifted the trophy.

Australia was way too good for New Zealand right from the start. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

This victory and that inevitability is both a measure of how far the game has come and a reminder of the cost of that progress.

Through the development of the NRLW, Australia is so much better than everyone else that its dominance threatens the international game as a spectacle.

Australia has so many players who can light up a match. Chapman's speed, power and finishing abilities, Jessie Southwell's kicking game and Olivia Kernick's cunning and strength are all rugby league joys to behold.

But it always adds up to the same thing. We always end up in the same place and if the journey always has the same ending it makes it harder to follow it through to the end.

It has made this tournament a slog and there is no way out of it either, not for a while yet.

There is no end in sight to Australia's dominance. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

Samoa and Fiji both have improvement in them and New Zealand will get better as the Warriors settle back into the NRLW, but the depth of Australia's talent is near bottomless.

For any other nation, losing a player like Millie Elliott to retirement would be a hammer blow that leaves behind an enormous space to fill.

But the only problem for Australia will be choosing between the excellent options at their disposal.

Sarah Togatuki, fresh off making the Dally M team of the year, can't make this side. Neither can Cronulla's Ellie Johnston or Tigers signing Rima Butler.

For any other nation, they'd be automatic selections every single time. For Australia, they must wait their turn.

Couple that with the fact that the best football is still ahead of someone like Jesse Southwell, a World Cup winner at 21, and this era of Australian domination has no end in sight.

They are not a big fish in a small pond; they are a leviathan in a bathtub and even as they crush all comers, they keep growing.

World.title: Shark attack hero breaks through for Iron Series win
World.content:
An emotional Charlie Verco has described his journey from a shark-attack rescue to a maiden Iron Series win as a "roller coaster".

Five months after saving Leah Stewart at Coogee Beach, Verco claimed the third round of the series by prevailing in a sprint finish in Sunday's race at Thirroul Beach.

In June, the 25-year-old paddled towards the danger and pulled the unconscious woman from the surf.

This shark attack hero believes Olympic inclusion could save lives The top seed in this year's Iron Series, who made headlines by helping save a shark attack victim earlier this year at Coogee, says having surf life saving in the Brisbane Olympic Games would help raise the profile of the sport.

After 12 days in a critical condition in hospital and a series of surgeries to amputate her arm, Stewart woke from an induced coma and was reunited with her daughter.

"Being able to manage the ups and downs of it, like the stressful rescue with Leah — I'm so happy that she was able to be alright," Verco said.

"It meant that I was able to keep focused on what I love, which is the sport.

"But realistically, we all do this sport as part of surf lifesaving. It certainly doesn't feel like we were doing a race like that.

"It feels like we're all just really wanting to win and compete against each other.

"But I like that we have the skills to be able to go and help people when they need it."

Verco beat home Ethan Callaghan and Henry Simpson in a breakthrough victory, which comes after the 25-year-old had entered this year's Iron Series as the top seed following the legendary Ali Day's retirement.

"It is a step up to try and put yourself at the front of the race as opposed to just being happy that you're here," Verco said.

"And for so long that was my goal, was just to get here. It's all about confidence.

"I've spent a long time doing races trying to get myself comfortable being at the front and setting my own pace, and I think that definitely helps."

Naomi Scott took out the women's event, with the Northcliffe athlete pipping Emma Woods in a sprint up the beach.

Before the Iron Series heads to Newcastle in January, Scott will travel to South Africa next week to defend her global Ironwoman title at the world lifesaving championships.

World.title: Chapman hat-trick fires Jillaroos to Rugby League World Cup glory
World.content:
The Jillaroos have defended their Rugby League World Cup title, dominating New Zealand 34-10 in the tournament decider at Lang Park.

The victory was all but assured after a dominant first half, with winger Jaime Chapman crossing for a hat-trick in sweltering Brisbane heat.

The win saw Australia claim a fourth-straight crown in the fifth-consecutive final featuring the Trans-Tasman rivals.

Rugby League World Cup finals live: Follow all the action in our blog.

Chapman's, whose treble brought her World Cup tally to 13, has told ABC Sport it was a dream end to the campaign after a difficult run with injury.

"I've fought so hard to get here and I'm just proud of all of us," Chapman said.

"And I'm super proud of myself as well for making it back into this team and winning it for our country."

Chapman scored a stunning treble in sweltering Brisbane heat. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

Lessons seemingly learnt from a lethargic start to their semifinal win over Fiji, the Jillaroos were dominant from the first minute in the tournament decider.

It took Chapman just two minutes to score the first try of the day by breaking wide, stutter stepping and rampaging through the New Zealand defence, allowing for the recalled Jesse Southwell to nail a difficult conversion.

A spectacular dive and one-handed putdown saw Chapman cross for her second in the 14th minute, before the winger put on the afterburners to complete her treble with a scintillating breakaway effort.

By half-time, Australia had run in six tries to the Kiwi Ferns' one, with Shaylee Best, Jess Sergis and Tamika Upton having also registered four-pointers, and Southwell having nailed all but one of the conversions.

Sergis's effort came after a breathtaking breakaway, while Upton completed a neat give and go with Abbi Church to compound New Zealand's misery in the shadows of half-time.

Shannon Mato's 23rd-minute converted effort was the Kiwi Ferns' only contribution to a half-time 34-6 scoreline.

Only a try-saving tackle prevented the Jillaroos from going further ahead five minutes after the break, but the Australians struggled for any cut through in an energy-sapping second half in which the still taxing conditions restricted the quality of play.

New Zealand winger Mackenzie Wiki was denied a late score thanks to a try-saving Isabelle Kelly tackle, but proceeded to find the only points of the second period by diving over with the full-time siren seconds from sounding.

Their 4-0 second-half scoreline meant the Kiwi Ferns went the entire tournament without conceding a point after half-time.

World.title: Albanese stands by Ukraine but won't rule out photo with Putin
World.content:
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has not ruled out appearing in a photograph alongside Russian President Vladimir Putin at an upcoming summit, despite condemning the invasion of Ukraine as "illegal and immoral".

The expected appearance of Mr Putin at APEC in China later this week has created a diplomatic challenge for many world leaders, with Mr Albanese leaving the door open to joining the traditional leaders' family photo at the event.

"I will respect and of course take into consideration the wishes of our host country," he told reporters in Manila on Sunday.

Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney has indicated he would take part in the photo out of respect for China, but other leaders are yet to indicate their position.

Mr Albanese is in the Philippines for the Association of South-East Asian Nations (ASEAN) leaders' summit and will travel to Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) meeting on Wednesday.

Anthony Albanese at a signing ceremony for the Philippines-Australia Defense Cooperation Arrangement ahead of the 49th ASEAN summit in Manila. (Reuters: Hollie Adams)

Mr Albanese welcomed the prospect of talks between Mr Putin, US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of APEC, amid concerns the three leaders could seek to carve up the world into spheres of influence.

"We think that dialogue is a good thing, and we await the outcome of that dialogue," Mr Albanese said.

"We want to see something constructive come out of that, including, we want to see a de-escalation [of] conflict from around the world."

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has likened the proposed three-way meeting to a "Yalta 2.0" moment, invoking the 1945 conference at which allied leaders discussed the post-war order in Europe.

Asked if the trilateral talk undermined Australia's push for greater cooperation between middle powers, Mr Albanese said he would continue to engage with the US and China, while standing firmly behind Ukraine.

"What's important about the struggle of the people of Ukraine is that they're not just standing up for their sovereignty; they're standing up for the international rule of law."

Mr Albanese played down any prospect of a direct interaction with Mr Putin at APEC but said he would make Australia's position clear if the two leaders found themselves in the same room.

"This is a bigger country being a bully in contravention of international law," he said.

Australia signs defence pact with Philippines

Mr Albanese witnessed the signing of a new defence cooperation between Australia and the Philippines that is expected to bolster freedom of navigation in the contested South China Sea.

Australia will also make an additional investment in maritime security capabilities, including drone technology and equipment and training to improve the detection of threats.

Australia, Philippines to ink defence deal Australia and the Philippines are set to sign a major defence cooperation agreement amid tensions in the South China Sea.

The Philippines has been involved in increasingly tense confrontations with Chinese vessels in disputed waters, where Beijing asserts sweeping territorial claims.

But Mr Albanese rejected suggestions that Australia's agreement was designed to counter China's growing military influence.

"This isn't aimed at any one country," he said.

"This is about supporting sovereignty of every country.

" [The] majority of our trade goes through the South China Sea, this is important. "

The prime minister, who also met with Australian sailors aboard HMAS Stalwart in Manila, confirmed Australia would continue its freedom of navigation activities in the region, despite repeated criticism from Beijing.

"We have exercises that are important; we have no intention of changing that," he said.

Anthony Albanese has welcomed the prospect of talks between the leaders of the US, China and Russia at the APEC Summit. (Reuters: Tingshu Wang)

Mr Albanese will travel to China later this week for APEC and talks with President Xi, but declined to confirm if he would directly raise issues in the South China Sea.

"We'll engage diplomatically rather than … through the media," he said.

In a lighter moment during his Manila visit, Mr Albanese also welcomed news that Filipino fast food giant Jollibee would open 35 stores across Australia over the next five years, creating an estimated 900 jobs.

"It's fantastic food, fantastic food," he declared after visiting one of the chain's restaurants.

Trump to push US-led AI initiative

The prime minister is also expected to use this week's ASEAN and East Asia summits to push for a de-escalation of conflict in the Middle East, warning its economic consequences are being felt throughout the region.

Mr Albanese said he would continue to make Australia's position known to Mr Trump, who is due to attend the East Asia and Quad leaders' summits in Manila on Tuesday.

The US president is expected to use the summits to push South-East Asian countries to join the US-led Pax Silica initiative, which offers funding and technical support to governments that adopt American AI systems for public services.

Australia is a member of the initiative, but Mr Albanese emphasised the government's own approach to AI safety and the need for international regulations.

Albanese apologises for 'dick' hot mic gaffe

Mr Albanese also apologised for a recent hot mic incident involving a conversation with Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen about the potential impact of mobile phone radiation on their "dicks".

Albanese and Bowen's hot mic gaffe The prime minister's office says Anthony Albanese and Chris Bowen were sharing a joke when a private conversation was inadvertently recorded.

"Of course I regret that, I apologise," the prime minister said of the remarks made on the sidelines of the COP31 UN climate summit last week.

"This was a private conversation, we thought, between two friends having … a light-hearted banter.

"No one was hurt or harmed."

Meanwhile, Mr Albanese confirmed he would raise the case of Australian man Tran Kip, who is detained in Vietnam on alleged terrorism charges, during a meeting with his Vietnamese counterpart.

Mr Albanese said the government would pursue the matter through diplomatic channels, pointing to previous efforts to secure the release of Australians detained overseas.

"Australia engages respectfully and diplomatically," he said.

World.title: Weekend deaths push WA road toll to grim record high
World.content:
Western Australia is on track to record its worst road toll in a decade, with five deaths recorded in the past 48 hours.

The horror weekend has pushed the state to a grim milestone, with the road toll now sitting at 186 deaths so far this year, above the 184 fatalities recorded for all of 2025.

Three young people were killed on Friday morning when their Ford Falcon collided with trees near the Wheatbelt town of Narrogin, 192 kilometres south-east of Perth.

Leigh Ballard is urging drivers to be more careful. (ABC News: Rosemary Murphy)

The shire's president, Leigh Ballard, described the deaths of the 21-year-old man, 22-year-old woman and 23-year-old man as a "terrible tragedy for the town."

"We've had too many accidents on the road this year, I just want everyone to slow down and drive safe," Mr Ballard said.

On Friday evening, two motorcycles collided on Mandurah Road in Dudley Park.

Regional roads are busier this time of year, which can mean more accidents. (ABC News)

The 35-year-old male rider of a Kawasaki bike died at the scene, while the rider of a Triumph motorcycle sustained non-life-threatening injuries.

The fifth death was a 41-year-old man, who was behind the wheel of a Toyota Landcruiser on the Donnybrook-Boyup Brook Road when it hit a tree.

'Heartbreaking' milestone

Julie Freeman, the opposition spokesperson for road safety, said the deaths should ring "alarm bells" in government.

"Today is a heartbreaking milestone that no Western Australian wanted to see," Ms Freeman said.

The WA government has invested millions into improving regional roads. (ABC South West WA: Bridget McArthur)

"There is a great paradox: our cars are getting safer, our penalties are getting tougher … and yet the road toll keeps going up, and I think there needs to be a concerted effort into investigating why that is."

While improvements on main regional roads have had an impact, Ms Freeman said these needed to be rolled out more extensively.

"What is being neglected is the 8,000-kilometre network of the local government roads; those roads also need these same treatments," she said.

The state government is investing $3.6 billion in regional roads over the next four years, a spokesperson said.

The state government has expanded the Regional Road Safety Programme. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Brianna Melville )

"The Regional Road Safety Program, which, since launching in 2020, has invested around $1 billion to deliver safety treatments to 10,000km of regional roads, including nearly 700km of local roads," the spokesperson said.

"The Cook Labor government has committed $125 million over five years to expand the Regional Road Safety Program to local roads."

Government minister Amber-Jade Sanderson said more than a billion dollars has been spent on road safety, and drivers must change their behaviour.

Amber-Jade Sanderson wants drivers to change their behaviour. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

"It has been a terrible few days on the roads, and there are some very traumatised and grieving families who have lost young people in their families," she said.

"We have spent a billion dollars over the past 10 years making our roads safer, AI cameras changing behaviours, education programs; we will continue supporting the community."

AI cameras are among the government's road safety measures. (ABC News)

There is significantly higher traffic on country roads across southern WA, with harvest underway, and roads are only expected to get busier as the summer holidays approach.

World.title: After tragically losing a mate, Herbert is helping businesses with his shirt
World.content:
Golfer Lucas Herbert has returned to Australia on a mission to use his platform to help those struggling in the tough economic climate.

Herbert has played in this week's NSW Open at the Hunter Valley, finishing in a tie for third.

But Herbert, fresh off the collapse of LIV Golf, entered this week's tournament without something synonymous with professional sport: sponsorships.

The end of LIV Golf brought an end to many commercial arrangements Herbert had, meaning he entered this week's NSW Open with his clothing as a blank canvas.

But Herbert decided he wanted to use his platform to help, following the tragic death of a mate earlier this year.

The 30-year-old from Bendigo put a call out to small businesses in the lead-up to the tournament, offering to promote them on his clothing.

He said small business owners were doing it tough, and said he wanted to help out.

He told golf journalist Tom Hobbs earlier this week that he was inspired to help small Australian businesses following the passing of a friend.

"Just seeing local business getting destroyed over here makes me sad," he said.

"One of my good friends took his own life in January because he was a small business owner and couldn't take the pressures of working 60 hours a week to keep the lights on any longer.

"I thought it would be better than coming home wearing blank hats and clothes."

A mental health charity, electrical and a lawn care business were among the sponsors Herbert carried on his clothing this week.

Herbert will also be part of the Australian Open and Australian PGA Championship during this golf season.

World.title: Man in custody after police helicopter search near Devonport
World.content:
A man allegedly linked to a series of incidents in Tasmania's north-west, including a service station robbery, is in police custody following a multi-hour search.

Police said they were first notified about the man shortly after 9am on Sunday, when they received reports he was "acting erratically" on Macfie Street in Devonport.

They said members of the public reported he was "knocking on doors and demanding keys to their vehicles" before he left the scene in a white Toyota.

Police said a service station in Railton, about 22 kilometres south of Devonport, was robbed just before 10am, with a quantity of cash taken from the premises.

Police were scouring the area around Devonport. (ABC News: Duncan Bailey)

The man is then alleged to have stolen a silver Alfa Romeo from Kimberley, about 9 kilometres south-east of Railton.

Police resources, including a helicopter, were deployed to search for the man and the stolen vehicle.

The suspect was described as being about 5 feet 8 inches in height, with short hair, olive complexion and facial tattoos.

Police said the man was then detected in the Penguin area, about 30 kilometres west of Devonport, just before 5pm following information from the public.

They said he fled from the Alfa Romeo near Preservation Bay, and attempted to escape on foot before surrendering to police and being taken into custody.

Investigations into the incidents are continuing.

World.title: ‘I can’t lead a normal life’: Why this former Bulldog is fighting for his future
World.content:
Exclusive SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘I can’t lead a normal life’: Why this former Bulldog is fighting for his future Jon Pierik November 15, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A former player who was forced into medical retirement after suffering eight brain bleeds and a fractured skull has been left shocked after an AFL-ordered clinical assessment ruled that he had sustained only a “mild” brain injury. That clinical reclassification – delivered more than two years after Western Bulldogs draftee Aiden O’Driscoll was forced out of the game before playing a senior match – has left the 21-year-old traumatised, derailed his bid for a $600,000 severe injury payout and put his management on a collision course with the league. Seeking recompense: Bulldogs draftee Aiden O’Driscoll was forced to retire without playing an AFL game. Getty O’Driscoll retired at just 18 in May 2024 before he had made his senior AFL debut, having suffered a major “head-on-head” concussion during a pre-season match simulation session and rushed to The Alfred hospital. He suffered a seizure and a fracture behind his ear, an MRI later revealing that the collision had left him with eight brain bleeds. While he received a career-ending injury payment of more than $150,000 in 2024, his application for a $600,000 severe injury benefit (SIB) payment was rejected this year by the AFL and AFL Players’ Association, which found he did not meet the criteria.



Related Article Exclusive

AFL injury ward ‘Vague and embarrassing’: Cats’ doctors hit back at Rooke class action concussion claim That decision was based on a neuropsychological assessment report completed in Perth in March by a group of clinicians specialising in the diagnosis and management of neuropsychological and behavioural conditions, which concluded that O’Driscoll suffered only a “mild TBI [traumatic brain injury]” – leaving O’Driscoll and his agent Peter Jess in shock. An AFL medical panel’s report in April 2024 revealed the extent of O’Driscoll’s injury, going as far as declaring “Aiden has more micro-haemorrhages than the panel has seen in other athletes”. He was medically retired by the AFL’s independent concussion panel. He struggles with daily memory loss, nausea and anxiety, dizziness and has difficulty sleeping as a result of the brain trauma stemming from the training incident. “It [mild assessment] does not add up. My memory for basic things is shocking, really bad. It has progressively got worse over time. It’s a horrible thing for a 21-year-old to go through. Literally yesterday, when I went to the shops for three things … avocado, it literally took me 15 minutes to remember, and it was one of three things. But I forgot one of the things, which was the reason for going to the shops, and that was the dishwashing liquid,” O’Driscoll told this masthead.



View post on X “Things like that have happened to me a lot since I had the hit. “I have lost a couple of girlfriends [relationship break-ups] along the way, and I honestly think it’s to do with this as well. “The basic things I forget. I obviously can’t live a normal life.” AFL chief medical officer Michael Makdissi, in a discharge summary letter dated May 18, 2026, did not comment on the “mild TBI” assessment, leaving Jess stunned.



Related Article Exclusive

Australian cricket ‘Misconceived’: Brighton Grammar hits back at Will Pucovski concussion lawsuit “The medical classification for Aiden’s type of injury is moderate/severe TBI, not a mild brain trauma as assessed … the assessment is flawed and cannot be relied upon,” Jess, a prominent concussion campaigner for athletes in all sports, said. The neuropsychological report, which Jess gave to this masthead on behalf of O’Driscoll, said: “He [O’Driscoll] sustained a mild TBI on 26/01/2024 during a pre-season simulation match, which resulted in a single seizure episode and loss of consciousness. Neuroimaging scans have identified micro-haemorrhages primarily in his right temporal lobe. “After medical assessments and review by an independent concussion panel, Aiden retired from professional football and contact sport in May 2024. “Prior to his TBI, Aiden underwent cognitive evaluation as part of the Western Bulldogs baseline cognitive testing program. At baseline, Aiden was observed to display variability across his results, with weaknesses more apparent on memory tasks and when the complexity and attentional demands were greater.



Related Article AFL 2026 Hanson’s ‘dehumanising’ comments spur former footy star in AFL legal fight “These outcomes largely reflected a long-standing pattern of cognitive strengths and weaknesses, noting his pre-existing ADHD and dyslexia diagnoses. “At 41 days post-TBI, neuropsychological review noted that Aiden had generally been making a good recovery. Formal testing revealed largely stable results compared to his baseline, though memory scores were slightly weaker. On the current assessment, Aiden’s basic attention processing speed, visual spatial skills, and executive functions were broadly at age-expected levels. His verbal language abilities were comparatively weaker, and vulnerabilities were apparent with his working memory and mental flexibility, attentional shift. “There were limitations and efficiencies with Aiden’s new learning encoding, as well as his memory recall, likely related to feelings of overwhelm and attentional weakness.” This masthead is not accusing the AFL or the AFLPA of any wrongdoing.



O’Driscoll, who has expressed frustration with the AFL and the overall process on social media, said it had been a traumatic experience. “It has been [traumatic], it has been very difficult,” O’Driscoll said. “The severity of my injury … it has had severe impacts on me. When it first happened, I just wanted to get back out there and keep playing. I wasn’t affected a heap, but it got to six months down the line, that’s when I started to feel it.” The AFLPA said in a rejection letter in March that O’Driscoll had not demonstrated a “permanent impairment of cognitive function”, meaning his future earning capacity would not be reduced by at least 40 per cent. Jess described that claim as “nonsense”, and had already begun examining legal action against several parties.



Related Article AFL 2026 ‘You’ve been nothing but a joke’: Ex-AFL player criticises league over concussion support The AFLPA did not wish to comment because of confidentiality reasons. The AFL was contacted for comment. Jess said the mild, rather than moderate or severe, assessment meant O’Driscoll’s bid for a disability pension was also impacted. “It’s frightening what has gone on here. It has destroyed the kid’s life,” Jess said. “He hasn’t done anything for months. He is not earning any money. This is setting a dangerous precedent.”



In the discharge letter, seen by this masthead, Makdissi said that O’Driscoll had not attended his final case review, with his bid to have a non-related third party, in his case Jess, accompanying him “deemed inappropriate” by the league. He said O’Driscoll’s working history included one-on-one football training, and disability support work with children and adults, but “his current work capacity is limited due to ongoing symptoms”. Makdissi noted that of the initial neuropsychological review in March 2024, O’Driscoll had reported that most of his initial concerns, including headaches, fatigue and memory concerns, had “largely resolved”. He said a follow-up in August 2024 had shown “stable or improved cognitive performance … with improved memory relative to the March assessment”. Of this year’s review, Makdissi said O’Driscoll reported “mildly increased cognitive and physical fatigue, slightly slower processing speed, reduced time management, intermittent forgetfulness, difficulty initiating tasks, and long-standing attention/memory weaknesses, though he can complete tasks once started”. “Aiden has returned to exercise but cannot tolerate AFL-level exertion due to nausea and feeling unwell. He remains restricted from contact sport,” Makdissi said.



Makdissi’s overall recommendations for O’Driscoll included ongoing psychological support, encouraging physical exercise and cognitive stimulation, specialist physiotherapy for exercise-related nausea and symptoms, and a referral to memory rehabilitation services. Manila, Philippines: Australia will ramp up its investment in drones and other defence measures in a pact with the Philippines to protect important trade routes and increase maritime surveillance as Beijing extends its reach over the South China Sea. The new pact was inked as Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and other world leaders arrived in Manila for this week’s ASEAN summit, where middle powers will seek to form strong positions on energy security and global volatility before heads of three of the world’s most powerful countries come together on the sidelines of APEC in China. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese tastes a burger during a visit to Jollibee on the sidelines of the 2026 ASEAN summit in Manila on Sunday. AAP Albanese signalled he would focus on de-escalating conflicts, including in his private meetings with US President Donald Trump, as the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East continue to drive inflation worldwide. “That’s something that’s impacting everyone who will be at the ASEAN summit tomorrow,” he said. “We’ll be discussing how we can work together to mitigate the impacts of the war, but also we want to see a de-escalation. And the coming days will be really important [to that].”



Albanese endorsed a historic meeting due later this week between Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. “We think that dialogue is a good thing, and we await the outcome of that dialogue. It’s obviously quite significant,” he said. As part of his visit to the Philippines, Albanese stopped for lunch at the country’s Jollibee’s franchise for some gastronomic diplomacy. The globally successful chain, famous for its fried chicken and gravy, spaghetti and hot dogs, plans to invest $60 million opening 35 outlets in Australia during the next five years. During a press conference with travelling Australian media earlier in the day, Albanese apologised for a crude joke he shared with Environment Minister Chris Bowen, which was captured on tape during the UN’s COP 31 climate conference in Turkey. Albanese will meet Trump and Xi as he attends ASEAN, APEC and a Quad meeting this week. While he does not expect a meeting with Putin, the prime minister said he would be forthright if they had their first encounter.



“If he’s in a room where I am, I’m sure they will hear my contribution during the ASEAN summit … This is an illegal and an immoral invasion. This is a bigger country being a bully, in contravention of international law,” he said. Albanese did not rule out appearing in an APEC leaders’ photo with Putin, if that was the wish of China as the host country. “But we will make very clear our views about Russia’s invasion of Ukraine,” he said. Philippine President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr is to meet Albanese on Monday. AP The prime minister also held a meeting with Vietnam’s Prime Minister Lê Minh Hung on Sunday, at which he said he would raise the case of detained Australian man Hiep Tran, and is due to meet Philippine President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr on Monday. The meeting with Marcos follows Sunday’s signing of a new defence agreement that includes intelligence sharing, coastguard operations and joint training exercises with the Philippines. Australia will also make additional investments in maritime surveillance capabilities, including drone technology.



“These activities will contribute to making our region more safe, more secure, and more prosperous,” Albanese said. The Philippines is on the front line of territorial disputes over the South China Sea, which is a key global trade route. China claims almost the entire waterway as its territory despite overlapping claims by other countries, and has built artificial islands in the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone. Hunter Marston, the South-East Asia program director at the Lowy Institute, said Australia and the Philippines already had fairly robust defence ties, with Australia boosting its activities as the United States scaled down some of its military exercises in the region. “In the last year, Australia has been providing more underwater and surface vessel unmanned aquatic vehicles to enhance Philippines coastguard abilities,” he said. “This agreement locks into place that already strong security co-operation, and provides some more institutional architecture for it.” The move will bolster support for the Philippines in contested waters where clashes are common between coastguards, and both China and the Philippines have accused each other of provoking tensions.



In July Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong warned Beijing against destabilising conduct in the region, earning a rebuke from China’s ministry of foreign affairs, which demanded Australia stop “exaggerating tensions and inciting confrontation”. Related Article Political leadership ‘No one was hurt’: Albanese responds after his crude ‘hot mic’ incident Marston said Australia’s attempts to stabilise China ties in recent years had been largely successful, stopping the relationship from erupting as it did around the COVID-19 inquiry five years ago. “That doesn’t mean there’s not tension,” he said. “Australia’s more active security role in South-East Asia certainly will rattle China to some degree, although it’s not to the nature or level that US has, so it’s not as acute a point of friction as US presence in the region.” Asked whether Sunday’s announcement was sending a message to China, Albanese said it “isn’t aimed at any one country”.



“This is about supporting sovereignty of every country … [International law of the sea] is really important, freedom of navigation. The majority of our trade goes through the South China Sea. That is important,” he said. “One of the reasons why Australia has to engage internationally is that one in four Australian jobs depend upon our trade.” Asked whether he would raise the Philippines agreement and China’s behaviour in the South China Sea when he meets Xi and Chinese Premier Li Qiang at the end of the week, Albanese said he would “engage diplomatically”. South-East Asian countries had planned to finalise a long-negotiated code of conduct on the South China Sea at this month’s ASEAN summit, but the process has stalled. “The sticking point is the question of whether the code of conduct will be legally binding – that seems to be the fine print that Beijing will not back down on,” Marston said. World.title: Jess we can – but campaign launch serves a reminder the Liberals haven’t yet
World.content:
Analysis PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election Jess we can – but campaign launch serves a reminder the Liberals haven’t yet Chip Le Grand November 15, 2026 — 6:38pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. We are moments from the start of the Liberal election campaign launch and Brian Loughnane, one of the party’s most experienced political strategists, is looking with furrowed brow over a room crammed with placard-waving kids, T-shirted candidates and party volunteers. One of the reasons for his concerned expression is that, as Victoria’s state party president, he’ll soon have to make a speech to them. Over his decades involved in Liberal politics, most notably as John Howard’s campaign director, Loughnane has always preferred standing in the wings to centre stage. Opposition Leader Jess Wilson speaks at the Liberal campaign launch on Sunday. Luis Enrique Ascui The other reason for concern is that, of all the elections he has worked on, none are as complicated as the one nearing its climax in Victoria. Rarely, in a state or federal election, are there so many genuine, four- and five-cornered contests and unpredictable seats. Never in a previous Victorian election has One Nation been a serious player. The Greens’ vote is up. The West Party is a thing. The teals are still around. The socialists insist we should pay them attention, too.



Yet not since 1992, when the financially stricken Labor administration inherited by Joan Kirner was limping towards election day, have the Liberals been so heavily expected to win. Loughnane is worried those expectations are running out of control. In the numbers he is crunching, he sees little margin for error. Called to the stage by former party leader Brad Battin, he makes clear this message. Liberal state president Brian Loughnane reminds supporters the campaign is at a “critical stage”. Getty Images “We’re now at a critical stage in this campaign,” Loughnane says. “All of us have seen elections won or lost in the last fortnight. This election is not over, and we must not think it’s over. “This is a very complex election, much more so than the public commentary and the polls would suggest. We need an historic swing to win, and as things stand, the election will be close.”



Jess Wilson takes her cue from the party elder she personally asked to oversee the state division after she became leader. Dressed in a pantsuit that shimmers somewhere between a shade of cobalt and electric blue, Wilson reminds the room that 16 additional seats – the basic arithmetic required for the Coalition to secure a lower house majority – is a mountain to climb. “The heightened media interest has seen much reporting, but polls are headlines, not outcomes,” Wilson says. Wilson and son Patrick in a sea of blue at the Liberal campaign launch. Luis Enrique Ascui “Make no mistake – this election will be close. There is much that is unusual about this election and with that comes great risk.” The Coalition parties have good reason to think they will form Victoria’s next government. A weary Labor administration, on its third leader in as many years, is being dogged to election day by a royal commission into the Big Build, five rate rises in a year by the Reserve Bank, and petrol prices hovering above $2 a litre.



Much of the state is by now on a first-name basis with Wilson, who is young, smart and if she were any politically cleaner, would squeak when she walks. “Jess we can!” the party members cheer. The Liberal campaign bus has been dubbed the Jess Express. At the end of her speech, the function room pulses with chants of “Jess, Jess, Jess!” Bev McArthur, a Liberal MP and conservative queen-maker who helped deliver Wilson the leadership from Battin last year, tells The Age that two things stand out about this campaign. The first is that everyone actually knows the November 28 election date. The second is everyone can recite the purported $15 billion pricetag on Big Build corruption. Robyn Baillieu takes a selfie with her husband Ted (right) and another former Victorian premier, Jeff Kennett. Luis Enrique Ascui A party that spent a decade warring among itself over the spoils of opposition presents as weirdly united. Former leaders Matthew Guy, John Pesutto and Battin are all on hand for Sunday’s launch and in line to become ministers in a Wilson government. The Liberals’ three living former premiers, Jeff Kennett, Ted Baillieu and Denis Napthine, are in VIP seats near the stage. By contrast, former premiers Daniel Andrews and Jacinta Allan were no-shows at the Labor launch across town. Their only appearance on Sunday was in Liberal Party campaign bumper stickers and leaflets.



Former Liberal leaders Matthew Guy (left) and Brad Battin in parliament last year. Jason South Battin is the day’s master of ceremonies. Only a year ago his leadership was torn down by the backers of McArthur and Wilson, but when he sits down to talk to The Age on Sunday, he is sweaty from warming up the crowd for the woman who took his job. “People want change,” he says. “We’ve got to remind them we’ve got the plan, we’ve got the plan and as you saw today, we’ve got Jess Wilson. I think we’re well and truly ready to roll. “We’ve got a very organised campaign. We’ve got a very disciplined team. We’ve got a group that are willing to work together to ensure that can deliver.” Battin predicts that when early voting opens on Wednesday, there will be a stampede at some polling places.



In Australian politics, the timing of campaign launches makes them less about making an opening pitch than delivering a closing argument. Related Article Opinion

Victorian election Is that a whiff of arrogance we detect from the Liberal leader? Jeff Kennett seems to think so Chip Le Grand State political editor For the Jess-led Liberals, it is a promise of repair – from Victoria’s books to the potholes in our roads to a less tangible vibrancy absent from the state. In a 35-minute speech which recounted a long list of campaign pledges already made and a new one to establish a bootcamp for youth offenders on the grounds of the old Dhurringile minimum security prison near Shepparton, Wilson promises to restore hope and, borrowing a line from Howard, “make Victorians feel relaxed and comfortable once more”. She mentions Labor 27 times and One Nation, a party which potentially stands between the Coalition and majority government, only once. She says that people are right to be frustrated and angry, but urges them to put their vote to better use.

World.title: The Roosters told Sam Walker he was free to leave. Now they want him to stay for 2027
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 The Roosters told Sam Walker he was free to leave. Now they want him to stay for 2027 Christian Nicolussi November 15, 2026 — 6:36pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The Sydney Roosters want Sam Walker to fulfil the final year of his contract to help them win a second straight NRL premiership, rather than a desire to keep him out of the clutches of hated rivals South Sydney. Having told Walker he was free to leave immediately after pulling their offer of a $4.2 million, three-year extension, the Roosters contacted Walker’s manager Clinton Schifcofske over the weekend to inform them they were now open to the halfback staying put in 2027. Sam Walker is expected to return to Bondi in 2027. Getty Images Roosters players had been vocal about the need for Walker to play for the club next season if they were any chance of defending their title. Skipper James Tedesco told this masthead a few weeks ago while in Kangaroos camp with Walker: “He’ll be hard to replace – we need him next year.”



It was widely reported the Roosters were prepared to tip in part of Walker’s salary if he could find a new home for 2027, but there was no way they were going to contribute towards any deal with Souths. Rabbitohs officials met with Walker in Brisbane last week, but the Bunnies would have to move on at least one senior player to accommodate Walker under the salary cap. South Sydney officials have met with Roosters and Australia half Sam Walker regarding his future in the NRL. Getty Images One name mentioned was Jack Wighton, who is about to enter the final year of an $800,000-a-season deal and had a three-year offer on the table from Hull FC in the Super League. But sources with knowledge of the situation not authorised to speak publicly confirmed on Sunday that Wighton was not interested in a move to England.





The 24-year-old Walker will join Roosters teammates in the US next week, where they will visit schools and run coaching clinics in LA. Meanwhile, Hudson Young will return to pre-season training with the Raiders on Monday for the first time since the club confirmed he would not return in 2028 and was free to join the PNG Chiefs. Young is expected to make a call this week about whether to take up the Chiefs’ offer. There were reports the Raiders were open to an immediate swap involving Young and Penrith’s Liam Martin, but privately the club do not expect the Panthers to entertain the idea.
