World.title: Testing times to continue until cricket digs deep
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

I agree with columnists Peter FitzSimons (“Cummins on the front foot, Khawaja caught out of his crease”, November 14) and Greg Baum’s call (“Enough white lies: It’s time for sandpaper’s truth commission”, The Sun-Herald, November 15) for Cricket Australia to reopen its investigation into the 2018 ball-tampering scandal in South Africa. Each argues this should not be trial by media – which is occurring now. Khawaja needs to back up his allegations with specifics and provide whatever evidence he has to a formal independent inquiry or “truth commission”. FitzSimons and Baum note the original inquiry was rushed and prioritised protecting the team’s reputation rather than establishing the truth. Cricket Australia’s refusal to reopen the inquiry is misguided, because the controversy is not going away. When another player from that tour retires and publishes a memoir, fresh allegations could reopen old wounds. An independent inquiry is the best hope of establishing what happened and holding people to account; the public feuding between players is unedifying, and will probably worsen without such an inquiry. Salvatore Sorbello, Campsie Related Article Updated

Ball tampering Twist in David Warner’s bombshell Sandpapergate claims involving ex-teammates The return of sandpaper to the headlines is puzzling. If it is illegal to roughen up one side of the cricket ball, why is it legal to polish the other side of the same ball? Each technique aims to modify the ball’s surface. And if the aim of such a modification is to assist the bowlers, why do none of them know anything about it? David Oliver, Orange Just a suggestion … As it appears that bowlers worldwide roughen cricket balls in to achieve the perfect swing, why don’t manufacturers make them that way so that everyone plays on an even field? Helen Robinson, Killcare If we can have an Enhanced Games why can’t we have a Sandpaper Test? Sponsors could include Bunnings and Greyhound Buses. Bernie Bourke, Ourimbah I am an English Test cricket fan who thinks “sandpapergate” is a storm in a teacup. I was rewatching the Fifth Test in Sydney from the 2010-11 Ashes when a zoomed-in camera shot showed Jimmy Anderson holding the ball behind his back while waiting to bowl to Michael Clarke. Tony Greig was commentating at the time and his shock at the condition of the ball was clear: “One side looks like the dog has been chewing on it and the other side is glowing.” I thought it more likely that a potato peeler had been applied. Jimmy Anderson delivered the ball and took Michael Clarke’s wicket, caught behind. So, the English used the same trick to alter the ball years earlier. It was an action practised in international cricket by other teams, which is why I don’t feel that there should be such a brouhaha about it, and especially not by the English. Rhod Jeffrey, Surry Hills Loading



Thank goodness our Australian cricket captain, Pat Cummins, has shone an honest light on the over-eight-year-old, rejuvenated, resurrected ball scandal (“Cummins rejects Khawaja claims’, November 14). In just over an hour, he answered the questions in an extremely intense TV press conference. He displayed exceptional calm and honesty in his answers, reacting to matters raised by Usman Khawaja and backed up by David Warner. The skipper disputed and reburied all the stuff Usman and David had exhumed. He proved that he is the leader to take us through an intensive period ahead on the field. It has often been said that the best of Aussie cricket captains could have been successful Australian prime ministers. The quality of his answers may have uncovered a future candidate. Bob Brenner, Beacon Hill I suggest that a separate edition be published about sandpaper and balls so that the rest of us can live in peace. Judy Hungerford, Narraweena Corporate obligations Andrew Irvine, the NAB chief executive, complains bitterly about the cost of payroll tax in Australia (“Like taxing blood donors: Bank boss slams ‘atrocious tax’”, November 14). He must be speaking in jest. Since 2024, NAB has reportedly made redundant or moved offshore some 3350 positions. Meanwhile, the bank employs 5000 people in India and another 2000 in Vietnam. Many of these are surely jobs that could be performed by Australians, earning Australian wages and paying Australian taxes. NAB appears to inhabit a different world from the rest of us. It complains about state revenue measures while reducing domestic employment, shifting costs and responsibilities onto the wider community, and retaining the financial benefits of offshoring, all while reducing the community tax-take from having people employed – in Australia. Australia’s economy depends on the contributions of employers and employees alike. Payroll tax is part of that contribution. Corporations cannot reasonably demand the benefits of operating in Australia while treating their obligations to the Australian community as an intolerable burden. Corporate social licence is not simply a matter of profitability. It carries responsibilities, too. Chris Rivers, Port Macquarie Negative currents The prime minister is right to say that Australia is a world leader when it comes to the decarbonisation of its electricity grid, but there is more to climate action than just that (“‘Entitled to her views’: PM on the defensive over Thunberg’s ‘snail’ jibe”, November 14). Unfortunately, we have been tardy with regard to the electrification of transport, have made little progress with the decarbonisation of industry and have been downright regressive when it comes to feeding the world’s addiction to fossil fuels. If we really do fancy ourselves as climate champions, we must at the very least stop approving new coal and gas projects. Ken Enderby, Concord The federal government budgeted $32,000 for coffee at the Australian pavilion in Turkey for the COP31 climate summit. AAPIMAGE



The fuss over the $32,000 coffee tab at COP31 in conservative quarters is predictable. But while people queued for an hour for a free coffee there, here in Oz we subsidised the fossil fuel industry with another $1,861,200. So it’s also no wonder the PM stuck to talking about how sad he was for his friends in the Pacific. And it’s equally unsurprising that Ms Thunberg, and many of us at home, are unimpressed. Lesley Walker, Northcote (Vic) Of more concern than the $32,000 spent on free coffee at COP31 is the use of plastic throw-away cups, made by the fossil fuel industry and adding to our greenhouse gases. Did no one who planned the marketing really not see the connection? Karen Joynes, Bermagui Your correspondent is correct in saying that whether NSW or Australia exports coal will make little difference to greenhouse gas production (Letters, November 14). There is no shortage of coal in the world and those burning it will continue to do so regardless of where it comes from. Likewise, gas. What is wrong is that we gain so little from these exports and regulate them so poorly at source. We should be using the proceeds to modernise our own system. At present, we have a total capacity of about 92 gigawatts. China installed 315 gigawatts of solar last year. Already some companies are saying coal-fired electricity is too expensive and last year renewables exceeded coal in global electricity production for the first time. The political parties, some of which are basically owned by the coal and gas industry, need to think about the future instead of looking backwards. Jock Webb, Narromine One Nation leader Pauline Hanson may be regretting a touch of Trump mania. Jason South Beware the clown show Pauline Hanson’s vision for Australia harkens back to simpler times (“Hanson’s stuck with Trump link”, November 14). Simpler times were not necessarily better times. The faces were whiter, the prejudices more pronounced, our original peoples still largely dispossessed and unable to vote. Hanson, by endorsing and aping Trump’s “tear it all down approach”, made a commitment that cannot be unmade simply by removing information from her website. Peter Hartcher’s reference to the “clown show” is apt, much wider than the obvious red faces and bright red hair. You never stop wondering what is coming next. Hanson, by bending the knee and kissing the ring of the MAGA sovereign, pledged her commitment to his lack of values and ham-fisted approach. At least the Australian people can see how Trump’s approach has failed and have extra information with which to judge Hanson’s lack of suitability for high office. Those who aspire to the highest office must be judged by a higher standard. Geoff Nilon, Mascot Peter Hartcher is adamant it was a terrible idea for the US and Israel to attack Iran in February but just because the war was badly prosecuted doesn’t mean it was wrong. Hartcher cites the need for US cabinet secretaries to live in military bases for fear of Iranian operatives, but that illustrates why the rogue regime can’t be left to its own devices, literally. He says Iran wasn’t developing nuclear weapons in February but, as Marco Rubio explained, the concern was Iran was building impenetrable bunkers and a massive missile arsenal, which would have allowed it to subsequently develop nuclear weapons without interference. Hartcher also cites the International Atomic Energy Agency saying it didn’t see a structured nuclear weapons program, but the IAEA has also repeatedly said Iran was enriching uranium to levels higher than needed for any civil purpose and was blocking IAEA inspections and oversight. Danny Samuels, Malvern (Vic)



Leaders gotta lead Sussan Ley is right that participation in a robust democracy, with a belief that change is possible, is vital to its success and needed now more than ever (“Apathy democracy’s biggest threat”, November 14). However, our leaders are beginning to look the same in the solutions they offer, and that is why we have become hopeless that we cannot effect change. No one wants to take bold action except when in opposition, when they champion the battler and deride income inequality. Perhaps that is why we see the rise of One Nation, as they are offering something totally radical and disruptive that gives some people hope. However, once in power, and the parties find we are not ready for decisive action, they start melding into safer alternatives and all is the same again. Perhaps leaders need to start leading and they will find that our apathy turns into hope. Manbir Singh Kohli, Pemulwuy Minns’ non-local fail Related Article Updated

One Nation One Nation reveals four upper house candidates, including controversial anti-trans campaigner I could not let the statement by Chris Minns that he was not running a charity as justification for nominating a candidate from outside the Wallsend electorate to possibly replace Sonia Hornery (“Minns defies anger over captain’s calls”, November 14). Surely he is still part of running a democratic system that is designed to have local people representing their local area in parliament. His attitude screams that nobody within the electorate of Wallsend is capable of representing them. Shame on him. Ken Berry, Hamilton East World of religion I do hope that our MPs and relevant executives in the education department read, consider and respond to points raised in Helen Paterson’s excellent article (“Religion classes are a dividing factor just when social cohesion is among our highest hopes”, November 14). Canada’s public education system, in which students learn about world religions (rather than be divided into religion or non-religion classes), certainly sounds like a great model to emulate! Brenda Mattick, Neutral Bay



By all means religion can be taught but, comparatively, as part of general studies, not elevated to the status of orthodoxy. Proselytising should have no place in public schools. Edward Grieve, Woolloomooloo I am not a religious person or a churchgoer. However, I value the religious instruction I received as a child at the local Presbyterian church and at secondary school (Letters, November 13). I remember the rousing Presbyterian hymns, stories from the King James Version of the Bible, and the teachings of Jesus. The hymns led me to the discovery of classical music and the pleasure of singing in large choirs for many years. The biblical stories enabled me to appreciate the great works of art seen in galleries and churches throughout Europe. So much of our language and daily expressions have come from the Bible, and many of the teachings of Jesus, particularly about love and forgiveness, are worth following. A compulsory course in comparative religions would be very useful, and may assist in fostering empathy for other cultures. The Church of England scripture classes at school had another advantage for all faiths. It was a convenient time to catch up with the homework you hadn’t done, and many of the Jewish girls joined us regularly for this purpose. Nora Hinchen, Naremburn Workers handle a painting called “Christ on the Cross Adored by Two Donors” by Spanish painter El Greco amid works at the Louvre. AP Dennis Fardy is spot on (Letters, November 14): add the option of primary ethics in secondary schools alongside religious instruction. For six years I facilitated discussions among 10- to 12-year-old primary school pupils. They taught me that children all have a view about the big philosophical issues, including love, truth telling, democracy, community, etc. After an enthusiastic discussion of tit-for-tat behaviour (they agreed it was futile) I asked: “So why do we do it?” An angel-faced 10-year-old girl quietly summed it up: “Revenge”. Religion and ethics are two perspectives on the same issue: morality. Discussions like the ones I was part of stimulated their thinking and mine, and had the benefit of linking our generations. Glenda Gartrell, Newtown Slam the brakes on AI Related Article Analysis

China relations Nvidia scandal raises new concerns about scale of Chinese spying James Massola’s brutally honest overview of the AI tsunami sweeping our world needs to be on page one (“Pacific jewel is in the grip of an AI fever-dream – deranged but oh so real”, November 12)! It seems that if humanity is not hit over the head with prescient warnings of danger, it’s all ‘keep calm and carry on’. We have become bedazzled by the positives of glittering AI technology to the extent that we are largely oblivious to the devastating negatives that put us at risk of losing our humanity. We are on the brink of annihilation as a species, and instead of actively listening to dismayed experts in the field, we are courting more and more rampaging AI technology in case we miss the bus! Our leaders are failing us just when we need their honesty and courage to severely slam on the brakes. Judy Finch, Taree

World.title: ‘Disgusted and appalled’: Sydney MP Alex Greenwich’s office graffitied with homophobic slur
World.content:
PoliticsNSWPolice ‘Disgusted and appalled’: Sydney MP Alex Greenwich’s office graffitied with homophobic slur Megan Gorrey November 15, 2026 — 6:11pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Independent Sydney MP Alex Greenwich has condemned the actions of graffiti vandals who sprayed a homophobic slur on his inner-city electorate office as “extremely distressing”. Images supplied by Greenwich show the alleged offenders had sprayed the word “pedo” on the sandstone walls and glass doors of the corner building on Oxford Street in Darlinghurst on Sunday. Police are investigating homophobic slurs graffitied on Greenwich’s inner Sydney office. Greenwich, who is openly gay and led the Yes campaign for marriage equality, said police were investigating and no one should have to be confronted with such an incident in their workplace – “especially on the nine-year anniversary of the marriage equality Yes vote”. “This homophobic attack was extremely distressing for me and my staff,” he told the Herald.



“If it was designed to intimidate me, it has had the opposite effect. I’m more determined than ever before to ensure Sydney and NSW is a safer and fairer place for my community.” NSW Police said officers set up a crime scene after they were called to the building before midday. Greenwich said it was the first time vandals had targeted his office with homophobic graffiti. Investigators are reviewing CCTV footage and making inquiries to identify offenders. The graffiti incident follows grave injuries suffered by federal MP Helen Haines in regional Victoria in October, which placed renewed attention on the hostility frequently directed at politicians.



Wentworth MP Allegra Spender, who attended a fundraising event with Greenwich on Sunday, was “disgusted and appalled” that his office was targeted with the “vile homophobic slur”. “There is no place for homophobia or hate in our community, and certainly not in Australian politics,” Spender said on social media. “Words matter, and this kind of attack is designed to intimidate and harm.” Greenwich, who has been Sydney MP since 2012, will recontest his seat at the March state election.



He considered leaving politics after taking on former NSW One Nation MP Mark Latham in a series of court battles after the one-time federal Labor leader tweeted a highly graphic and homophobic remark about Greenwich in 2023. Greenwich won his defamation case against Latham (who lost an appeal against the ruling) but conceded the hate directed his way from others wore him down. Sydney MP Alex Greenwich. Steven Siewert Last year, he told gay magazine DNA the tweet attacking his sexuality was the start of a long period of sustained online hate, death threats – which police believed to be credible – and self-doubt. But Greenwich said the Bondi massacre on December 14, and the rise of Pauline Hanson’s One Nation, had ultimately compelled him to stay in politics and fight “for the sensible centre”.



Related Article Updated

One Nation One Nation reveals four upper house candidates, including controversial anti-trans campaigner “I’ve seen how the far right can destabilise politics, and [how] a sensible centrist crossbench [can provide] stability in minority governments. As the only gay member of the lower house, I’m often reminded that if you are not at the table, you are on the menu, and hard-fought wins like abortion decriminalisation, voluntary assisted dying and LGBTQ rights can, and have, come under attack,” Greenwich said in March. World.title: This school’s black and red blazers are more than a uniform. They’re a passport to a prestigious network
World.content:
In its 148 years, Xavier has produced a Queensland premier, a lord mayor of Melbourne, and 18 federal and state MPs. Schoolboys who enter the exclusive Kew Catholic school’s gates are “Xaverians for life”.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

W alking into Xavier College – with its Great Hall, its 250-space underground temperature-controlled car park, 600-strong rotating art collection, lush sporting ovals and view of the city skyline – feels less like entering a school and more like gaining access to Melbourne’s upper echelons. And that’s just for a visitor. For the boys who enter the Kew college’s gates, the black and red blazer is a passport that will gain them entry to an exclusive network that can open doors throughout their lives – in business, politics and sport. Xavier is exclusive and prestigious, with annual fees above $44,000 for every secondary year level. For that fee, families gain access to not only great facilities and teaching, but to one of the largest alumni communities in Australia, according to Xavier. Xavier College rector Father Chris Middleton with students in front of the school’s chapel. Simon Schluter But enrolments at the Catholic boys’ school have been declining for more than a decade. The decline has occurred alongside the cost-of-living crisis and changing demographics, and as most boys’ schools battle the general perception that single-sex schools can breed hypermasculine culture.





And at the end of last year, former Xavier student Tom Silvagni, the son of AFL legend Stephen Silvagni, was convicted of two counts of rape. Interim principal Lee MacMaster, who is about to retire after 46 years as an educator, said the news of Silvagni’s conviction sent reverberations through the whole school. “Things like this should never happen,” he said. MacMaster said the school had strong relationships with girls’ schools, there were female staff in senior roles, and a no-tolerance approach was taken to misogyny. “What we’re trying to educate our boys is there’s something much bigger than yourself,” he said. In its 148 years, Xavier has produced a Queensland premier, a lord mayor of Melbourne, and 18 federal and state members of parliament – including former leader of the federal opposition Bill Shorten and federal member for Wannon Dan Tehan. Tehan, who graduated in 1985, said Xavier taught him not to take things at face value but to prosecute, interrogate and always seek the truth.



Tehan said he also gained a group of lifelong friends. “That is to me what a great education should be about,” he said. Celebrity chef Adam D’Sylva and his son Javier at Xavier College. Luis Enrique Ascui Xavier alumni include 16 graduates who have been knighted, two Rhodes Scholars and a High Court judge. There have also been 62 OAM recipients and a United Nations special rapporteur. Celebrity chef Adam D’Sylva, who has appeared on MasterChef and Snack Masters and is the owner of newly hatted restaurant Decca, is among the famous alumni. “Once you go to Xavier, you are a Xaverian for life,” said D’Sylva. “What Xavier gave me, aside from the academic side, it gave me the feeling that you can be invincible, you can do anything and be anything you want in life.” He said his teenage daughter jokingly calls his network of Xavier friends a cult.



“But it’s a really good cult,” he said. Academically, Xavier achieved a median VCE study score of 33 in 2025, above the state average of 30, yet it wasn’t among the state’s top-performing schools last year. But as a founding member of the Associated Public Schools of Victoria (APS Sport), Xavier’s sporting teams are among the state’s most competitive. While Xavier doesn’t offer standalone sports scholarships, the school has produced more than 149 AFL players, 17 Olympians and a Paralympian. Head of sports Michael Wilson said sporting scouts often visit games, and AFL teams use the school’s football oval. He said the school had replicated a professional sporting environment on campus where they could. “We put GPS units on our footballs so we can track the distances they run, ice baths after class, world-class gym with gym instructors; it’s a unique opportunity for our boys to taste-test what they are going into,” Wilson said.

World.title: ‘Good riddance’: One of the most popular HSC subjects is being overhauled. Teachers are thrilled.
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWHSC ‘Good riddance’: One of the most popular HSC subjects is being overhauled. Teachers are thrilled. Emily Kowal November 15, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

High school students will finally learn how to start a business before they bankrupt one, under a major syllabus overhaul of NSW’s most popular elective HSC subject. The NSW Education Standards Authority has unveiled a new business studies curriculum, to the delight of teachers who have long criticised the existing course as illogical and outdated. Under the current syllabus, which has been in place since 2010, students begin year 11 learning about concepts like bankruptcy and liquidation but end the year learning how to start a business. Castle Hill High School head teacher of social science Michelle O’Brien. KATE GERAGHTY “That doesn’t really make sense,” said a NESA subject-matter expert spokesperson. “It didn’t really have a logical flow or progression, and that also led to quite a lot of duplication where you might learn a concept in one place and have to come back and re-teach it later on.”



The course has been flipped so students explore how to start a business before learning how to grow and manage one. The new syllabus also explores modern entrepreneurial concepts and business models such as subscriptions, affiliate models and crowdfunding. After almost 30 years of teaching the same course, Castle Hill High School head teacher Michelle O’Brien is ready for change. She is glad the syllabus is updating to a more logical flow. Michelle O’Brien with students Amy Maher and Arshan Jam. KATE GERAGHTY “There’s a lot of repetition. It’s been around since 2010, so there are a lot of things that are pretty outdated,” she said, noting her textbooks discuss “e-marketing” with no mention of social media or AI. She said the subject is adored by students who “have aspirations to own their own businesses and become millionaires”. It was the third-most popular HSC course this year, with almost 21,000 students. It’s known as an accessible course, teaching teenagers to start, grow and manage a business.



The old course was critiqued for being too content-heavy, especially its in-depth focus on complex financial topics like hedging, derivatives and international payments. “They didn’t understand it. They didn’t understand why they had to understand it,” said O’Brien. “Good riddance,” she said of its departure. Editor's pick Private schools Why this Sydney private school should be banned from new enrolments “We’ve removed that out of the course so that there’s more space for students to learn about and practise those foundational finance skills,” said a NESA spokesperson. In a major change, students will now have to study a real-world business case study for every focus area in the syllabus, including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander businesses.



Previously students would often study just one or two case studies – often Qantas, Coca-Cola or Apple – and reuse them across different content requirements. Student Arshan Jam said the case-study change was “interesting” as most students make up their case studies. “That’s going to be really hard to do if you have to have a different business for every area,” he said. Schools will have more than a year to get to know the new syllabus. It will be taught from 2028 and examined in the HSC for the first time in 2029. World.title: The Wallabies desperately need more power. A missing weapon is nearing his return
World.content:
SportRugby UnionWallabies The Wallabies desperately need more power. A missing weapon is nearing his return Jonathan Drennan November 15, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A damning statistic in last Sunday’s 23-point defeat against England laid bare the Wallabies’ lack of muscle in the forwards: the 73 metres from 22 carries by England No. 8 Ben Earl was nearly as much as the cumulative total of the entire starting Australian pack, which managed 83. Les Kiss could have been forgiven for casting a rueful eye in the direction of Langi Gleeson this week. The powerful back-rower added starch to the Wallabies pack in wins over the British & Irish Lions and South Africa last year before heading overseas to join Montpellier. Langi Gleeson of the Wallabies muscles through against the British & Irish Lions in the second Test in Melbourne. Getty Images According to informed sources, Rugby Australia want Gleeson to return home after his contract expires next June, but Gleeson knows he needs to deliver on the field before planning his future ahead of next year’s World Cup. The 25-year-old is on the comeback trail after a nightmare nine months recovering from an ACL injury. Since joining the French giants last October, Gleeson has only played two games, after battling a heel problem then damaging his ACL in January. Making his first start for Montpellier, on a muddy field in Wales against the Ospreys, Gleeson lasted just 20 minutes after an opponent awkwardly landed on his knee during a routine tackle.



Gleeson had surgery but, speaking only limited French and with his circle of family and friends from Sydney’s northern beaches thousands of miles away, struggled when it came to the lonely hours of rehabilitation. “I was lucky to have my partner over from last Christmas in Montpellier because as soon as I got injured I was basically useless,” Gleeson said. Langi Gleeson was named the Waratahs’ best player in 2025. Getty Images “She was cooking, cleaning, doing everything, while I was on the bed the whole time. I think if I didn’t have anyone here I don’t know how I would have survived, to be honest. In Australia you’ve got family and stuff that look after you … “It’s been one of the toughest parts of my life because when you come into a new team and you want to earn the respect of the boys and you get injured … now you’re just watching them from the sideline.”



For the past nine months Gleeson has arrived early at Montpellier’s training base and worked on his rehabilitation in a separate area away from the main team, which includes fellow Australians Tom Banks and Jordan Uelese. The back-rower loves the history and architecture of his new home town in France but his day job has become tougher than ever. “It does get lonely when you’re in the gym and you’re watching the boys train and doing all these things that you wish you could do on the field,” he said. “It’s a bit depressing but I knew my time would come. I just keep putting my head down, keep working. Nothing lasts forever.” Gleeson’s game is built on explosive ball-carrying and breaking the gain line. He is back in training and building strength in his left knee, and hopes to get back on the field in December. After surgery Gleeson had to teach himself how to run again, and has been working hard to regain his fitness. The days are long and the training is tough but he is in a far happier place. “The training might be difficult but trust me, it’s better than sitting at home with a fat knee watching French TV where you don’t know what’s going on,” Gleeson said.



Related Article Opinion

Australian rugby Enough with all the ‘learnings’. It’s time for the Wallabies to pass a big test Iain Payten Senior Sports Reporter Gleeson remains open-minded about returning to Australia and is still motivated to play for the Wallabies. He knows he needs to get back on the field to prove – not only to his club but to himself – that he can regain the speed that made him a standout for club and country last year. “With all my conversations with my manager, everything is just waiting until I get on the field and start playing because the main thing is I’m here to play,” Gleeson said. “I just feel like I owe it to Montpellier as well. I’ve missed a big chunk of time here. “I was talking to my partner the other day, [asking] ‘Do I regret coming here or should I have stayed in Australia?’ “I believe that when you make your bed, you lie in it – and I’m still happy I made this decision to come here.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport are sent every Friday.

World.title: ‘I can’t lead a normal life’: Why this former Bulldog is fighting for his future
World.content:
Exclusive SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘I can’t lead a normal life’: Why this former Bulldog is fighting for his future Jon Pierik November 15, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A former player who was forced into medical retirement after suffering eight brain bleeds and a fractured skull has been left shocked after an AFL-ordered clinical assessment ruled that he had sustained only a “mild” brain injury. That clinical reclassification – delivered more than two years after Western Bulldogs draftee Aiden O’Driscoll was forced out of the game before playing a senior match – has left the 21-year-old traumatised, derailed his bid for a $600,000 severe injury payout and put his management on a collision course with the league. Seeking recompense: Bulldogs draftee Aiden O’Driscoll was forced to retire without playing an AFL game. Getty O’Driscoll retired at just 18 in May 2024 before he had made his senior AFL debut, having suffered a major “head-on-head” concussion during a pre-season match simulation session and rushed to The Alfred hospital. He suffered a seizure and a fracture behind his ear, an MRI later revealing that the collision had left him with eight brain bleeds. While he received a career-ending injury payment of more than $150,000 in 2024, his application for a $600,000 severe injury benefit (SIB) payment was rejected this year by the AFL and AFL Players’ Association, which found he did not meet the criteria.



Related Article Exclusive

AFL injury ward ‘Vague and embarrassing’: Cats’ doctors hit back at Rooke class action concussion claim That decision was based on a neuropsychological assessment report completed in Perth in March by a group of clinicians specialising in the diagnosis and management of neuropsychological and behavioural conditions, which concluded that O’Driscoll suffered only a “mild TBI [traumatic brain injury]” – leaving O’Driscoll and his agent Peter Jess in shock. An AFL medical panel’s report in April 2024 revealed the extent of O’Driscoll’s injury, going as far as declaring “Aiden has more micro-haemorrhages than the panel has seen in other athletes”. He was medically retired by the AFL’s independent concussion panel. He struggles with daily memory loss, nausea and anxiety, dizziness and has difficulty sleeping as a result of the brain trauma stemming from the training incident. “It [mild assessment] does not add up. My memory for basic things is shocking, really bad. It has progressively got worse over time. It’s a horrible thing for a 21-year-old to go through. Literally yesterday, when I went to the shops for three things … avocado, it literally took me 15 minutes to remember, and it was one of three things. But I forgot one of the things, which was the reason for going to the shops, and that was the dishwashing liquid,” O’Driscoll told this masthead.



View post on X “Things like that have happened to me a lot since I had the hit. “I have lost a couple of girlfriends [relationship break-ups] along the way, and I honestly think it’s to do with this as well. “The basic things I forget. I obviously can’t live a normal life.” AFL chief medical officer Michael Makdissi, in a discharge summary letter dated May 18, 2026, did not comment on the “mild TBI” assessment, leaving Jess stunned.



Related Article Exclusive

Australian cricket ‘Misconceived’: Brighton Grammar hits back at Will Pucovski concussion lawsuit “The medical classification for Aiden’s type of injury is moderate/severe TBI, not a mild brain trauma as assessed … the assessment is flawed and cannot be relied upon,” Jess, a prominent concussion campaigner for athletes in all sports, said. The neuropsychological report, which Jess gave to this masthead on behalf of O’Driscoll, said: “He [O’Driscoll] sustained a mild TBI on 26/01/2024 during a pre-season simulation match, which resulted in a single seizure episode and loss of consciousness. Neuroimaging scans have identified micro-haemorrhages primarily in his right temporal lobe. “After medical assessments and review by an independent concussion panel, Aiden retired from professional football and contact sport in May 2024. “Prior to his TBI, Aiden underwent cognitive evaluation as part of the Western Bulldogs baseline cognitive testing program. At baseline, Aiden was observed to display variability across his results, with weaknesses more apparent on memory tasks and when the complexity and attentional demands were greater.



Related Article AFL 2026 Hanson’s ‘dehumanising’ comments spur former footy star in AFL legal fight “These outcomes largely reflected a long-standing pattern of cognitive strengths and weaknesses, noting his pre-existing ADHD and dyslexia diagnoses. “At 41 days post-TBI, neuropsychological review noted that Aiden had generally been making a good recovery. Formal testing revealed largely stable results compared to his baseline, though memory scores were slightly weaker. On the current assessment, Aiden’s basic attention processing speed, visual spatial skills, and executive functions were broadly at age-expected levels. His verbal language abilities were comparatively weaker, and vulnerabilities were apparent with his working memory and mental flexibility, attentional shift. “There were limitations and efficiencies with Aiden’s new learning encoding, as well as his memory recall, likely related to feelings of overwhelm and attentional weakness.” This masthead is not accusing the AFL or the AFLPA of any wrongdoing.



O’Driscoll, who has expressed frustration with the AFL and the overall process on social media, said it had been a traumatic experience. “It has been [traumatic], it has been very difficult,” O’Driscoll said. “The severity of my injury … it has had severe impacts on me. When it first happened, I just wanted to get back out there and keep playing. I wasn’t affected a heap, but it got to six months down the line, that’s when I started to feel it.” The AFLPA said in a rejection letter in March that O’Driscoll had not demonstrated a “permanent impairment of cognitive function”, meaning his future earning capacity would not be reduced by at least 40 per cent. Jess described that claim as “nonsense”, and had already begun examining legal action against several parties.



Related Article AFL 2026 ‘You’ve been nothing but a joke’: Ex-AFL player criticises league over concussion support The AFLPA did not wish to comment because of confidentiality reasons. The AFL was contacted for comment. Jess said the mild, rather than moderate or severe, assessment meant O’Driscoll’s bid for a disability pension was also impacted. “It’s frightening what has gone on here. It has destroyed the kid’s life,” Jess said. “He hasn’t done anything for months. He is not earning any money. This is setting a dangerous precedent.”



In the discharge letter, seen by this masthead, Makdissi said that O’Driscoll had not attended his final case review, with his bid to have a non-related third party, in his case Jess, accompanying him “deemed inappropriate” by the league. He said O’Driscoll’s working history included one-on-one football training, and disability support work with children and adults, but “his current work capacity is limited due to ongoing symptoms”. Makdissi noted that of the initial neuropsychological review in March 2024, O’Driscoll had reported that most of his initial concerns, including headaches, fatigue and memory concerns, had “largely resolved”. He said a follow-up in August 2024 had shown “stable or improved cognitive performance … with improved memory relative to the March assessment”. Of this year’s review, Makdissi said O’Driscoll reported “mildly increased cognitive and physical fatigue, slightly slower processing speed, reduced time management, intermittent forgetfulness, difficulty initiating tasks, and long-standing attention/memory weaknesses, though he can complete tasks once started”. “Aiden has returned to exercise but cannot tolerate AFL-level exertion due to nausea and feeling unwell. He remains restricted from contact sport,” Makdissi said.



Makdissi’s overall recommendations for O’Driscoll included ongoing psychological support, encouraging physical exercise and cognitive stimulation, specialist physiotherapy for exercise-related nausea and symptoms, and a referral to memory rehabilitation services. AFL players fund the severe injury benefit fund from their slice of the AFL’s revenue. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Drones, intelligence and a bucket of chicken: Australia and the Philippines sign new defence pact
World.content:
PoliticsFederalDefence Drones, intelligence and a bucket of chicken: Australia and the Philippines sign new defence pact Natassia Chrysanthos November 15, 2026 — 6:58pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Manila, Philippines: Australia will ramp up its investment in drones and other defence measures in a pact with the Philippines to protect important trade routes and increase maritime surveillance as Beijing extends its reach over the South China Sea. The new pact was inked as Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and other world leaders arrived in Manila for this week’s ASEAN summit, where middle powers will seek to form strong positions on energy security and global volatility before heads of three of the world’s most powerful countries come together on the sidelines of APEC in China. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese tastes a burger during a visit to Jollibee on the sidelines of the 2026 ASEAN summit in Manila on Sunday. AAP Albanese signalled he would focus on de-escalating conflicts, including in his private meetings with US President Donald Trump, as the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East continue to drive inflation worldwide. “That’s something that’s impacting everyone who will be at the ASEAN summit tomorrow,” he said. “We’ll be discussing how we can work together to mitigate the impacts of the war, but also we want to see a de-escalation. And the coming days will be really important [to that].”



Albanese endorsed a historic meeting due later this week between Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. “We think that dialogue is a good thing, and we await the outcome of that dialogue. It’s obviously quite significant,” he said. As part of his visit to the Philippines, Albanese stopped for lunch at the country’s Jollibee’s franchise for some gastronomic diplomacy. The globally successful chain, famous for its fried chicken and gravy, spaghetti and hot dogs, plans to invest $60 million opening 35 outlets in Australia during the next five years. During a press conference with travelling Australian media earlier in the day, Albanese apologised for a crude joke he shared with Environment Minister Chris Bowen, which was captured on tape during the UN’s COP 31 climate conference in Turkey. Albanese will meet Trump and Xi as he attends ASEAN, APEC and a Quad meeting this week. While he does not expect a meeting with Putin, the prime minister said he would be forthright if they had their first encounter.



“If he’s in a room where I am, I’m sure they will hear my contribution during the ASEAN summit … This is an illegal and an immoral invasion. This is a bigger country being a bully, in contravention of international law,” he said. Albanese did not rule out appearing in an APEC leaders’ photo with Putin, if that was the wish of China as the host country. “But we will make very clear our views about Russia’s invasion of Ukraine,” he said. Philippine President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr is to meet Albanese on Monday. AP The prime minister also held a meeting with Vietnam’s Prime Minister Lê Minh Hung on Sunday, at which he said he would raise the case of detained Australian man Hiep Tran, and is due to meet Philippine President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr on Monday. The meeting with Marcos follows Sunday’s signing of a new defence agreement that includes intelligence sharing, coastguard operations and joint training exercises with the Philippines. Australia will also make additional investments in maritime surveillance capabilities, including drone technology.



“These activities will contribute to making our region more safe, more secure, and more prosperous,” Albanese said. The Philippines is on the front line of territorial disputes over the South China Sea, which is a key global trade route. China claims almost the entire waterway as its territory despite overlapping claims by other countries, and has built artificial islands in the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone. Hunter Marston, the South-East Asia program director at the Lowy Institute, said Australia and the Philippines already had fairly robust defence ties, with Australia boosting its activities as the United States scaled down some of its military exercises in the region. “In the last year, Australia has been providing more underwater and surface vessel unmanned aquatic vehicles to enhance Philippines coastguard abilities,” he said. “This agreement locks into place that already strong security co-operation, and provides some more institutional architecture for it.” The move will bolster support for the Philippines in contested waters where clashes are common between coastguards, and both China and the Philippines have accused each other of provoking tensions.



In July Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong warned Beijing against destabilising conduct in the region, earning a rebuke from China’s ministry of foreign affairs, which demanded Australia stop “exaggerating tensions and inciting confrontation”. Related Article Political leadership ‘No one was hurt’: Albanese responds after his crude ‘hot mic’ incident Marston said Australia’s attempts to stabilise China ties in recent years had been largely successful, stopping the relationship from erupting as it did around the COVID-19 inquiry five years ago. “That doesn’t mean there’s not tension,” he said. “Australia’s more active security role in South-East Asia certainly will rattle China to some degree, although it’s not to the nature or level that US has, so it’s not as acute a point of friction as US presence in the region.” Asked whether Sunday’s announcement was sending a message to China, Albanese said it “isn’t aimed at any one country”.



“This is about supporting sovereignty of every country … [International law of the sea] is really important, freedom of navigation. The majority of our trade goes through the South China Sea. That is important,” he said. “One of the reasons why Australia has to engage internationally is that one in four Australian jobs depend upon our trade.” Asked whether he would raise the Philippines agreement and China’s behaviour in the South China Sea when he meets Xi and Chinese Premier Li Qiang at the end of the week, Albanese said he would “engage diplomatically”. South-East Asian countries had planned to finalise a long-negotiated code of conduct on the South China Sea at this month’s ASEAN summit, but the process has stalled. “The sticking point is the question of whether the code of conduct will be legally binding – that seems to be the fine print that Beijing will not back down on,” Marston said.
