World.title: Jess we can – but campaign launch serves a reminder the Liberals haven’t yet
World.content:
Analysis PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election Jess we can – but campaign launch serves a reminder the Liberals haven’t yet Chip Le Grand November 15, 2026 — 6:38pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

We are moments from the start of the Liberal election campaign launch and Brian Loughnane, one of the party’s most experienced political strategists, is looking with furrowed brow over a room crammed with placard-waving kids, T-shirted candidates and party volunteers. One of the reasons for his concerned expression is that, as Victoria’s state party president, he’ll soon have to make a speech to them. Over his decades involved in Liberal politics, most notably as John Howard’s campaign director, Loughnane has always preferred standing in the wings to centre stage. Opposition Leader Jess Wilson speaks at the Liberal campaign launch on Sunday. Luis Enrique Ascui The other reason for concern is that, of all the elections he has worked on, none are as complicated as the one nearing its climax in Victoria. Rarely, in a state or federal election, are there so many genuine, four- and five-cornered contests and unpredictable seats. Never in a previous Victorian election has One Nation been a serious player. The Greens’ vote is up. The West Party is a thing. The teals are still around. The socialists insist we should pay them attention, too.



Yet not since 1992, when the financially stricken Labor administration inherited by Joan Kirner was limping towards election day, have the Liberals been so heavily expected to win. Loughnane is worried those expectations are running out of control. In the numbers he is crunching, he sees little margin for error. Called to the stage by former party leader Brad Battin, he makes clear this message. Liberal state president Brian Loughnane reminds supporters the campaign is at a “critical stage”. Getty Images “We’re now at a critical stage in this campaign,” Loughnane says. “All of us have seen elections won or lost in the last fortnight. This election is not over, and we must not think it’s over. “This is a very complex election, much more so than the public commentary and the polls would suggest. We need an historic swing to win, and as things stand, the election will be close.”



Jess Wilson takes her cue from the party elder she personally asked to oversee the state division after she became leader. Dressed in a pantsuit that shimmers somewhere between a shade of cobalt and electric blue, Wilson reminds the room that 16 additional seats – the basic arithmetic required for the Coalition to secure a lower house majority – is a mountain to climb. “The heightened media interest has seen much reporting, but polls are headlines, not outcomes,” Wilson says. Wilson and son Patrick in a sea of blue at the Liberal campaign launch. Luis Enrique Ascui “Make no mistake – this election will be close. There is much that is unusual about this election and with that comes great risk.” The Coalition parties have good reason to think they will form Victoria’s next government. A weary Labor administration, on its third leader in as many years, is being dogged to election day by a royal commission into the Big Build, five rate rises in a year by the Reserve Bank, and petrol prices hovering above $2 a litre.



Much of the state is by now on a first-name basis with Wilson, who is young, smart and if she were any politically cleaner, would squeak when she walks. “Jess we can!” the party members cheer. The Liberal campaign bus has been dubbed the Jess Express. At the end of her speech, the function room pulses with chants of “Jess, Jess, Jess!” Bev McArthur, a Liberal MP and conservative queen-maker who helped deliver Wilson the leadership from Battin last year, tells The Age that two things stand out about this campaign. The first is that everyone actually knows the November 28 election date. The second is everyone can recite the purported $15 billion pricetag on Big Build corruption. Robyn Baillieu takes a selfie with her husband Ted (right) and another former Victorian premier, Jeff Kennett. Luis Enrique Ascui A party that spent a decade warring among itself over the spoils of opposition presents as weirdly united. Former leaders Matthew Guy, John Pesutto and Battin are all on hand for Sunday’s launch and in line to become ministers in a Wilson government. The Liberals’ three living former premiers, Jeff Kennett, Ted Baillieu and Denis Napthine, are in VIP seats near the stage. By contrast, former premiers Daniel Andrews and Jacinta Allan were no-shows at the Labor launch across town. Their only appearance on Sunday was in Liberal Party campaign bumper stickers and leaflets.



Former Liberal leaders Matthew Guy (left) and Brad Battin in parliament last year. Jason South Battin is the day’s master of ceremonies. Only a year ago his leadership was torn down by the backers of McArthur and Wilson, but when he sits down to talk to The Age on Sunday, he is sweaty from warming up the crowd for the woman who took his job. “People want change,” he says. “We’ve got to remind them we’ve got the plan, we’ve got the plan and as you saw today, we’ve got Jess Wilson. I think we’re well and truly ready to roll. “We’ve got a very organised campaign. We’ve got a very disciplined team. We’ve got a group that are willing to work together to ensure that can deliver.” Battin predicts that when early voting opens on Wednesday, there will be a stampede at some polling places.



In Australian politics, the timing of campaign launches makes them less about making an opening pitch than delivering a closing argument. Related Article Opinion

Victorian election Is that a whiff of arrogance we detect from the Liberal leader? Jeff Kennett seems to think so Chip Le Grand State political editor For the Jess-led Liberals, it is a promise of repair – from Victoria’s books to the potholes in our roads to a less tangible vibrancy absent from the state. In a 35-minute speech which recounted a long list of campaign pledges already made and a new one to establish a bootcamp for youth offenders on the grounds of the old Dhurringile minimum security prison near Shepparton, Wilson promises to restore hope and, borrowing a line from Howard, “make Victorians feel relaxed and comfortable once more”. She mentions Labor 27 times and One Nation, a party which potentially stands between the Coalition and majority government, only once. She says that people are right to be frustrated and angry, but urges them to put their vote to better use.

World.title: Australia dispatch Kiwi Ferns to retain Rugby League World Cup women's crown
World.content:
The queens of rugby league have extended their reign to four successive World Cups, delivering another ruthless reminder of the gulf that exists between the champions and their rivals.

The Jillaroos cantered to a fourth title on the trot, crushing the Kiwi Ferns 34-10 in Brisbane.

It was a clinic in attacking efficiency, the Jillaroos showcasing their class in a flawless first half, before taking the foot off the gas somewhat in the second with the title already firmly secured.

Up by 32 points at half-time, the Kiwi Ferns simply had no answers for the rampant Australians, their 18-year wait for a World Cup to continue.

What was once a rivalry dominated by the women in black has become increasingly one-sided, Australia now just one win away form squaring the overall head to head ledger which once read 15-3 in favour of the Ferns.

Superstar Jamie Chapman cut capers in the Kiwi Ferns defence, as the Aussies took metres at will.

The would have one hand on the trophy after only twenty minutes as the defending champs raced out to a 24-0 lead.

Chapman struck twice, Shaylee Bent and Jessica Sergis also dotting down to put Australia firmly in control.

Finally getting some decent possession, the Ferns hit back with their one and only try of the half through Shannon Mato on the back of a a deft ball out of dummy half from Ashleigh Quinlan, reducing the margin to three converted tries.

But any hopes of a miracle were crushed when Chapman once again ripped the Ferns line wide open, sprinting 50 metres away to finish a first half hat-trick.

Tamika Upton drove the nail in further right on the brink of the break with a sixth try, for a commanding 34-6 half-time lead.

After the 35-minute scoring blitz, the second would remarkably be scoreless right up until the 70th.

New Zealand managed to end things in style as Mackenzie Wiki got over for a consolation right on the siren, the only points produced in the second spell.

But this was Australia's afternoon, the dynasty showing no signs of slowing.

Recap all the action in our live blog below:

World.title: NZ Nurses Organisation claim Auckland hospital patients unable to vote
World.content:
The NZ Nurses Organisation is surveying its members at two Auckland hospitals to determine the extent to which patients missed out on voting in the general election.

Delegate Sophie Tomes said the Electoral Commission had mobile voting teams at North Shore and Middlemore Hospitals only on the day before the election.

She claimed at least 12 North Shore patients were unable to vote, because they were bed-ridden.

"Our patients have been denied democracy," Tomes said. "We have confirmed that at least 12 patients at North Shore were unable to vote, including five from the Elective Surgery Centre, four from Ward 4 and three from Ward 15.

"These patients were bedridden and unable to get to the mobile voting team. They have been denied their democratic right.

"NZNO members reported voting for them personally was more challenging than previous elections, with long queues on the Friday also preventing busy nurses from having their say."

Tomes said union delegates had previously urged the Electoral Commission to make the mobile voting teams available on election day, but the patients were denied their democratic right.

"We work with hospitals directly, and the type of service we provide will depend on what works for them and the space available," said the Electoral Commission. "For example, we had a mobile team at Middlemore Hospital all day Friday, 6 November, to issue takeaway votes to patients in the wards.

"Patients were able to request a takeaway vote from the ward staff, who would record their details and pass it on to our team to prepare a takeaway vote. Our team returned on election day, as well, to pick up completed votes.

World.title: NZ First still considering MP Michael Laws' future in the party
World.content:
New Zealand First are yet to give an update on MP Michael Laws' future in the party - after promising to do so following the election.

Laws was reprimanded by the party only a few days before election day for comments he made about Opportunity Party MP Kayla Kingdon-Bebb mocking her demeanour and appearance, describing her as "rather severe-looking" and making sexual remarks while broadcasting on his online talkshow.

Laws apologised for those remarks, which were panned by Kingdon-Bebb and her party, National Leader Christopher Luxon and Laws' leader Winston Peters who told RNZ they were "simply unacceptable".

Laws was initially reprimanded by Peters, who said there could be further consequences after the election when the party had time to meet.

"The board can't meet as well, and so as a consequence, we have to defer it until after the election when we can deal with it properly."

"Properly and soberly," Peters told RNZ at the time.

However, more than a week on from election day, a spokesperson for the party confirmed to RNZ there was no update on Laws' future in the party as yet.

Laws made it back into Parliament following the election after being ranked sixth on the party list.

World.title: 'Flood' of weka sightings in Dunedin becomes a trickle
World.content:
Weka look likely to disappear from Dunedin again, despite a breeding pair making their home in a northern suburb last year.

They used to live in the area - Otago Peninsula's iconic Hereweka translates to 'catch the weka' - but they were wiped out along the east coast of the South Island and now the nearest populations live a few hundred kilometres away.

Retired ornithologist Bruce McKinlay started to record weka sightings in the city over the last five years, after receiving credible reports.

"In February, March 2025, there was a real flood of them," he said.

McKinlay recorded about 76 sightings by September last year.

Audio player for " Weka sightings spark debate over possible Dunedin return " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/environment/2607793%2Fflood-of-weka-sightings-in-dunedin-becomes-a-trickle

Weka sightings spark debate over possible Dunedin return Morning Report Download MP3 3m

There were three clearly different groups of weka - a breeding pair in Normanby that had three broods of chicks, one at Seconds Beach at St Clair and one on the Otago Peninsula, he said.

Then the reporting unexpectedly stopped.

The last sighting of the St Clair weka was in October last year and reports of the Normanby weka stopped from about March, he said.

Only the weka on the peninsula remained.

"Weka, no matter how confident or bolshy you think they look, are susceptible to predation," he said.

Stories from iwi suggested weka were an important seasonal food in the area before European settlement and hapū would travel to harvest weka at the right time, he said.

A trail camera photo of a weka on the Otago Peninsula. Supplied/Supplied/Fiona Morrison, Otago Peninsula Biodiversity Group

They were vulnerable to environmental changes, and the introduction of mustelids, cats and dogs.

McKinlay said people had to be involved in the return of weka to Dunedin, as it was too far for weka to walk.

He urged people not to bring weka into the area, although acknowledged the curious birds could have become stowaways.

"If you're going to think it's fun to bring a weka home, you are condemning it to eventually die," he said. "If we wanted weka back in Dunedin, it will take quite a lot of effort and co-ordination."

McKinlay believed the decision should not be taken lightly, and was not risk free to weka or other native species.

Weka were a known predator of sooty shearwater and the one on the peninsula lived near the colony at Sandfly Bay.

"If you've got one precious taonga like the sooty shearwater and you've got another one that eats it, which one do you actually want?

"How do you actually make these choices to actually accommodate a predator within your landscape?"

Weka are slowly disappearing from Dunedin. Tess Brunton/RNZ

McKinlay encouraged anyone who spotted a weka in Dunedin to log it with the DOC Hotline 0800 362 468.

He has reached out to previous weka spotters, but none of them reported further sightings.

McKinlay recorded their absences, saying it was part of their story in the city and painted a picture of how vulnerable weka were, if their arrival was not managed properly.

"One of the problems with this sort of work is the absence of records really doesn't attract people's attentions as much as the positive," he said.

World.title: Live cricket: Black Caps v India fifth ODI
World.content:
Follow all the action as the Black Caps take on India at Bay Oval in Mt Maunganui for their ffith ODI.

Embedded content removed for printing

New Zealand has been forced to make numerous changes during the T20 and ODI series mainly due to injuries and Central Districts pace bowler Brett Randell is the latest to be called up.

Randell has been called into the squad to bolster their bowling stocks for the fourth and fifth ODIs at Mt Maunganui this weekend.

The 31-year-old right-arm bowler has 145 professional caps to his name including five appearances for New Zealand A, and recently returned from a County Championship stint with Derbyshire.

Fellow Central Districts allrounder Josh Clarkson will also come into the squad for the fifth and final ODI against India on Sunday.

"We're very pleased for Brett, he's been a consistent performer in domestic cricket for some time now and has earned this opportunity," said head coach Rob Walter.

"There's been a few movements throughout the series so we're fortunate to be able to bring in Brett and Josh."

World.title: Nations Championship: Fiji remain winless after Irish loss
World.content:
The Flying Fijians' losing run in the Nations Championship continued in Dublin, as they were hammered 43-15-by Ireland.

In the Nations Cup, Tonga could not hold out Georgia, losing 55-31 in Tbilisi, while Samoa grabbed their second consecutive win on the road, beating Portugal 36-5 in Lisbon.

For Fiji, costly errors - including the inability to win their own lineout throws, conceding the scrum battles and losing the ball when in possession - continued to plague their campaign.

The loss means the Pacific Islanders have lost all five of their championship matches so far, with just one more game to go for them in the series.

Match commentators said it was a tale of what might have been once again for the islanders, just like they had done in the last five championship matches they have played so far this year.

Although they stayed in the contest in the first 40 minutes, their inability to keep the basics right worked against them, as Ireland took advantage and piled the points on in the second 40 minutes to keep their record against Fiji at home safe.

Ireland managed to score seven tries, two each to wingers Tommy O'Brien and Robert Baloucoune. Other tryscorers were Ronan Kelleher, Andrew Porter and Nick Timoney.

Flyhalf Sam Prendergast added six points from three successful conversions, while replacement Ciaran Frawley also got a kick through for two points.

Fiji managed only two tries to captain Peceli Yato and Josua Tuisova, while flyhalf Ben Volavola added five points through a conversion and a successful penalty kick.

New head coach Jake White has had just one victory with the side, since taking over last month, that coming against Japan in a one-off international.

He has now had two setbacks, losing to France last weekend and today's beating by the Irish at the Aviva Stadium.

White's disappointment in the coaching box was caught on television during the game and he told the media his Fiji side "did Ireland a favour".

"Let me put it that way, because I think Ireland deep down know that, if they play like that against South Africa, they're going to be up against it."

Ireland led 17-15 at halftime.

Ireland started well

The hosts started the game well, with O'Brien claiming the first try of the game in the eighth minute. Prendergast kicked the conversion for the 7-0 advantage.

Eight minutes later, halfback Jamison Gibson-Park went over the Fiji line, after he picked up from the base of the scrum five metres out, but referee Agnus Gardner and the TV match official ruled that out, after replays showed Gibson-Park had lost the ball over the line.

The Flying Fijians did not let go of their hold on the Irish lead and that resulted in Tuisova's try in the 18th minute.

'The Bus' ran onto a Frank Lomani pass off a lineout win close to the Irish line, bulldozed his way through the defensive wall and planted the ball firmly for his try. Volavola missed the conversion attempt.

Then in the 22nd minute, captain Yato, who was getting some assistance with his knee inside the Irish 22-metre zone, stood up to take a pass from Jiuta Wainiqolo, who had broken free from the Irish grasp, to dive over and put the visitors ahead 12-7 on the scoreboard.

However, Baloucoune was on hand to score a double from out wide, running into free space both times, after the Irish had sucked the Fijian defence in to create overlaps on the flanks.

Volavola slotted in a late penalty, after the hooter had sounded for halftime, keeping Fiji in the game, as the two teams ran off for the break.

Irish domination

A disappointing second-half performance from the Flying Fijians saw Ireland take control.

The islanders failed to score any points after the break, as the Irish rallied to score 26 unanswered points and keep their hopes of topping the Nations Championship northern hemisphere standings alive.

Two early knock-ons from Fiji - one unforced from a lineout maul - gave the possession back to Ireland early.

Four minutes after the restart, the hosts drove a lineout maul towards the Fijian line and hooker Kellaher was over in the corner.

Replacement prop Inoke Ravuiwasa was yellow-carded for a swinging arm tackle nine minutes later and the Irish extended their lead with Potter going over.

O'Brien had his second for the match, when he chased a Prendergast grubber kick, and then Timoney crashed through under the crossbar for his try with three minutes remaining, as Ireland clocked off with another good win.

Tonga second best

Meanwhile, in the Nations Cup, Georgia marked their 300th international match with a fifth straight win to be crowned Pool B champions with a round to spare.

They defeated Tonga 55-31, their biggest win over the Friendly Islanders to date.

Captain Theo McFarland scored two tries for Manu Samoa against Portugal. Supplied/World Rugby

The bonus-point success was rapturously received by the home crowd, as the Lelos outscored their opponents by eight tries to five in a fiery clash.

Georgia captain Davit Niniashvili, who played outstandingly during the game, said it was great to have won against Tonga and create a bit of history.

"It feels good," he said. "We prepared for this and knew Tonga are big boys.

"The second half was good and, when we have this support behind us, it gives us even more energy, so I hope they will keep coming to support us."

Tonga captain Ben Tameifuna said they gave Georgia the opportunities, which their hosts successfully converted into points.

"You can't give easy ball to a team like Georgia, especially with the set-piece they have," he said. "I'm definitely proud of the team and I feel like we are definitely heading in the right direction, but congratulations to Georgia."

Tameifuna put Tonga ahead with a close-range score early, but they lost Patrick Pellegrini to the sinbin for a deliberate knock-on.

Georgia scored twice in six minutes through Vano Karkadze, after they took advantage of the one-man advantage.

His first was an easy close-range finish and he repeated the trick for his second try with a similar effort, before scrumhalf Vasil Lobzhanidze added a third home score.

Tonga cut the hosts' lead, when flanker Semisi Paea claimed their second try, following a superb maul.

Georgia led 22-14 at halftime, but lost Akaki Tabutsadze to a yellow card after the second half resumed, and winger John Tapueluelu collected a stunning offload from full-back Taniela Filimone to run in from the corner to score for Tonga.

Georgia came back strong with three more tries, while Tonga responded with tries to Veikoso Poloniati and Lotu Inisi.

The 'Ikale Tahi also had Fetuli Paea sin-binned late.

Samoa victorious in Lisbon

Samoa showed their class to comfortably dispatch Portugal 36-5 in an impressive bonus-point victory at Estadio do Restelo.

The visitors surged into a commanding 24-0 lead over Os Lobos in the Portuguese capital.

Tries from Peter Umaga-Jensen, captain Theo McFarland, Niko Jones and Latrell Ah Kiong put them in total control at the break in the first-ever test match between the sides.

Portugal hit back through Domingos Cabral, but Samoa added further late scores through McFarland and Miracle Faiilagi in the second spell to win the contest.

Manu Samoa kept with the same side that beat Zimbabwe so impressively last weekend.

They led in the sixth minute, when former Hurricanes centre Umaga-Jensen brilliantly burst through midfield to score, before captain McFarland added a second with a pick-and-go try.

Then Jones, son of All Blacks and Manu Samoa legend Sir Michael, got into the act with a similar close-range effort, as the islanders found top gear early.

Ah Kiong, who scored a hattrick against Zimbabwe seven days previously, added Samoa's fourth, when he raced clear from halfway, after intercepting an errant Portugal pass.

World.title: Five charged after police uncover drug lab in Avondale
World.content:
Five people are due to appear in court on Monday, after police were led to a clandestine drug laboratory in the Auckland suburb of Avondale.

Detective Senior Sergeant Anthony Darville says officers received a report of a person with a firearm on St Jude Street just before 6pm Saturday.

The police Eagle helicopter guided armed officers to a property, where equipment associated with a clan lab was found.

Three women aged 39, 43 and 53, and a 57-year-old man were charged with possessing equipment with intent and further charges have not been ruled out.

World.title: New study shows what does and doesn't work for ADHD kids
World.content:
A new study says giving kids with ADHD extra time for tasks and more frequent breaks while in class may not affect their behaviour.

Researchers from Florida International University got more than 200 primary school children at summer camps in the US to switch between taking and not taking medication and different classroom environments.

The study, published in the Jama Pediatrics medical journal found medication improved the kids' rule-following and test results but the adaptations in the classroom, including extended time for tasks, frequent breaks, using a standing desk and having a low distraction space, didn't affect their behaviour or achievement.

University of Auckland development neuropsychology expert Professor Karen Waldie said the study came as no surprise to those who work with children with ADHD and do research in the area.

"Procrastination and time blindness are one of the key symptoms of ADHD. The main reason for the benefits of medication and behavioural therapy comes down to the brain chemical dopamine and the reward system of the brain.

"Stimulant medication such as Ritalin works to increase dopamine in the prefrontal cortex and this helps those with ADHD focus on the task at hand: right now."

Waldie said the study found that medication and behaviour therapy improved academic productivity and rule-following behaviour in the classroom, but accommodations such as extended time on tasks had no effect.

"Another thing that works in a similar way as stimulant meds is a hard deadline and quick consequences of actions - so basically people with ADHD work very well under pressure, which gives them a dopamine reward hit, and do less well when there is time available to perform a task like a test or when there is a distant or inconsequential reward."

Consultant clinical psychologist and honorary senior lecturer at University of Auckland's Te Ara Hāro Centre for Infant, Child and Adolescent Mental Health, Dr Melanie Woodfield, said the study is an important signal from a carefully designed experiment, but needs testing in the real world.

"Positive behaviour supports, medication, or both, are known to improve academic performance and decrease challenging behaviour for many children with ADHD."

Woodfield said the study leaned towards strict control, excluding children with low IQ or autism alongside ADHD, and taking place in a specialist American summer camp treatment classroom, where staff even counted the ratio of teacher praise to commands, to ensure it was 3:1.

"That's quite far removed from a messy, complex, real world classroom with fewer resources, stretched teachers, and children with higher needs. The authors themselves recommend the study now needs to be repeated in real- world classrooms, where they expect the effects would be weaker.

"Ideally, we should also acknowledge that some accommodations do work for some children, some of the time," Woodfield said.

"However, this research suggests that a blanket, Oprah-style giveaway 'You get extra time! And you get extra time' may not return reliable dividends, compared to behavioural approaches and/or medication."

Clinical psychologist Giselle Bahr said there's been no specific research about what happens when children with ADHD are offered structured classroom changes, and while the study showed they did not make a difference to behaviour in this instance, it was food for thought.

"It's like, of course it would make sense to give a child more time if they're struggling, but it looks like it's not as simple as that," she said.

"What we already know is that behavioural strategies help children and they don't have any adverse effects, there's no risks associated with them. We already know that methylphenidate changes children's behaviour in the short term, but over the long term it leads to worse outcomes."

However, Waldie did not agree and said she had not seen that supported in scientific literature.

Bahr said the study had not been done in a normal classroom setting, but at a summer camp during one-hour class periods, and the adjustments were randomised.

"The rest of the hours of the day they were doing fun activities and the classes were small. They only had 15 to 18 students in them and there were two adults in each of those classrooms. It's not an exact match with how a classroom generally run, so we have to be careful about what we extrapolate from that.

"It doesn't look like they matched a child's kind of need for what's going to help them learn better in a classroom, they just kind of trailed these adaptations."

She said the researchers, Fabiano and Pelham, had authored papers about children and ADHD for decades and said behavioural interventions remained an important, low-risk strategy for supporting children with ADHD.

"Some of their previous work looked at the best order for interventions. They found that starting with behavioural strategies was more effective than starting with medication. Also, that ADHD medication made things worse for children in the long term, even if it produced improvements in the short-term."

Bahr said ADHD medication came with serious risks, including reduced growth, a risk of psychotic symptoms, and cardiovascular problems.

Waldie said the only well-established effect would potentially be with appetite, however research on that aspect was conducted with fast-acting mythylphenidate before the slow-release medication was available.

Waldie said methylphenidate was the most-studied pediatric medication, with evidence showing it reduced rates of mortality, accidents, and self-medication.

Waldie was interested in understanding the study's findings in relation to the dopamine system in a person with ADHD, procrastination and the need to go down to the wire before panic set in.

"That's when the ADHD person tends to excel, it's like a light flipping, that's when things get done," Waldie said.

Bahr said the findings challenged the common-sense assumptions that adaptations like extra time or low distraction spaces would always improve outcomes, but more research was needed to determine how classroom adjustments could benefit kids with ADHD.

Study details: The study evaluated the single and combined effects of academic accommodations, behaviour therapy, and stimulant medication (methylphenidate, 0.3mg/kg).

The academic accommodations were: extended time on tasks, frequent breaks during task, a low-distraction workspace with the option of using noise-cancelling headphones, and the ability to stand at the desk. A general classroom setting was compared with a classroom with enhanced behaviour interventions including a daily report card with contingent rewards, and lots of praise.

Results: 255 children with a mean age of 8 years and 8 months, took part in the study. 201 (79%) of the children were male, and 235 (84%) completed the study.

World.title: England sets Australia big run chase after opener's century
World.content:
England opener Tom Banton has clubbed a century as the visitors set Australia 356 runs to win their second one-day international.

Underpinned by Banton's 121 from 99 balls, England posted 6-355 after the hosts won the toss at Adelaide Oval on Sunday.

Banton, Jordan Cox (67 from 49 balls), Joe Root (62 from 68) and Will Jacks (54 not out from 40) dominated as England seek to level the three-match series after losing the opening fixture in Perth.

Paceman Xavier Bartlett (3-72 from 10 overs) was the only Australian bowler to take multiple wickets.

After Ben Duckett (9) fell in the fifth over, he smacked a Bartlett delivery straight to Cooper Connolly (1-11 from three overs) at point, Banton and Root took control.

The duo produced a 137-run partnership from 136 balls for the second wicket, taking England to a powerful position of 1-156 in the 28th over.

But their union ended when Root, trying to smack a short Connolly delivery to the leg side, got a leading edge and was caught at cover.

England captain Harry Brook (5) lasted only 11 balls. He attempted a leg-side ramp but chopped on to give Riley Meredith (1-75 from 10 overs) a wicket.

Banton, a 28-year-old wicketkeeper-batsman from Somerset, soon reached his second ODI ton from only 86 balls.

He departed in the 35th over when he cracked a pull shot from Bartlett's bowling to Cameron Green who, diving forward at deep midwicket, completed a fine catch centimetres from the turf.

Cox and Jacks then combined for a 102-run stand in less than 12 overs as England accelerated to its imposing total.

Australia rested paceman Mahli Beardman, two days after his stunning one-day international debut of 6-24 in a seven-wicket win at Optus Stadium. He was replaced by Meredith.

After the ODI series concludes in Hobart on Wednesday, the Australians play five T20 games against England from next Saturday.

Australian quick Nathan Ellis has been ruled out of that series as he continues to recover from a side strain, with Ben Dwarshuis drafted in.

AAP

World.title: Aussie quick says 'everyone knew' about sandpaper, as Warner doubles down
World.content:
Former Australian cricketer Chadd Sayers, who played his lone Test after Sandpapergate on the infamous 2018 South African tour, has said he is comfortable stating he believed everyone in the team knew about ball-tampering.

The notorious Cape Town Test match, where Cameron Bancroft was filmed using sandpaper on the cricket ball, was thrust into the spotlight this week after Usman Khawaja in his memoir, Sabr, claimed ball-tampering was commonplace and the entire team needed to take responsibility.

The memoir has caused a rift in Australian cricket.

David Warner, who was suspended with Cameron Bancroft and then-captain Steve Smith over the incident, backed Khawaja's account in Sabr, saying it was "100 per cent accurate".

Meanwhile, Test captain Pat Cummins, who was part of the infamous 2018 side, held a 70-minute press conference on Friday, again denying he had any knowledge of sandpaper being used and claiming Khawaja had been "casual" with people's lives and reputations.

Sayers, who was part of the Australian touring squad in 2018, said ahead of Australia's second ODI against England in Adelaide on Sunday that he was comfortable saying every member of the team knew sandpaper was being used.

"I'm comfortable saying where I'm sitting now that everyone knew what was going on [in South Africa in 2018]," Sayers said on the SEN broadcast.

"It [sandpaper] was used in two Test matches and there were discussions in change rooms … I'm not taking sides; it's just my recollection of what took place."

Sayers also said there was a meeting held in the wake of the team being caught with sandpaper, which lasted between 60 and 90 minutes.

Cameron Bancroft was caught using sandpaper on the ball during the Test match in Cape Town, with an investigation determining he, Smith and vice-captain Warner were responsible for the ball tampering.

The trio was suspended, while the bowlers in that Test have always denied knowledge that sandpaper was being used on the ball.

In his memoir, Khawaja claimed he knew sandpaper was being used on the ball and told Bancroft to be careful.

Khawaja also said ball-tampering was commonplace in cricket.

Test captain Pat Cummins, who was part of the infamous 2018 side, held a 70-minute press conference on Friday, again denying he had any knowledge of sandpaper being used and claiming Khawaja had been "casual" with people's lives and reputations.

Cummins hits out at Khawaja Australian Test cricket captain Pat Cummins rubbishes Usman Khawaja's ball-tampering claims in a long and passionate press conference.

"When he says 'we all knew', if by that he means we knew sandpaper was going out on the field, he's 100 per cent wrong," Cummins said on Friday.

"I've said that consistently for the last eight years; I did not know that was happening.

"But I think Usman actually says things that are far more serious than that. He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball tamper with sandpaper; that's complete and utter nonsense.

"I was genuinely shocked this week when I found out Usman admitted that he told Cam [Bancroft] to be careful when using sandpaper. That's not the Usman that I know. It's not the Usman that has been part of the team that's helped rebuild the Australian cricket culture over the last eight years, and the Usman that would have stopped that from happening there and then.

"Usman's a friend, but friends aren't casual with each other's lives and reputations. In his book Ussie's been casual with my [life] and the lives of many others, and I think Australian cricket. I support his right to tell a story, 100 per cent. I'm really glad he feels like he can, but we have to be accountable for the things that we say and do."

Warner doubles down on Cricket Australia on social media

David Warner has hit out at Cricket Australia as Sandpapergate continues to dominate headlines. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

David Warner has made another statement on social media, claiming he was not aware of all the facts before taking the brunt of punishment for Sandpapergate.

On Saturday, Warner accused Cricket Australia of a potential cover-up by claiming he believed the bowlers were not interviewed by the organisation about the incident.

Cape Town inquiry spoke to all Aussie bowlers, ABC understands Sources connected to the Australian bowling group say they all spoke to investigators as part of the inquiry into Cape Town ball tampering, which runs counter to claims by David Warner.

"As far as I am aware, CA did not interview Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc or Nathan Lyon in their 2018 investigation," he wrote on Instagram.

"If that's correct then how can CA push the idea that the bowlers didn't know?

"It looks like they had decided who they wanted to blame from the very beginning … ran a shoddy investigation to serve the purpose and now they want to maintain the false narrative that the bowlers had no idea.

"That stinks of a cover-up."

Multiple media outlets, including ABC Sport, have reported the bowlers were interviewed by Cricket Australia.

On Sunday, Warner then doubled down on his criticism of Cricket Australia and supported his previous post.

"Just to clarify 'As far as I am aware' was the POINT," he wrote.

"I was never told the bowlers had been interviewed or provided statements.

"That information would've been pretty useful when I was forced to make decisions back in 2018.

"Why weren't we given all the evidence by CA?"

World.title: Live: Kangaroos try to back up Jillaroos' thrashing in World Cup final against Kiwis
World.content:
(Getty)

There was nothing resembling a speed bump for the Aussie women through the group stages as they won their three games against Samoa, England and Wales by a combined 242-6.

Then came the semifinal against Fiji, which was supposed to be a similar story but the Bulikula staged an early ambush for an early 8-0 lead. It may not sound like much, but it wasn't just the score, it was the way Fiji went about it, dominating with physicality and skill.

The Jillaroos eventually resettled for a 30-14 win, and more than a few of them said it was just the sort of hit-out they needed before the final.

(Getty)

Fiji was also right in the game against the Kiwi Ferns to kick off their tournament, before a last-minute Leianne Tufuga try gave New Zealand an 18-12 win.

Then they went 92-0 over France, 40-12 over Papua New Guinea, and 32-0 over Samoa.

Pretty similar journeys, albeit in reverse order, for both teams. So hopefully it leads to a very even contest this afternoon.

World.title: How Swim GP may have given a glimpse of the future of para-sport
World.content:
Swim GP's made for TV, all-action racing format has proven a hit with swimmers and spectators alike.

But the biggest benefit may well be the innovations that placed para-swimmers front and centre of the competition at the Melbourne Sports and Aquatics Centre.

In front of a sold-out crowd, four teams: Kraken, Wahoo, King Tide and Tsunami, competed in a variety of races ranging from skins events through to mystery medley relays.

Times are not important. It's all about who touches the wall first.

"It is an opportunity for our athletes, our Paralympic team and our Olympic team, to come together and really showcase what they do," Swimming Australia Paralympic head coach Mel Tantrum said ahead of Saturday's evening events.

"This is about building the brand, building the profile of the athletes, swimming in prime time in preparation for the next six years."

The Melbourne Sports and Aquatic Centre was sold-out for day two. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

Swim GP is not a new idea, and indeed has built on the concepts reintroduced at last year's Australia vs the World in Brisbane.

However, crucially, Swim GP has seen para-swimmers take a leading role.

Swimming Australia chief executive Rob Woodhouse told ABC Sport that involving the para-swimmers "was one of the most important factors" and a "no-brainer" in Swim GP's planning for a couple of reasons.

"Both our head coaches, Mel Tantrum and Rohan Taylor, they absolutely want a packed stadium for our trials, ideally Sydney next year, but particularly the Olympic/Paralympic trials in '28 in Chandler, one of the reasons being, for the Olympics, SoFi Stadium, with 40,000 screaming Americans and Long Beach for the Paralympics," Woodhouse said.

"Some of those [para-]athletes do have sensory issues, so for them to have some experience coming out to all of that noise and those bright lights, the flashing lights and all those sorts of things is really, really important.

"So there's quite an important benefit from Swim GP for those para-athletes that do have to deal with those things to get more accustomed to a noisy venue, to a bright flashy venue and things like that.

"[Also] that aspirational view that these athletes can provide, whether they're para-athletes or able-bodied athletes, to the young kids at home, and there's a lot of kids with various disabilities that don't have opportunities to get into a pool or to even just get involved in the other sports. So, just being able to showcase our amazing para-athletes and what they do is a really critical factor."

A big atmosphere is vital for Australia's swimmers to prepare for LA Olympic Games in 2028. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

Tantrum agreed, saying integrating the two programs was vital.

"Swimming Australia is really inclusive in terms of the parity between Olympic and Paralympic programs and making sure our swimmers across both programs are really profiled and really supported," Tantrum said.

"The athletes are loving being part of a bigger team. Those sort of innovative, creative competitions make the athletes feel they're part of an elite team.

"It's not just para, it's not separate, it's part of being the Australian Dolphins swim team and both programs coming together.

"The athletes are fully integrated team members. They don't sit separately. They've got the same uniform, same bleachers, same team meetings.

"And I think that's, for the athletes, it's a chance for them to really showcase their athleticism.

"It's not about, oh, you're a para-athlete, it's about elite swimming at its best.

"The world's best swimmers are here in the pool. And yeah, whether you're Olympic or Paralympic, you know, able-bodied or have a disability, it doesn't matter. You're an elite athlete first and you're here to perform."

New tech bringing para-sport into the mainstream

Victoria Belando Nicholson (right) was a member of the King Tide team. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

One of the biggest challenges in para-sport when there are a limited number of athletes, is integrating multiple classifications and how to accurately, and fairly, ensure a level playing field.

In a standard multi-class meet, swimmers with varied impairments all start their races at the same time, with the winner determined by how close a swimmer gets to the world record in their particular classification.

That's all well and good but, for spectators, it can get confusing as to who as actually won because the winner does not always touch the wall first.

Swim GP gets around this by having a staggered start, with lights on the blocks for each swimmer.

The time-gap is determined based on a swimmer's season best in a particular distance and should result in a blanket finish — far more appealing for spectators.

"I think it's a really good idea to then see everyone come up towards each other and finish pretty closely," Paralympic legend Lakeisha Patterson told ABC Sport.

"It makes it an exciting race, I think, towards the end.

"I think for an event that isn't preparing for a world champs or a major international meet, this is really good for fans to see how multi-class swimming works."

Lakeisha Patterson said she was nervous before her race, perhaps made more so when Ben Hance literally ripped the shirt off his back when walking out. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

Patterson competed in, and won, Saturday night's opening race, a multi-class, mixed 100m event where each swimmer swam a different stroke, with Patterson unusually swimming butterfly, which she noted "definitely" won't be on her program for next year's world championships.

Perhaps she should reconsider. Patterson, who is classified as an S9 swimmer, swam a PB to blitz the field, although the other three swimmers; Tim Hodge (S9), Ben Hance (S14) and Keira Stephens (S10), were far closer together.

"It doesn't matter what their classification is and, in some cases, what their gender is," Tantrum explained.

"It's some new tech that we're trialling for the first time on the block so that athletes, no matter what their class or their gender, they can race together.

"With this [Swim GP] format, it's basically who touches the wall first is the winner.

"These staggered starts and close finals make the crowd get right into it. It makes it exciting if someone's got a 20-second stagger to catch up on in 100 metres. It makes for exciting racing, and the crowd really got into that last night and you could feel the crowd lift.

"That's what swimming should be, right? It should be exciting."

The future of para-sport?

Lakeisha Patterson (right) and Rowan Crothers (second right) were key members of Team Tsunami. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

Patterson noted that giving para-swimmers the same platform was crucial for the development of the sport.

"I think it's incredibly important to showcase that our athletes aren't just here for participation," she said.

"We are athletes showcasing what is possible, and I think Australia is leading the way in that inclusion space and how we can involve our entire team.

"Leading into Brisbane we can really build on that and hopefully have all of Australia behind us, and showing to the people watching at home that they may have a space in Paralympic sport as well."

Fully integrated competitions remain a rarity for para and able-bodied sporting events, the Commonwealth Games being a notable exception.

Given the success of this format, Tantrum said that innovations like the staggered starts seen in Swim GP could inspire more innovation elsewhere, perhaps even adding more athletes to future Commonwealth Games fields.

"If we could influence Commonwealth Games Federation … we could potentially have a greater number of athletes and a greater number of classes competing together," Tantrum said.

"We left a number of athletes at home [from the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games] because they simply didn't have events for those classes.

"So something that is more of a multi-class format for Commonwealth Games would be a great innovation to at least consider.

What should the future of para sport look like? Birmingham 2022 celebrated the largest para sport program in history, but there's still a large gap between wealthy and developing nations. What should integration look like?

"There's potential there that we could make this more integrated, fun, with exciting finishes and more athletes involved from Australia."

Perhaps even other sports could take note?

"Our immediate purpose is to showcase swimming," Tantrum said.

"But you know, if we can lead other sports and things like track and field to follow a similar format, where the para-athletes are standing alongside their Olympic athlete colleagues?

"You know, it's humans, right? It's human story, it's humans doing the best that they can do.

"If other sports such as athletics or cycling, want to come in and do what we're doing, if we're the trailblazers of that space, we'd love others to join in as well."

World.title: Swimming stars tipped for big 2027 despite illness, injury hiccups
World.content:
Battered by illness and injury, a trio of Australian Olympic swimming stars are being backed to be ready for Los Angeles Games.

Between them, Kaylee McKeown, Mollie O'Callaghan and Kyle Chalmers have won 11 Olympic gold medals.

McKeown returned to competition over the weekend at the inaugural Swim GP in Melbourne, having not raced since last year because of glandular fever.

Chalmers was poolside at the event, in the midst of a six-week break from swimming as he manages long-term back problems.

O'Callaghan, who nursed back and shoulder injuries through the Glasgow Commonwealth Games, was a late withdrawal from the Swim GP because of a skin infection.

McKeown said the one positive of her illness was that it had happened this year, not next.

Australian swimming head coach Rohan Taylor echoed that sentiment about the three stars in the context of the four-year Olympic cycle.

Mollie O'Callaghan missed competing at Swim GP due to an infection. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

"No-one will remember what happens in 2026 [in terms of injury or illness]. You can't worry about that now," Taylor told AAP.

"You have to get them right, you have to remember their talent won't go anywhere.

"It's about getting them healthy and then letting the fitness build. We know they can race and we just have to get ourselves to the arena fit and healthy, then we will be right."

McKeown made a successful return to racing at the Swim GP and Taylor was pleased with the backstroke queen's progress after the illness knocked her flat.

"I live on the Sunshine Coast, so I get to see it up close and see the progression," Taylor said.

"It's really good to see her back racing. She's such a competitor.

"She just looked back to her normal self, competitive, focused when the race was on, but enjoying herself.

"She just has to build momentum back."

McKeown gave a glimpse of her blistering backstroke speed on Saturday night, storming home after the staggered start to beat Ella Ramsay's breaststroke in the 50m skins champions race.

It was her first racing since the world championships in July last year.

Kaylee McKeown is one of Australian swimming's biggest stars. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

"I've been doing some pretty solid sessions, but it's hard to come into these races — not racing all year — and then my body just hasn't recovered as quickly as it would," McKeown said.

"It's good, nice practice and gives a bit of confidence that I'm still swimming well.

"It's great there are no times, which takes the pressure off. It's just about racing."

As McKeown notes, glandular fever affects people differently and in her case, "it just really knocked me flat".

So competing for the Tsunami team at the Swim GP, with nothing riding on the results, was an ideal stepping stone as McKeown looks to next year's world championships and then the 2028 Olympics.

"It's really good fun and I'm glad we can race in this format," she said.

"It's taken a long time to build back and then I have to build to where I was, which is even more of a gap.

"I'm lucky it was this year and not next year, when it counts, so it's a blessing in disguise. I've had some nice time at home."

Swim GP is a points-based competition in a 25m pool, with no official times recorded and a variety of relay and individual race formats.

The Wahoo team, lead by Meg Harris and Sam Short, dominated the two-night Swim GP and comfortably won on 222 points.

McKeown's Tsunami were next on 173, ahead of Kraken (170) and KingTide (149).

AAP

World.title: Carpenter leads Chelsea to victory against Manchester City
World.content:
Ellie Carpenter has continued her thunderous campaign for Chelsea, helping set up the winner in the Blues' table-topping Women's Super League (WSL) victory over champions Manchester City.

By assisting on Sandy Baltimore's stunning goal that sealed the 1-0 win at Stamford Bridge on Saturday (Sunday AEDT), the on-song wing back also earned the bragging rights over Matildas' teammate Mary Fowler, who was taken off by City with half an hour to go after a much more ineffective afternoon.

By inflicting City's first league defeat of the season, Chelsea went back to the top, leapfrogging the champs to go a point clear after 10 matches.

And as usual this season, the energetic 26-year-old Carpenter, who has looked one of the best players in the WSL this term, was at the heart of the win, already having caused plenty of problems with her crossing from the right flank even before her key contribution deep into stoppage time in the first half.

Carpenter found Baltimore in the box with a short pass and then sped off to take the return pass while dragging her defender with her.

That simply opened up more space for French international Baltimore, who had time to set her sights and curl home a superb left-footed strike beyond keeper Ayaka Yamashita.

It was Carpenter's first assist of her exceptional league season to go with her four goals.

However, across all competitions she's the club leader with nine goal involvements, five goals and four assists.

City looked as if they could eke out an equaliser but their hopes were finally dashed with a quarter of an hour left when Yamashita was sent off, losing out in a race to the ball with Alyssa Thompson and clumsily bringing her down.

Fowler, whose recent form has helped her really nail down a starting spot at City, had already been taken off by that point, replaced by fit-again WSL legend Vivianne Miedema, but the visitors still could not find an equaliser, Lauren Hemp missing a sitter from point-blank range in the 64th minute.

It was City's first defeat in any competition since April 25.

Elsewhere, Manchester United captain Maya le Tissier marked her 150th appearance for the club with a goal in a 2-0 victory at Crystal Palace that moved them to fourth, while Tottenham drew 0-0 at home to Everton and Liverpool won 3-0 at Brighton.

AAP

World.title: All Blacks suffer 73-year first in defeat to Wales
World.content:
Wales has ended a 73-year winless sequence against New Zealand with a stunning 35-28 victory in the Nations Championship.

Wales, who last overcame the All Blacks in 1953 and have endured a dismal recent run, outscored the visitors five tries to four on Saturday and produced a defensive performance for the ages to end a run of 34 losses to the three-times world champions.

They caught New Zealand cold with two early tries and two more at the start of the second half, and heroic Welsh defence resisted waves of attacks in the closing stages to hold on for a famous victory.

"It's come from belief. Obviously, we've got the crowd behind us, and the energy and the noise was unbelievable," Welsh man of the match James Botham said.

"We've been training on the defensive side of things, and it shows how training has come on and just how much we have got each other's back."

The Wales players team were in tears at the end amid raucous celebrations at Cardiff's Principality Stadium after Tomos Williams, Dewi Lake, Archie Griffin, Eddie James and Louis Rees-Zammit scored tries and Sam Costelow was immaculate with the boot.

New Zealand were stunned, held up over the line three times in the closing minutes at a raucous Cardiff. (Getty Images: Dan Istitene)

New Zealand's tries were scored by Cortez Ratima, Wallace Sititi, Fehi Fineanganofo and Peter Lakai, all converted by Richie Mo'unga, but were held up over the line three times, with the Welsh defenders making a total of 346 tackles by the end of the game.

It was only the fourth time Wales had beaten New Zealand in 39 meetings.

"A hell of a defensive effort from them," New Zealand coach Dave Rennie said.

"They were excellent tonight."

One consolation for the All Blacks is that the bonus points they have picked up have put them above South Africa in the Northern Hemisphere standings as they seek a place in the new competition's final at Twickenham.

Elsewhere, England thrashed Eddie Jones's Japan 78-15 Nations Championship at Twickenham, with England winger Will Joseph scoring a record-equalling five tries.

Joseph was making only his second appearance for England, more than four years after his debut, and started his return with a try from his first touch inside the opening 65 seconds before adding three more in the first 25 minutes.

The 24-year-old scored a fifth after the interval to equal the record set by Rory Underwood in 1989 and matched by Josh Lewsey in 2003 and Henry Arundell at the last World Cup.

England ran in 13 tries in a record score against Japan, and in the new Nations Championship competition.

And in Genoa, Argentina beat Italy 19-14, condemning the hosts to their fifth defeat in five matches in the competition.

Reuters

World.title: Hoffman delivers best Alpine World Cup finish in 27 years
World.content:
Australia's Madison Hoffman has delivered the nation its best FIS Alpine World Cup result in almost three decades with a phenomenal eighth place in Levi, Finland.

The 26-year-old finished in eighth place in the slalom at the World Cup opener, her first career World Cup top 10.

The result was Australia's best since Olympic bronze medallist Zali Steggall's eighth place in 1999 at the French resort of Serre Chevalier.

Steggall had two career World Cup podiums, winning at Park City, Utah, in 1997 and a second in 1998, finishing her World Cup career with 11 top 10 finishes.

Hoffman, who has twice endured lengthy spells off the snow due to ACL injuries in 2022 and 2024, said the performance would take some time to settle in.

"It hasn't hit me yet, but I'm definitely proud, especially after a long slog with some injuries," Hoffman told the Olympic Winter Institute of Australia.

"Tearing both my knees in 2024 and coming back last year, it feels good to be back racing."

Madi Hoffman was the lowest-ranked starter in the top 30. (Supplied: FIS/Christopher Pallot)

Hoffman's achievement was all the more remarkable given she was wearing bib 57, meaning 56 skiers had already attempted the course before her.

As skiers complete a course, particularly in slalom races, their skis cut through the snow, making it all the more difficult for those following to carve their own line through the gates.

To illustrate the point, the top three finishers, Emma Aicher, Lara Colturi and Katharina Truppe, wore bibs 1, 2 and 3 respectively, with seven of the top 10 in single-digit bib numbers.

Hoffman was the lowest-ranked starter to ski in the second run, limited to the fastest 30 finishers from the first run.

No Australian had finished as high as eighth in a World Cup event since Zali Steggal in 1999. (Supplied: FIS/Christopher Pallot)

The Sydney athlete defied those conditions to register the 13th-fastest opening run, before completing the job with a sublime second run that pushed her personal boundaries even further.

"In the first run I chose to trust myself and not try to do anything more or anything less than training," Hoffman, who finished 23rd in the slalom at the Milano-Cortina Olympic Games, said.

"In the second run I thought I'd try to give it a little bit more oomph, but it was the same stuff, trying not to do anything crazy on race day, just normal skiing."

Hoffman's fellow Milano-Cortina Olympian Phoebe Heaydon just missed out on making the top 30, finishing 0.12 outside the cut off in 31st place, although that was still a lifetime World Cup personal best for the 21-year-old.

While Australia has had incredible success in freestyle skiing in recent years, winning multiple medals in moguls, aerials and park and pipe disciplines, alpine and nordic skiing has proven a tougher nut to crack.

Results like these from Hoffman suggest that the only way is up heading into Winter Olympic Games in the French Alps in 2030 and Utah in 2034.

Tech.title: Watch SpaceX successfully execute the first ‘chopstick’ catch of Starship
Tech.content:
After aborting a planned catch of Starship Flight 15’s booster, SpaceX successfully captured Starship with its “Mechazilla” launch and catch tower for the first time. The company has performed ‘ chopstick ’ catches of its boosters before, but this is the first time the maneuver has successfully been executed on the Starship vehicle itself.

SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said during the company’s third-quarter earnings call that “success is not guaranteed on these first flights, but I’d say it’s more likely than not that this succeeds next flight.” While not a complete success, in that the company was unable to recover the entire launch vehicle, it still stands as a milestone for the Starship program. And, since it has previously caught boosters on previous launches, there is reason to believe the failure today was not an insurmountable obstacle. SpaceX is still trying to determine what caused the booster to abort its landing and detonate over the Gulf of Mexico.

Tech.title: Magic: The Gathering is getting a Netflix animated series. For real this time.
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

“It’s really happening. I promise. For real.” Those are the first words from Roy Graham, Head of Story at Magic: The Gathering, in a video posted yesterday announcing Planeswalker, the animated series heading to Netflix in 2027.

An animated Magic: The Gathering series was first teased back in 2019 with Joe and Anthony Russo at the helm. But that fell apart. In 2024, Netflix announced it still planned to make a series based on the game, but it decided to rework it from the ground up.

Now fans are finally getting their first glimpse of the show, which will be called Planeswalker. According to the sneak peek, because each plane exists in its own pocket universe, it will have a unique design, animation, and filmmaking style.

According to a synopsis of the show shared with IGN, Planeswalker will focus on Chandra Nalaar, a “volatile pyromancer hunted for her gifts, and haunted by her past.” Storyline details beyond that are vague, other than mentioning an “insidious force” that Chandra and other Planeswalkers will team up to confront “to prevent a cataclysmic war that threatens to consume their very existence.”

Tech.title: Work to replace old copper wire led to the FAA’s ground stop
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

At a press conference today, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that Friday’s nationwide ground stop ordered by the FAA was related to work replacing outdated copper wire with a fiber optic line at a “remote FAA facility.” The secretary said that this was “routine maintenance,” rather than the result of a major modernization effort. He told reporters that it was “such an old wire that it was being discontinued, meaning that line was going to get shut down,” necessitating the upgrade.

What wasn’t clear, according to Secretary Duffy, was the root cause of the problem. He said that it could have been faulty hardware, a misconfigured router, or “incompetence” on the part of contractor L3Harris. Regardless, what followed was the newly installed router “flooding” other routers in the Air Traffic Control system. Duffy said that there were “over 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds,” causing disruption to radar feeds and communication with planes.

Secretary Duffy also took the opportunity to call on additional funding from Congress for modernizing the Air Traffic Control system, and to tout the work the FAA has done so far. “We are building, we are building safely, but we are building fast,” he said, but said that Congress had only given him a “partial payment” to complete the necessary work.

In a statement posted to their site, L3Harris said:

L3Harris has been modernizing the communications infrastructure supporting the National Airspace System in close coordination with the FAA. With safety and reliability as our highest priorities, L3Harris, together with its telco partners and the FAA, has completed more than 70% of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber optic system. We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation’s air travel. L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.

Update November 14th: Added a statement from L3Harris.
